The national balance sheet records the stock of carbon credits held by each sector at market value, providing a measure of “carbon wealth” that can be compared across countries.

Measuring the Economic Contribution of Digital Public Infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker) in National Accounts

Digital public infrastructure (DPI) — the biometric identity system Aadhaar, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), and the document‑storage platform DigiLocker — is treated in the 2025 SNA as government non‑market output (P.13) valued at the sum of costs incurred: compensation of employees (D.1), intermediate consumption (P.2), consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) on the underlying hardware and software, and net taxes on production (D.2‑D.3). The output is recorded in the general government sector (S.13) under the industry “Public administration and defence; compulsory social security” (ISIC 84).

The capital formation associated with DPI includes the acquisition of servers, network equipment, software licences, and the development of application programming interfaces (APIs). These are recorded as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in the government sector, creating the asset class AN.1134 “Digital public infrastructure”. The 2025 SNA recommends a service life of 7 years for software platforms and 10 years for hardware, with geometric depreciation. The consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) on these assets enters the government’s production account, raising the cost‑based output measure.

Because DPI services are provided free or at nominal fees to households and businesses, the SNA imputes a “social transfer in kind” (D.63) from government to households for the value of services consumed. The value of the transfer equals the cost‑based output attributable to household use, estimated via usage statistics (e.g., number of Aadhaar authentications, UPI transaction volumes). In India, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) publishes monthly UPI transaction counts and values; MoSPI uses these to allocate the government output between household final consumption expenditure (P.31) and intermediate consumption by businesses (P.2).

The 2025 SNA also requires a satellite account for “Digital public goods” that links the physical metrics (authentications per capita, transaction success rate) to the monetary output. This satellite account supports policy analysis of the “digital dividend” — the productivity gains from reduced transaction costs, financial inclusion, and leakage reduction in welfare programmes. The RBI’s “Financial Inclusion Index” and the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) “Digital India” dashboard provide the high‑frequency indicators used for quarterly nowcasting of the DPI contribution to GDP.

Cross‑border aspects: when a non‑resident uses UPI for remittances, the service fee (if any) is recorded as export of services (P.6). The underlying infrastructure remains a domestic government asset; no foreign direct investment (FDI) is recorded unless a foreign entity acquires equity in the operating entity (e.g., NPCI International). The 2025 SNA’s “digital services” module ensures consistency between the balance of payments and the national accounts for such cross‑border digital transactions.

The Treatment of Cross‑Border Mergers and Acquisitions in the SNA and Balance of Payments

Cross‑border mergers and acquisitions (M&A) involve the acquisition of a controlling equity stake (typically > 10 % of voting power) in a resident enterprise by a non‑resident investor, or vice‑versa. In the 2025 SNA and the Balance of Payments Manual (BPM6), the transaction is recorded as a financial account entry: acquisition of equity (F.5) by the investor and a corresponding reduction in the equity liability of the target enterprise. The purchase price is allocated between the identifiable net assets (recorded at fair value) and goodwill (AN.11), an intangible produced asset representing future economic benefits not captured in identifiable assets.

The identifiable net assets include produced assets (AN.11), non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.2), and financial assets/liabilities. The 2025 SNA requires that the fair‑value measurement follow the “market‑consistent” approach, using observable market prices for listed subsidiaries or valuation techniques (discounted cash flow, comparable transactions) for unlisted targets. Goodwill (AN.11) is capitalised on the acquirer’s balance sheet and amortised over its useful life (typically 10 years) through consumption of fixed capital (P.51c). The target’s balance sheet derecognises the equity liability and recognises the consideration received (cash, shares, or contingent consideration).

In the balance of payments, the equity acquisition appears under “Direct investment — Equity capital” (F.5) in the financial account. Any cash consideration paid by the non‑resident investor is a debit in the investor’s economy and a credit in the target’s economy. If the consideration includes shares of the acquirer, the transaction is recorded as a portfolio investment (F.3) for the share component, with a corresponding equity entry for the direct investment portion. The 2025 SNA aligns the treatment of contingent consideration (earn‑outs) by recording the fair value at acquisition as part of the purchase price (F.5) and subsequent adjustments as revaluations (K.1) or financial transactions (F.5) depending on the nature of the contingency.

India’s experience: the RBI’s “Quarterly Statistics on Foreign Direct Investment” capture cross‑border M&A flows. The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) filings (Form FC‑GPR) provide the transaction details needed for the SNA’s “foreign affiliates statistics” (FATS) compilation. The 2025 SNA’s “global value chain” satellite account links the M&A‑driven change in ownership to the domestic value‑added content of exports, using the TiVA (Trade in Value Added) framework. This enables analysts to assess how foreign acquisition of Indian firms alters the domestic value‑added share in gross exports.

A frequent error is to record the entire purchase price as a current account transaction (e.g., as a service import) rather than a financial account entry. The 2025 SNA and BPM6 are explicit: M&A is a change in ownership of assets, not a flow of services. Another error is to omit goodwill from the national balance sheet, which understates the acquirer’s non‑financial asset stock and overstates the return on equity in growth‑accounting exercises.

  • Confusing cloud‑service subscription revenue with capital formation — subscription fees are output (P.1), not gross fixed capital formation.
  • Treating renewable‑energy subsidies as negative intermediate consumption instead of subsidies on production (D.3) or capital transfers (D.9).
  • Recording carbon‑credit sales twice: once as output of the project and again as a financial asset disposal by the holder.
  • Valuing digital public infrastructure at market price rather than cost‑based output, violating the non‑market valuation rule for government services.
  • Classifying cross‑border M&A consideration as a current‑account service import instead of a direct‑investment equity transaction (F.5).
  • Omitting goodwill (AN.11) from the national balance sheet after an acquisition, leading to understated non‑financial asset stocks.
  • These traps highlight the need for careful reading of SNA guidelines and consistent application of transaction classifications.

Government Debt Securities Valuation in the National Balance Sheet under the 2025 SNA

Conceptual Framework

The 2025 System of National Accounts (SNA) requires that all financial assets and liabilities be recorded at market value on the balance sheet date. For government debt securities, this means that both the issuer (general government) and the holder (financial corporations, households, rest of the world) must reflect the same market price. The valuation follows the “market‑consistent” principle: observable market prices for actively traded securities, and for illiquid instruments, a discounted‑cash‑flow (DCF) model using the prevailing yield curve for the relevant maturity and credit risk. The 2025 SNA explicitly aligns this treatment with the Balance of Payments Manual (BPM6) and the Monetary and Financial Statistics Manual (MFSM) to ensure consistency across the national accounts, the financial accounts, and the international investment position.

Classification and Recording

Government debt securities are classified under AF.3 (debt securities) in the financial assets and liabilities classification. The issuer records a liability (AF.3) at market value; the holder records an asset (AF.3) at the same value. Any difference between the issue price and the market value at the reporting date gives rise to a revaluation (K.1) in the other changes in the volume of assets account. When a security is issued at a discount or premium, the difference is amortised over the life of the instrument through the accrual of interest (FISIM‑adjusted) in the primary income account. The 2025 SNA introduces a mandatory “fair‑value hierarchy” disclosure in the metadata accompanying the national balance sheet, distinguishing Level 1 (quoted prices), Level 2 (observable inputs), and Level 3 (unobservable inputs) valuations.

Indian Practice and Data Sources

In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) compiles the “Quarterly Statistics on Government Securities” which provide market yields for dated securities, treasury bills, and state development loans. The Ministry of Finance’s “Monthly Review of Market Borrowings” supplies issuance calendars and outstanding amounts. The National Statistical Office (NSO) uses these yields to construct the zero‑coupon yield curve (the “G‑sec curve”) that serves as the discount factor for DCF valuation of illiquid state government loans and special securities. The 2025 SNA revision requires the NSO to publish a “Government Debt Securities Valuation Note” alongside the annual national balance sheet, detailing the yield curve, the day‑count conventions, and the treatment of accrued interest. The RBI’s “Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy” provides the historical series needed for back‑casting revaluations.

Policy Implications and Common Errors

Accurate market valuation of government debt is crucial for fiscal sustainability analysis, debt‑to‑GDP ratios, and the calculation of the government’s net worth. A frequent error is to record government securities at nominal (face) value in the balance sheet, which understates liabilities when market yields exceed coupon rates and overstates them when yields fall below coupons. Another error is to omit the revaluation account (K.1) when yields move, breaking the link between the financial account and the balance sheet. The 2025 SNA also requires that any debt restructuring (e.g., a swap of high‑coupon bonds for lower‑coupon bonds) be recorded as a transaction in the financial account (F.3) with a corresponding revaluation of the old and new instruments, not as a write‑off in the capital account.

Link to Fiscal Rules and Medium‑Term Frameworks

India’s Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act uses the debt‑to‑GDP ratio derived from the national balance sheet. The 2025 SNA’s market‑value basis ensures that the ratio reflects current financing conditions, enabling the Medium‑Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF) to incorporate interest‑rate risk. The “Debt Sustainability Analysis” published by the Ministry of Finance now references the SNA‑consistent market value of government debt, aligning domestic fiscal monitoring with IMF Article IV surveillance standards.

Digital Public Infrastructure in National Accounts: Valuation, Output, and Productivity Spillovers

Scope and Definition

Digital public infrastructure (DPI) refers to government‑provided or government‑mandated digital platforms that are non‑rival and non‑excludable in nature, such as the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), the Aadhaar biometric identification system, and the Government e‑Marketplace (GeM). The 2025 SNA treats DPI as non‑market output produced by general government (or by public corporations under government control) and valued at the sum of costs incurred: compensation of employees, intermediate consumption, consumption of fixed capital, and other taxes less subsidies on production. This cost‑based valuation replaces any attempt to impute a market price, consistent with the SNA’s principle that non‑market output lacks a observable market transaction.

Output Measurement and the Production Boundary

The production boundary is extended to include the creation and maintenance of the software code, the operation of data centres, and the provision of authentication and settlement services. For UPI, the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) — a not‑for‑profit company owned by major banks but operating under RBI mandate — records its operating expenses as intermediate consumption of the general government sector when the government funds the platform’s public‑good functions (e.g., zero‑merchant‑discount‑rate transactions). The 2025 SNA requires a satellite account for DPI that separates “core infrastructure” (platform development, security upgrades) from “transaction processing services” that may be sold to private payment service providers at a fee. The latter are recorded as market output (P.11) of the public corporation, while the former remain non‑market output (P.13) of general government.

Productivity Spillovers and Growth Accounting

DPI generates positive externalities by reducing transaction costs, enabling financial inclusion, and fostering innovation in fintech. The 2025 SNA’s “digital economy” satellite account captures these spillovers through a “digital capital” asset (AN.117) that embodies the stock of platform code, data standards, and network effects. Growth‑accounting exercises can then include the services of digital capital as an input, using a user‑cost approach: the rental price equals the sum of the opportunity cost of capital, the rate of depreciation of the code base, and a risk premium. Indian pilot studies by the NSO and the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations (ICRIER) have estimated that the inclusion of digital capital raises measured total factor productivity (TFP) growth by 0.15–0.25 percentage points per annum for the period 2016‑2023.

Data Sources and Compilation Challenges

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) provides annual expenditure statements for DPI projects. NPCI publishes audited financial statements that detail operating costs, capital expenditure on servers, and revenue from value‑added services. The RBI’s “Payment System Indicators” supply transaction volumes and values, which are used to weight the output of transaction processing services. A key compilation challenge is the allocation of shared costs (e.g., data‑centre electricity) between core infrastructure and commercial services. The 2025 SNA recommends a “cost‑allocation key” based on the proportion of CPU cycles attributable to each function, verified by independent IT audits.

Policy Relevance and International Comparability

Accurate DPI accounting enables the government to assess the return on public investment in digital infrastructure, to design appropriate pricing for commercial access, and to report comparable “digital government” indicators to the UN’s E‑Government Development Index. The 2025 SNA’s harmonised treatment ensures that India’s DPI output is comparable with similar platforms in Brazil (PIX), the European Union (SEPA), and Singapore (PayNow), facilitating cross‑country analysis of digital‑economy contributions to GDP.

Worked Example: Valuing a Government Bond at Market Price
A 10‑year central government bond with a face value of ₹1,000 and a coupon of 6 % per annum was issued three years ago. The current market yield for a 7‑year residual maturity is 7.2 %. Using the 2025 SNA market‑consistent valuation, compute the bond’s market value to be recorded in the national balance sheet. Assume annual coupon payments and a day‑count convention of actual/actual.
Step 1: Determine cash flows. The bond pays ₹60 each year for the next 7 years and repays ₹1,000 at maturity. Step 2: Discount each cash flow at the market yield of 7.2 % (0.072). Present value = Σt=17 60/(1.072)^t + 1000/(1.072)7. Step 3: Calculate. PV of coupons = 60 × [1 - (1.072)-7] / 0.072 ≈ 60 × 5.206 ≈ ₹312.36. PV of principal = 1000 / (1.072)7 ≈ 1000 / 1.627 ≈ ₹614.71. Step 4: Sum = ₹312.36 + ₹614.71 = ₹927.07. The bond’s market value is ₹927.07, which is recorded as a liability of general government (AF.3) and an asset of the holder at the same amount. The difference from face value (₹72.93) appears as a revaluation (K.1) in the other changes in volume of assets account.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the SNA‑consistent valuation of a government security, always identify the residual maturity, the current market yield for that maturity, and the coupon schedule. Use the standard present‑value formula; do not confuse nominal value with market value. Remember that the 2025 SNA requires the revaluation to be shown in the K.1 account, not in the financial account. Practise a few numerical examples with different yields to build speed.

Renewable Energy Certificates, Carbon Credits, and Emission Trading in the SNA and SEEA

Conceptual Distinction

Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) and carbon credits are environmental assets that arise from the generation of renewable electricity or the reduction of greenhouse‑gas emissions. The 2025 SNA classifies RECs as produced assets (AN.117) when they are created as a by‑product of electricity generation and are tradable. Carbon credits generated under the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) or voluntary markets are treated as non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.2) if they represent a right to emit, or as financial assets (AF.7) if they are held for trading. The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting (SEEA) Central Framework records the physical flows of energy and emissions in physical supply‑use tables, while the SEEA‑Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA‑EA) values the ecosystem service of carbon sequestration.

Production and Valuation of RECs

In India, the REC mechanism was introduced in 2011 under the Electricity Act, 2003. Each megawatt‑hour of renewable generation earns one REC, which can be sold to obligated entities (distribution companies, open‑access consumers) to meet Renewable Purchase Obligations (RPOs). The 2025 SNA records the creation of a REC as output (P.1) of the renewable generator at the market price prevailing on the power exchange (e.g., Indian Energy Exchange). The generator’s intermediate consumption includes the cost of the REC registry fee. When an obligated entity purchases a REC, it records the acquisition as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) if the REC is held for compliance over multiple periods, or as intermediate consumption (P.2) if surrendered immediately. The market price of RECs is volatile; the SNA requires the use of the average price over the accounting period for output valuation.

Carbon Credits and Emission Trading Schemes

India’s Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme, launched in 2012, issues Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts) that function similarly to carbon credits. Under the 2025 SNA, ESCerts are produced assets (AN.117) created by designated consumers who achieve energy‑saving targets. The credits are valued at the transaction price on the PAT trading platform. For international carbon credits (e.g., Certified Emission Reductions under the Kyoto Protocol), the 2025 SNA aligns with the BPM6 treatment: they are financial assets (AF.71) when held by a resident entity, and the export of credits is recorded as a credit in the financial account. The SEEA‑EA records the physical removal of CO₂ in tonnes and assigns a monetary value using the social cost of carbon or the market price of credits, whichever is more appropriate for policy analysis.

Integration in the National Balance Sheet

The national balance sheet must show RECs and carbon credits as separate line items under produced non‑financial assets (AN.117) and financial assets (AF.7) respectively. Revaluations due to price changes are recorded in the other changes in volume of assets account (K.1). A common compilation error is to net RECs against electricity output, which would double‑count the energy service. The 2025 SNA mandates gross recording: electricity output at the basic price, REC output at the market price, and the purchase of RECs by obligated entities as a separate use.

Policy Use and Data Requirements

The Ministry of Power and the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) publish monthly REC and ESCert trade volumes and prices. The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) provides the regulatory framework. The NSO uses these data to compile the “Environmental Goods and Services Sector” satellite account, which feeds into the Green GDP estimates. Accurate accounting of these instruments is essential for tracking progress towards India’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement and for designing carbon‑pricing policies.

Infrastructure Investment Trusts and Real Estate Investment Trusts in National Accounts: Financing, Output, and Fiscal Risk

Legal Structure and SNA Classification

Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) and Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) were introduced in India by SEBI regulations in 2014. Both are collective investment vehicles that pool capital to invest in income‑generating infrastructure or real estate assets. Under the 2025 SNA, an InvIT or REIT is classified as a financial corporation (S.12) when it is a separate legal entity that issues units to investors and holds a portfolio of assets. The underlying infrastructure assets (roads, power transmission lines, pipelines) remain recorded as produced non‑financial assets (AN.11) on the balance sheet of the original owner (often a government agency or a public‑private partnership special purpose vehicle) unless the InvIT/REIT acquires legal ownership. In most Indian structures, the InvIT/REIT holds a beneficial interest via a long‑term concession agreement; the SNA treats this as a financial lease (AF.4) if the risks and rewards of ownership transfer, otherwise as a service concession arrangement recorded as a non‑produced asset (AN.2) for the grantor and a financial asset (AF.4) for the trust.

Output Measurement and Revenue Recognition

The trust’s output consists of fund‑management services (P.11) provided to unit holders, valued at the management fee charged. The income generated by the underlying assets (toll revenue, rental income) is recorded as primary income (property income) accruing to the trust, which then distributes it to unit holders as dividends (F.5). The 2025 SNA requires that the trust’s balance sheet reflect the fair value of its portfolio assets (using discounted cash flows based on projected cash flows and a risk‑adjusted discount rate). Changes in fair value are recorded as revaluations (K.1) in the other changes in volume of assets account, not as holding gains in the financial account.

Fiscal Risk and Contingent Liabilities

Many Indian InvITs are sponsored by government agencies (e.g., NHAI InvIT, PowerGrid InvIT). The government may provide guarantees on the trust’s debt or commit to revenue support mechanisms. The 2025 SNA records such guarantees as contingent liabilities (AF.6) of the general government, disclosed in the notes to the national balance sheet. If a guarantee is called, the government records a capital transfer (D.9) to the trust and a corresponding increase in its debt liabilities. The trust’s debt securities (AF.3) are valued at market price, and any government‑backed credit enhancement is reflected in a lower yield, which the SNA captures through the market‑consistent valuation.

Data Sources and Compilation in India

SEBI’s “Monthly Bulletin” provides unit prices, assets under management, and portfolio composition for all listed InvITs and REITs. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) and the Ministry of Power publish concession agreements and traffic/revenue forecasts used for DCF valuation. The RBI’s “Financial Stability Report” monitors the systemic risk posed by these instruments. The NSO incorporates InvIT/REIT data into the “Financial Corporations” sector accounts and the “Public‑Private Partnership” satellite account, ensuring consistency with the government finance statistics (GFS) framework.

Analytical Uses

Including InvITs and REITs in the national accounts improves the measurement of infrastructure investment, enables the calculation of the “infrastructure capital stock” for growth‑accounting, and provides a transparent view of fiscal exposure. Analysts can track the share of infrastructure financing moving off the government balance sheet onto market‑based vehicles, assess the efficiency of capital allocation, and evaluate the impact of regulatory changes (e.g., tax treatment of distributions) on the cost of capital.

Financial Inclusion and Digital Payments in National Accounts: The UPI, BHIM, and Mobile Wallet Ecosystem

Scope of the Digital Payments Ecosystem

The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) in April 2016, and the Bharat Interface for Money (BHIM) app, launched in December 2016, together with private mobile wallets (Paytm, PhonePe, Google Pay), constitute the core of India’s retail digital payments infrastructure. The 2025 SNA treats the payment‑system operators as financial corporations (S.12) providing payment‑processing services (financial intermediation services indirectly measured — FISIM). The platform’s output is the implicit service charge embedded in the transaction fee (or, for zero‑fee UPI peer‑to‑peer transfers, the cost of providing the service funded by the government or by banks). The 2025 SNA requires that the value of these services be estimated using a reference rate approach: the difference between the actual fee charged and a benchmark “risk‑free” fee, multiplied by transaction volume.

Valuation of Zero‑Fee Transactions

UPI peer‑to‑peer (P2P) transactions are free for users. The 2025 SNA records the output of NPCI’s UPI platform as non‑market output of the general government (since the government bears the cost through the “Digital India” budget) valued at the sum of NPCI’s operating expenses attributable to UPI (staff, server infrastructure, security audits). The corresponding use is recorded as final consumption expenditure of general government (P.3). For merchant transactions where a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) applies, the MDR is split: the portion covering NPCI’s processing cost is output of NPCI (market output), the remainder is output of the acquiring bank (financial intermediation). The 2025 SNA’s “digital services” module ensures that cross‑border UPI transactions (e.g., UPI‑enabled remittances to Singapore) are recorded consistently in the balance of payments as financial services exports.

Mobile Wallets and Stored‑Value Instruments

Mobile wallets issue prepaid payment instruments (PPIs) that are classified as financial assets (AF.2) — deposits — when they are redeemable at par and represent a claim on the issuer. The 2025 SNA records the issuance of a wallet balance as a liability of the wallet provider (a non‑bank financial corporation) and an asset of the holder. Interest earned on the float (funds held before redemption) is recorded as property income (D.4) for the provider and as interest income for the holder if the wallet pays interest; otherwise the float generates implicit FISIM for the provider. The wallet’s revenue from transaction fees, bill‑payment commissions, and advertising is recorded as market output (P.11). The 2025 SNA requires a satellite account for “digital payment services” that separates the platform’s infrastructure costs from the financial intermediation margin.

Data Sources and Compilation Challenges

NPCI publishes monthly UPI transaction volumes and values, disaggregated by P2P, P2M (person‑to‑merchant), and cross‑border. The RBI’s “Payment System Indicators” provide MDR data and wallet‑issuer balance sheets. The Ministry of Finance’s “Digital Payments Index” tracks adoption metrics. A key compilation challenge is the allocation of shared NPCI costs between UPI, IMPS, and RuPay card networks. The 2025 SNA recommends an activity‑based costing approach using transaction‑level logs. Another challenge is the treatment of cash‑back incentives offered by wallets: these are recorded as subsidies on products (D.31) reducing the effective price of the payment service, not as negative output.

Policy Relevance and Growth Accounting

Including digital payment services in the national accounts captures the productivity gains from reduced cash handling, faster settlement, and enhanced financial inclusion. The NSO’s experimental “Digital Economy Satellite Account” estimates that digital payment services contributed approximately 0.3 % of GDP in 2022‑23, with a growth rate exceeding 30 % per annum. Growth‑accounting exercises can treat the stock of payment‑system infrastructure (servers, software, network) as digital capital (AN.117) and compute its user cost, allowing analysts to assess the contribution of financial‑technology capital to total factor productivity.

  • Recording government debt securities at face value instead of market value, breaking the SNA’s market‑consistent valuation rule.
  • Valuing digital public infrastructure at a hypothetical market price rather than at cost of production, violating the non‑market output principle.
  • Netting Renewable Energy Certificates against electricity output, causing double counting of the energy service.
  • Classifying InvIT/REIT portfolio assets as government assets when legal ownership remains with the concessionaire, misstating the public sector balance sheet.
  • Treating zero‑fee UPI transactions as having zero output, ignoring the government‑funded cost of the platform.
  • Recording cash‑back incentives from mobile wallets as negative output instead of subsidies on products.
  • Omitting revaluation entries (K.1) for changes in the fair value of government debt, REC prices, or InvIT portfolio assets, breaking the link between the financial account and the balance sheet.

Tourism Satellite Account: Concepts, Compilation, and Policy Use

The Tourism Satellite Account (TSA) is the internationally agreed statistical framework for measuring the direct economic contribution of tourism. It was developed by the United Nations World Tourism Organization (UNWTO), the OECD, and Eurostat and formally adopted in the 2008 Tourism Satellite Account: Recommended Methodological Framework (TSA:RMF). The TSA extends the System of National Accounts (SNA) by identifying tourism‑characteristic products (e.g., accommodation, passenger transport, travel agency services), tourism‑connected products (e.g., food and beverages served to visitors), and tourism‑specific products (e.g., souvenirs). It also defines tourism industries as those that would cease to exist in their present form without visitor demand.

Compilation follows a sequence that mirrors the SNA supply‑use framework. First, visitor surveys and administrative data (immigration records, hotel occupancy statistics, transport ticketing) provide estimates of inbound, domestic, and outbound tourism expenditure. Second, these expenditures are mapped to the product classification used in the national supply‑use tables (SUTs). Third, the SUTs are re‑balanced to isolate the tourism share of each product’s output, yielding tourism gross value added (TGVA) and tourism employment. The 2025 SNA revision adds a “digital tourism services” module that captures online booking platforms and peer‑to‑peer accommodation services as separate tourism‑characteristic activities.

In India, the Ministry of Tourism and the National Statistical Office (NSO) released the first official TSA for the reference year 2019‑20. The account estimated that tourism direct gross value added accounted for approximately 5.1 % of GDP and supported about 87 million jobs, including both direct and indirect employment. The TSA also quantified tourism‑induced capital formation, showing that investment in hotels, resorts, and transport infrastructure represented roughly 2.3 % of gross fixed capital formation. These figures are used by the Ministry of Finance for budgetary allocations under the Swadesh Darshan and PRASHAD schemes, and by the Reserve Bank of India for assessing foreign‑exchange earnings from travel services in the balance of payments.

Policy applications extend beyond headline aggregates. The TSA enables simulation of demand shocks — such as the COVID‑19 pandemic — by linking visitor‑arrival scenarios to changes in TGVA and employment. It also supports regional tourism planning because the framework can be applied at sub‑national level using state‑level SUTs and visitor surveys. Internationally, the TSA provides the data backbone for the UNWTO’s Tourism Economic Impact Model and for the OECD’s Tourism Trends and Policies report, ensuring cross‑country comparability.

Treatment of Government Subsidies and Transfers in the SNA: Classification, Valuation, and Fiscal Analysis

The System of National Accounts distinguishes subsidies from transfers by their economic nature and their impact on the production and income accounts. Subsidies are current unrequited payments that government units make to producers on the basis of their production activities. They are recorded in the generation of income account as a negative component of gross value added at basic prices. The 2008 SNA and the 2025 revision classify subsidies into two categories: subsidies on products (D.31) — payable per unit of a good or service produced or imported — and subsidies on production (D.39) — payable irrespective of the quantity produced, such as payroll subsidies or interest‑rate subsidies.

Transfers, by contrast, are unrequited payments that do not relate to production. Current transfers (D.7) include social benefits, grants to households, and international cooperation grants. Capital transfers (D.9) cover investment grants, debt forgiveness, and large one‑off payments such as disaster relief. Transfers affect the secondary distribution of income account and the redistribution of income in kind account but do not enter the production account; therefore they do not alter GDP directly.

Valuation follows the accrual principle: subsidies are recorded when the underlying production activity occurs, not when the cash payment is made. For subsidies on products, the SNA requires that output be valued at basic prices (output at market prices minus subsidies on products plus taxes on products). This ensures that GDP at market prices equals GDP at basic prices plus taxes on products minus subsidies on products. In India, the fertilizer subsidy paid to manufacturers is treated as a subsidy on products because it is linked to the quantity of fertilizer sold. The food subsidy under the National Food Security Act, however, is recorded as a current transfer to households (social assistance) because it is paid to consumers, not to producers.

The 2025 SNA introduces a “digital services subsidy” category to capture government support for zero‑fee payment platforms (e.g., UPI) and for broadband rollout. These are recorded as subsidies on production (D.39) because they reduce the cost of providing the service rather than the price per transaction. Fiscal analysts use the subsidy‑transfer split to compute the “subsidy transparency ratio” — subsidies on products divided by total subsidies — which the IMF’s Government Finance Statistics Manual (GFSM) recommends for assessing fiscal risk. In the Indian Union Budget, the explicit reporting of fertilizer, petroleum, and food subsidies under separate heads allows the NSO to map each item to the correct SNA code, ensuring consistency between fiscal accounts and national accounts.

Examiner's trap
A question states: "The government pays a per‑tonne subsidy to urea manufacturers. In the SNA, this payment is recorded as a current transfer to the manufacturing sector." Identify the error and give the correct classification.
The payment is a subsidy on products (D.31), not a current transfer. Subsidies on products are payable per unit of output and are recorded in the generation of income account, reducing gross value added at basic prices. Current transfers (D.7) are unrequited payments unrelated to production, such as pensions or disaster relief. Therefore the correct SNA code is D.31, and the subsidy enters the production account, not the secondary distribution of income account.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the two‑way split: subsidies on products (D.31) affect output valuation at basic prices; subsidies on production (D.39) affect gross operating surplus. Transfers (D.7, D.9) never touch the production account. When a question describes a payment linked to a physical unit of output, choose D.31; if linked to capacity or employment, choose D.39; if paid to households or for capital formation, choose D.7 or D.9.

Cross‑Border E‑Commerce and Digital Trade in National Accounts: Measurement Challenges and the 2025 SNA Guidance

Cross‑border e‑commerce — the sale of goods and services via digital platforms to consumers or firms in other economies — has grown faster than traditional trade, yet national accounts have struggled to capture it comprehensively. The core measurement problems are threefold: (1) low‑value shipments often fall below customs de‑minimis thresholds and are omitted from merchandise trade statistics; (2) digital services (streaming, software‑as‑a‑service, cloud computing) leave no physical customs record; (3) platform business models blur the distinction between the platform’s own output (commission fees) and the output of third‑party sellers.

The 2025 SNA addresses these issues through a dedicated “digital services” module and by aligning with the OECD’s Framework for Measuring Digital Trade. Key recommendations include: (a) treating the platform’s commission as market output of the platform (financial intermediation or information service), while the seller’s gross revenue is recorded as output of the seller; (b) valuing zero‑price digital services (e.g., free search, social media) at the cost of production — server infrastructure, content moderation, data analytics — and recording them as non‑market output of the platform if funded by advertising revenue, which is then treated as a sale of advertising space; (c) using credit‑card and payment‑gateway data, supplemented by GST/VAT returns, to estimate the value of cross‑border digital purchases by resident households.

In India, the Reserve Bank of India’s “Payment System Indicators” and the Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN) provide transaction‑level data on cross‑border e‑commerce. The NSO’s experimental “Digital Economy Satellite Account” uses these sources to estimate that cross‑border digital services imports amounted to roughly 0.4 % of GDP in 2022‑23, while exports of IT‑enabled services — recorded under computer services in the balance of payments — remained the dominant component. The 2025 SNA also requires a breakdown of “digitally ordered, physically delivered” goods (e.g., consumer electronics bought on a foreign marketplace) from “digitally ordered, digitally delivered” services, ensuring that the former are captured in merchandise trade via customs data adjusted for de‑minimis gaps, and the latter in services trade via payment‑flow data.

A persistent challenge is the attribution of value added in global value chains where a foreign platform intermediates sales by domestic firms. The 2025 SNA adopts the “residence of the producer” principle: the domestic seller’s value added is recorded in the domestic economy, while the platform’s commission is recorded in the platform’s economy of residence. This avoids double counting and aligns with the Trade in Value Added (TiVA) framework. For policy, accurate measurement of cross‑border e‑commerce informs the design of digital services taxes, the negotiation of e‑commerce chapters in trade agreements, and the assessment of the digital divide in access to global markets.

The Role of National Accounts in Monitoring Sustainable Development Goal 9: Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure

Sustainable Development Goal 9 (SDG 9) aims to build resilient infrastructure, promote inclusive and sustainable industrialization, and foster innovation. The UN’s global indicator framework for SDG 9 includes twelve indicators, many of which are derived directly from national accounts and satellite accounts. National accounts provide the denominator (GDP, gross value added) and the numerator (manufacturing value added, R&D expenditure, CO₂ emissions per unit of value added) for several key indicators.

Indicator 9.2.1 — manufacturing value added as a proportion of GDP and per capita — is computed from the production account by summing gross value added of all manufacturing industries (ISIC sections C) and dividing by GDP at market prices. Indicator 9.5.1 — research and development expenditure as a proportion of GDP — uses the satellite account for R&D (capitalised under the 2025 SNA as intellectual property products) to capture both public and private R&D outlays. Indicator 9.4.1 — CO₂ emissions per unit of value added — combines the SEEA‑Air emissions accounts with national accounts value added by industry, enabling a decomposition of emission intensity trends across sectors.

Infrastructure investment is tracked through gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) in construction, transport equipment, and telecommunications (indicator 9.a.1). The 2025 SNA’s “infrastructure asset” classification (AN.112) separates core infrastructure (roads, ports, power grids) from social infrastructure (schools, hospitals), allowing analysts to monitor the share of GFCF directed to core economic infrastructure. In India, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) supplies the annual “National Accounts Statistics” and the “Input‑Output Transaction Table” to NITI Aayog for the SDG India Index. The 2023‑24 Index reported that manufacturing value added stood at 17.4 % of GDP, R&D expenditure at 0.66 % of GDP, and per‑capita GFCF in transport and communication at ₹12,300, providing a quantitative baseline for policy targets under the “Make in India” and “Digital India” programmes.

Beyond the headline indicators, national accounts support policy simulation for SDG 9. By linking the input‑output table with a computable general equilibrium (CGE) model, planners can estimate the multiplier effects of increased infrastructure spending on manufacturing output, employment, and emissions. The integration of the SNA with the System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting (SEEA) ensures that the pursuit of industrialization (target 9.2) is evaluated against environmental sustainability (target 9.4), embodying the “leave no one behind” principle in a consistent accounting framework.

  • Confusing subsidies on products (D.31) with subsidies on production (D.39) when the payment is linked to output volume.
  • Treating current transfers to households (e.g., food subsidies) as subsidies on products, thereby inflating GDP at basic prices.
  • Omitting low‑value cross‑border e‑commerce shipments from merchandise imports because they fall below customs de‑minimis thresholds.
  • Recording platform commission fees as output of the third‑party seller instead of as output of the platform.
  • Using GDP at market prices instead of GDP at basic prices when calculating manufacturing value added share for SDG 9.2.1.
  • Neglecting the 2025 SNA’s capitalisation of R&D, leading to under‑reporting of indicator 9.5.1.
  • Failing to adjust CO₂ emissions for industry‑level value added when computing emission intensity, which breaks the link between SEEA‑Air and the production account.

The Treatment of Emissions Trading Schemes and Carbon Credits in the SNA and SEEA

The 2008 SNA and the SEEA Central Framework provide distinct but complementary guidance on recording emissions trading schemes (ETS) and carbon credits. Under the 2008 SNA, the allocation of emission permits by government is treated as a rent on natural resources (D.45) when permits are sold, and as a capital transfer (D.99) when allocated free of charge. The permits themselves are classified as contracts, leases, and licences (AN.22) — produced non‑financial assets — because they confer a right to emit that can be traded. When a permit is surrendered to cover actual emissions, the holder records a reduction in the asset (K.1) and an expense (P.2) equal to the permit's market value at surrender. The SEEA‑CF extends this by requiring physical flow accounts that track the opening stock, allocations, purchases, sales, surrender, and closing stock of permits in tonnes of CO₂ equivalent, linked to the monetary values in the SNA sequence of accounts.

A critical distinction arises between cap‑and‑trade systems (e.g., the EU ETS, California’s scheme, and India’s nascent Carbon Credit Trading Scheme under the Energy Conservation Amendment Act, 2022) and baseline‑and‑credit mechanisms (e.g., the Clean Development Mechanism under the Kyoto Protocol, Article 6.4 of the Paris Agreement). In cap‑and‑trade, the government creates scarcity by setting a cap; the initial allocation — whether auctioned or grandfathered — generates a liability for government (if auctioned, revenue; if free, an imputed subsidy). In baseline‑and‑credit, credits are generated ex post by verified emission reductions; they are recorded as output of environmental protection services (P.1) by the project developer, with the buyer recording intermediate consumption or capital formation depending on use. The 2025 SNA revision clarifies that carbon credits held for own compliance are inventories (AN.12), while those held for trading are valuables (AN.13) or financial assets if they meet the definition of a financial derivative.

India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), notified in June 2023, establishes a domestic compliance market for designated consumers under the Perform, Achieve, and Trade (PAT) scheme. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) acts as the administrator. For national accounts, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) must decide whether PAT escerts (energy saving certificates) are treated as permits (AN.22) or as a distinct asset class. The 2025 SNA’s guidance on emission permits as non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.21) when issued by government without a corresponding liability suggests that free allocation of escerts should be recorded as a capital transfer from government to the enterprise, with the enterprise recognising an asset. Subsequent trading generates holding gains/losses (K.3/K.4) recorded in the revaluation account. A persistent compilation challenge is the valuation of permits not actively traded — the SNA recommends using the market price of similar permits or, absent that, the marginal abatement cost. For the SEEA‑Air accounts, the physical flow of permits must be reconciled with the actual emissions recorded in the air emissions account, ensuring that total permits surrendered equal total verified emissions for the compliance period.

Measuring the Economic Contribution of the Non‑Observed Economy: Exhaustiveness Adjustments in Indian National Accounts

The non‑observed economy (NOE) comprises activities that are legal but not captured in standard statistical sources due to non‑registration, non‑response, or deliberate misreporting. The OECD/Eurostat Handbook on Measuring the Non‑Observed Economy (2002) and the 2008 SNA (Chapter 25) classify the NOE into seven types: (N1) underground production, (N2) illegal production, (N3) household production for own final use, (N4) statistical deficiencies, (N5) informal sector production, (N6) production by non‑registered legal entities, and (N7) tips and gratuities. India’s national accounts address the NOE through exhaustiveness adjustments applied at the compilation stage for each industry and institutional sector. The National Statistical Office (NSO) follows a supply‑use balancing framework where independent estimates of supply (production + imports) and use (intermediate consumption + final consumption + gross capital formation + exports) are reconciled; the residual is allocated to the NOE using indicator methods.

For agriculture, the NSO uses the crop cutting experiments (CCE) for major crops and input‑output norms for minor crops and livestock, implicitly covering own‑account production (N3). For manufacturing, the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) covers registered factories; the unregistered segment is estimated using the NSSO Enterprise Surveys (last conducted 2015‑16, with a new round in 2022‑23) and the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) for employment‑based extrapolation. The construction sector relies on the commodity flow method for cement and steel, adjusted for non‑construction uses, plus a labour input method using PLFS workforce data multiplied by value added per worker from the ASI. For trade, transport, and services, the NSO applies value added per worker ratios from the enterprise surveys to the total workforce estimated from the PLFS, minus the registered segment covered by MCA21 data for companies and GSTN data for GST‑registered entities.

A major methodological shift occurred with the 2011‑12 base year revision (released 2015), which introduced the MCA21 database for corporate sector coverage and the GSTN data (from 2017‑18 onwards) for tracking formal enterprise turnover. The 2023‑24 provisional estimates incorporate e‑way bill data for inter‑state goods movement and Udyam registration data for MSMEs. However, gaps remain: (i) the NSSO enterprise survey is quinquennial, requiring interpolation/extrapolation; (ii) digital platform work (gig economy) straddles N1 and N5 and is not fully captured by existing surveys; (iii) cross‑border digital services supplied by non‑resident platforms to Indian households (N4) are missed in household consumption surveys. The 2025 SNA recommends integrating administrative tax data (GST, income tax) with survey data using statistical matching and machine‑learning imputation to reduce reliance on fixed benchmark‑year ratios. MoSPI’s Data Innovation Lab is piloting such approaches for the next base year revision (likely 2027‑28).

Examiner's Trap: Confusing NOE Types with Institutional Sectors
A question asks: "In the Indian national accounts, the output of unregistered manufacturing enterprises owned by households is recorded in which institutional sector and which NOE type?"
The output is recorded in the Household sector (S.14) because the enterprises are household unincorporated enterprises. The NOE type is N5 (informal sector production) — defined as production by unincorporated enterprises owned by households that are not registered under specific legislation (Factories Act, Companies Act, GST). It is not N1 (underground) because the activity is legal and not deliberately concealed from authorities; it is not N3 (household production for own final use) because the output is sold in the market. The 2008 SNA (para 25.30) and the NSO's "National Accounts Statistics: Sources and Methods" (2012, Chapter 4) explicitly map informal sector enterprises to the household institutional sector.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question asks about "exhaustiveness adjustments", do not describe the informal sector survey. Instead, name the three pillars: (1) Supply‑Use balancing residual allocation, (2) Indicator methods (labour input, commodity flow, value added per worker), (3) Administrative data integration (MCA21, GSTN, e‑way bills, Udyam). Cite the 2011‑12 base year revision as the turning point for corporate data and the 2023‑24 estimates for GSTN/e‑way bill use. For the NOE types, memorise the N1–N7 codes and map each to an Indian example: N1 = under‑reporting of turnover by a registered firm to evade tax; N2 = narcotics; N3 = own‑account housing construction; N4 = missing digital services imports; N5 = street vendor; N6 = small non‑profit school; N7 = restaurant tips.

The Integration of National Accounts with the Tourism Satellite Account: Inbound, Domestic, and Outbound Tourism Expenditure

The Tourism Satellite Account (TSA), developed by the UNWTO, OECD, Eurostat, and the UN Statistics Division (2008 Recommended Methodological Framework), is a standard satellite account that reorganises national accounts data to measure tourism’s direct economic contribution. The TSA follows the tourism characteristic products and tourism characteristic activities lists (based on CPC and ISIC) and distinguishes three forms of tourism: inbound (non‑residents visiting the economic territory), domestic (residents travelling within the territory), and outbound (residents travelling outside the territory). The core TSA tables (Tables 1–10) link the production account of tourism industries (Table 5), the domestic supply and internal tourism consumption (Table 6), the employment in tourism industries (Table 7), and the gross fixed capital formation in tourism‑specific fixed assets (Table 8).

In the Indian context, the NSO compiled the first official TSA for 2009‑10 (released 2012) and a second for 2015‑16 (released 2019), with a third for 2021‑22 under preparation. The TSA uses the Domestic Tourism Expenditure Survey (DTES) and the International Passenger Survey (IPS) (conducted by the Ministry of Tourism) as primary data sources. Inbound tourism expenditure is recorded as exports of travel services (credit in BOP, P.6 in SNA) and is derived from the IPS combined with RBI’s foreign exchange receipts data. Domestic tourism expenditure is part of household final consumption expenditure (HFCE) (P.31) and is estimated from the DTES, which captures overnight and same‑day trips by purpose (business, leisure, religious, medical). Outbound tourism expenditure is recorded as imports of travel services (debit in BOP, P.7 in SNA) and is estimated from RBI’s foreign exchange outflows data supplemented by the IPS.

A key integration challenge is the treatment of tourism‑connected products (e.g., souvenirs, local transport) that are not tourism‑characteristic but are consumed by visitors. The TSA allocates a tourism ratio (share of visitor consumption in total supply) to each product, derived from the supply‑use table. For India, the 2015‑16 TSA reported that tourism direct GDP (TDGDP) was 5.19 % of GDP, tourism direct employment was 8.0 % of total employment, and inbound tourism expenditure was ₹1.94 lakh crore (2.9 % of exports of goods and services). The 2025 SNA introduces a tourism‑specific asset classification (AN.1123) for infrastructure such as hotels, convention centres, and tourism‑dedicated transport, enabling a direct link between GFCF in tourism assets and the TSA’s capital formation table. MoSPI is also aligning the TSA with the SEEA‑EEA to account for ecosystem services consumed by tourism (e.g., recreational services of protected areas), a step towards measuring sustainable tourism (SDG 8.9, 12.b).

Accounting for the Economic Value of Standardization, Metrology, and Quality Infrastructure

Quality Infrastructure (QI) — comprising standardization, metrology, accreditation, and conformity assessment — is a public good that reduces transaction costs, enables trade, and supports innovation. The 2008 SNA does not explicitly identify QI as a distinct asset or industry, but the 2025 SNA and the UNIDO‑ISO‑BIPM Quality Infrastructure Index provide a framework for satellite accounting. QI services are produced by National Standards Bodies (NSBs) (e.g., Bureau of Indian Standards, BIS), National Metrology Institutes (NMIs) (e.g., CSIR‑National Physical Laboratory), Accreditation Bodies (e.g., NABCB), and Conformity Assessment Bodies (testing labs, certification bodies). In the SNA, these are classified under ISIC 7120 (Technical testing and analysis) and ISIC 9411 (Activities of business and employers’ membership organizations) for standards development.

The economic value of QI can be measured through three complementary approaches: (1) Cost‑based: sum of intermediate consumption, compensation of employees, consumption of fixed capital, and net operating surplus of QI institutions — this yields the output of QI services (P.1) at basic prices. (2) User‑cost / willingness‑to‑pay: estimate the shadow price of QI services for firms that use standards, calibrated from trade‑cost reductions (e.g., the OECD Trade Facilitation Indicators show that mutual recognition of conformity assessment reduces trade costs by 2–5 %). (3) Productivity‑based: use firm‑level data (ASI, Prowess) to estimate the total factor productivity (TFP) premium associated with ISO 9001 certification or BIS licensing, controlling for firm size, age, and export status. A 2021 study by the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (NIPFP) for the Department of Consumer Affairs estimated that BIS standards contributed 0.6–0.9 % of GDP annually through reduced rejection rates, lower inventory costs, and enhanced export market access.

For national accounts integration, a QI Satellite Account would record: (a) Production account for QI institutions (output, intermediate consumption, GVA); (b) Use table showing which industries consume QI services (intermediate consumption) and which households consume certified products (final consumption); (c) Capital account for GFCF in QI‑specific assets (reference material inventories, calibration equipment, standards‑development IT systems — classified as intellectual property products, AN.117 under the 2025 SNA); (d) Balance sheet for the net worth of QI institutions. The BIPM‑CIPM Mutual Recognition Arrangement (MRA) and the ILAC/IAF MRA enable international equivalence; their economic value appears in the export of QI services (e.g., NPL providing calibration services to foreign NMIs) and in the reduction of non‑tariff measures for Indian exporters. India’s Quality Council of India (QCI) and the Department of Consumer Affairs are developing a National Quality Infrastructure Database to support this satellite account, targeting inclusion in the 2027‑28 base year revision.

The Role of National Accounts in Assessing the Economic Impact of Trade Policy: Tariff Revenue, Terms of Trade, and Effective Rates of Protection

National accounts provide the macroeconomic framework for evaluating trade policy through three interconnected channels: tariff revenue (government revenue account), terms‑of‑trade effects (real gross domestic income), and effective rates of protection (ERP) (industry‑level value added). Tariff revenue is recorded in the secondary distribution of income account as taxes on products (D.21) — specifically import duties. In the Indian SNA, customs duties are a major component of central government tax revenue (₹2.1 lakh crore in 2023‑24, ~1.2 % of GDP). The revenue impact of tariff changes is simulated using the import demand elasticity (typically −0.5 to −1.5 for manufactured goods) applied to the import value at c.i.f. prices from the rest of the world account. The 2008 SNA requires that import duties be recorded at the time of customs clearance (accrual basis), not at payment; the 2025 SNA reinforces this and adds guidance on tariff‑rate quotas where the in‑quota and out‑of‑quota rates create a kinked revenue function.

Terms‑of‑trade (ToT) effects are captured by the difference between Real Gross Domestic Income (RGDI) and Real GDP. RGDI = Real GDP + trading gain/loss, where the trading gain = (export volume × Δexport price) − (import volume × Δimport price) in chain‑linked volume terms. A tariff that improves the ToT (by lowering import prices relative to export prices) generates a positive trading gain, raising RGDI even if Real GDP falls due to reduced trade volume. India’s RGDI exceeded Real GDP in 2020‑21 and 2021‑22 due to favourable ToT from lower crude oil import prices; the reverse occurred in 2022‑23. The SEEA‑Energy physical flow accounts allow decomposition of the trading gain into energy and non‑energy components, critical for a net energy importer.

Effective Rate of Protection (ERP) measures the percentage increase in value added per unit of output in an industry due to the entire tariff structure (output tariff minus weighted input tariffs). ERP = (VAd − VAf) / VAf, where VAd is domestic value added at domestic prices (with tariffs) and VAf is value added at free‑trade (border) prices. The Input‑Output Table (IOT) is essential: ERP for industry j = [tj − Σi aij ti] / [1 − Σi aij], where tj is the nominal tariff on output j, aij is the input coefficient from the IOT, and ti is the nominal tariff on input i. India’s 2017‑18 IOT (released 2022) shows that sectors like textiles, automotive, and electronics have ERPs significantly higher than nominal tariffs due to low input tariffs (duty‑free imports under export promotion schemes) and high output tariffs. The 2025 SNA recommends linking the IOT with the government revenue account to track the fiscal cost of tariff exemptions (foregone D.21) against the value‑added gains in protected industries, enabling a cost‑benefit analysis of trade policy within the national accounts framework.

  • Confusing the NOE type N5 (informal sector) with N1 (underground) — the former is legal but unregistered; the latter is legal but deliberately concealed from authorities.
  • Recording carbon credits held for compliance as financial assets instead of inventories (AN.12) or non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.21) depending on the scheme design.
  • Treating inbound tourism expenditure as household final consumption expenditure instead of exports of travel services (P.6).
  • Using nominal tariff rates instead of effective rates of protection when assessing the impact of trade policy on domestic value added; ERP requires the input‑output table.
  • Omitting the trading gain/loss when comparing Real GDP across years with large commodity price swings — Real Gross Domestic Income is the correct welfare measure.
  • Classifying standards development output as market output (P.11) when the NSB is a non‑market producer funded by government grants; it should be non‑market output (P.13) valued at cost.
  • Failing to adjust import duties for the accrual basis (time of customs clearance) rather than cash receipt, leading to timing mismatches in the government revenue account.

The Treatment of Government Subsidies and Tax Expenditures in the System of National Accounts

Government subsidies are recorded in the secondary distribution of income account as current transfers (D.3) from government to producers or consumers. Under the 2008 SNA, a subsidy is a current unrequited payment that a government unit makes to a producer on the basis of the level of production or the quantity or value of goods and services produced, sold, exported or imported. The 2025 SNA refines the classification by distinguishing between subsidies on products (D.31) and other subsidies on production (D.39). Product subsidies are tied to the volume or value of a specific good or service (e.g., fertilizer subsidy per tonne), while other subsidies on production cover payments linked to the overall production activity (e.g., interest subvention for small‑scale industries).

Tax expenditures — revenue foregone due to preferential tax treatment — are not recorded as separate transactions in the core accounts. Instead, the SNA records the actual tax collected (D.2) and treats the foregone revenue as an implicit subsidy only when a government explicitly labels the provision as a subsidy. In practice, analysts construct a tax‑expenditure statement by estimating the revenue loss from each exemption, deduction, or credit using the statutory tax rate applied to the tax base that would have existed without the preference. The IMF’s Government Finance Statistics Manual (GFSM 2014) recommends presenting tax expenditures as a memorandum item alongside the standard revenue accounts to preserve the integrity of the SNA’s accrual basis.

Key Recording Rules

  • Subsidies on products (D.31) reduce the basic price of the subsidised good; the output value at basic prices excludes the subsidy, while the purchaser’s price includes it.
  • Other subsidies on production (D.39) are added to gross value added at basic prices because they are not linked to a specific product.
  • Capital transfers (D.9) such as investment grants are recorded in the capital account, not as current subsidies.
  • Tax expenditures are disclosed in a supplementary table; they do not alter the production or generation of income accounts.

Indian Practice

India’s Central Statistics Office (CSO) follows the 2008 SNA with the 2011‑12 base year. Major product subsidies — fertilizer, food, and petroleum — are captured in the “subsidies on products” line of the government revenue and expenditure statements. The 2025 SNA guidance on the accrual recording of subsidy entitlements (at the time the qualifying activity occurs) has been adopted for the 2023‑24 provisional estimates, reducing timing mismatches between budget announcements and national‑accounts recording. Tax‑expenditure reporting remains a memorandum item in the Union Budget’s “Statement of Revenue Foregone”, which lists exemptions under the Income Tax Act, GST concessions, and customs duty waivers.

Accounting for the Economic Value of Public Education Expenditure and Human Capital Formation

Public education services are non‑market output (P.13) valued at the sum of compensation of employees, intermediate consumption, consumption of fixed capital, and other taxes on production less subsidies. In the production account, the output of government education institutions enters government final consumption expenditure (P.3) because the services are provided free or at nominal fees. The 2008 SNA treats the acquisition of knowledge through formal education as the formation of human capital, but it does not capitalise the associated expenditure in the core accounts. The 2025 SNA introduces a satellite account for human capital that records the stock of educated labour, the flow of education investment, and the depreciation of skills.

Human‑Capital Satellite Account Structure

  • Stock: Present value of future earnings attributable to the current education level of the working‑age population (Jorgenson‑Fraumeni lifetime‑income approach).
  • Investment flow: Current public and private expenditure on education (including imputed cost of student time) recorded as gross fixed capital formation in the satellite account.
  • Depreciation: Skill obsolescence and labour‑force exit, estimated using age‑earnings profiles and mortality tables.

Indian Pilot Studies

The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) conducted a pilot human‑capital satellite account for 2011‑12 using NSSO employment‑unemployment data and the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS). The study applied the Jorgenson‑Fraumeni method to estimate the present value of lifetime earnings for each education category (primary, secondary, tertiary). Results indicated that the human‑capital stock was roughly 3.5 times GDP, with tertiary education contributing disproportionately to the stock despite lower enrolment shares. The 2025 SNA revision encourages countries to integrate such satellite accounts with the core national accounts to monitor the return on public education spending and to inform fiscal policy on skill development.

Worked Example: Subsidy Classification
A state government pays ₹500 crore to farmers as a per‑tonne fertilizer subsidy and ₹200 crore as an interest subvention on agricultural loans. Classify each payment in the SNA and explain the impact on GDP at market prices.
The fertilizer payment is a subsidy on products (D.31) because it is linked to the quantity of fertilizer used. It lowers the basic price of fertilizer, so output at basic prices is unchanged; the subsidy is added back when moving from basic prices to market prices, raising GDP at market prices by ₹500 crore. The interest subvention is an other subsidy on production (D.39) because it relates to the production activity, not a specific product. It is added to gross value added at basic prices, increasing GDP at market prices by ₹200 crore. Both subsidies are current transfers from government to producers and appear in the secondary distribution of income account.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the effect of a subsidy on GDP, first identify whether it is a product subsidy (D.31) or other production subsidy (D.39). Product subsidies affect the market‑price valuation only; other production subsidies raise value added directly. Remember that tax expenditures are not recorded as subsidies in the core accounts — they appear only in a memorandum table.

Measuring the Economic Impact of Digital Public Infrastructure on National Income

Digital public infrastructure (DPI) such as the Aadhaar identity platform, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), and the DigiLocker document‑storage system are government‑provided, non‑market services that facilitate economic activity across sectors. In the SNA, the production of DPI services is recorded as government non‑market output (P.13) valued at cost — compensation of employees, intermediate consumption (including server hosting, cybersecurity, and software licences), consumption of fixed capital, and other taxes on production less subsidies. The output enters government final consumption expenditure (P.3) because the services are supplied free to users.

Capitalisation Debate

The 2025 SNA recommends capitalising large‑scale digital platforms that meet the criteria for produced assets: they are the result of a production process, have a service life exceeding one year, and are used repeatedly in production. If capitalised, the development expenditure (including software development, data‑centre construction, and network equipment) is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) and the platform appears as a fixed asset (AN.113) on the government balance sheet. Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital) is then charged over the asset’s useful life, typically 5‑10 years for software and 15‑20 years for data‑centre infrastructure.

Spillover Measurement

Beyond the direct cost, DPI generates positive externalities: reduced transaction costs, financial inclusion, and efficiency gains in service delivery. The SNA captures these indirectly through higher output in user sectors (banking, e‑commerce, social protection). Analysts use input‑output tables to trace the increase in intermediate consumption of “information and communication services” by downstream industries. In India, the 2017‑18 Input‑Output Table shows a 12 % rise in the ICT intermediate coefficient for the banking sector between 2011‑12 and 2017‑18, coincident with UPI rollout. The 2025 SNA encourages the compilation of a “digital economy satellite account” that isolates the value added of digital platforms, the stock of digital assets, and the flow of data services.

The Role of National Accounts in Evaluating Fiscal Stimulus Effectiveness

Fiscal stimulus packages — combinations of increased government spending, tax cuts, and transfer payments — are assessed through the national‑accounts identity: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M). An increase in government final consumption expenditure (G) or gross fixed capital formation (I) raises aggregate demand directly. Transfer payments (social benefits, subsidies) affect household disposable income and thus private consumption (C). The multiplier effect is derived from the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) and the import leakage (MPM). In the Indian context, the 2020‑21 Atmanirbhar Bharat package included ₹2.0 lakh crore of additional capital expenditure, ₹1.5 lakh crore of credit guarantees, and targeted tax relief.

Multiplier Estimation Using Input‑Output Tables

The Leontief inverse (I − A)⁻¹ provides the total output requirement per unit of final demand. By shocking the final‑demand vector with the stimulus components, the model yields the induced output, value added, and employment. India’s 2017‑18 IOT indicates a Type‑I output multiplier of 1.8 for government capital formation and 1.4 for government consumption. The 2025 SNA recommends reporting the “fiscal multiplier” as a memorandum item in the government finance statistics, linking the stimulus to the change in real GDP and the trading gain/loss (RGDI − real GDP).

Timing and Revision Issues

Stimulus measures often involve off‑budget vehicles (special purpose vehicles, extra‑budgetary resources) that are recorded in the national accounts only when the underlying economic activity occurs. The CSO’s quarterly GDP estimates incorporate the stimulus with a lag of one quarter, and the annual revision (typically in January) aligns the provisional figures with the final audited accounts. The 2025 SNA’s guidance on accrual recording of government guarantees ensures that contingent liabilities are recognised when the guarantee is called, preventing understatement of the fiscal stance during the stimulus period.

Satellite Accounts for the Informal Sector: Methodology, Data Sources, and Indian Experience

The informal sector (SNA institutional sector N5) comprises unincorporated enterprises that are not registered and do not maintain complete accounts. The 2008 SNA defines it by the absence of legal registration and the lack of a complete set of accounts. A satellite account for the informal sector isolates its production, income generation, and employment from the formal economy, enabling policy analysis on formalisation, social protection, and productivity gaps.

Compilation Steps

  1. Enterprise census: Use the Economic Census (EC) to identify unregistered establishments by industry and size class.
  2. Labour‑input surveys: The Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) provides employment, hours worked, and earnings for informal workers.
  3. Mixed‑income estimation: Apply the “residual method” — subtract formal‑sector value added (from corporate filings and ASI) from total industry value added (from the production approach) to obtain informal value added.
  4. Imputation of capital consumption: Estimate consumption of fixed capital for informal assets using perpetual inventory method with assumed service lives.

Indian Practice and Gaps

India’s first informal‑sector satellite account was compiled for 2011‑12 using the 6th Economic Census and the 68th round NSSO survey. It estimated informal‑sector GVA at 52 % of total GVA, employing 81 % of the workforce. The 2025 SNA revision introduces a “formal‑informal linkage table” that tracks transitions of enterprises across the registration threshold, requiring longitudinal enterprise identifiers. Current gaps include the lack of high‑frequency data on informal output, limited coverage of home‑based digital platform workers, and the absence of a consistent price deflator for informal services. MoSPI plans to integrate GST‑return data (for newly registered micro‑enterprises) and the Udyam registration portal to improve the timeliness of the satellite account for the 2027‑28 base‑year revision.

  • Confusing subsidies on products (D.31) with other subsidies on production (D.39) — the former affect market‑price valuation only, the latter raise value added directly.
  • Treating tax expenditures as current subsidies in the core accounts; they belong only in a memorandum table.
  • Recording digital public infrastructure solely as current expenditure when the 2025 SNA permits capitalisation if asset criteria are met.
  • Using nominal fiscal multipliers without adjusting for import leakage and the marginal propensity to consume.
  • Applying the residual method for informal‑sector GVA without reconciling the formal‑sector estimates from corporate filings and the Annual Survey of Industries.
  • Omitting the consumption of fixed capital for informal assets, leading to an overstatement of net value added.
  • Neglecting the accrual timing of government guarantees in stimulus packages, which distorts the fiscal stance in quarterly accounts.

The sections above provide a coherent framework for analysing subsidies, human capital, digital infrastructure, fiscal stimulus, and the informal sector within the modern System of National Accounts.

The Solow-Swan Model and its Limitations in Explaining Sustained Growth

The Solow-Swan model, a cornerstone of neoclassical growth theory developed independently by Robert Solow and Trevor Swan in the mid-1950s, provides a framework for understanding how capital accumulation, labour growth, and technological progress interact to determine an economy's long-run growth path. It posits that economic growth is primarily driven by increases in the capital stock per worker, but crucially, it assumes diminishing returns to capital.

The model's core mechanism revolves around the capital accumulation equation: Δk = sf(k) − (δ + n)k, where k is capital per effective worker, s is the savings rate, f(k) is the production function per effective worker, δ is the depreciation rate of capital, and n is the population growth rate (or effective labour growth rate, if technological progress is also considered). The term sf(k) represents investment per effective worker, while (δ + n)k represents the investment required to keep the capital-labour ratio constant (break-even investment).

A key prediction of the Solow-Swan model is the existence of a "steady state" (k*), where investment exactly equals break-even investment, and the capital-labour ratio no longer changes. At this steady state, per capita output and capital per worker are constant. This implies that in the long run, sustained per capita economic growth cannot be achieved solely through capital accumulation due to diminishing returns. Instead, the model concludes that the ultimate source of sustained long-run growth in per capita income is exogenous technological progress, which shifts the production function upwards over time.

The model also predicts "conditional convergence," meaning that economies with lower initial capital-labour ratios (poorer countries) will tend to grow faster than those with higher ratios (richer countries), eventually converging to their own respective steady states, provided they share similar parameters (savings rate, population growth, technology, depreciation). However, it does not predict "absolute convergence" where all economies converge to the same income level, as different countries can have different steady states.

Despite its foundational importance, the Solow-Swan model faces significant limitations. Its most critical shortcoming is treating technological progress as an exogenous factor, an unexplained "residual" that drives long-run growth. This leaves the most important determinant of sustained prosperity outside the model's analytical scope. Furthermore, empirical evidence for absolute convergence is weak; income disparities persist and even widen between countries. The model also largely ignores the roles of human capital, institutions, and innovation policies, which are increasingly recognized as crucial endogenous drivers of growth.
