Produced capital is measured at replacement cost using perpetual inventory methods consistent with the 2008 SNA. Human capital is valued via the lifetime income approach (Jorgenson‑Fraumeni) or the cost‑based approach (education expenditure plus health expenditure). Natural capital follows the System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting (SEEA) – Central Framework for physical stocks and the SEEA‑Ecosystem Accounting for ecosystem services.

India’s National Statistical Office (NSO) launched a pilot Inclusive Wealth Account in 2021, covering the period 2005‑2019. The pilot used the World Bank’s Changing Wealth of Nations database for cross‑country comparability and applied the SEEA‑Energy and SEEA‑Water physical flow accounts for natural capital. Produced capital was derived from the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) and the National Accounts’ gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) series. Human capital estimates relied on the National Sample Survey (NSS) education and health modules, combined with the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) for earnings profiles. The 2021 pilot reported that India’s inclusive wealth per capita grew at an average annual rate of 2.3 % over 2005‑2019, driven primarily by human capital accumulation (≈1.4 % per year) while natural capital declined by 0.6 % per year due to forest degradation and groundwater depletion.

The 2025 SNA revision strengthens the link between national accounts and inclusive wealth by recognising natural capital as a non‑produced asset on the balance sheet and by capitalising research and development (R&D) and data as produced assets. This alignment permits a consistent “wealth‑account” presentation where the change in net worth equals saving plus capital gains minus depletion. For policy, the inclusive wealth framework highlights that GDP growth alone can mask asset erosion; a country may record rising GDP while its natural capital stock shrinks, implying an unsustainable trajectory. The Indian pilot therefore recommends supplementing the quarterly GDP press release with an annual “Inclusive Wealth Bulletin” that tracks the three capital stocks and their contributions to net worth changes.

The Treatment of Intellectual Property as a Produced Asset: Capitalisation, Amortisation, and Cross‑Border Licensing in the 2025 SNA

The 2008 System of National Accounts (SNA) treated research and development (R&D) as intermediate consumption, so the output of R&D‑intensive industries excluded the value of the knowledge created. The 2025 SNA revises this by capitalising R&D, software, databases, and intellectual property products (IPPs) as gross fixed capital formation (GFCF). An IPP is defined as a produced asset that provides a stream of future economic benefits through the use of knowledge, creativity, or innovation. The main categories are patents, copyrights, trademarks, industrial designs, and trade secrets. Capitalisation occurs at the sum of costs incurred in developing the asset (labour, materials, overheads) plus a mark‑up for own‑account production. When market prices are observable — for example, a patent sold in an arm’s‑length transaction — that price is used; otherwise the cost‑based approach applies.

Amortisation follows the asset’s expected service life. For patents the legal life (typically 20 years) is the upper bound, but economic life may be shorter; the SNA recommends using the shorter of legal and economic life. Software and databases are amortised over 3‑5 years unless evidence supports a longer period. The consumption of fixed capital (CFC) on IPPs enters the production account as a cost, raising gross value added (GVA) relative to the 2008 treatment. In India, the Central Statistics Office (CSO) published an experimental “IP Satellite Account” in 2023 covering patents filed by Indian residents (≈ 55 000 in 2022) and copyright registrations (≈ 1.2 lakh). The account estimated the stock of IP assets at ₹ 12.4 lakh crore at end‑2022, contributing roughly 0.7 % of GDP through CFC.

Cross‑border licensing generates royalty flows that are recorded as exports or imports of services (code SI in the Balance of Payments). The 2025 SNA aligns with the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines: royalties must reflect arm’s‑length prices. When a multinational enterprise (MNE) shifts IP to a low‑tax jurisdiction, the SNA requires the host country to record the corresponding GFCF and the source country to record the royalty outflow. India’s 2022‑23 Balance of Payments showed royalty receipts of ₹ 1.1 lakh crore and payments of ₹ 2.3 lakh crore, reflecting net IP import. The SNA’s “global value chain” satellite tables (TiVA) now allow analysts to trace the domestic value added embodied in IP‑intensive exports, improving the measurement of technology‑driven competitiveness.

Worked Example
Explain how the 2025 SNA reclassifies research and development expenditure and its effect on GDP.
Under the 2008 SNA, R&D expenditure was treated as intermediate consumption, so it reduced gross value added (GVA) of the performing industry. The 2025 SNA reclassifies R&D as gross fixed capital formation (GFCF), creating a new produced asset — an intellectual property product. The expenditure is now recorded as investment, not consumption. Consequently, the industry’s GVA rises by the amount of R&D spending (since intermediate consumption falls), and the economy’s GDP (expenditure side) increases by the same amount through higher GFCF. The asset is then amortised over its useful life via consumption of fixed capital (CFC), which enters the production account as a cost in subsequent periods. The net effect on GDP in the year of spending is positive; over the asset’s life the cumulative GDP impact is neutral, but the timing shift improves the measurement of knowledge‑intensive production.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about the GDP impact of capitalising R&D, remember the two‑step logic: (1) immediate rise in GFCF and GVA because intermediate consumption falls; (2) later CFC charges that offset the initial boost. Quote the 2025 SNA terminology — “intellectual property product”, “GFCF”, “CFC” — to show precision.

The Use of Satellite Accounts for the Digital Economy: Cloud Services, Platform Intermediation, and Data as a Factor of Production

The rapid expansion of cloud computing, digital platforms, and data‑driven business models has outpaced the core SNA’s production boundary. The OECD’s “Digital Economy Satellite Account” (DESA) framework, published in 2020, proposes a modular extension that isolates digital activities without altering headline GDP. The DESA defines three core modules: (i) Cloud Services — measuring the output of cloud service providers (CSPs) at basic prices, using revenue from infrastructure‑as‑a‑service (IaaS), platform‑as‑a‑service (PaaS), and software‑as‑a‑service (SaaS); (ii) Platform Intermediation — capturing the value added by digital platforms that match buyers and sellers (e‑commerce, ride‑hailing, food delivery) via the “platform fee” or commission revenue; (iii) Data as a Produced Asset — valuing data generated by users, sensors, and transactions using either the cost‑of‑production method (collection, cleaning, storage costs) or the user‑cost method (discounted future service flows).

India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) and the NSO jointly piloted a Digital Economy Satellite Account in 2022‑23. The pilot used GST‑N (Goods and Services Tax Network) invoice data to identify CSP revenues (≈ ₹ 1.8 lakh crore in FY 2022‑23) and platform commission revenues from major e‑commerce and ride‑hailing firms (≈ ₹ 0.9 lakh crore). Data valuation relied on the cost‑of‑production approach applied to the National Data Repository (NDR) and the Open Government Data Platform, yielding an experimental data stock of ₹ 0.4 lakh crore. The satellite account showed that digital‑economy GVA contributed 4.2 % of total GVA in FY 2022‑23, up from 2.8 % in FY 2018‑19.

Key methodological challenges remain. First, many cloud services are consumed by the same enterprise that produces them (own‑account), requiring imputation of market‑equivalent prices. Second, platform intermediation often involves multi‑sided markets where the “price” to one side is zero; the SNA recommends allocating the total platform revenue across sides using demand elasticities. Third, open‑source data and user‑generated content (e.g., social media posts) have zero market price but generate substantial downstream value; the 2025 SNA treats such data as a non‑market produced asset valued at cost, while the DESA suggests a supplementary “data‑value” table for analytical purposes. The Indian pilot recommends annual updates aligned with the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) and the Quarterly GDP release cycle.

The Measurement of Multidimensional Poverty and Its Integration with National Income Accounts: The Alkire‑Foster Method and Policy Linkages

The Alkire‑Foster (AF) counting methodology, developed by Sabina Alkire and James Foster at the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI), underpins the Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) published jointly by UNDP and OPHI since 2010. The AF method identifies deprivations across a set of weighted indicators, applies a deprivation cutoff (k) to classify a person as multidimensionally poor, and aggregates using the adjusted headcount ratio (M₀ = H × A), where H is the incidence (share of poor) and A is the intensity (average share of weighted deprivations among the poor). The standard global MPI uses ten indicators grouped into three dimensions — health (nutrition, child mortality), education (years of schooling, school attendance), and living standards (cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, assets) — each dimension weighted equally (1/3) and each indicator equally within its dimension.

India’s National MPI, released by NITI Aayog in 2021 (based on NFHS‑4, 2015‑16) and updated in 2023 (NFHS‑5, 2019‑21), adapts the global framework by adding indicators such as maternal health and bank account ownership. The 2023 report estimated the national MPI at 0.069, with 14.96 % of the population multidimensionally poor (down from 24.85 % in 2015‑16). The intensity among the poor was 42.3 %. The MPI is disaggregated by state, district, urban/rural, and social groups, enabling targeted policy interventions such as the Aspirational Districts Programme.

Integrating MPI with national income accounts is achieved through Distributional National Accounts (DNA), which break down aggregate household income, consumption, and saving by income decile and link them to MPI status. The NSO’s 2022‑23 experimental DNA tables show that the bottom two deciles account for 55 % of the multidimensionally poor population but only 12 % of national disposable income. This linkage allows policymakers to simulate the impact of cash transfers or in‑kind subsidies on both income poverty and multidimensional deprivations. For instance, a universal basic income (UBI) of ₹ 7 500 per month per adult would raise the income share of the poorest decile by 3.2 percentage points and reduce the MPI incidence by an estimated 2.1 percentage points, assuming no behavioural response. The 2025 SNA’s expanded household sector accounts (including imputed rent, own‑account production, and social transfers in kind) improve the consistency of such simulations.

The Role of National Accounts in Assessing the Economic Impact of Demographic Transition: Ageing, Labour Supply, and Fiscal Pressure

Demographic transition — the shift from high fertility and mortality to low fertility and mortality — reshapes the age structure, labour force participation, and fiscal balances. National accounts provide the macroeconomic framework to quantify these effects through three channels: (1) Potential output estimation using a production‑function approach where labour input is measured as quality‑adjusted hours worked (QALI). The CSO’s 2023 potential output model incorporates cohort‑specific participation rates from the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) and projects them using the United Nations World Population Prospects 2022 revision. (2) Generational accounting, which computes the net present value of future government expenditures (pensions, health, long‑term care) minus revenues for each birth cohort. India’s 2022‑23 Economic Survey presented a generational account showing that cohorts born after 2000 face a net fiscal burden of ₹ 1.8 lakh crore (present value) under current policies, driven by rising old‑age pension outlays and health‑care costs. (3) The national balance sheet, expanded under the 2025 SNA to include pension entitlements as liabilities of the general government sector, makes the inter‑temporal fiscal position transparent. The 2023‑24 provisional balance sheet recorded government pension obligations at ₹ 45 lakh crore (≈ 12 % of GDP), up from ₹ 38 lakh crore in 2020‑21.

India’s demographic dividend window — the period when the working‑age share peaks — is projected to last until the early 2040s. The 2023‑24 Economic Survey estimates that a 1 percentage‑point increase in the labour force participation rate (LFPR) of women (currently 24 % vs. 76 % for men) could raise potential GDP growth by 0.3 percentage points annually. National accounts capture this through the “labour input” component of growth accounting: the KLEMS database for India (released 2022) provides industry‑level QALI series that separate quantity (hours) from quality (education, experience). Simulations using the KLEMS data show that closing the gender LFPR gap by 2030 would add ₹ 12 lakh crore to real GDP (2023‑24 prices) over the decade.

Fiscal pressure from ageing is reflected in the rising share of “social protection” in government final consumption expenditure (GFCE). In 2022‑23, social protection (pensions, health insurance, cash transfers) accounted for 14.2 % of GFCE, up from 11.5 % in 2015‑16. The 2025 SNA’s accrual recording of pension liabilities forces governments to recognise the full cost of defined‑benefit schemes at the time of accrual, not at cash payment. This improves the credibility of medium‑term fiscal frameworks and informs the design of parametric reforms (e.g., raising retirement age, indexing pensions to inflation rather than wages). The integration of demographic projections with national accounts thus provides a coherent evidence base for both monetary policy (potential output) and fiscal policy (debt sustainability).

  • Confusing inclusive wealth growth with GDP growth — inclusive wealth can fall while GDP rises if natural capital depletion exceeds produced and human capital accumulation.
  • Treating intellectual property royalties as factor income rather than service exports/imports — the 2025 SNA classifies them under “charges for the use of intellectual property” (code SI).
  • Assuming satellite‑account digital‑economy GVA is additive to headline GDP — DESA figures are a re‑classification, not an addition.
  • Using a single‑year MPI headcount to infer income poverty trends — MPI incidence and intensity must be read together, and linked to distributional national accounts for income‑poverty mapping.
  • Ignoring the quality‑adjusted labour input (QALI) when projecting potential output — raw hours worked overstate labour contribution if education and experience are rising.
  • Recording pension obligations only on a cash basis in the national balance sheet — the 2025 SNA requires accrual valuation, which materially changes the government’s net worth.
  • Applying a uniform discount rate across all generational accounts — cohort‑specific discount rates reflecting risk and time preference are essential for credible fiscal sustainability analysis.

The Role of National Accounts in Measuring the Economic Impact of Trade in Services and Digital Delivery Modes

The System of National Accounts (SNA) records exports and imports of services through the balance of payments (BOP) framework, distinguishing four modes of supply defined by the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS): Mode 1 (cross‑border supply), Mode 2 (consumption abroad), Mode 3 (commercial presence), and Mode 4 (movement of natural persons). Digital delivery — primarily Mode 1 — has expanded the share of services trade that never crosses a physical border, creating measurement challenges for national accountants. The 2008 SNA treats digitally delivered services as standard service exports, valued at the transaction price agreed between resident and non‑resident parties. However, the rise of platform‑mediated transactions, cloud computing, and data‑driven services has blurred the line between a service export and a royalty or licence fee. The 2025 SNA revision introduces a dedicated “digital services” product classification (CPC 2.1 – Digital intermediation services) and requires compilers to separate platform fees from the underlying service value, using the “principal‑agent” principle where the platform acts as an agent. In practice, statistical offices such as India’s Central Statistics Office (CSO) have begun linking GST invoice data with BOP surveys to identify the residence of the counterparty and the mode of supply. The OECD’s “Measuring the Digital Economy” framework further recommends the use of “digital supply‑use tables” that map the flow of data, software, and cloud services across industries, enabling a more granular decomposition of value added attributable to digital trade. These extensions allow policymakers to assess the contribution of services exports to GDP growth, to evaluate the impact of trade‑policy changes (e.g., the removal of data‑localisation requirements) on national income, and to feed consistent service‑trade data into the Trade in Value‑Added (TiVA) database for global value‑chain analysis.

The Use of Administrative Tax Data for Real‑Time Household Consumption Expenditure Estimation

Traditional household consumption expenditure (HCE) estimates rely on quinquennial consumer expenditure surveys (CES) that suffer from recall bias, long lags, and limited granularity. Since the introduction of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India (July 2017), the CSO has piloted the use of monthly GST return data (GSTR‑1 and GSTR‑3B) to nowcast private final consumption expenditure (PFCE). The methodology aggregates taxable turnover at the HSN‑code level, applies industry‑specific markup ratios derived from the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) to convert turnover into final consumption values, and adjusts for the share of business‑to‑business (B2B) transactions using the input‑output table. A parallel track exploits income‑tax return (ITR) data to capture consumption of high‑income households that are under‑represented in survey samples. The 2025 SNA encourages the integration of administrative micro‑data through “statistical registers” that link enterprise identifiers (GSTIN, PAN) with household identifiers (Aadhaar‑seeded) while preserving confidentiality via secure‑multiparty computation. Early results from the CSO’s 2023‑24 experimental series show that the GST‑based nowcast reduces the revision magnitude of PFCE by roughly 30 % compared with the survey‑only benchmark, and provides a monthly frequency that aligns with the quarterly national accounts compilation calendar. Remaining challenges include the treatment of exempt supplies, the informal sector’s low GST coverage, and the need for robust imputation models for non‑taxable consumption such as imputed rent and own‑account production.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which of the following statements about the use of GST data for real‑time PFCE estimation is correct? (a) GST data alone can replace the Consumer Expenditure Survey. (b) GST turnover must be adjusted for B2B transactions using input‑output tables. (c) The 2025 SNA prohibits the use of administrative tax data in national accounts. (d) GST data captures all household consumption including imputed rent."
Correct answer: (b). GST turnover reflects total taxable sales, which include both final consumption and intermediate purchases. The CSO methodology uses the input‑output table to strip out B2B flows and derive a final consumption estimate. Statement (a) is false because GST excludes exempt and informal consumption; (c) is false — the 2025 SNA explicitly encourages administrative data integration; (d) is false because imputed rent is non‑market and not captured in GST invoices.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes national‑accounts concepts with tax‑administration details, identify the statistical principle first (e.g., production vs. expenditure approach, residence principle). Then match the administrative source to the specific account it feeds (GST → PFCE, ITR → household income). Eliminate options that claim a single source can fully replace a survey or that a new SNA revision bans administrative data.

The Treatment of Carbon Credits and Emission Trading Schemes in the System of National Accounts

Emission allowances and carbon credits are classified in the 2008 SNA as non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.22) when they are tradable and have a market price. The initial allocation of allowances by a government is recorded as a capital transfer (D.9) to the recipient enterprise, increasing the enterprise’s net worth. Subsequent purchases and sales of allowances are recorded as acquisitions less disposals of non‑produced non‑financial assets (NP.1), affecting the capital account and the net lending/borrowing position. The 2025 SNA revision refines this treatment by introducing a “carbon‑asset” sub‑classification that distinguishes between compliance‑market allowances (e.g., EU ETS Phase IV allowances) and voluntary‑market credits (e.g., Verified Carbon Standard units). Valuation follows the market‑price principle: the balance‑sheet value at each reporting date equals the prevailing spot price on the relevant exchange. For countries operating a domestic cap‑and‑trade system, the government’s holding of unsold allowances appears as an asset on the general government balance sheet, while the liability to surrender allowances for verified emissions is recorded as a provision (AF.8) under the 2025 SNA’s expanded provisions framework. The flow accounts capture the cost of compliance as intermediate consumption (P.2) when allowances are surrendered, and any revenue from auctioning allowances as a tax on production (D.2) if the auction is compulsory. These entries ensure that the macroeconomic impact of carbon pricing — on sectoral value added, profitability, and government revenue — is transparently reflected in GDP, net domestic product, and the government’s fiscal balance.

The Integration of Satellite Imagery and Remote Sensing for Agricultural Output and Rural Income Estimation

Satellite‑derived indicators such as the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI), and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) backscatter have become core inputs for the CSO’s “Crop‑Cutting Experiment” (CCE) calibration and for the construction of the “Agricultural Production Index” (API). The National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) provides fortnightly NDVI composites at 250 m resolution, which are aggregated to the district level and regressed against historical CCE yields to produce early‑season yield forecasts. These forecasts feed the quarterly estimates of gross value added (GVA) for the “crops” sub‑sector, reducing the lag between harvest and national‑accounts publication from six months to two months. In parallel, night‑time lights (NTL) data from the VIIRS sensor are used to proxy rural economic activity where formal surveys are sparse; the CSO’s 2022‑23 pilot combined NTL intensity with the Socio‑Economic and Caste Census (SECC) household‑level asset data to impute per‑capita income for villages lacking a Primary Agricultural Credit Society (PACS) survey. The 2025 SNA’s “big‑data” annex recognises satellite imagery as a “non‑traditional data source” and prescribes quality‑assurance protocols: metadata documentation, uncertainty quantification (e.g., cloud‑cover bias), and version‑controlled processing pipelines. The integration of these geospatial layers with the System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting for Agriculture (SEEA‑Agri) enables a consistent accounting of land‑use change, soil carbon stocks, and water‑use efficiency alongside monetary output, supporting both the Green GDP initiative and the monitoring of Sustainable Development Goal 2 (Zero Hunger).

The Role of National Accounts in Assessing the Fiscal Implications of Digital Services Taxation and OECD Pillar One Implementation

The OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework’s Pillar One reallocates a portion of the residual profit of the largest multinational enterprises (MNEs) to market jurisdictions based on a revenue‑allocation key, while Pillar Two introduces a global minimum corporate tax. National accounts record the resulting revenue flows as “taxes on production and imports” (D.2) when they are levied on the gross revenue of digital services (e.g., India’s 2 % equalisation levy) and as “current taxes on income, wealth, etc.” (D.5) for the profit‑allocation component. The 2025 SNA introduces a new tax‑type code (D.29 – Digital services taxes) to separate these receipts from traditional turnover taxes, enabling analysts to trace their incidence across sectors via the supply‑use tables. For the government sector, the additional revenue improves the primary balance and reduces the gross financing need, but the macroeconomic impact depends on the behavioural response of MNEs — potential price pass‑through to consumers (affecting household final consumption expenditure) and profit shifting that alters the gross operating surplus of the non‑financial corporations sector. The CSO’s 2024‑25 “Digital Tax Satellite Account” links the tax revenue series with the TiVA database to estimate the domestic value‑added content of taxed digital services, providing a metric for the “effective tax rate on domestic value added”. This satellite account also feeds the medium‑term fiscal framework by projecting the revenue trajectory under alternative scenarios of MNE profit‑allocation rules, exchange‑rate movements, and digital‑service growth rates, thereby informing both fiscal policy and the design of compensatory measures for affected domestic firms.

  • Confusing the classification of carbon allowances as financial assets rather than non‑produced non‑financial assets.
  • Assuming GST turnover equals final household consumption without adjusting for B2B flows using input‑output tables.
  • Treating digital services taxes as income taxes in the government revenue account instead of taxes on production.
  • Neglecting the residence principle when attributing cross‑border digital service flows in the balance of payments.
  • Overstating the coverage of satellite‑based yield forecasts by ignoring cloud‑cover bias and sensor‑resolution limits.
  • Recording the initial allocation of emission allowances as a sale of goods rather than a capital transfer.
  • Using a single‑year night‑time lights composite to infer long‑term rural income trends without controlling for seasonal lighting variations.

The advanced sections above extend the national‑accounts toolkit into digital trade, real‑time fiscal data, carbon markets, geospatial estimation, and international tax reform, equipping candidates to tackle the most current analytical questions.

Measuring the Economic Impact of Digital Public Infrastructure on National Income

Digital public infrastructure (DPI) — exemplified by Aadhaar (launched 2009), the Unified Payments Interface (UPI, 2016) and DigiLocker (2015) — has become a general‑purpose technology that lowers transaction costs across the economy. In the System of National Accounts (SNA) the production of DPI services by government agencies is recorded as non‑market output valued at the sum of compensation of employees, consumption of fixed capital and intermediate consumption (2008 SNA, §6.31). Because the services are provided free or at nominal fees, the output does not generate a market price; the cost‑of‑production approach therefore imputes a value that enters government final consumption expenditure (GFCE) and, through the production account, gross value added (GVA) of the general government sector. The 2025 SNA revision introduces a “digital platform” asset class (AN.117) that permits capitalisation of the underlying software, data‑management systems and network effects when they meet the criteria of a produced asset — i.e. they are created through a production process, have a lifespan exceeding one year and are used repeatedly in production. When the DPI platform satisfies these conditions, the initial development outlays are re‑classified from intermediate consumption to gross fixed capital formation (GFCF), raising the government’s capital stock and altering the depreciation profile (consumption of fixed capital) in subsequent periods.

The macroeconomic impact of DPI is traced through three channels. First, the reduction in payment‑settlement costs raises the marginal productivity of commerce, which appears as higher gross operating surplus in the non‑financial corporations sector. Second, the inclusion of previously unbanked households in the formal financial system expands the household sector’s financial assets (currency and deposits) and liabilities (loans), improving the coverage of the financial account and the flow‑of‑funds matrix. Third, the data generated by DPI — transaction logs, authentication records — constitute a public data asset that can be valued either at the cost of collection and curation (the “cost‑based” method) or at the estimated willingness‑to‑pay of downstream users (the “user‑value” method). The 2025 SNA recommends a satellite account for public data assets that records both the production cost and the imputed user value, enabling analysts to assess the net contribution of DPI to national income beyond the cost‑of‑production baseline.

Empirical work in India uses the “UPI transaction volume” series (monthly, published by the National Payments Corporation of India) as a high‑frequency indicator of real‑time economic activity. Researchers regress quarterly GVA growth on lagged UPI volume, controlling for seasonality and the monetary policy stance, and find a statistically significant elasticity of 0.12‑0.15. This elasticity is then used in the CSO’s nowcasting model to adjust the quarterly GVA estimate for the “financial services” sub‑sector before the final survey‑based estimates are available. A common examiner trap is to treat the entire UPI transaction value as final consumption expenditure; the correct treatment recognises that only the fee component (merchant discount rate) is a service output, while the principal transfer is a financial intermediation flow recorded in the financial account.

Accounting for the Economic Value of Public Data Assets and Open Government Data in the SNA

Open government data (OGD) portals such as data.gov.in publish thousands of datasets ranging from geospatial layers to health‑facility registers. Under the 2008 SNA, data that are the direct output of a statistical production process (e.g., a census) are recorded as a non‑market service (government output) valued at cost. However, datasets that are compiled, curated and disseminated as a reusable resource — meeting the definition of a “knowledge‑capturing product” — qualify as intellectual property products (IPP) under the 2025 SNA (AN.117). The 2025 revision explicitly lists “databases” and “data‑as‑a‑service” as produced assets when they are created through a deliberate production process, have a measurable lifespan and are used repeatedly in further production. Capitalisation of OGD therefore moves the initial outlays (data collection, cleaning, metadata creation, portal development) from intermediate consumption to GFCF, creating a capital stock that yields a flow of services (data access) recorded as output of the general government sector.

Valuation of the resulting asset can follow three approaches. The cost‑based approach sums the actual expenditures incurred by the statistical office and the IT ministry, adjusted for consumption of fixed capital on the portal infrastructure. The market‑price approach uses observable licence fees for comparable commercial datasets (e.g., satellite imagery licences) to impute a market value. The user‑value approach estimates the aggregate willingness‑to‑pay of downstream users — researchers, start‑ups, policy analysts — by applying a demand‑curve estimation to download statistics and citation counts. The 2025 SNA recommends presenting all three valuations in a satellite account for public data assets, together with a “data‑quality” indicator (completeness, timeliness, granularity) that adjusts the user‑value estimate for usability.

In practice, the Indian Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) piloted a “Public Data Satellite Account” in 2023‑24. The account recorded the 2022‑23 cost of the National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (NDSAP) implementation at ₹1,240 crore, capitalised ₹860 crore as a database asset (AN.117) and imputed a user‑value of ₹3,450 crore based on a contingent‑valuation survey of 1,200 data‑intensive firms. The satellite account feeds the supply‑use tables by adding a “data services” row, allowing the calculation of a data‑intensity multiplier for sectors such as fintech, agritech and e‑governance. A frequent exam error is to record the entire download count as a volume indicator of output; the SNA requires that only the service of providing access (the “data‑as‑a‑service” activity) be measured, not the number of downloads per se.

Worked Example: Classifying a Government‑Run API Platform
A ministry launches an open API that provides real‑time air‑quality data to private app developers. The development cost is ₹45 crore, the annual server cost is ₹5 crore, and the platform generates no direct revenue. In the 2025 SNA, how should the initial development cost and the annual server cost be recorded in the production and capital accounts?
The API platform is a produced asset (database + software) with a lifespan > 1 year, used repeatedly in production. The initial development cost (₹45 crore) is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) in the government capital account, creating an asset AN.117. The annual server cost (₹5 crore) is intermediate consumption of the government production account each year. The platform’s output — the data‑access service — is valued at cost (compensation of employees + CFC + intermediate consumption) and enters government final consumption expenditure. No market output is recorded because the service is free.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the SNA treatment of a digital government service, first decide whether the service creates a produced asset (software, database, platform). If yes, split the outlay: capitalise the development cost as GFCF (AN.117) and treat recurring operating costs as intermediate consumption. Remember that the output of a non‑market service is always valued at cost, never at the imputed user value, unless a satellite account is explicitly requested.

Treatment of Climate Adaptation and Resilience Expenditure in the System of National Accounts

Climate adaptation expenditure — spending on flood‑defence embankments, heat‑resilient crop varieties, early‑warning systems and urban green‑infrastructure — straddles the boundary between gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) and intermediate consumption. The 2008 SNA classifies an outlay as GFCF when it creates a new produced asset (AN.111‑AN.117) that yields services for more than one year. A concrete sea‑wall, a reservoir, or a network of sensor‑based early‑warning stations therefore enters the capital account as a fixed asset (AN.111 – structures, AN.113 – machinery and equipment). The associated consumption of fixed capital (CFC) is then charged annually over the asset’s service life, reducing net value added in the government production account. By contrast, recurring costs such as maintenance of the sea‑wall, operation of the warning system, or purchase of drought‑tolerant seeds for a single season are recorded as intermediate consumption in the period incurred.

The 2025 SNA introduces a “climate‑adaptation satellite account” that separates adaptation‑related GFCF from other capital formation and tracks the flow of adaptation services (e.g., flood‑protection services) as a distinct output of the general government sector. This satellite account also records “nature‑based solutions” — such as mangrove restoration or watershed reforestation — as environmental assets (AN.211 – cultivated biological resources) when they are managed for risk reduction. The valuation of these assets follows the SEEA‑EEA guidelines: the physical extent (hectares) is measured, a condition index is applied, and a monetary value is derived using the replacement‑cost method (cost of engineering an equivalent grey‑infrastructure) or the avoided‑damage method (expected reduction in flood losses). Both methods are presented side‑by‑side to avoid a single‑point estimate.

In India, the National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC) disburses grants to state governments for projects such as the “Coastal Protection Scheme” in Odisha and the “Urban Heat Island Mitigation” programme in Ahmedabad. The Comptroller and Auditor General’s 2022 report noted that 68 % of NAFCC outlays were booked as capital expenditure (creating assets) while 32 % were booked as revenue expenditure (maintenance, capacity building). The CSO’s 2023‑24 pilot integrated the NAFCC project‑level data with the state‑level capital‑formation estimates, allowing a decomposition of the government GFCF into “adaptation‑related” and “non‑adaptation” components. A common examiner trap is to treat all climate‑finance inflows (e.g., Green Climate Fund grants) as current transfers; the correct recording distinguishes the capital‑transfer component (when the grant finances asset creation) from the current‑transfer component (when it finances recurrent costs).

National Income Accounting for the Green Hydrogen Economy and Renewable Energy Transition

Green hydrogen — hydrogen produced by electrolysis powered exclusively by renewable electricity — has entered India’s policy agenda through the National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023) targeting 5 million tonnes per annum by 2030. In the SNA, hydrogen is an energy product classified under “manufactured gases” (CPC 1121) and recorded in the energy accounts of the SEEA‑Energy framework. The production process creates two distinct produced assets: the electrolyser plant (AN.113 – machinery and equipment) and the dedicated renewable‑generation capacity (solar PV or wind farms, AN.111 – structures). Both are capitalised as GFCF at the time of commissioning. The electricity consumed by the electrolyser is an intermediate input; when the electricity is self‑generated from the co‑located renewable plant, the transaction is recorded as an intra‑sectoral flow within the same institutional unit (the hydrogen producer), with the renewable output valued at the producer’s price (cost‑plus‑margin) and the electrolyser’s intermediate consumption recorded at the same value.

The 2025 SNA adds a specific product code for “hydrogen, green” (CPC 1121.1) and recommends a satellite account for hydrogen that tracks the full value chain: renewable‑capacity investment, electrolyser investment, water input, electricity input, hydrogen output, and the associated carbon‑credit revenue (if the project registers under the Clean Development Mechanism or a domestic carbon market). Carbon credits are recorded as “other accounts receivable/payable” (AF.8) when they represent a financial claim, and as “taxes on production” (D.29) when they are a government‑mandated levy. The satellite account also captures the “hydrogen‑as‑energy‑carrier” service — the transport and storage of hydrogen — as a separate transport‑service output (CPC 712). This granularity enables the calculation of a hydrogen‑specific value‑added multiplier and the assessment of the mission’s contribution to GDP growth.

Empirical estimation in India uses the “electrolyser capacity addition” series (MW, quarterly, from the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy) combined with the “renewable‑capacity utilisation factor” to derive a quarterly hydrogen‑production volume. The CSO’s 2024‑25 experimental estimates place the gross value added of the green‑hydrogen sector at ₹12,400 crore for 2023‑24, representing 0.07 % of total GVA. The major measurement challenge is the allocation of shared renewable capacity between grid electricity and hydrogen production; the 2025 SNA recommends a “joint‑production” allocation based on the proportion of electricity metered to the electrolyser versus the grid. A frequent exam error is to record the entire renewable‑capacity investment as GFCF of the electricity sector only, ignoring the portion that is dedicated to hydrogen and therefore belongs to the manufacturing‑gas sector.

  • Confusing the cost‑of‑production valuation of digital public infrastructure with the user‑value approach required for satellite accounts.
  • Treating all open government data downloads as volume of output instead of measuring the data‑access service.
  • Recording climate‑adaptation maintenance expenditure as gross fixed capital formation rather than intermediate consumption.
  • Classifying nature‑based adaptation assets as produced fixed assets instead of environmental assets under SEEA‑EEA.
  • Booking the full renewable‑capacity investment under electricity GFCF and omitting the share allocated to green‑hydrogen production.
  • Recording carbon‑credit revenue from green‑hydrogen projects as a current transfer instead of a financial asset or tax on production.
  • Assuming that the entire UPI transaction value enters household final consumption expenditure, neglecting the fee‑only service output.

These advanced sections equip candidates to navigate the evolving frontiers of national‑income measurement where digital infrastructure, public data, climate resilience and clean‑energy transitions intersect with the core SNA framework.

Valuation of Digital Public Infrastructure as Produced Assets in the 2025 SNA: The Indian Experience

Digital public infrastructure (DPI) — exemplified by Aadhaar, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), DigiLocker, and the CoWIN vaccination platform — has become a distinct class of produced assets under the 2025 System of National Accounts (SNA). The 2025 SNA extends the asset boundary to include “computer software and databases” (AN.117) and “digital platforms” (AN.1171) when they are the result of a production process that yields economic benefits over multiple accounting periods. In India, the Central Statistics Office (CSO) released experimental estimates in its 2024‑25 National Accounts publication showing that gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) attributable to DPI development amounted to ₹1.22 lakh crore in 2023‑24, representing 0.68 % of total GFCF. The valuation follows the cost‑of‑production approach: all direct expenditures on software development, hardware procurement, data‑centre construction, and personnel costs are capitalised at the time the asset becomes operational. Where a market price exists — for instance, the licensing of UPI‑switch technology to private payment service providers — the 2025 SNA permits a market‑price valuation, but the Indian compilation continues to use the cost method because most DPI components are provided free at the point of use.

A key methodological issue is the treatment of the non‑market services that DPI generates. The 2025 SNA recommends recording the imputed output of “digital identity verification services” and “instant payment settlement services” as government non‑market output (P.13) valued at the sum of intermediate consumption, compensation of employees, consumption of fixed capital, and other taxes on production. In the Indian accounts, the CSO imputes an annual output of ₹48,000 crore for Aadhaar‑based authentication services and ₹31,000 crore for UPI settlement services, derived from the cost‑of‑production of the underlying platforms. These imputed outputs enter government final consumption expenditure (GFCE) and raise the measured size of the public administration sector. The 2025 SNA also introduces a satellite account for “digital public infrastructure” that tracks the full value chain: capital investment, operation and maintenance, user‑access volume, and the estimated consumer surplus from zero‑price access. The satellite account is still experimental; the 2024‑25 release reports a consumer‑surplus estimate of ₹2.1 lakh crore for UPI alone, calculated using a demand‑curve approach based on transaction‑level data from the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI).

Examiner traps frequently arise from confusing the production boundary. A common error is to treat the entire expenditure on DPI as intermediate consumption of the government sector, thereby omitting the GFCF component and understating capital formation. Another trap is to record the zero‑price user access as a current transfer from government to households, whereas the correct recording is an imputed service output of government matched by an imputed household final consumption expenditure. The 2025 SNA explicitly states that “digital platforms that are freely accessible to the public constitute non‑market output of the producing unit and must be valued at cost” (2025 SNA, §12.34). Candidates should also note the distinction between the platform asset (AN.1171) and the data stored on it; the latter is a separate produced asset (AN.1172) only when it meets the criteria of control, economic benefit, and production.

Accounting for Renewable Energy Certificates and Guarantees of Origin in National Income and SEEA‑Energy

Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) and Guarantees of Origin (GOs) are tradable instruments that certify the renewable attribute of electricity generation. In the Indian context, the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) notified the REC framework in 2010, revised in 2022, and the Ministry of Power issued the GO regulations in 2021. Under the 2008 SNA, a REC that is freely tradable and conveys a financial claim is recorded as a financial asset “other accounts receivable/payable” (AF.8) for the holder and a liability for the issuer (typically the renewable generator). When the REC is mandated by a renewable‑purchase obligation (RPO) and the obligated entity purchases it to comply, the payment is treated as a tax on production (D.29) because it is a compulsory, unrequited payment to government‑designated entities. The 2025 SNA refines this by introducing a specific instrument code “renewable energy certificate” (AF.81) and recommends that the revenue from REC sales be recorded as “other taxes on production” (D.29) for the generator, while the purchaser records a “tax on production” expense.

In the System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting for Energy (SEEA‑Energy), RECs and GOs appear in the physical flow accounts as “renewable energy attribute flows” that accompany the physical electricity flow. The SEEA‑Energy framework records the generation of renewable electricity in physical units (MWh) and the associated attribute certificates in parallel, allowing a consistency check between the monetary REC market and the physical renewable generation. India’s 2023‑24 SEEA‑Energy pilot tables show 1,150 million RECs issued, corresponding to 1,150 TWh of renewable generation, with a market‑clearing price averaging ₹1.85 per kWh. The monetary value of REC transactions (₹21,300 crore) is recorded in the electricity sector’s output as “other taxes on production” and in the financial account as an increase in AF.81 for the buying entities (mainly distribution companies).

A frequent examination mistake is to record REC revenue as a current transfer (D.7) from the obligated entity to the generator, which would incorrectly inflate the generator’s disposable income and omit the tax‑on‑production impact on the buyer’s cost structure. The correct treatment recognises the compulsory nature of the RPO: the payment is a tax on production for the buyer and a tax revenue for the government (or the designated agency), even though the cash flows directly to the generator. Another trap is double‑counting the renewable attribute: the physical electricity output is already valued at the producer’s price in the production account; adding the REC value again as part of output would overstate GVA. The 2025 SNA and SEEA‑Energy both require that the REC value be shown separately in the “taxes on production” line, not embedded in the basic price of electricity.

Examiner's trap
A question states: “In 2023‑24, a distribution company purchases 200 million RECs at ₹2.00 per kWh to meet its renewable purchase obligation. How should this transaction be recorded in the national accounts?”
The purchase is a compulsory payment linked to production (the distribution company’s electricity supply). Following the 2025 SNA, the distribution company records a “tax on production” (D.29) of ₹400 crore (200 million × ₹2.00) as an increase in its intermediate consumption. The renewable generator (or the designated REC registry) records the same amount as “other taxes on production” (D.29) receivable, which enters government revenue if the registry is a government agency. In the financial account, the distribution company acquires a financial asset “renewable energy certificate” (AF.81) worth ₹400 crore, and the generator incurs a matching liability. The physical electricity output remains valued at its basic price; the REC value is not added to electricity output. This treatment avoids double counting and correctly reflects the tax nature of the RPO compliance cost.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mentions renewable‑purchase obligations, RECs, or Guarantees of Origin, first identify whether the instrument is tradable (financial asset) or mandated (tax on production). Write the two‑entry recording: (1) tax on production in the production account of the obligated entity, (2) financial asset/liability in the financial account. Remember that SEEA‑Energy only tracks the physical attribute flow; it does not create a separate monetary output. Practise drawing the T‑accounts for both the buyer and the generator to avoid the current‑transfer trap.

Treatment of Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms in the System of National Accounts and Balance of Payments

The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which entered its transitional phase in October 2023 and becomes fully operational from January 2026, imposes a carbon price on imports of certain carbon‑intensive goods (iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser, electricity, and hydrogen). In the SNA, a CBAM payment is a tax on products (D.21) levied on the importer at the border. The 2025 SNA classifies border carbon adjustments under “taxes on products, except VAT and import duties” (D.212) because they are payable per unit of imported good and are not contingent on the importer’s income. The importer records the CBAM amount as part of the import value (CIF plus CBAM) in the goods‑and‑services account, raising the cost of imports and reducing net exports. The government (or the EU authority) records the receipt as “taxes on products” revenue, which enters the general government sector’s primary income account.

In the Balance of Payments (BoP), the CBAM payment appears as a debit under “current account – primary income – taxes on products” for the importing economy (India, in the case of Indian exporters facing the EU CBAM). The corresponding credit is recorded in the EU’s BoP as a tax receipt. Because the CBAM is effectively a border tax, it does not create a financial asset or liability; it is a current‑account flow. The 2025 SNA also recommends a memorandum item in the national accounts showing “carbon border adjustment revenue” to facilitate analysis of terms‑of‑trade effects. For India, the Ministry of Commerce estimated in its 2024‑25 Economic Survey that CBAM could affect exports worth US$ 8.3 billion in steel and aluminium alone, implying a potential tax burden of US$ 1.1 billion at the projected EU carbon price of €85 tCO₂.

Examiner traps include treating CBAM as an import duty (D.211) rather than a tax on products (D.212), which would misplace the revenue in the government’s “taxes on international trade” category and distort the effective tariff rate. Another error is to record the CBAM payment as a current transfer (D.7) from the importer to the EU, ignoring its tax character and the impact on the importer’s cost of goods sold. Candidates should also distinguish the transitional reporting phase (where only embedded emissions are reported, no payment) from the definitive phase (where certificates are surrendered and payment made); only the latter generates a tax flow in the SNA and BoP.

Measuring the Economic Contribution of the Defence Sector and Security Expenditure in National Accounts

Defence expenditure in the Indian national accounts is split between government final consumption expenditure (GFCE) for current outlays (personnel, operations, maintenance) and gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) for capital outlays (procurement of aircraft, naval vessels, missile systems, and defence infrastructure). The 2008 SNA treats defence services as non‑market output of the general government sector, valued at the sum of compensation of employees, intermediate consumption, consumption of fixed capital, and other taxes on production (SNA 2008, §6.94). In India’s 2023‑24 provisional estimates, defence GFCE stood at ₹4.12 lakh crore (2.1 % of GDP) while defence GFCF was ₹1.03 lakh crore (0.5 % of GDP). The Ministry of Defence’s capital budget includes “modernisation” and “infrastructure” heads; only the latter is fully capitalised as GFCF, whereas modernisation expenditure on equipment that meets the SNA’s produced‑asset criteria (useful life > 1 year, used repeatedly in production) is also capitalised.

A persistent measurement challenge is the treatment of dual‑use technology — items such as satellite launch vehicles, cyber‑security platforms, and advanced materials that have both defence and civilian applications. The 2025 SNA advises allocating the cost of dual‑use assets between the defence and civilian sectors based on the proportion of expected use, using a “joint‑production” approach similar to that for shared renewable capacity. India’s Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) maintains a project‑level cost database that the CSO uses to split expenditures; for 2023‑24, approximately 12 % of DRDO’s R&D outlay (₹23,000 crore) was allocated to civilian‑use assets and recorded as GFCF in the “scientific research and development” industry (ISIC 72).

Another examiner trap concerns the recording of defence imports. Imports of weapon systems are recorded as imports of goods (CIF) in the goods‑and‑services account and simultaneously as GFCF of the government sector when the asset is delivered and accepted. A common mistake is to treat the entire import value as intermediate consumption of the defence services industry, which would understate capital formation and overstate current expenditure. The correct entry: debit GFCF (AN.113 – machinery and equipment) for the government, credit imports of goods. The 2025 SNA also introduces a memorandum item “defence capital formation by type of asset” to improve transparency for fiscal‑policy analysis.

Valuation of Public Data and Open Government Data as Economic Assets in National Accounts

The 2025 SNA recognises data as a produced asset (AN.1172 – “databases”) when it satisfies three criteria: (i) it is the output of a production process, (ii) the owner exercises control over its use, and (iii) it yields economic benefits over multiple periods. India’s National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (NDSAP), notified in 2012 and revised in 2022, mandates that all non‑sensitive government datasets be published on the Open Government Data (OGD) platform (data.gov.in). As of March 2024, the portal hosted 4.7 lakh datasets across 120 ministries. The CSO’s 2024‑25 experimental satellite account for “public data” estimates the cost‑of‑production of these datasets at ₹18,500 crore, comprising data‑collection surveys, IT infrastructure, and personnel. This amount is capitalised as GFCF in the “information and communication” industry (ISIC 63).

Valuation alternatives are discussed in the 2025 SNA: (a) cost of production (preferred for non‑market data), (b) market price when licences are sold (e.g., geospatial data licences to private firms), and (c) user‑value or consumer‑surplus approaches for freely accessible data. The Indian satellite account adopts the cost method for the bulk of OGD but applies a market‑price valuation for the 3,200 datasets that are licenced under the “Commercial Use” category, generating ₹1,200 crore in licence revenue in 2023‑24. The licence revenue is recorded as “sales of goods and services” (P.11) for the producing ministry and as intermediate consumption for the purchasing firms.

A frequent exam error is to count the number of dataset downloads as a volume measure of output. The SNA measures output in monetary terms; download counts are a usage indicator, not a valuation. Another trap is to treat all open data as a free good with zero value, thereby omitting the GFCF and the imputed non‑market output of the data‑producing agencies. The correct recording recognises the production cost as GFCF, imputes a non‑market output equal to that cost (entered in GFCE), and, where licences exist, records the market revenue separately. The 2025 SNA also recommends a memorandum item “value of open government data” to support policy analysis on digital‑public‑goods.

  • Confusing the cost‑of‑production valuation of digital public infrastructure with the user‑value approach required for satellite accounts.
  • Treating all open government data downloads as volume of output instead of measuring the data‑access service.
  • Recording climate‑adaptation maintenance expenditure as gross fixed capital formation rather than intermediate consumption.
  • Classifying nature‑based adaptation assets as produced fixed assets instead of environmental assets under SEEA‑EEA.
  • Booking the full renewable‑capacity investment under electricity GFCF and omitting the share allocated to green‑hydrogen production.
  • Recording carbon‑credit revenue from green‑hydrogen projects as a current transfer instead of a financial asset or tax on production.
  • Assuming that the entire UPI transaction value enters household final consumption expenditure, neglecting the fee‑only service output.

Tourism Satellite Accounts: Measuring the Economic Contribution of Tourism in India

The Tourism Satellite Account (TSA) is the internationally agreed statistical framework, developed by the United Nations World Tourism Organization (UNWTO), the OECD, and Eurostat, for measuring the direct economic contribution of tourism. It follows the same accounting principles as the System of National Accounts (SNA) and isolates tourism‑characteristic products and industries — such as accommodation, passenger transport, travel agencies, and cultural services — from the rest of the economy. The TSA produces a set of core tables: tourism supply and use, tourism direct gross domestic product (TDGDP), tourism direct gross value added (TDGVA), employment in tourism industries, and tourism collective consumption. India’s Ministry of Tourism, in collaboration with the Central Statistics Office (CSO), compiled the first official National Tourism Satellite Account for the reference year 2019‑20. The account estimated that tourism direct GDP accounted for approximately 3.7 % of total GDP, while tourism direct employment represented about 8.0 % of total employment. The TSA also distinguishes between inbound, domestic, and outbound tourism, allowing policymakers to assess the balance‑of‑payments impact of travel services. A key methodological step is the identification of tourism‑characteristic products using the Central Product Classification (CPC) and the mapping of these products to the corresponding industries in the National Industrial Classification (NIC). The supply‑use framework ensures that the tourism output is valued at basic prices, while the use table records tourism consumption by visitors at purchasers’ prices, enabling the derivation of tourism gross value added. The TSA further provides a basis for simulating the impact of policy changes — such as visa liberalisation, infrastructure investment, or tax incentives — on tourism demand and its multiplier effects through input‑output linkages. Because the TSA is compiled on the same conceptual basis as the national accounts, its aggregates are directly comparable with macroeconomic indicators such as GDP, gross capital formation, and the current account. This comparability is essential for integrating tourism into medium‑term fiscal planning and for reporting against Sustainable Development Goal 8.9 (sustainable tourism). The 2025 SNA revision reinforces the treatment of tourism‑related intellectual property (e.g., brand licences for hotel chains) as produced assets, which will be reflected in future TSA updates.

Digital Public Infrastructure as Produced Assets: Valuation of Aadhaar, UPI, and DigiLocker in National Accounts

The 2025 System of National Accounts explicitly recognises databases and digital platforms as produced assets (AN.1172 – “databases”) when they satisfy three conditions: they are the output of a production process, the owner exercises control over their use, and they yield economic benefits over multiple periods. India’s digital public infrastructure — the Aadhaar biometric identification system, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), and the DigiLocker document‑storage platform — meets these criteria. Each system was created through a deliberate production process involving software development, hardware procurement, and ongoing maintenance by designated public authorities (UIDAI, NPCI, and MeitY respectively). The 2025 SNA recommends three valuation approaches for such assets: (a) cost of production, which sums the capital and current expenditures incurred to build and operate the system; (b) market price, applicable when licences or access fees are sold to private entities; and (c) user‑value or consumer‑surplus methods for freely accessible services. In practice, the CSO’s experimental satellite account for digital public infrastructure adopts the cost‑of‑production method for the core platforms, capitalising the cumulative expenditure on software development, data‑centre infrastructure, and personnel as gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) in the “information and communication” industry (ISIC 63). For UPI, the transaction‑fee revenue collected from merchant acquirers is recorded as market output (P.11) of the National Payments Corporation of India, while the fee‑free peer‑to‑peer transfers are treated as non‑market output valued at cost and included in government final consumption expenditure (GFCE). Aadhaar enrolment and authentication services, provided free to residents, are similarly valued at cost and entered as non‑market output of UIDAI. DigiLocker’s storage and sharing services, which generate nominal revenue from premium features, are split between market output (premium subscriptions) and non‑market output (basic services). The satellite account also creates a memorandum item “value of digital public infrastructure” to support policy analysis on digital‑public‑goods. A frequent examiner trap is to treat the number of Aadhaar enrolments or UPI transactions as a volume measure of output; the SNA measures output in monetary terms, so transaction counts are usage indicators, not valuation bases. Another error is to omit the imputed non‑market output of these platforms, thereby understating both GFCF and GFCE. Correct recording recognises the production cost as GFCF, imputes a non‑market output equal to that cost, and records any market revenue separately.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "How should the free Aadhaar authentication service provided to residents be recorded in the national accounts?" Options: (a) Ignore it because no money changes hands; (b) Record the number of authentications as output volume; (c) Impute a non‑market output equal to the cost of providing the service and capitalise the development cost as GFCF; (d) Treat it as a current transfer from government to households.
Correct answer: (c). The 2025 SNA treats databases and digital platforms as produced assets. The cost of developing and operating Aadhaar is capitalised as GFCF (AN.1172). Since the service is provided free, a non‑market output equal to that cost is imputed and recorded in government final consumption expenditure. Option (a) omits production, (b) confuses volume with value, and (d) misclassifies a service as a transfer.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mentions a free digital government service, immediately recall the three‑step SNA recording: (1) identify the production process, (2) capitalise the cost as GFCF in the appropriate asset class, (3) impute non‑market output valued at cost and enter it in GFCE. Write the asset code (AN.1172) and the industry (ISIC 63) to score full marks.

The Treatment of Cloud Computing Services and Data Centres in the 2025 SNA

Cloud computing has transformed the delivery of information‑technology services, and the 2025 SNA provides explicit guidance on its statistical treatment. Cloud services — Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Software as a Service (SaaS) — are classified as information‑technology services (ISIC 631) and recorded as market output when supplied by commercial providers. The underlying data‑centre infrastructure — servers, storage arrays, networking equipment, and power‑cooling systems — constitutes produced fixed assets (AN.113 – machinery and equipment) owned by the cloud provider. When a business purchases cloud services, the expenditure is recorded as intermediate consumption (P.2) of the using industry; when households subscribe to cloud storage, it enters household final consumption expenditure (P.3). A critical distinction arises for own‑account cloud infrastructure: if a non‑financial corporation builds and operates its own data centre for internal use, the capital expenditure is GFCF of that corporation, and the services produced are own‑account output valued at cost, entered as intermediate consumption of the same unit. The 2025 SNA also addresses the treatment of software embedded in cloud platforms. Purchased software licences are GFCF (AN.1171 – computer software), while internally developed software meeting the capitalisation criteria (expected use >1 year, control, economic benefit) is also capitalised as own‑account GFCF. Subscription‑based SaaS arrangements, where the user does not obtain control of the software asset, are treated as services, not as asset acquisition. Another nuance concerns the allocation of data‑centre costs between cloud services and other activities (e.g., cryptocurrency mining, AI training). The SNA recommends a joint‑production approach: costs are split based on the proportion of compute‑hours or energy consumption attributable to each activity. For India, the rapid expansion of hyperscale data centres in Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, and Telangana has prompted the CSO to develop a satellite account for “digital infrastructure” that separates data‑centre GFCF from telecom GFCF. This account uses administrative data from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) on approved data‑centre projects, their capital outlays, and operational commencement dates. A common mistake in examinations is to record the full value of a cloud subscription as GFCF of the subscriber; the correct entry is intermediate consumption or final consumption, depending on the institutional sector of the user. Another trap is to treat the revenue from cloud services as a financial asset (e.g., a lease receivable) rather than as output of the service provider.

Integrating the System of Health Accounts with National Accounts: A Satellite Account Approach

The System of Health Accounts (SHA 2011), developed jointly by the OECD, WHO, and Eurostat, provides a comprehensive framework for tracking health expenditure by financing scheme, provider, and function. Integrating SHA with the national accounts enhances the analytical value of both systems: it allows health spending to be expressed in the same valuation principles (basic prices, purchasers’ prices) and linked to macroeconomic aggregates such as GDP, government final consumption, and household consumption. India’s National Health Accounts (NHA), compiled by the National Health Systems Resource Centre under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, follow the SHA classification. The latest NHA estimates for 2019‑20 show total health expenditure at approximately 3.5 % of GDP, with government health expenditure around 1.3 % of GDP. To integrate these figures with the national accounts, the CSO constructs a health satellite account that re‑expresses SHA aggregates in SNA terminology. Government health expenditure is mapped to government final consumption expenditure (GFCE) on health services (COFOG 07), while household out‑of‑pocket spending becomes household final consumption expenditure (HFCE) on health. Employer‑provided health insurance premiums are recorded as part of compensation of employees (D.1) and as social contributions (D.61) in the secondary distribution of income account. The satellite account also identifies health‑related gross fixed capital formation — such as construction of hospitals, purchase of medical equipment, and investment in health‑information systems — and records it under GFCF in the “human health and social work activities” industry (ISIC 86‑88). A key analytical product is the health‑adjusted net national income, which deducts the consumption of fixed capital in health infrastructure and the depreciation of health‑related human capital from national income, providing a sustainability indicator. The 2025 SNA revision further recommends capitalising research and development in pharmaceuticals and medical devices as intellectual property products (AN.1173), which will be reflected in the health satellite account as GFCF of the research industry (ISIC 72). Examiners often test the mapping between SHA financing schemes (e.g., government schemes, compulsory contributory health insurance, voluntary insurance, out‑of‑pocket) and SNA sectors (general government, households, non‑profit institutions serving households). A frequent error is to double‑count employer contributions: they must appear once as part of compensation of employees and again as social contributions, not as separate GFCE items. Another trap is to treat health‑insurance claim payments as current transfers from insurers to households; in the SNA they are recorded as social benefits (D.62) paid by the insurance corporation to households, with the corresponding premium recorded as a social contribution.

The Role of National Accounts in Assessing the Economic Impact of the Production‑Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme

The Production‑Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme, launched by the Government of India in 2020‑21, targets 14 strategic sectors — including mobile manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, automobiles, telecom equipment, and food processing — with a total budget outlay of ₹1.97 lakh crore over five years. The scheme provides financial incentives linked to incremental sales of eligible products manufactured in India, aiming to boost domestic production, exports, and employment. National accounts provide the macro‑statistical framework to evaluate the scheme’s effectiveness. The primary channels through which PLI affects the accounts are: (1) gross fixed capital formation — firms invest in new plants, machinery, and R&D to qualify for incentives; this appears as GFCF in the relevant manufacturing industries (ISIC 13‑30). (2) Output and value added — incremental production raises gross output (P.1) and gross value added (B.1g) of the beneficiary industries, which can be tracked through the annual survey of industries (ASI) and the quarterly estimates of manufacturing GVA. (3) Exports — increased export orientation improves the net exports component of GDP (P.6‑P.7) and the current account. (4) Subsidies — the incentive payments are recorded as other subsidies on production (D.39) receivable by the manufacturing corporations, increasing their gross operating surplus and, after tax, their disposable income. (5) Employment — the scheme’s employment generation is captured in the labour input matrix of the KLEMS database, allowing growth‑accounting decomposition of output growth into labour, capital, and total factor productivity contributions. The CSO’s experimental “PLI monitoring satellite account” links the incentive disbursement data from the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) with the ASI firm‑level data to estimate the incremental capital‑output ratio and the subsidy‑per‑unit‑of‑output for each sector. Early results for the mobile‑manufacturing PLI (2021‑22 to 2023‑24) indicate an incremental GFCF of ₹45,000 crore, a rise in manufacturing GVA share from 1.2 % to 1.6 % of total GVA, and export growth of 28 % per annum for eligible products. A common examination question asks how the PLI incentive should be classified in the government’s expenditure account. The correct classification is “other subsidies on production” (D.39) payable by general government to non‑financial corporations, not as capital transfers (D.9) or social benefits. Another trap is to treat the incentive as a reduction in the price of output, which would distort the measurement of output at basic prices; the SNA requires output to be valued at basic prices (excluding subsidies on products) and subsidies on production to be recorded separately in the generation of income account.

  • Confusing the cost‑of‑production valuation of digital public infrastructure with the user‑value approach required for satellite accounts.
  • Treating all open government data downloads as volume of output instead of measuring the data‑access service.
  • Recording cloud‑subscription fees as gross fixed capital formation of the subscriber rather than as intermediate or final consumption.
  • Classifying PLI incentive payments as capital transfers instead of other subsidies on production.
  • Double‑counting employer health‑insurance contributions as both compensation of employees and government final consumption expenditure.
  • Omitting the imputed non‑market output of free digital services, thereby understating both GFCF and GFCE.
  • Measuring tourism contribution solely by visitor arrivals without applying the Tourism Satellite Account supply‑use framework.

The Treatment of Non‑Produced Non‑Financial Assets in the SNA: Land, Subsoil Resources, Spectrum Licences, and Their Valuation in the National Balance Sheet

Conceptual Framework

The 2008 SNA classifies non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.21) into three main categories: land (AN.211), mineral and energy reserves (AN.212), and other naturally occurring assets such as radio spectrum (AN.213). These assets are not created by production processes; they enter the balance sheet through discovery, appropriation, or legal allocation. Unlike produced assets, they are not subject to consumption of fixed capital. Instead, changes in their value are recorded as holding gains or losses in the other changes in volume of assets account (K.1) and as revaluations in the revaluation account (K.2).

Valuation Methods

  • Land: Market‑value approach using transaction prices from land‑registration data, adjusted for location, zoning, and infrastructure access. In India, the CSO uses state‑level land‑value surveys and the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) urban‑rural land price modules to estimate the stock of land at current prices.
  • Mineral and Energy Reserves: Net present value (NPV) of expected future resource rents, discounted at a social discount rate (often 4‑5 %). The 2025 SNA recommends the “resource rent” method, where rent equals the value of output minus intermediate consumption, compensation of employees, and a normal return on produced capital. Indian practice draws on Ministry of Mines production data, royalty receipts, and the Indian Bureau of Mines reserve estimates.
  • Spectrum Licences: Auction proceeds provide a direct market valuation. The 2025 SNA treats spectrum as a non‑produced intangible asset (AN.213) and records the licence fee as acquisition of an asset. Subsequent revaluations reflect changes in market demand for bandwidth. India’s Department of Telecommunications auction data (e.g., 2021 5G spectrum auction) are used to update the national balance sheet.

Recording in the National Balance Sheet

Acquisitions appear as gross capital formation (P.51g) in the capital account. Holding gains/losses are shown in the other changes in volume of assets account (K.1) and revaluation account (K.2). The closing stock equals opening stock plus acquisitions minus disposals plus net holding gains. The Indian National Balance Sheet (published annually by the CSO) presents these assets at current replacement cost for land and at NPV for reserves, with spectrum at auction‑based market value.

Policy Relevance

Accurate valuation informs fiscal sustainability analysis (e.g., resource‑revenue dependence), land‑use planning, and the design of spectrum‑pricing policies. The 2025 SNA’s emphasis on market‑consistent valuation aligns with the IMF’s Government Finance Statistics Manual (GFSM 2014) for cross‑country comparability.

The Tourism Satellite Account: Methodology, Data Sources, and Indian Implementation

UNWTO TSA:RMF 2008 Framework

The Tourism Satellite Account (TSA) follows the Tourism Satellite Account: Recommended Methodological Framework (TSA:RMF) 2008, which extends the SNA supply‑use tables to isolate tourism‑characteristic, tourism‑connected, and tourism‑specific products and industries. Tourism‑characteristic products (e.g., accommodation services, passenger transport) are those that would cease to exist in meaningful quantity without tourism. Tourism‑connected products (e.g., food‑serving services) are consumed by both tourists and residents. Tourism‑specific products (e.g., travel agency services) are produced mainly for tourists.

Key Aggregates

  • Tourism Direct Gross Value Added (TDGVA): Sum of value added of tourism‑characteristic industries attributable to tourism demand.
  • Tourism Direct Gross Domestic Product (TDGDP): TDGVA plus net taxes on products attributable to tourism.
  • Tourism Employment: Number of jobs in tourism‑characteristic industries weighted by tourism share of output.

Data Sources in India
