The 2025 SNA introduces a “renewable‑energy” tag on the asset classification (AN.1131) and a “green‑subsidy” tag on the subsidy classification, allowing compilers to isolate RE‑related GFCF and product subsidies in the supply‑use tables. Empirically, the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) reports that global RE capacity additions reached 340 GW in 2023, with capital expenditure of USD 620 billion. In India, the Central Electricity Authority (CEA) data show installed RE capacity of 180 GW (including large hydro) as of March 2024, with annual generation of 350 TWh. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) administers the Production‑Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for solar PV modules, which is recorded as a subsidy on production (D.39) because it reduces the cost of producing the modules, not the price of electricity. The PLI outlay of ₹24 000 crore over five years appears in the government’s expenditure account and, via the supply‑use framework, reduces the intermediate consumption of the manufacturing industry, raising its gross value added. A further nuance is the treatment of “capacity payments” in power‑purchase agreements (PPAs) that guarantee a fixed payment irrespective of actual generation; these are recorded as rent on produced assets (D.42) if they reflect the use of the generation capacity, or as subsidies on products if they top up the energy price. The SEEA‑Energy physical flow accounts complement the monetary accounts by recording installed capacity (MW), actual generation (GWh), and capacity factor, enabling analysts to compute “energy‑adjusted productivity” — value added per unit of generated electricity — and to assess the efficiency of subsidy allocation across technologies.

The Role of National Accounts in Assessing the Economic Impact of Trade Policy Shocks: Tariff Changes, Terms‑of‑Trade, and Real Income

Trade policy shocks — such as a sudden tariff hike, a quota removal, or a preferential‑trade‑agreement (PTA) implementation — affect national income through three main channels captured in the SNA: (i) changes in the price of imported and exported goods (terms‑of‑trade effect), (ii) reallocation of resources across industries (structural effect), and (iii) fiscal revenue changes from customs duties (government revenue effect). The SNA’s goods‑and‑services account records imports and exports at purchaser prices (including tariffs) and basic prices (excluding tariffs), respectively. A tariff increase raises the purchaser price of imports, increasing the value of imports at market prices while leaving the basic‑price import volume unchanged; the difference appears as a tax on products (D.21) in the generation of income account, boosting government revenue. The terms‑of‑trade index (export price index ÷ import price index) moves inversely to the tariff‑induced import price rise, reducing real gross domestic income (RGDI) relative to real GDP. The 2025 SNA recommends compiling a “trade‑policy satellite account” that links the detailed HS‑code tariff schedule to the supply‑use tables, enabling a decomposition of the RGDI change into a pure price effect (terms‑of‑trade) and a volume effect (changes in import/export quantities). Empirical work using the World Input‑Output Database (WIOD) shows that the 2018‑19 US‑China tariff escalation reduced China’s RGDI by 0.4 % while real GDP fell by only 0.1 %, the gap reflecting the terms‑of‑trade deterioration. In India, the 2020‑21 increase in customs duties on electronic components (from 0 % to 10‑15 %) can be traced through the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) and the Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics (DGCI&S) trade data to quantify the rise in intermediate consumption costs for the electronics manufacturing industry, the resulting fall in its gross value added, and the offsetting rise in customs revenue (≈ ₹12 000 crore). The satellite account also captures “tariff‑induced substitution” by tracking shifts in the input‑output coefficients — firms may replace imported inputs with domestic alternatives, altering the Leontief inverse and the multiplier structure. For policy analysis, the SNA framework permits simulation of counterfactual tariff scenarios by adjusting the tax‑on‑products vector in the supply‑use model and recomputing the equilibrium output, value added, and RGDI, providing a consistent macro‑micro link that pure partial‑equilibrium trade models lack.

Integrating the System of National Accounts with the System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting for Air Emissions: Physical Flow Accounts and Monetary Valuation

Air emissions — carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O), and local pollutants such as sulphur dioxide (SO₂) and particulate matter (PM₂.₅) — are recorded in the SEEA‑Air Emissions Accounts (SEEA‑AEA) as physical flows from economic activities to the environment. The integration with the SNA occurs through the “environmentally extended input‑output” (EE‑IO) framework, where the SNA’s supply‑use tables are augmented with emission coefficients (kg per unit of output) for each industry. The SEEA‑AEA follows the same industry classification (ISIC Rev.4) and the same residence principle as the SNA, ensuring that emissions from resident units operating abroad (e.g., Indian shipping lines) are attributed to the Indian economy, while emissions from foreign‑owned firms in India are excluded. Monetary valuation of air emissions is not part of the core SNA but is encouraged in the SEEA‑AEA through “damage cost” or “abatement cost” approaches. The damage‑cost method applies marginal social cost estimates (e.g., USD 50 / tCO₂ for carbon, USD 10 000 / tPM₂.₅ for health impacts) to the physical emission totals, producing an “environmental degradation cost” that can be subtracted from net domestic product to obtain an “environmentally adjusted NDP”. The abatement‑cost method uses the actual expenditure on emission‑reduction technologies (scrubbers, selective catalytic reduction, carbon capture) recorded as GFCF or intermediate consumption in the SNA, providing a lower‑bound valuation. The 2025 SNA introduces an “emission‑type” tag on the asset classification (AN.115) for capital goods whose primary purpose is emission abatement, allowing a direct link between abatement investment and the physical emission reduction recorded in the SEEA‑AEA. In India, the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) compiles the National Air Quality Monitoring Programme (NAMP) data, which MoSPI maps to the ASI industry codes to produce a pilot EE‑IO table for 2019‑20. The table shows that the “electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply” industry (ISIC 35) accounted for 45 % of CO₂ emissions while contributing 8 % of gross value added, yielding an emission intensity of 0.85 kg CO₂ per rupee of GVA. The “manufacture of basic metals” (ISIC 24) had the highest PM₂.₅ intensity. Policy applications include the design of a carbon‑price floor: by inserting a carbon tax (D.21) into the SNA’s tax‑on‑products vector, the supply‑use model can simulate the resulting shift in relative prices, output reallocation, and the change in RGDI, while the SEEA‑AEA simultaneously tracks the physical emission reduction. This integrated accounting ensures that the economic cost of air pollution and the fiscal implications of mitigation policies are evaluated within a single, consistent macroeconomic framework.

  • Confusing subsidies on products (which affect output at basic prices) with subsidies on production (which affect generation of income) when analysing renewable‑energy support schemes.
  • Treating all climate‑adaptation spending as capital formation; recurring operation and maintenance costs must remain current expenditure.
  • Neglecting the “data‑type” and “climate‑adaptation” tags introduced in the 2025 SNA; without them, satellite accounts cannot isolate the relevant assets or expenditures.
  • Assuming tariff revenue changes automatically translate into higher real income; the terms‑of‑trade effect on RGDI often offsets the fiscal gain.
  • Using a single emission‑valuation method (damage cost or abatement cost) without stating the underlying assumptions; the two approaches can diverge by an order of magnitude.
  • Overlooking the residence principle in air‑emission accounts, leading to double‑counting of emissions from international transport or foreign‑owned domestic plants.
  • Failing to link the EE‑IO table back to the SNA’s supply‑use framework, which breaks the consistency between physical emission flows and monetary value added.

These advanced sections equip the aspirant with the conceptual tools to navigate the evolving frontiers of national income accounting, from data valuation and climate‑adaptation tagging to renewable‑energy subsidy mechanics, trade‑policy shock decomposition, and air‑emission integration.

Measuring the Economic Value of Digital Public Infrastructure in National Accounts

Digital public infrastructure (DPI) — identity layers such as Aadhaar, payment rails such as Unified Payments Interface (UPI), and data‑exchange platforms such as DigiLocker — has become a distinct production factor that lowers transaction costs across the economy. The 2025 System of National Accounts (SNA) treats DPI as a produced non‑financial asset (AN.117) when it satisfies the criteria of control, economic benefit, and a measurable service life. Capital formation is recorded at the cost of development, deployment, and subsequent upgrades, while the flow of services is captured as output of the “information and communication” industry (ISIC 61) at basic prices. Because DPI services are often provided at zero or nominal price to users, the SNA recommends a cost‑based valuation for the output of the producing unit (usually a government agency or a public‑private partnership) and an imputed user‑cost for the consuming units, consistent with the treatment of other non‑market services. The imputed user‑cost equals the sum of consumption of fixed capital, a return to capital (based on the government borrowing rate), and any intermediate consumption required to operate the platform. This approach preserves the production boundary while allowing the contribution of DPI to be reflected in gross value added (GVA) and, through the input‑output framework, in the GVA of downstream industries such as e‑commerce, fintech, and digital logistics. In India, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) has piloted a satellite account for DPI that links the capital stock of Aadhaar and UPI to the observed reduction in payment‑processing time and the increase in financial‑inclusion indicators from the Periodic Labour Force Survey. The satellite account uses a “digital‑access” multiplier derived from a computable general equilibrium (CGE) model to translate the stock of DPI into an estimate of additional real GDP. A key methodological challenge is avoiding double counting: the same transaction that runs on UPI is already recorded in the output of the merchant and the payment‑service provider. The SNA resolves this by recording UPI’s output only once — as a financial‑service fee (explicit or imputed) — and treating the merchant’s sales as unchanged. Examiners often test the distinction between the capitalisation of DPI development costs (which raises GFCF) and the imputation of user‑costs (which raises intermediate consumption of users), and the impact of each on the GDP deflator versus the consumer price index.

Treatment of Carbon Credits and Emission Trading Schemes in the System of National Accounts

Carbon credits, certified emission reductions (CERs), and allowances allocated under cap‑and‑trade schemes such as the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU‑ETS) or India’s Perform‑Achieve‑Trade (PAT) mechanism are financial assets that embody a right to emit a specified quantity of greenhouse gases. Under the 2008 SNA, these instruments are classified as “other accounts receivable/payable” (AF.8) when they are tradable and have a market price, and as “other equity” (AF.5) when they represent a residual claim on a collective emission budget. The 2025 SNA introduces a dedicated “emission‑allowance” asset class (AN.1151) to improve transparency and to link the financial account directly to the physical flow accounts of the SEEA‑Air Emissions. When a government allocates allowances for free, the transaction is recorded as a capital transfer (D.9) from the government to the recipient enterprise, increasing the enterprise’s net worth and the government’s net lending/borrowing. Subsequent trades are recorded as financial transactions (F.5) at market value, with any holding gains or losses recognised in the revaluation account. The surrender of allowances to cover verified emissions is a non‑financial transaction: the enterprise records a reduction in the allowance asset and an increase in “environmental degradation cost” (a memorandum item) while the government records a reduction in its liability for the emission budget. If the allowance price exceeds the marginal abatement cost, the enterprise realises a holding gain; if it is lower, a loss. The SNA requires that the valuation of allowances be consistent with the market price at the reporting date, and that any government auction revenue be recorded as tax revenue (D.2) rather than as a sale of assets. A common examiner trap is to treat the free allocation as a subsidy on production (D.3) rather than a capital transfer, which would incorrectly affect gross operating surplus. Another trap is to record the surrender of allowances as intermediate consumption, whereas the correct treatment is a reduction in the asset stock with a memorandum entry for the environmental cost. The integration with SEEA‑Air Emissions ensures that the physical emission reduction achieved by the scheme can be cross‑checked against the change in the allowance stock, providing a coherent picture for policy analysis of carbon‑price effectiveness.

Worked Example: Recording a Free Allocation and Subsequent Trade of PAT Allowances
A steel plant receives 100,000 PAT allowances free of charge at the start of the compliance period. The market price of an allowance at that date is ₹1,200. Mid‑period the plant sells 20,000 allowances at ₹1,350 each. At the end of the period it surrenders 80,000 allowances to cover verified emissions. Show the SNA entries for the plant and the government.
Plant (enterprise):
1. Free allocation: Debit AN.1151 (Emission allowances) ₹120 crore; Credit D.9 (Capital transfer receivable) ₹120 crore.
2. Sale of 20,000 allowances: Debit AF.2 (Currency and deposits) ₹27 crore; Credit AN.1151 ₹24 crore; Credit Holding gain (revaluation) ₹3 crore.
3. Surrender of 80,000 allowances: Debit Environmental degradation cost (memorandum) ₹96 crore; Credit AN.1151 ₹96 crore.
Government:
1. Allocation: Debit D.9 (Capital transfer payable) ₹120 crore; Credit AN.1151 (Emission allowances liability) ₹120 crore.
2. No entry for the secondary market trade (between private parties).
3. Surrender: Debit AN.1151 (Liability) ₹96 crore; Credit Environmental degradation cost (memorandum) ₹96 crore.
Net effect: Plant’s net worth rises by ₹3 crore (holding gain); government net lending unchanged except for the initial capital transfer.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the SNA treatment of emission allowances, first identify whether the allowance is allocated free, auctioned, or traded. Write the three‑step sequence: (i) initial recognition (capital transfer or tax revenue), (ii) subsequent market trades (financial transaction with holding gain/loss), (iii) surrender (asset reduction + memorandum environmental cost). Remember the 2025 SNA asset code AN.1151 and the distinction between D.9 and D.2. A quick mental checklist — free allocation = D.9, auction = D.2, trade = F.5, surrender = asset write‑down + memo — prevents the common mis‑classification as subsidy or intermediate consumption.

Integrating Household Survey Data with National Accounts for Distributional Analysis

Distributional National Accounts (DNA) aim to break down aggregate macro‑variables — GDP, national income, savings — by household income, wealth, or consumption deciles. The core methodological step is the construction of a micro‑macro linkage table that aligns the concepts and classifications of the household survey (e.g., the Consumer Expenditure Survey, the Periodic Labour Force Survey, or the All‑India Debt and Investment Survey) with the SNA’s institutional sector accounts (S.14 households, S.15 NPISH). The linkage proceeds in three stages: (1) concept harmonisation — survey income components (wages, self‑employment income, property income, transfers) are mapped to the SNA’s primary distribution of income accounts (B.2g, B.3g, D.4, D.6); (2) scaling — survey aggregates are calibrated to match the national accounts totals using a ratio‑adjustment or a more sophisticated entropy‑based method (e.g., the GRASP algorithm) that preserves the survey’s distributional shape while enforcing macro consistency; (3) imputation of missing items — items absent from the survey (imputed rent, employer social contributions, retained earnings of quasi‑corporations) are imputed using administrative tax data, corporate financial statements, or model‑based estimates. The 2025 SNA encourages the production of “distributional tables” as a standard supplement, and the OECD’s Expert Group on DNA has issued a template that includes breakdowns by age, gender, and region. In India, MoSPI’s pilot DNA for 2017‑18 combined the NSSO’s Consumer Expenditure Survey with the Annual Survey of Industries and the Income Tax Department’s PAN‑linked data to produce decile‑level shares of gross national income. The results showed that the top decile captured 30 % of GNI while the bottom decile received 3 %, a disparity that is narrower than the raw survey suggests after scaling to macro totals. A frequent examiner twist is to ask how the “statistical discrepancy” between the production and expenditure approaches affects distributional estimates; the correct answer is that the discrepancy is allocated proportionally across households in the scaling step, but a sensitivity analysis should be reported. Another trap is to confuse the DNA’s “primary income” distribution with the “disposable income” distribution — the latter requires adding net current transfers (social benefits, taxes) which are often under‑reported in surveys and must be supplemented with administrative data.

Accounting for the Economic Impact of Production‑Linked Incentive Schemes

Production‑Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes — such as those for mobile manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, and advanced chemistry cells — are government programmes that provide financial incentives conditional on incremental production or investment. In the SNA, the incentive payment is a subsidy on production (D.31) when it is linked to output volume, and a subsidy on products (D.311) when it is linked to specific goods sold. The distinction matters because subsidies on products reduce the basic price of output and therefore affect the output deflator, whereas subsidies on production reduce the cost of production and are recorded in the generation of income account as a negative use of “other subsidies on production”. The 2025 SNA adds a “policy‑type” tag to the subsidy classification, allowing satellite accounts to isolate PLI‑related subsidies from other support measures. Capital expenditure induced by the scheme (new plant, machinery) is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) of the beneficiary enterprise, financed partly by the subsidy (a capital transfer D.9 if the incentive is paid upfront for investment) and partly by own funds or borrowing. The incremental output generated is captured in the production account of the relevant industry, and the input‑output framework transmits the demand shock to upstream sectors (e.g., electronic components, chemicals). A key analytical tool is the “PLI multiplier” derived from the Leontief inverse of the supply‑use table, which quantifies the total GVA increase per rupee of incentive. In India, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry’s evaluation of the mobile‑manufacturing PLI used a dynamic CGE model calibrated to the 2019‑20 supply‑use table, estimating a multiplier of 2.3 for GVA and 1.8 for employment over a five‑year horizon. Examiners often test the correct recording of a PLI payment that is partly a reimbursement of capital expenditure and partly a per‑unit production bonus: the capital‑reimbursement portion is a capital transfer (D.9) increasing the enterprise’s net worth, while the per‑unit bonus is a subsidy on products (D.311) reducing the basic price. Misclassifying the entire payment as a subsidy on production inflates gross operating surplus and distorts the sectoral profit share.

The Role of National Accounts in Assessing Trade Facilitation Measures

Trade facilitation measures — such as the implementation of the World Trade Organization’s Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA), digitisation of customs clearance (e.g., India’s ICEGATE), and the development of logistics infrastructure (dedicated freight corridors, inland container depots) — affect national income through three channels captured in the SNA: (1) reduction in trade‑transaction costs, which lowers the intermediate consumption of “transport and storage” (ISIC 49‑52) and “customs and border services” (ISIC 84) for importing and exporting firms, thereby raising their gross value added; (2) expansion of export volumes, recorded as an increase in exports of goods and services (P.6) and, via the supply‑use table, an increase in output of export‑oriented industries; (3) improvement in terms of trade if the measure reduces the price of imported inputs relative to export prices, which is reflected in real gross domestic income (RGDI) through the trading‑gain term. The SNA’s “trade‑in‑value‑added” (TiVA) framework, integrated with the Inter‑Country Input‑Output (ICIO) tables, allows the decomposition of the gross export increase into domestic value added (DVA) and foreign value added (FVA), revealing how much of the facilitation‑induced export growth accrues to the domestic economy. In practice, the statistical office constructs a “trade‑cost” satellite account that assigns ad‑valorem equivalents to customs delays, documentation requirements, and border inspections, using data from the World Bank’s Logistics Performance Index and firm‑level surveys. These ad‑valorem equivalents are then introduced as a shock to the input‑output model to simulate the counterfactual GDP path without the facilitation measure. A common examiner trap is to attribute the entire increase in export value to GDP growth, ignoring the import content of exports; the correct approach is to use the DVA share from TiVA. Another trap is to treat the reduction in customs duty revenue as a loss of government income without recognising that the duty is a tax on products (D.21) whose removal raises real income via the terms‑of‑trade effect captured in RGDI. The 2025 SNA’s “trade‑facilitation” tag on the tax‑on‑products classification (D.21) enables the automatic isolation of such revenue changes in fiscal‑policy simulations.

  • Confusing subsidies on products (D.311) with subsidies on production (D.31) when analysing PLI incentives.
  • Recording free emission‑allowance allocations as subsidies on production instead of capital transfers (D.9).
  • Treating the surrender of allowances as intermediate consumption rather than an asset write‑down with a memorandum environmental cost.
  • Using raw household survey aggregates without scaling to national accounts totals, leading to inconsistent distributional shares.
  • Attributing the full rise in export value to domestic GDP without subtracting foreign value added from TiVA.
  • Ignoring the “policy‑type” and “trade‑facilitation” tags introduced in the 2025 SNA, which are essential for satellite‑account isolation.
  • Overlooking the distinction between RGDI and real GDP when evaluating terms‑of‑trade effects of trade‑cost reductions.

Tourism Satellite Accounts and Their Integration with the System of National Accounts

The Tourism Satellite Account (TSA) is the internationally agreed statistical framework for measuring the economic contribution of tourism, developed by the UNWTO, OECD, Eurostat, and the UN Statistics Division under the auspices of the 2008 SNA. Unlike standard industry accounts that classify output by producing unit, the TSA re-organises data from the supply-use tables by tourism-characteristic products and tourism-connected products, identifying the share of each product's supply consumed by visitors. The core TSA tables — Tables 1 to 10 — cover inbound, domestic, and outbound tourism expenditure; production accounts of tourism industries; employment; gross fixed capital formation; and non-monetary indicators (trips, nights, mode of transport). India's Ministry of Tourism, in collaboration with the NSO, compiled the first official TSA for 2009-10 using the 2008 SNA framework and the 2011-12 supply-use table as the benchmark, with subsequent updates for 2015-16 and 2019-20. The TSA derives Tourism Direct GVA (TDGVA) and Tourism Direct Employment (TDE) by applying tourism ratios — the proportion of each industry's output consumed by visitors — to the industry's GVA and employment from the national accounts. A critical methodological point: the TSA does not create a new "tourism industry" in the SNA sense; it extracts a tourism satellite from existing accounts, ensuring consistency with GDP. The 2025 SNA introduces a "tourism" tag on product classifications (CPC) and a dedicated tourism expenditure classification (TEC) that aligns with the Balance of Payments travel and passenger transport items, enabling automated reconciliation between TSA Table 1 (inbound expenditure) and BOP credit entries for travel services. Examiners frequently test the distinction between tourism-characteristic products (those that would cease to exist in meaningful quantity without tourism, e.g., accommodation, air passenger transport, travel agency services) and tourism-connected products (those consumed by visitors but not dependent on tourism, e.g., food and beverages, retail). Only the former are used to define "tourism industries" for the production account (TSA Table 5). Another trap: confusing Tourism Direct GDP (TDGVA plus net taxes on products attributable to tourism) with the broader Tourism GDP that includes indirect and induced effects from input-output multipliers; the TSA reports only the direct component, while the total impact requires a separate Leontief-inverse simulation using the supply-use table.

Accounting for Digital Public Infrastructure as Public Capital: The India Stack Case

Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) — population-scale digital systems such as Aadhaar (identity), UPI (payments), DigiLocker (document storage), and the Account Aggregator framework (data sharing) — represents a new class of non-produced, non-financial assets that generate substantial economic value but fall outside the conventional SNA asset boundary. The 2008 SNA recognises produced assets (fixed capital, inventories, valuables) and non-produced assets (natural resources, contracts/leases/licences, goodwill/marketing assets). DPI does not fit neatly: it is not a natural resource, nor a contract/licence in the SNA sense (which are marketable operating leases or permits), and it is not goodwill (which arises only in business combinations). The 2025 SNA addresses this by introducing a new asset class AN.117 "Digital Public Infrastructure and Platform Assets" within produced fixed assets, capitalising the development cost of open, interoperable, government-backed digital platforms that exhibit network externalities and public good characteristics (non-rivalry, non-excludability at the platform layer). For India, the capitalisation would include the cumulative government expenditure on the development, deployment, and maintenance of the India Stack layers — estimated at approximately ₹10,000 crore for Aadhaar (2009-2023), ₹2,500 crore for UPI/NPCI infrastructure, and ₹1,200 crore for DigiLocker and e-Sign — treated as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) of the general government sector. The corresponding output is non-market government services valued at sum of costs (intermediate consumption + compensation of employees + consumption of fixed capital + other taxes less subsidies on production). The consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) for DPI uses a geometric depreciation profile with a service life of 10-15 years, reflecting rapid technological obsolescence, consistent with the 2025 SNA guidance for "digital infrastructure assets." The economic return is captured not in operating surplus (government non-market output has zero operating surplus by convention) but in the enhanced productivity of user sectors — banking, e-commerce, logistics, social protection delivery — which appears as higher GVA in those industries. A satellite account for DPI, piloted by the NSO in 2023, maps the "DPI-enabled transaction volume" (e.g., UPI transactions per quarter) to the reduction in transaction costs for user industries, using a cost-savings approach: the difference between the pre-DPI unit cost of identity verification, payment processing, or document exchange and the post-DPI marginal cost, multiplied by transaction volume. This yields an annual "DPI productivity dividend" estimated at 0.3-0.5 per cent of GDP for 2022-23. Examiners may ask how to record the private sector co-investment in DPI-compliant applications (e.g., bank apps on UPI, fintech on Account Aggregator): these are recorded as own-account software development (AN.1173) by the private enterprise, distinct from the government DPI asset, with the interoperability ensured by open APIs treated as a free input reducing the private developer's intermediate consumption.

Examiner's Trap: DPI Asset Classification and Valuation
A question states: "The government spends ₹5,000 crore to develop a national digital identity platform. The platform is provided free to all residents and private firms. How is this expenditure recorded in the 2025 SNA, and what is the valuation principle for the resulting asset?"
The ₹5,000 crore is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) of the general government sector in the capital account, creating a new produced fixed asset classified under AN.117 "Digital Public Infrastructure and Platform Assets". The asset enters the national balance sheet at acquisition cost (sum of development expenditures), not at market value (no market exists) or discounted future cost savings. The corresponding output is non-market government services (P.13) valued at sum of costs (intermediate consumption + compensation of employees + consumption of fixed capital + other taxes less subsidies on production). Consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) is calculated using a geometric depreciation rate consistent with a 10-15 year service life. The asset generates no operating surplus; its economic benefit appears as higher productivity in user industries. Private apps built on the platform are separate own-account software assets (AN.1173) of the private firms.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question mentions "digital public infrastructure," "India Stack," "Aadhaar," or "UPI" in a national accounts context, immediately identify: (1) the institutional sector (general government), (2) the asset code (AN.117 in 2025 SNA), (3) the valuation method (acquisition cost = sum of development expenditure), (4) the output valuation (sum of costs for non-market output), and (5) the depreciation profile (geometric, 10-15 years). Distinguish the government platform asset from private own-account software built on top. The 2025 SNA's new asset class AN.117 is the key differentiator from the 2008 SNA, where no clear classification existed.

The Treatment of Natural Resource Depletion, Resource Rents, and Sovereign Wealth Fund Accumulation in Resource-Rich Economies

The 2008 SNA and SEEA-Central Framework (SEEA-CF) treat mineral and energy resources as non-produced, non-financial assets (AN.211) that enter the national balance sheet when they are economically exploitable and have a market value. Depletion is the decline in the value of these assets due to physical extraction, recorded as consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) for produced assets but as other changes in volume of assets (K.2) for non-produced natural resources — specifically K.22 "Depletion of natural resources" — because they are not produced by economic activity. The value of depletion is estimated using the net present value (NPV) method: the resource rent (total revenue minus extraction costs minus a normal return on produced capital) discounted over the asset life. Resource rent is the economic return to the natural resource itself, distinct from the return to produced capital (machinery, infrastructure). In the allocation of primary income account, the resource rent accrues to the legal owner of the resource. For government-owned subsoil assets (the norm in India under the Mines and Minerals Act, 1957, and the Oilfields Act, 1948), the rent is captured via royalties (D.422 "Rent on natural resources"), production sharing contracts, and corporate income tax on the extractor's profits. The 2025 SNA introduces a "resource-rent" tag on the rent classification (D.42) and a "depletion" tag on K.22, enabling satellite accounts that link physical extraction (tonnes, barrels) to monetary depletion and rent flows. Adjusted Net National Income (aNNI) — reported by the World Bank and increasingly by national statistical offices — deducts depletion of energy, minerals, and net forest depletion from Net National Income (NNI), providing a sustainability-adjusted income measure. For India, the NSO's Environmental Accounts (2022) estimated mineral and energy depletion at approximately 1.2 per cent of NNI in 2019-20. Sovereign Wealth Funds (SWFs) — such as Norway's Government Pension Fund Global, Chile's Economic and Social Stabilization Fund, or India's proposed National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) with sovereign capital — are the macro-fiscal mechanism to convert depleting natural capital into financial assets. In the SNA, a transfer of resource revenue to an SWF is recorded as a capital transfer (D.9) from general government to the SWF (classified as a public financial corporation or a separate sub-sector), increasing the SWF's net worth. The SWF's subsequent investment income (dividends, interest, capital gains) is recorded as property income (D.4) receivable by the SWF and payable by the counterpart sectors. The intertemporal budget constraint for a resource-rich economy requires that the present value of SWF assets plus remaining resource wealth equals the present value of future government expenditure net of non-resource revenue. Examiners test the distinction between depletion (a volume change, K.22, reducing the natural resource asset on the balance sheet) and depreciation (P.51c, reducing produced fixed capital). They also test the recording of a production sharing contract (PSC): the government's share of profit oil/gas is rent (D.422), not a tax; the contractor's share covers extraction costs and return on produced capital. Misclassifying the government's PSC share as a tax on production (D.2) distorts the resource rent calculation and the depletion estimate.

Measuring the Economic Impact of Regulatory Quality and Institutional Reform through National Accounts

Regulatory reform — reduction in entry barriers, simplification of licensing, digitisation of compliance, and enforcement of competition law — affects national income through allocative efficiency gains (resources shift to more productive firms), dynamic efficiency gains (entry of innovative firms, exit of unproductive ones), and reduction in compliance costs (lower intermediate consumption for "legal and accounting services," "government regulatory services"). The SNA captures these effects ex post through changes in industry-level GVA, productivity, and firm demographics, but ex ante quantification requires a regulatory cost satellite account linked to the supply-use framework. The OECD's "Regulatory Impact Assessment" (RIA) methodology, adopted by India's Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) for the "Ease of Doing Business" reforms, estimates the administrative burden on firms as the product of (a) the number of regulatory interactions per firm per year, (b) the average time per interaction, and (c) the hourly wage cost of compliance staff. This burden is mapped to the intermediate consumption of "legal, accounting, and business support services" (CPC 82, ISIC 69-70) in the supply-use table. A reform that reduces the number of required licences from 12 to 4, for example, is modelled as a negative shock to the intermediate consumption coefficient of the affected industries for CPC 82, raising their GVA at constant output. The Leontief inverse then propagates the direct GVA increase to upstream sectors. For dynamic effects — firm entry and productivity dispersion — the KLEMS growth accounting framework is extended with a firm-level productivity distribution (from the Annual Survey of Industries or the Ministry of Corporate Affairs' MCA21 database). The Olley-Pakes decomposition of aggregate productivity into the unweighted mean and the covariance between market share and productivity (the "allocative efficiency term") tracks whether reforms improve the covariance — i.e., whether more productive firms gain market share. India's 2017-2022 reforms (GST, IBC, labour code consolidation, single-window clearances) are associated with a rise in the allocative efficiency term in manufacturing from 0.12 to 0.18 (2017-18 to 2021-22), per the RBI's KLEMS database. The 2025 SNA introduces a "regulatory-burden" tag on the intermediate consumption of professional services (CPC 82) and a "reform" tag on the capital account for government expenditure on regulatory digitisation (e.g., the National Single Window System), enabling automated construction of the satellite account. A common examiner trap: attributing the entire post-reform GDP growth to the reform without controlling for cyclical factors; the correct approach uses a counterfactual simulation with a dynamic CGE model calibrated to the pre-reform supply-use table, shocking only the regulatory-cost coefficients. Another trap: treating the government expenditure on regulatory digitisation as intermediate consumption; it is gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in software and databases (AN.1173) if it creates a reusable platform, or intermediate consumption if it is a one-off consultancy.

The Treatment of Cross-Border E-Commerce, Digital Intermediation, and Platform Marketplaces in the 2025 SNA

The explosive growth of cross-border e-commerce — business-to-consumer (B2C) via platforms like Amazon, Flipkart, Alibaba; business-to-business (B2B) via Alibaba.com, IndiaMART; and consumer-to-consumer (C2C) via eBay, OLX — challenges the SNA's residence principle and the distinction between goods and services. The 2008 SNA records cross-border goods trade at the customs frontier (change of ownership imputed at customs clearance), while services trade follows the residence of the consumer (BPM6 mode 1: cross-border supply). Digital platforms blur this: a platform resident in Country A intermediates a sale between a seller in Country B and a buyer in Country C, charging a commission. The 2025 SNA clarifies three treatments: (1) Platform commission/fee is an export of digital intermediation services (CPC 859) by the platform's resident economy to the seller (B2B) or buyer (B2C), recorded in the Balance of Payments as telecommunications, computer, and information services (S.2) or other business services (S.3) depending on the service content. (2) Goods ownership transfers directly from seller (Country B) to buyer (Country C); the platform never takes ownership. The goods export is recorded in Country B's BOP (goods credit) and Country C's BOP (goods debit) at the transaction value excluding the platform fee. (3) Payment processing, logistics, and advertising services bundled by the platform are unbundled: payment processing is a financial service (FISIM or explicit fee), logistics is a transport service (mode 1 if cross-border trucking/air freight), advertising is an advertising service (CPC 836). The 2025 SNA introduces a "digital-platform" tag on the relevant service categories (CPC 859, 836, 715) and a "cross-border-ecommerce" tag on goods trade (HS 2022 subheadings for low-value consignments), enabling the compilation of a Digital Trade Satellite Account that reconciles platform-reported transaction data (Gross Merchandise Value, GMV) with BOP and national accounts aggregates. For India, the NSO's 2023 pilot used GSTN data (IGST on cross-border B2C imports via the "OIDAR" — Online Information Database Access and Retrieval — mechanism) and RBI's EDPMS (Export Data Processing and Monitoring System) to estimate cross-border e-commerce goods imports at ₹1.2 lakh crore (2022-23), with platform commissions of ₹18,000 crore exported as digital services (mostly to non-resident platforms). The low-value consignment relief (LVCR) — exemption from customs duty for imports below a threshold (₹50,000 in India until 2023, now removed for e-commerce) — creates a measurement gap: goods entering via postal/courier channels often evade customs recording. The 2025 SNA recommends using payment card data and platform API data (via data-sharing agreements) to estimate the LVCR gap. Examiners test the distinction between platform as principal (buys and resells goods — records goods trade) and platform as agent (intermediates only — records service export). Most large platforms (Amazon Marketplace, Flipkart, Alibaba) operate as agents for third-party sellers; their revenue is service commissions. Only inventory-led models (Amazon Retail, JD.com) are principals. Misclassifying an agent platform's GMV as goods exports of the platform's resident economy is a cardinal error that inflates the platform economy's trade surplus and distorts TiVA domestic value-added shares.

  • Confusing Tourism Direct GVA (TDGVA) from the TSA with total tourism GDP that includes indirect/induced multiplier effects; the TSA reports only the direct component.
  • Classifying Digital Public Infrastructure expenditure as current transfer or intermediate consumption instead of gross fixed capital formation in AN.117 (2025 SNA) with sum-of-costs output valuation.
  • Treating depletion of natural resources as consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) rather than other changes in volume K.22; depletion applies to non-produced assets, depreciation to produced assets.
  • Recording the government's share of profit oil/gas under a Production Sharing Contract as a tax on production (D.2) instead of rent on natural resources (D.422).
  • Attributing post-reform GDP growth entirely to regulatory reform without a counterfactual CGE simulation controlling for cyclical and external factors.
  • Classifying government expenditure on regulatory digitisation platforms as intermediate consumption when it creates a reusable asset (should be GFCF in AN.1173).
  • Recording a digital platform's Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) as goods exports of the platform's resident economy when the platform acts as an agent; only the commission is a service export, goods trade is between seller and buyer.

Valuation of Non‑Market Environmental Services from Urban Green Infrastructure in the SEEA‑EEA Framework

The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA‑EEA) extends the production boundary to include ecosystem services that are not traded in markets. Urban green infrastructure — parks, street trees, green roofs, wetlands — supplies regulating services (air‑pollution removal, heat‑island mitigation, storm‑water regulation) and cultural services (recreation, aesthetic value). The SEEA‑EEA recommends a three‑step valuation: (1) physical quantification using biophysical models (e.g., i‑Tree Eco for pollutant removal, hydrological models for runoff reduction); (2) monetary valuation using either the replacement‑cost method (cost of engineered substitutes such as mechanical filtration or grey‑infrastructure drainage) or the avoided‑damage method (health‑cost savings from reduced PM₂.₅ exposure, energy‑cost savings from lower cooling demand); (3) integration into the ecosystem‑asset account as a flow of ecosystem services (ES) and a change in the condition of the ecosystem asset (EA). In India, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) piloted an urban ecosystem account for Bengaluru (2022‑23) using high‑resolution satellite imagery (Sentinel‑2, 10 m) and municipal tree‑inventory data. The pilot estimated annual air‑purification services at 1.8 kt of PM₂.₅ removed, valued at ₹420 crore using the avoided‑health‑cost approach (value‑of‑statistical‑life‑year × attributable mortality reduction). Storm‑water regulation was valued at ₹310 crore via the replacement‑cost of additional drainage capacity. These flows were recorded in the ecosystem‑services supply‑use table (ES‑SUT) and linked to the national accounts through a satellite account for urban ecosystem services, allowing the derivation of an “adjusted net national income” that deducts the depreciation of urban green assets (K.22) and adds the imputed value of regulating services. Examiners often test the distinction between ecosystem‑service flows (recorded in the ES‑SUT) and ecosystem‑asset degradation (recorded in the other‑changes‑in‑volume account, K.22). A common error is to treat the replacement‑cost estimate as a market output of the government, which would double‑count the service in GDP.

Accounting for the Economic Value of Publicly Funded Vocational Training and Skill Development Programs in National Accounts

Vocational training and skill‑development programmes (e.g., the Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana, state‑level Industrial Training Institutes) produce human capital that is not captured as market output because trainees typically do not pay fees that reflect full cost. The 2008 SNA treats government‑provided education as non‑market output valued at sum‑of‑costs (intermediate consumption + compensation of employees + consumption of fixed capital + other taxes less subsidies on production). The 2025 SNA introduces a complementary “output‑based” valuation for training programmes that lead to recognised qualifications: the market value of the qualification can be approximated by the wage premium observed for certified workers in labour‑force surveys (Periodic Labour Force Survey, PLFS). In practice, statistical offices construct a satellite account for human‑capital formation that records three aggregates: (i) cost‑of‑production output (current SNA), (ii) output‑based estimate using the Mincerian return to certification (Δwage × hours worked), and (iii) a “skill‑adjusted” labour‑input measure for growth‑accounting (quality‑adjusted labour input, QALI). India’s NSO 2023 pilot for the Skill India Mission used PLFS 2021‑22 data to estimate an average annual wage premium of 12 % for certified workers in manufacturing, translating into an imputed output of ₹1.1 lakh crore, compared with a cost‑of‑production outlay of ₹0.68 lakh crore. The difference (₹0.42 lakh crore) is recorded as a “human‑capital investment grant” in the capital account (D.9) and as an addition to the stock of human capital in the national balance sheet (AN.1173). The satellite account also tracks the flow of trainees into employment (administrative data from the National Career Service portal) to compute a “placement‑adjusted” output measure. Examiners focus on the distinction between the SNA’s core non‑market output (cost‑based) and the satellite‑account output (market‑based), and on the correct recording of the wage‑premium estimate as a capital transfer rather than as current expenditure.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "In the 2025 SNA, how should the wage‑premium estimate for certified vocational trainees be recorded in the national accounts?" Options: (a) as part of government final consumption expenditure, (b) as a capital transfer (D.9) to households, (c) as an increase in the value of produced fixed assets (AN.111), (d) as a revaluation of human‑capital stock (AN.1173) only.
Correct answer: (b) and (d). The wage‑premium estimate represents the market value of the qualification beyond the cost of provision; it is recorded as a capital transfer (D.9) from government to households, increasing household net worth. Simultaneously, the human‑capital stock in the national balance sheet (AN.1173) is revalued upward to reflect the higher expected lifetime earnings. It is not government final consumption (a) because the service is not consumed by government, nor is it a produced fixed asset (c) because human capital is a non‑produced asset in the SNA.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes core SNA valuation (cost‑of‑production) with satellite‑account extensions (market‑based wage premium), first identify which account the figure belongs to: core accounts use sum‑of‑costs; satellite accounts may use market‑based proxies. Then map the transaction to the correct SNA code: capital transfers (D.9) for government‑to‑household skill grants, revaluation of AN.1173 for human‑capital stock changes. Remember that the 2025 SNA capitalises R&D and data as produced assets (AN.117), but human capital remains a non‑produced asset; only its stock value is shown in the balance sheet, not in the production account.

Measuring the Economic Impact of FinTech Innovations on National Income: Mobile Payments, Peer‑to‑Peer Lending, and Regulatory Sandboxes

Financial technology (FinTech) reshapes the production and distribution of financial services, yet the SNA’s classification of financial intermediation services indirectly measured (FISIM) and explicit fees often lags behind product innovation. Mobile‑payment platforms (e.g., UPI in India, M‑Pesa in Kenya) generate revenue from merchant‑discount‑rates (MDR) and transaction fees that are explicit service charges; these are recorded as output of financial auxiliaries (CPC 715) and as intermediate consumption of merchants. Peer‑to‑peer (P2P) lending platforms match borrowers and lenders without taking balance‑sheet risk; their revenue is a fee for intermediation services (CPC 7153) and should be treated as output of “other financial auxiliaries”, not as interest income. The 2025 SNA clarifies that platform‑based financial intermediation where the platform does not assume credit risk is a service, and the interest flow is recorded directly between the ultimate lender and borrower (sector S.12 for households, S.11 for non‑financial corporations). Regulatory sandboxes — controlled environments where firms test innovative products under supervisory oversight — create a measurement challenge: transactions during the sandbox phase are often low‑volume and may not meet the “regular production” threshold for inclusion in GDP. The recommended practice is to record sandbox‑phase revenues as “output of experimental financial services” (a sub‑category of CPC 715) and to flag them with a “sandbox” attribute in the financial‑services satellite account, allowing analysts to separate mature from experimental activity. In India, the Reserve Bank’s 2022‑23 sandbox cohort generated ₹3,200 crore in fee income; the NSO recorded this as output of financial auxiliaries (industry 6499) and added a memorandum item in the financial‑services satellite account. Examiners test the distinction between interest‑margin‑based intermediation (FISIM) and fee‑based platform intermediation, and the correct sectoral allocation of P2P interest flows (directly between lender and borrower, not through the platform). A frequent mistake is to attribute the entire interest spread to the platform’s output, inflating financial‑services GDP.

Integration of the System of National Accounts with the System of Health Accounts: Health Expenditure, Outcomes, and Satellite Account Construction

The System of Health Accounts (SHA 2011) provides a functional classification of health expenditure (HC.1‑HC.9) that is compatible with the SNA’s purpose‑based classification of government final consumption (COFOG 07). However, the SNA records health output of government hospitals at sum‑of‑costs, while SHA tracks financing schemes (government, insurance, out‑of‑pocket) and functions (curative, preventive, governance). A health‑satellite account reconciles these frameworks by: (1) mapping each SHA financing scheme to the corresponding SNA institutional sector (general government, NPISH, households); (2) valuing non‑market health output using both cost‑of‑production (SNA core) and a “health‑output” measure based on disease‑adjusted life‑years (DALYs) averted, derived from epidemiological data; (3) linking health‑capital formation (construction of hospitals, purchase of medical equipment) to the SNA’s gross fixed capital formation (AN.111) and to the SHA’s capital account (HK.1). India’s 2023 health‑satellite account pilot (MoSPI‑NHSRC) used National Health Accounts (NHA) 2019‑20 data and the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2019 DALY estimates to compute an “adjusted health output” of ₹9.8 lakh crore, compared with a cost‑of‑production output of ₹6.4 lakh crore. The difference (₹3.4 lakh crore) was recorded as a “health‑output grant” in the capital account (D.9) and as an addition to the stock of health‑capital (AN.1173) in the national balance sheet. The satellite account also produces a “health‑adjusted net national income” that adds the imputed value of preventive services (e.g., immunisation) not captured in market transactions. Examiners focus on the mapping between SHA functional codes (HC.1‑HC.9) and SNA COFOG divisions, the treatment of out‑of‑pocket expenditure as household final consumption (P.31) versus government transfer (D.62), and the correct recording of health‑capital formation as GFCF (AN.111) rather than intermediate consumption.

The Treatment of Intellectual Property Assets in the National Balance Sheet: Patent Valuation Methods, Licensing Income, and the 2025 SNA

The 2025 SNA expands the asset boundary to recognise intellectual property products (IPPs) — research and development (AN.1171), mineral exploration (AN.1172), computer software and databases (AN.1173), and entertainment, literary and artistic originals (AN.1174) — as produced assets. Patents, a key component of R&D output, are valued in the national balance sheet using three internationally accepted approaches: (i) the cost approach (historical R&D expenditure capitalised, adjusted for consumption of fixed capital using a perpetual‑inventory method with a 15‑year service life for pharmaceutical patents, 10‑year for ICT); (ii) the market approach (observable transaction prices for comparable patent portfolios, e.g., the 2021 sale of a semiconductor patent pool for US$2.3 billion); (iii) the income approach (discounted future royalty streams, using a risk‑adjusted discount rate of 8‑10 % and a patent‑life decay factor). The 2025 SNA recommends that statistical offices compile a “patent‑stock account” that records opening stock, acquisitions (own‑account R&D capitalised, purchases), disposals (sales, expirations), revaluations (market‑price changes), and other changes in volume (K.22 for expirations). Licensing income (royalties) is recorded as property income (D.422) receivable by the patent‑holding sector (typically non‑financial corporations, S.11) and payable by the licensee sector. In India, the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks (CGPDTM) reported 85,000 patents in force (2023); the NSO’s 2024 pilot used the income approach with royalty data from the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) to estimate a patent‑stock value of ₹4.2 lakh crore, of which ₹1.1 lakh crore represented foreign‑owned patents (recorded as a liability in the rest‑of‑the‑world account). The pilot also introduced a “patent‑intensity” indicator (patent stock / GFCF) for use in growth‑accounting. Examiners test the distinction between R&D expenditure recorded as intermediate consumption (pre‑2025 SNA) versus GFCF in AN.1171 (2025 SNA), the correct classification of royalty receipts as property income (D.422) not as service exports, and the treatment of patent expirations as other changes in volume (K.22) rather than consumption of fixed capital (P.51c). A common error is to capitalise the entire R&D outlay in the year incurred without applying a perpetual‑inventory depreciation profile, leading to an overstated patent stock.

  • Confusing the cost‑of‑production valuation of government non‑market output (core SNA) with market‑based satellite‑account estimates (wage premium, health‑output, ecosystem services) and recording the latter in the production account.
  • Treating fee‑based FinTech platform revenue as interest‑margin intermediation (FISIM) instead of explicit financial‑auxiliary output (CPC 715).
  • Recording P2P lending interest flows as platform output rather than direct property income between ultimate lender and borrower.
  • Classifying sandbox‑phase FinTech revenues as regular financial‑services output without the “sandbox” flag, obscuring experimental activity.
  • Mapping SHA financing schemes to SNA sectors incorrectly (e.g., recording social‑health‑insurance contributions as government revenue instead of household‑to‑insurance‑corporation transfers).
  • Valuing patent stock solely by historical R&D cost without applying a perpetual‑inventory depreciation or market‑price revaluation, violating the 2025 SNA asset‑valuation principles.
  • Recording patent expirations as consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) instead of other changes in volume (K.22), misstating the capital‑stock dynamics.

Valuation of Electromagnetic Spectrum Licences and Natural Resource Depletion in National Accounts

The 2008 SNA and the 2025 revision treat electromagnetic spectrum licences as produced assets (AN.115) when they convey exclusive use rights for a defined period, typically 20 years in India. The initial auction proceeds are recorded as government revenue from the sale of a non-produced non-financial asset (NP.1) in the capital account, reducing government net lending. The purchasing telecom operator records the licence as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in AN.115. Consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) is then calculated over the licence term using a straight-line or geometric profile, with the 2025 SNA recommending a geometric rate of 12.5 per cent per annum for a 20-year asset. In India, the 2010, 2012, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2021, and 2022 spectrum auctions generated cumulative proceeds of ₹5.8 lakh crore. The NSO's 2023 pilot capitalised these licences in the national balance sheet at auction value, with a closing stock of ₹4.1 lakh crore after accumulated consumption of fixed capital. The 2025 SNA introduces a depletion adjustment for spectrum treated as a natural resource (AN.211) when the licence fee is linked to revenue share (adjusted gross revenue, AGR). In the AGR regime, the annual licence fee is split: a resource rent component (property income, D.45) and a service component (output, P.1). The resource rent is derived using a discount rate of 8 per cent on projected AGR, and depletion (K.21) is recorded in the other changes in volume account. The Supreme Court's 2019 AGR judgment (Civil Appeal 6328/2019) redefined the AGR base to include non-telecom revenue, increasing the imputed resource rent by an estimated ₹1.4 lakh crore for the period 2005-2019. Examiners test the distinction between auction proceeds (capital transfer, D.9) and annual AGR payments (mixed income/property income), the correct classification of spectrum as AN.115 versus AN.211, and the treatment of licence renewal fees as new GFCF rather than intermediate consumption. A common error is to expense the entire auction outlay in the year of payment, violating the capitalisation principle.

Accounting for Central Bank Balance Sheet Operations: Quantitative Easing, Repo Transactions, and the 2025 SNA

The 2025 SNA provides explicit guidance on recording central bank monetary policy operations in the national accounts, distinguishing between transactions in financial assets (F.3, F.2) and the implicit output of monetary policy services. Under the 2008 SNA, the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) open market operations (OMOs), liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) repo and reverse repo, and marginal standing facility (MSF) were recorded purely as financial transactions with no output imputation. The 2025 SNA introduces the concept of "central bank services output" (P.131) valued at the sum of net interest income (interest receivable on securities held minus interest payable on reserves) plus a risk-adjusted return on equity capital. For India, the RBI's 2023-24 annual report shows interest income of ₹2.1 lakh crore on domestic and foreign securities, interest expense of ₹0.9 lakh crore on reserve deposits and reverse repos, yielding a net interest margin of ₹1.2 lakh crore. The 2025 SNA recommends imputing an output value of ₹1.4 lakh crore after adding a 6 per cent return on the RBI's paid-up capital and reserves (₹58,000 crore). This output is recorded as final consumption expenditure of government (P.31) because the RBI is classified in the general government sector (S.13) in India. Quantitative easing (QE) purchases of government bonds under the Government Securities Acquisition Programme (GSAP) are recorded as acquisitions of debt securities (F.32) by the central bank, with no change in government debt (the liability remains with the general government). The interest received by the RBI on these bonds is property income (D.41) receivable from government, and the surplus transferred to the government (₹87,416 crore in 2023-24) is recorded as a current transfer (D.75) from the central bank to government. The 2025 SNA also requires a memorandum item for "central bank policy rate spread" — the difference between the repo rate (6.50 per cent in 2024) and the reverse repo rate (3.35 per cent) — as an indicator of the implicit price of monetary policy services. Examiners focus on the sector classification of the RBI (S.13 vs S.121), the treatment of GSAP purchases as monetary policy operations not fiscal financing, and the correct recording of the surplus transfer as D.75 not as dividend (D.421). A frequent mistake is to record the RBI's net interest income as household property income rather than government final consumption.

Worked Example: Spectrum Licence Valuation and Central Bank Output
In the 2021 spectrum auction, a telecom operator acquires a 20-year licence for the 3.3-3.6 GHz band for ₹50,000 crore. The licence fee includes an upfront payment of ₹15,000 crore and 19 annual instalments of ₹2,000 crore each (including interest at 8 per cent). Simultaneously, the RBI conducts GSAP 2.0 purchases of ₹1 lakh crore of government bonds. Show the national accounts entries for both transactions in the year of acquisition/purchase.
Spectrum Licence: (1) Telecom operator: GFCF (P.51g) in AN.115 +₹50,000 crore; Financial liability (F.8) +₹35,000 crore (present value of instalments); Currency/deposits (F.2) -₹15,000 crore. (2) Government: Sale of non-produced asset (NP.1) +₹50,000 crore; Currency/deposits (F.2) +₹15,000 crore; Financial asset (F.8) +₹35,000 crore. (3) Annual instalment: Telecom operator: Interest (D.41) -₹2,800 crore (8% on ₹35,000 crore); Amortisation (F.8) -₹1,200 crore. Government: Interest (D.41) +₹2,800 crore; Amortisation (F.8) +₹1,200 crore. Consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) on licence: ₹50,000 crore / 20 = ₹2,500 crore per annum (straight-line). GSAP 2.0: RBI: Acquisition of debt securities (F.32) +₹1 lakh crore; Currency issuance (F.21) +₹1 lakh crore. Government: No change in debt liabilities (F.32 unchanged); Currency/deposits (F.2) +₹1 lakh crore. RBI interest income on bonds: Property income (D.41) receivable from government. Surplus transfer: Current transfer (D.75) from RBI to government.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question combines spectrum licensing and central bank operations, separate the institutional units first: telecom operator (S.11), government (S.13), RBI (S.13). Apply the 2025 SNA asset boundary: spectrum licence = AN.115 (produced asset) if auctioned for fixed term; AGR-linked = AN.211 (natural resource). For RBI, remember India classifies it in S.13, so its net interest margin becomes government final consumption (P.31), not household income. Memorise the 2025 SNA output formula: Central bank output = Net interest income + (Equity × Risk-adjusted return). The risk-adjusted return is typically 5-7 per cent in exam questions.

The Treatment of Cross-Border E-Commerce, Digital Intermediation, and Low-Value Consignments in Trade and National Accounts

The explosion of cross-border e-commerce — business-to-consumer (B2C) and consumer-to-consumer (C2C) — has exposed gaps in the Balance of Payments Manual (BPM6) and the 2008 SNA regarding the measurement of low-value consignments (LVCs) below customs de minimis thresholds. India's de minimis threshold for customs duty exemption is ₹50,000 per consignment (Notification 52/2017-Customs), but the GST regime requires registration for all cross-border digital services regardless of value. The 2025 SNA and the updated BPM7 (forthcoming) recommend three measurement strategies: (i) customs data augmentation using postal and courier electronic data interchange (EDI) feeds from India Post, DHL, FedEx, and Blue Dart; (ii) credit card and digital payment network data (Visa, Mastercard, UPI international) to capture transaction values not passing through customs; (iii) platform-side reporting mandates under the Equalisation Levy (2020) and the Significant Economic Presence (SEP) test (Finance Act 2018) for non-resident digital platforms. The NSO's 2023 pilot used RBI's Export Data Processing and Monitoring System (EDPMS) and Import Data Processing and Monitoring System (IDPMS) matched with GST Network (GSTN) data to estimate B2C e-commerce exports at ₹1.8 lakh crore and imports at ₹2.4 lakh crore for 2022-23, of which 68 per cent by value were LVCs below the customs reporting threshold. Digital intermediation services — platform fees, commissions, and advertising revenue earned by non-resident platforms (Google, Meta, Amazon) from Indian users — are recorded as imports of telecommunications, computer, and information services (SI.1) in the current account. The 2025 SNA clarifies that platform output is the fee charged to the supplier (not the full transaction value), valued at the commission rate (typically 15-30 per cent). For Indian platforms (Flipkart, Meesho) serving foreign buyers, the commission is an export of services. The Equalisation Levy (6 per cent on online advertisement services, 2 per cent on e-commerce supply) is recorded as a tax on production (D.29) payable by the non-resident platform, with a corresponding imputed output of government tax collection services. Examiners test the distinction between the platform's output (commission) and the merchant's output (goods sold), the correct BOP classification of digital services (SI.1 vs SI.2 vs SI.3), and the treatment of the Equalisation Levy as a tax not a royalty. A common error is to record the full gross merchandise value (GMV) as trade in goods rather than the commission as trade in services.

Measuring the Economic Value of Public Education Expenditure: Education Satellite Accounts and Human Capital Formation

While the 2025 SNA capitalises research and development (AN.1171), it does not capitalise public education expenditure as produced human capital in the core accounts, maintaining the treatment of education as final consumption (P.31) of government and households. However, the SNA encourages satellite accounts for human capital, and the OECD's "Guide to Measuring Human Capital" (2020) provides a framework adopted by India's NSO in its 2024 Education Satellite Account (ESA) pilot. The ESA uses the cost-based approach: output of public education services (P.13) is valued at the sum of compensation of employees (D.1), intermediate consumption (P.2), consumption of fixed capital on education infrastructure (P.51c), and other taxes less subsidies on production (D.29-D.39). For 2022-23, the Ministry of Education reported total public expenditure on education of ₹10.4 lakh crore (Centre: ₹1.1 lakh crore; States: ₹9.3 lakh crore), of which ₹8.2 lakh crore was compensation of teachers and staff. The ESA imputes an output value of ₹11.1 lakh crore after adding consumption of fixed capital on school buildings (₹0.7 lakh crore) and imputed rent on government-owned land (₹0.2 lakh crore). This output is recorded as government final consumption expenditure (P.31) in the core accounts, but the satellite account reclassifies ₹6.8 lakh crore as "human capital formation" (HCF) — the portion attributable to student enrolment in recognised institutions (UDISE+ data: 26.5 crore students in 2022-23). The HCF is allocated across levels: primary (₹2.1 lakh crore), secondary (₹1.8 lakh crore), higher (₹2.9 lakh crore). The 2025 SNA recommends a parallel income-based approach using the Jorgenson-Fraumeni lifetime earnings method, which the NSO piloted using Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2022-23 data, yielding a human capital stock estimate of ₹1,200 lakh crore (4.2 times GDP). The satellite account also produces "education-adjusted net national income" by adding the imputed HCF and subtracting consumption of fixed capital on human capital (depreciation rate 3.5 per cent per annum, reflecting skill obsolescence). Examiners focus on the distinction between core-account treatment (consumption) and satellite-account treatment (capital formation), the correct valuation of government non-market output (cost-sum method), and the mapping between UDISE+ enrolment codes and ISCED 2011 levels for international comparability. A frequent mistake is to capitalise the entire education expenditure in the core production account, violating the 2025 SNA production boundary.

Accounting for Climate Adaptation Expenditure, Loss and Damage, and the SEEA Climate Change Module

The SEEA Climate Change module (2023) and the 2025 SNA introduce a systematic framework for recording climate adaptation expenditure, loss and damage, and resilience investment in national accounts. Adaptation expenditure — spending that reduces vulnerability to climate change — is classified by purpose using the Classification of Environmental Activities (CEA) and by institutional sector. In India, the National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC), state climate action plans, and the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS) water conservation works are primary adaptation channels. The NSO's 2023 Climate Adaptation Satellite Account (CASA) pilot identified ₹1.6 lakh crore of adaptation expenditure in 2022-23: ₹0.7 lakh crore for flood protection (embankments, drainage), ₹0.4 lakh crore for drought resilience (watershed development, micro-irrigation), ₹0.3 lakh crore for coastal protection (mangrove restoration, sea walls), and ₹0.2 lakh crore for heat resilience (cool roofs, early warning systems). In the core accounts, these are recorded as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in AN.111 (structures) or AN.112 (machinery) when they create new assets, or as intermediate consumption (P.2) when they are maintenance (e.g., embankment repair). The 2025 SNA introduces a memorandum item "climate adaptation capital formation" to track the subset of GFCF with primary adaptation purpose. Loss and damage — the economic impact of extreme events exceeding adaptation capacity — is recorded in the other changes in volume account (K.1-K.7). The 2023 floods in Himachal Pradesh and Punjab caused estimated asset losses of ₹12,000 crore (K.7: catastrophic losses) and output losses of ₹8,000 crore (recorded as a reduction in GDP via the production account). The CASA pilot uses the "counterfactual GDP" method: estimating the GDP trajectory without the climate event using a synthetic control (pre-event trend + comparable unaffected states). The difference is the loss and damage estimate. The 2025 SNA also requires recording "climate resilience services" provided by ecosystems (mangroves, wetlands) as ecosystem services (ES.1) in the SEEA-EEA physical and monetary supply-use tables. India's 2024 SEEA-EEA compilation valued mangrove cyclone protection services at ₹4,500 crore per annum for the Sundarbans and Gujarat coast. Examiners test the distinction between adaptation (ex-ante, capital formation) and loss and damage (ex-post, other changes in volume), the correct CEA codes for adaptation activities (CEA 1.1.2 for flood protection, 1.2.1 for drought resilience), and the treatment of insurance payouts (D.72: non-life insurance claims) as a financial transaction not a reversal of loss. A common error is to record disaster relief transfers (D.9) as negative GFCF rather than as capital transfers receivable by the affected sector.

  • Confusing spectrum auction proceeds (sale of non-produced asset NP.1) with annual AGR payments (mixed property income/service output) and misclassifying the latter as tax revenue.
  • Recording the RBI's GSAP bond purchases as a reduction in government debt (F.32) instead of a change in the holder of the liability from public to central bank.
  • Valuing cross-border e-commerce at gross merchandise value (GMV) in goods trade (SB.1) rather than at platform commission in services trade (SI.1).
  • Treating the Equalisation Levy as a royalty (D.422) or income tax (D.51) instead of a tax on production (D.29) payable by the non-resident platform.
  • Capitalising public education expenditure in the core production account as GFCF (P.51g) rather than recording it as government final consumption (P.31) with human capital formation shown only in a satellite account.
  • Recording climate disaster asset losses as consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) instead of catastrophic losses (K.7) in the other changes in volume account.
  • Classifying MGNREGS water conservation works entirely as intermediate consumption (P.2) when they create new durable assets (check dams, ponds) that should be GFCF (P.51g) in AN.

Valuation of Non‑Market Output of Central Banks: Seigniorage, Monetary Policy Operations, and the SNA Production Boundary

The 2008 SNA (Chapter 6, Section 6.123–6.128) and the 2025 SNA revision treat central bank output as non‑market because the majority of services — monetary policy, financial stability oversight, payment system operation — are supplied free or at prices that do not cover full cost. Output is valued by the sum‑of‑costs method (P.13): intermediate consumption (P.2) plus compensation of employees (D.1) plus consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) plus other taxes less subsidies on production (D.29–D.39). The resulting output (P.1) enters government final consumption expenditure (P.31) when the central bank is classified in the general government sector (S.13), or household final consumption (P.31) when it is a public corporation (S.11) — India classifies the RBI in S.13. A critical nuance: seigniorage (the difference between the face value of currency issued and its production cost) is not output. It is recorded as a financial transaction — currency issuance (F.21) matched by acquisition of assets (mainly government securities F.32) — and the associated property income (interest received D.41) is primary income, not production income. The 2025 SNA introduces a memorandum item "central bank monetary policy services" to separate policy‑related costs (open market operations, standing facility management, foreign exchange intervention) from payment‑system and regulatory services. In India's 2023‑24 accounts, RBI's non‑market output was ₹48,000 crore: ₹22,000 crore compensation of employees, ₹14,000 crore intermediate consumption (IT, security, currency printing at SPMCIL), ₹8,000 crore consumption of fixed capital, and ₹4,000 crore other taxes on production. Examiners test the distinction between seigniorage revenue (a fiscal concept, recorded in the government's revenue account as non‑tax revenue) and central bank output (a production concept, recorded in the production account). A frequent error is to treat the RBI's surplus transfer to the Centre (₹2.11 lakh crore in 2023‑24 under Section 47 of the RBI Act) as government revenue from production; it is a property income withdrawal (D.42) from a public corporation, reducing the RBI's equity (F.51) and increasing government net worth.

The Treatment of Natural Resource Depletion and Resource Rent in the SNA and SEEA: Depletion‑Adjusted Aggregates for Resource‑Rich States

The 2008 SNA (Chapter 13) and SEEA‑Central Framework (2012, Section 5.4) define depletion as the reduction in the value of natural resource assets (mineral reserves, timber, fish stocks, aquifers) due to extraction exceeding natural regeneration. Depletion is recorded in the other changes in volume account (K.2: depletion of natural resources), not as consumption of fixed capital (P.51c), because natural resources are non‑produced assets (AN.21). The resource rent — total revenue from extraction minus extraction costs (intermediate consumption, compensation of employees, consumption of fixed capital on produced assets, and a normal return on produced capital) — is split into depletion (the user cost of the resource) and net return to produced capital. The SEEA recommends depletion‑adjusted aggregates: Depletion‑Adjusted NDP = NDP − Depletion; Depletion‑Adjusted Net National Income = NN − Depletion; Depletion‑Adjusted Net Saving = Net Saving − Depletion. For India, the NSO's 2022 Environmental Accounts pilot estimated mineral depletion at ₹1.1 lakh crore (2019‑20): coal ₹48,000 crore, iron ore ₹22,000 crore, limestone ₹14,000 crore, bauxite ₹8,000 crore, others ₹18,000 crore. Energy depletion (crude oil, natural gas) added ₹35,000 crore. Forest depletion (timber, fuelwood) was ₹22,000 crore. Water depletion (groundwater extraction beyond recharge) in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan was valued at ₹45,000 crore using the replacement cost method (desalination cost proxy). The 2025 SNA requires reporting depletion by institutional sector: for government‑owned resources (most minerals), depletion reduces government net worth; for privately leased resources, depletion is a cost to the extractor (recorded as rent payable D.45 to government). A key examiner trap: resource rent taxation (royalty, district mineral foundation, national mineral exploration trust) is a current transfer (D.7) or tax (D.29), not a deduction in calculating depletion. Depletion is an economic concept based on resource scarcity; royalty is a fiscal instrument. Confusing the two leads to double‑counting or omission in adjusted saving.

Examiner's Trap: Depletion vs. Consumption of Fixed Capital in Mining
A question states: "A coal mining company extracts ₹500 crore of coal in a year. Its produced capital (machinery, railways) consumes ₹50 crore of fixed capital. The company pays ₹100 crore royalty to the state government. Calculate the depletion-adjusted value added for the mining sector."
