The 2025 SNA clarifies that border carbon adjustments are taxes on products (D.21) when levied on the good at importation, distinct from carbon taxes on production (D.29) levied on domestic output. India's steel and aluminium exporters face CBAM liabilities estimated at ₹8,000–12,000 crore annually (2026 onwards). The NSO's BoP compilation will need to coordinate with CBIC customs data to classify CBAM payments correctly. Examiners test the classification of CBAM as D.21 (tax on products) versus D.29 (tax on production) or D.59 (current taxes on income/wealth), the BoP recording (no entry in exporter's BoP if importer pays), and the impact on terms of trade (CBAM raises import prices for EU, deteriorating India's terms of trade if export prices are unchanged). A frequent trap is recording CBAM as an export tax in India's accounts — it is an EU import duty.

Central Bank Balance Sheet Operations and Their Recording in the System of National Accounts

The Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) balance sheet expansion — through open market operations (OMO), long-term repo operations (LTRO), targeted long-term repo operations (TLTRO), and the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) — has direct implications for national accounts compilation, particularly the financial account and the measurement of financial intermediation services indirectly measured (FISIM). Under the 2008 SNA, the central bank is a financial corporation (S.121) producing financial intermediation services. Its output (P.1) is measured as the sum of explicit fees and FISIM, where FISIM = (loan interest received − reference rate × loans) + (reference rate × deposits − deposit interest paid). The reference rate is the interbank lending rate (e.g., weighted average call rate). When the RBI conducts OMOs (outright purchase of government securities), it increases its asset holdings (AF.3, debt securities) and reserve money (liability: currency in circulation + bank reserves). This does not directly create FISIM because the securities are held to maturity and the interest earned is property income (D.41), not intermediation margin. However, LTRO/TLTRO operations — where the RBI lends to banks at a fixed repo rate against collateral — generate FISIM if the repo rate differs from the reference rate. The 2025 SNA refines FISIM calculation for central bank policy operations: (1) standing facility rates (marginal standing facility, standing deposit facility) serve as reference rates for corresponding assets/liabilities; (2) quantitative easing (QE) holdings of government bonds are treated as investment portfolio, not intermediation, so interest is D.41, not FISIM. The RBI's surplus transfer to the government (Section 47 of the RBI Act) is recorded as a withdrawal from income of quasi-corporations (D.422) in the allocation of primary income account, not as a tax. The 2025 SNA introduces a "central bank policy operations" satellite account tracking the stock and flow of policy instruments (OMO, LTRO, FX swaps) and their impact on the yield curve, separate from core financial intermediation. India's NSO uses RBI's Weekly Statistical Supplement (WSS) and annual report data for the monetary and financial statistics (MFS) compilation, which feeds into the financial account of the national accounts. A critical reconciliation item is the treatment of MSS bonds — issued by the government on behalf of the RBI for sterilisation. In the government's accounts, MSS bonds are a liability (AF.3); in the RBI's accounts, the proceeds are held as cash balances (AF.2), not lent out. The interest cost is borne by the government (D.41 payable), while the RBI earns interest on its cash investment (D.41 receivable). Examiners test the distinction between monetary policy operations (affecting financial account, not directly GDP) and financial intermediation (generating FISIM, part of GDP), the classification of RBI surplus transfer (D.422, not tax), and the 2025 SNA's reference rate framework for central bank facilities. A common error is including RBI's OMO gains/losses in GDP — they are holding gains/losses (K.3, K.4, K.5), recorded in the revaluation account, not the production account.

  • Confusing the fiscal treatment of spectrum auction proceeds (revenue receipt) with the national accounts treatment (disposal of non-produced asset, K.2) — they diverge by design.
  • Stating that SEZ output is excluded from GDP because it is "duty-free" — the SNA includes all resident production within the economic territory regardless of customs status.
  • Recording CBAM as an export tax in the exporting country's accounts — it is an import duty (D.21) levied by the importing country's government.
  • Treating UPI transaction values as direct GDP contributions — only the cost of providing the payment infrastructure (government non-market output) enters GDP; transaction values are financial flows.
  • Classifying the RBI's surplus transfer to government as a tax (D.2) — it is withdrawal from income of quasi-corporations (D.422) in the primary distribution of income account.
  • Assuming all central bank policy operations generate FISIM — outright OMO and QE holdings generate property income (D.41); only lending facilities at rates diverging from the reference rate generate FISIM.
  • Equating tax expenditures (SEZ income tax holidays, GST zero-rating) with government expenditure in the core SNA — they are memorandum items, not recorded in the production or generation of income accounts.

Special Drawing Rights Allocations and Reserve Asset Accounting in the SNA and BPM6

The International Monetary Fund's (IMF) Special Drawing Rights (SDR) allocations create distinct recording challenges across the System of National Accounts (SNA) and the Balance of Payments Manual, sixth edition (BPM6). An SDR allocation is recorded as the incurrence of a liability (AF.12, Special Drawing Rights) by the recipient central bank — in India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) — and the acquisition of a financial asset (AF.12) in the form of SDR holdings. The counterpart is an increase in reserve assets (BPM6: reserve assets, SDRs). No production or income is generated at the moment of allocation; it is a financial account transaction (F.12) with a corresponding other changes in volume account entry (K.7, reclassification) if the allocation is general, or a transaction if it is a specific allocation to a member. The 2009 general SDR allocation (SDR 161.2 billion) and the 2021 general allocation (SDR 456.5 billion, of which India received SDR 12.57 billion) were recorded as transactions in the financial account of the monetary and financial statistics (MFS) and the balance of payments.

Interest on SDR holdings (D.41, property income receivable) and interest on SDR allocations (D.41, property income payable) accrue continuously. The SDR interest rate (SDRi) is determined weekly as a weighted average of short-term interest rates on the instruments in the SDR basket (US dollar, euro, Chinese renminbi, Japanese yen, pound sterling). In the national accounts, the RBI's net SDR interest (receivable less payable) enters the allocation of primary income account of the financial corporations sector (S.12). The 2025 SNA clarifies that SDR holdings and allocations are measured at nominal value (face value) in the balance sheets, with holding gains and losses (K.3, K.4, K.5) arising from exchange rate movements between the SDR and the domestic currency recorded in the revaluation account. A critical reconciliation item for India is the valuation of SDR holdings in the RBI's Weekly Statistical Supplement (WSS) — reported in SDR millions and converted at the RBI's reference rate — versus the IMF's SDR valuation. The 2025 SNA introduces a memorandum item for "SDR allocation cumulative net interest position" to track the net fiscal cost of SDR allocations over time, relevant for debt sustainability analysis where SDR allocations are treated as long-term liabilities of the central government in some analytical presentations (e.g., IMF's Debt Sustainability Framework), though in the core SNA they remain central bank liabilities.

Examiners test the distinction between the SDR allocation (liability) and SDR holding (asset), the classification of SDR interest as property income (not FISIM), and the treatment of valuation changes as holding gains/losses (not transactions). A common error is recording the SDR allocation as government revenue or grant; it is a liability creation with no revenue implication. Another error is netting SDR holdings against allocations in the balance sheet — the 2008 SNA and BPM6 require gross presentation. The 2025 SNA further specifies that SDR allocations are not "debt securities" (AF.3) but a separate instrument category (AF.12), and that the central bank's SDR holdings are part of reserve assets (AF.1) only if they are readily available for meeting balance of payments needs; otherwise they are classified as other investment (AF.8). India's practice follows BPM6: SDR holdings are reserve assets; SDR allocations are other investment liabilities of the monetary authority.

Valuation of Digital Public Infrastructure as Public Capital Formation: The India Stack Experience

India's Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) — comprising the identity layer (Aadhaar), the payments layer (Unified Payments Interface, UPI), the data empowerment layer (Account Aggregator framework, DigiLocker), and the open network layer (Open Network for Digital Commerce, ONDC; Unified Health Interface, UHI) — represents a novel class of public capital formation that challenges conventional national accounts classification. Under the 2008 SNA, government expenditure on the development, deployment, and maintenance of these platforms is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in produced assets: specifically, computer software and databases (AN.117) and, where applicable, telecommunications equipment (AN.113). The 2025 SNA expands the asset boundary to explicitly recognise "data, databases, and digital platforms" as produced assets (AN.1173) when they are created through a production process and used repeatedly in production for more than one year. The India Stack components meet this criterion: they are developed under government direction (NPCI for UPI, UIDAI for Aadhaar, Sahamati for Account Aggregator), involve significant upfront R&D and software engineering, and generate a stream of services (authentication, payment processing, consent-based data sharing) used by households, businesses, and government agencies.

The valuation challenge is threefold. First, the initial development cost (capitalised R&D, software engineering, hardware procurement) is observable from budget documents (MeitY, NPCI, UIDAI annual reports) and forms the initial acquisition value. Second, the ongoing maintenance and upgrade expenditure (server costs, security audits, version upgrades) is recorded as intermediate consumption (P.2) if it maintains existing functionality, or as capital formation (P.51g) if it extends the asset's service life or adds new functionality — a distinction the 2025 SNA sharpens by requiring a "significant improvement" threshold. Third, the imputed user cost of DPI services provided free or at nominal cost (e.g., UPI zero merchant discount rate for small merchants, free Aadhaar authentication for government schemes) must be estimated for government non-market output (P.13). The 2008 SNA uses the sum-of-costs approach: output = intermediate consumption + compensation of employees + consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) + other taxes less subsidies on production. For DPI, consumption of fixed capital is derived using geometric depreciation profiles for software (typically 3-5 year service life) and hardware (5-7 years). India's NSO has initiated a satellite account for the digital economy (2023) that attempts to capitalise the stock of DPI assets and impute their service flows. A critical methodological issue is the treatment of network effects: the value of UPI grows with the number of users and transactions, but the SNA records only the cost of providing the infrastructure, not the consumer surplus or network externality value. The 2025 SNA's "digital platform" satellite account framework allows for supplementary presentation of user metrics (active users, transaction volumes, API calls) alongside monetary stocks and flows.

Examiners test the classification of DPI expenditure (capital formation vs. current expenditure), the asset category (AN.1173 data, databases, and digital platforms), the valuation method (sum-of-costs for non-market output), and the 2025 SNA's extension of the production boundary to include data as a produced asset. A common error is treating UPI transaction values as GDP — only the cost of operating the payment infrastructure enters GDP. Another error is classifying Aadhaar enrolment fees (where charged) as government revenue from sales (P.11) — they are treated as payments for non-market services at non-significant prices, recorded as other subsidies on production (D.39) if below cost.

Examiner's Trap: DPI Capitalisation vs. Expense
A question states: "The Government of India spends ₹5,000 crore on upgrading the UPI platform to support credit lines and international interoperability. In the national accounts, this expenditure is recorded as:" Options: (a) Intermediate consumption of general government, (b) Gross fixed capital formation in computer software and databases, (c) Government final consumption expenditure, (d) Subsidy to NPCI.
Correct answer: (b). The upgrade extends the asset's service life and adds new functionality (credit lines, cross-border interoperability), meeting the 2025 SNA's "significant improvement" criterion for capital formation. It is classified under AN.1173 (data, databases, and digital platforms). The expenditure is not intermediate consumption because it does not merely maintain existing functionality. It is not government final consumption expenditure because the asset is used repeatedly in production over multiple years. It is not a subsidy to NPCI because NPCI is the implementing agent; the government is the owner of the asset (or the asset is attributed to the general government sector as the beneficial owner). The consumption of fixed capital on this asset will be charged over its revised service life, entering the sum-of-costs calculation for government non-market output.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question mentions "digital public infrastructure", "India Stack", "Aadhaar", "UPI", or "ONDC" in a national accounts context, immediately identify: (1) the institutional sector of the owner (general government vs. public corporation), (2) the asset classification (AN.1173 under 2025 SNA), (3) the valuation method (sum-of-costs for non-market output), and (4) the distinction between capital formation (new functionality, extended life) and intermediate consumption (maintenance, security patches). Memorise the 2025 SNA asset code AN.1173 and the term "data, databases, and digital platforms".

The Global Minimum Tax (Pillar Two) and Its Recording in Government Finance Statistics and National Accounts

The OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework's Two-Pillar Solution to address the tax challenges of the digitalisation of the economy introduces a global minimum corporate tax (Pillar Two) with an effective date of 2024 for the Income Inclusion Rule (IIR) and 2025 for the Undertaxed Profits Rule (UTPR). India has not yet legislated Pillar Two but participates in the Inclusive Framework. The national accounts and Government Finance Statistics (GFS) recording of the Top-up Tax (the difference between the 15% minimum effective tax rate and the jurisdiction's effective tax rate) requires careful classification. Under the 2008 SNA and GFSM 2014, the Top-up Tax paid by a multinational enterprise (MNE) group to a jurisdiction (the "Ultimate Parent Entity" jurisdiction under IIR, or the "source" jurisdiction under UTPR) is recorded as a current tax on income, wealth, etc. (D.51, D.59) — specifically, D.51 (taxes on income) if it meets the definition of a tax on income (compulsory, unrequited, levied on income). The 2025 SNA confirms this classification but adds a memorandum item for "Pillar Two top-up tax revenue" to track the new revenue stream separately from domestic corporate income tax (CIT).

The mechanism: The MNE group calculates its Effective Tax Rate (ETR) per jurisdiction (GloBE ETR = Covered Taxes ÷ GloBE Income). If ETR < 15%, a Top-up Tax = (15% - ETR) × GloBE Income (net of substance-based income exclusion). The Top-up Tax is allocated first to the Ultimate Parent Entity (UPE) jurisdiction (IIR), then to intermediate parent jurisdictions, then to other constituent entities (UTPR). In the national accounts of the collecting jurisdiction, the Top-up Tax is a revenue transaction (D.51 receivable) in the allocation of primary income account of general government. In the paying jurisdiction (where the low-taxed entity resides), there is no direct recording unless the entity bears the economic burden — the SNA follows the legal liability principle. However, the 2025 SNA introduces a "tax transparency" satellite account that links the Top-up Tax to the specific MNE groups and jurisdictions involved, using Country-by-Country Reporting (CbCR) data.

A critical issue for India is the interaction with domestic tax incentives (SEZ tax holidays, Section 10AA, Section 80-IAC for startups). If a jurisdiction's domestic ETR is below 15% due to incentives, the Top-up Tax effectively neutralises the incentive from the MNE's perspective, but the revenue accrues to the UPE jurisdiction (often the US, EU, or Japan for Indian MNEs' foreign parents), not to India. In India's national accounts, the domestic CIT revenue forgone due to incentives is a tax expenditure (memorandum item), while the Top-up Tax collected by foreign jurisdictions on Indian-resident entities is not recorded as Indian revenue. The 2025 SNA's "distributional corporate tax" framework attempts to allocate the global tax burden to the ultimate owners, but this remains a research agenda. Examiners test the classification of Top-up Tax (D.51, not D.29 or D.59), the distinction between legal liability (UPE jurisdiction) and economic incidence, and the memorandum item treatment of tax expenditures vs. Pillar Two revenue.

Accounting for Carbon Markets: Emission Trading Schemes, Carbon Credits, and the SEEA-CF Integration

The proliferation of compliance carbon markets (EU ETS, China's national ETS, Korea ETS, California Cap-and-Trade) and voluntary carbon markets (Verra, Gold Standard, Article 6.4 mechanism under the Paris Agreement) creates a new class of environmental assets and liabilities that the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting — Central Framework (SEEA-CF) and the 2025 SNA are integrating into the asset boundary. Under the SEEA-CF, emission permits (allowances) allocated by governments are recorded as the creation of a non-produced, non-financial asset (AN.221, emission permits) for the holder and a liability for the government (AF.8, other accounts payable) if allocated free, or a financial transaction (sale of permit) if auctioned. The 2008 SNA treated permits as rent on natural resources (D.45) when allocated free, but the 2025 SNA aligns with SEEA-CF: free allocation is a capital transfer (D.99) from government to corporation, creating an asset (AN.221) for the corporation. Auction proceeds are government revenue from the sale of a non-produced asset (K.2, disposal of non-produced non-financial asset), not a tax.

Carbon credits (Certified Emission Reductions, CERs; Verified Carbon Units, VCUs; Article 6.4 credits) generated from mitigation projects are produced assets (AN.117, intellectual property products / other produced assets) when they result from a production process (e.g., renewable energy project, afforestation). The 2025 SNA classifies them as "emission reduction credits" (AN.1174) — a new sub-category of produced assets. Their valuation at inception is the cost of the mitigation activity (capitalised project costs). Subsequent valuation is at market price (quoted on exchanges or over-the-counter), with holding gains/losses (K.3, K.4) recorded in the revaluation account. When a credit is surrendered for compliance, it is a disposal of a produced asset (K.2) by the holder and a reduction of the government's permit liability. The SEEA-CF physical flow accounts track the stock and flow of permits and credits in tonnes of CO2 equivalent, linked to the monetary accounts via the permit/credit price.

India's Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001, and the upcoming Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) notified under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022, create domestic compliance instruments (Energy Saving Certificates, ESCerts; and future Carbon Credit Certificates). In the national accounts, ESCerts allocated free are capital transfers (D.99) creating AN.221 assets for designated consumers. PAT cycle targets and trading volumes are reported by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE). The voluntary market in India (e.g., credits from renewable projects registered under Verra) generates AN.1174 assets for project developers. A critical reconciliation item is the treatment of Article 6.2 Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs): the selling country records a disposal of a non-produced asset (K.2) and an export of a service (P.62, environmental protection services); the buying country records an acquisition of a non-produced asset (K.1) and an import of a service. The 2025 SNA introduces a "carbon market satellite account" integrating physical flows (tonnes), monetary stocks (permits, credits), and the government's net permit position (allocated minus surrendered). Examiners test the asset classification (AN.221 for permits, AN.1174 for credits), the revenue classification (auction proceeds = K.2, not tax), the treatment of free allocation (capital transfer D.99), and the Article 6.2 cross-border recording (export/import of environmental services).

The Treatment of Spectrum Licenses and Natural Resource Concessions as Produced Assets in the 2025 SNA

The 2025 SNA introduces a fundamental shift in the treatment of licenses to use natural resources — including radio spectrum, mineral rights, oil and gas concessions, and fishing quotas — by recognising them as produced assets (AN.115, licences to use natural resources) when they are granted for a significant period (typically >10 years) and the licensee bears the risks and rewards of resource extraction or use. Under the 2008 SNA, such licences were generally treated as rent on natural resources (D.45, property income) paid by the licensee to the government (the legal owner), with no asset recorded on the licensee's balance sheet. The 2025 SNA distinguishes three cases: (1) Short-term licences (<10 years) or licences where the government retains substantial risk (e.g., production-sharing contracts with cost recovery) remain rent (D.45); (2) Long-term licences where the licensee has de facto control over the resource (e.g., spectrum licences with renewal expectancy, mining leases with exclusive extraction rights) are reclassified as the acquisition of a produced asset (AN.115) by the licensee, financed by a loan (AF.4) from the government if paid in instalments, or by a financial transaction if paid upfront; (3) Perpetual licences or those with automatic renewal are treated as the sale of a non-produced asset (K.2, disposal of natural resource) by the government and acquisition of a produced asset (AN.115) by the licensee.

India's spectrum auctions (2010, 2012, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2021, 2022, 2024) involve upfront payments and deferred payment options (moratorium, equated annual instalments). Under the 2025 SNA, the winning bidder acquires AN.115 (licence to use spectrum) at the present value of the payment stream (discounted at the government bond yield). The upfront payment is a financial transaction (F.4, loan from government to bidder, or F.8, other accounts payable/receivable). The annual instalments are debt service (F.4 principal repayment + D.41 interest). The government's auction proceeds are not revenue (D.2) but the disposal of a non-produced asset (K.2, natural resource) and the creation of a financial asset (loan). This aligns with the 2025 SNA's treatment of spectrum as a "licence to use a natural resource" that is produced by the government through the auction process (the auction itself is a production process creating the licence). The consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) on AN.115 is calculated over the licence period (e.g., 20 years), entering the licensee's production account as a cost. For the government, the auction eliminates the natural resource asset (AN.21, radio spectrum) from its balance sheet.

Mineral concessions under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (amended 2015, 2021, 2023) involve auction of mining leases and composite licences. The 2025 SNA treatment depends on the contract form: revenue-sharing contracts (introduced 2021) where the bidder quotes a revenue share percentage are treated as rent (D.45) because the government retains resource price risk. Fixed upfront payment contracts (pre-2015) are treated as AN.115 acquisition. The District Mineral Foundation (DMF) and National Mineral Exploration Trust (NMET) contributions are current transfers (D.73/D.74) from the licensee to government, not part of the licence asset value. Examiners test the 2025 SNA reclassification (rent vs. asset acquisition), the asset code AN.115, the discounting of deferred payments, the consumption of fixed capital on the licence, and the government's revenue classification (K.2 disposal of natural resource, not tax revenue). A common error is recording spectrum auction proceeds as non-tax revenue (D.29) in the core accounts — they are K.2 in the capital account. Another error is treating the annual instalment as rent — it is debt service on the implicit loan.

  • Confusing SDR allocation (liability) with SDR holding (asset) and netting them in the balance sheet — the 2008 SNA and BPM6 require gross presentation; the allocation is AF.12 liability, the holding is AF.12 asset (reserve asset).
  • Recording UPI transaction values or Aadhaar authentication volumes as direct GDP contributions — only the cost of providing the digital infrastructure (sum-of-costs: intermediate consumption + compensation of employees + consumption of fixed capital) enters GDP as government non-market output.
  • Classifying the Global Minimum Tax (Pillar Two) Top-up Tax as a tax on production (D.29) or a capital transfer — it is a current tax on income (D.51) levied on the multinational enterprise group in the Ultimate Parent Entity jurisdiction.
  • Treating carbon permit auction proceeds as tax revenue (D.2) — under SEEA-CF and the 2025 SNA, they are disposal of a non-produced asset (K.2, emission permit); free allocation is a capital transfer (D.99) creating AN.221 for the recipient.
  • Recording spectrum auction proceeds as non-tax revenue (D.29) in the production or generation of income accounts — they are K.2 (disposal of natural resource) in the capital account, with the bidder acquiring AN.115 (licence to use natural resource) financed by an implicit loan (AF.4).
  • Assuming all carbon credits are financial assets — credits generated from mitigation projects (CERs, VCUs, Article 6.4 credits) are produced assets (AN.1174, emission reduction credits); only compliance permits (EUAs, China ETS allowances) are non-produced assets (AN.221) when allocated by government.
  • Equating the consumption of fixed capital on Digital Public Infrastructure with zero because services are free — the 2008/2025 SNA requires geometric depreciation on the capitalised development cost (AN.1173) over the asset's service life (3-5 years for software), which enters the sum-of-costs valuation of government non-market output.

Government Debt Securities: Valuation, Revaluation, and Balance‑Sheet Integration under the 2025 SNA

The 2025 System of National Accounts (SNA) refines the treatment of government debt securities (AF.3) by requiring market‑value valuation on the balance sheet and a clear separation of transactions, revaluations, and other changes in volume. Under the 2008 SNA, many compilers recorded government bonds at nominal (face) value, with interest accrued (D.41) but without a revaluation account for price changes. The 2025 revision mandates that each quarter the market price of each security be observed — using secondary‑market yields for actively traded issues and model‑based discount curves for illiquid ones — and that the resulting holding gains or losses be recorded in the revaluation account (K.11) rather than in the production or generation of income accounts. This aligns the SNA with the IMF’s Government Finance Statistics Manual 2014 (GFSM 2014) and the Balance of Payments Manual 6 (BPM6), which both require market‑value reporting for debt instruments.

Accrued interest continues to be recorded as property income (D.41) on an accrual basis, but the 2025 SNA introduces a “clean‑price” convention: the market value of a bond equals its clean price plus accrued interest. The clean price reflects the present value of future cash flows discounted at the current market yield; accrued interest is the coupon accrued since the last payment date. When a government issues a new bond at a premium or discount, the issue price determines the initial financial asset/liability value (AF.31 for short‑term, AF.32 for long‑term). Subsequent amortisation of the premium or discount is recorded as a negative or positive interest expense (D.41) over the life of the instrument, consistent with the effective‑interest method.

Central bank holdings of government securities (e.g., the Reserve Bank of India’s open‑market operations) are treated as a separate sub‑sector (S.121) in the financial corporations sector. The 2025 SNA requires that the central bank’s portfolio be valued at market prices, with revaluation gains/losses flowing through its own revaluation account. When the central bank purchases bonds in the secondary market, the transaction is recorded as an acquisition of AF.32 (liability of general government, asset of central bank) at the market price; the counterpart is a change in the central bank’s monetary base (currency in circulation and reserves). This ensures consistency between the monetary survey and the national accounts.

For index‑linked or inflation‑linked bonds, the principal adjustment for inflation is recorded as a holding gain (K.11) in the revaluation account, while the coupon payment (which may be fixed in real terms) is split into a real interest component (D.41) and an inflation compensation component (also K.11). The 2025 SNA also clarifies the treatment of sovereign‑guaranteed securities issued by public corporations: the guarantee creates a contingent liability (AF.8) for government, which is recognised on the balance sheet only when the guarantee is called. Until then, the security remains on the issuer’s balance sheet, and the government’s exposure is disclosed in the memorandum items.

In India, the Controller General of Accounts (CGA) and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) have begun aligning the Quarterly Public Debt Management Report with the 2025 SNA framework. The 2023‑24 Union Budget introduced a “market‑value based” reporting template for dated securities, treasury bills, and state development loans. The statistical discrepancy between the production‑side GDP and the expenditure‑side GDP is partly reduced when government debt is valued at market prices, because the interest‑payment component (D.41) becomes consistent with the accrual‑based primary deficit. Examiners often test the distinction between nominal‑value recording (legacy practice) and market‑value recording (2025 SNA), the placement of holding gains in K.11, and the correct sectoral classification of central‑bank holdings.

Digital Public Goods and Open Data Platforms: Extending the Production Boundary for Non‑Market Output

Digital public goods (DPGs) — open‑source software, open data platforms, and interoperable standards that are freely accessible — have become a distinct class of non‑market output. The 2025 SNA explicitly recognises that the production of DPGs by government agencies (or by non‑profit institutions serving households, NPISHs) falls within the production boundary when the output is “produced for own final use or for free distribution to the public” (SNA 2025, §6.124). The valuation follows the sum‑of‑costs method: intermediate consumption (e.g., cloud‑hosting fees, contractor payments) plus compensation of employees (including developers, data curators, and system administrators) plus consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) on the capitalised development cost (AN.1173, computer software and databases).

Capitalisation of DPG development costs requires that the software or database meet the SNA’s asset criteria: it must be used repeatedly in production for more than one year, be subject to control by the producing unit, and generate future economic benefits. For example, India’s DigiLocker platform (launched 2015) and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) architecture (operational since 2016) are capitalised as AN.1173. Their development expenditures — including the National Payments Corporation of India’s (NPCI) staff costs, server infrastructure, and third‑party integration work — are recorded as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in the government’s capital account. The subsequent consumption of fixed capital is charged over an estimated service life of three to five years, reflecting rapid technology obsolescence.

Open‑source contributions by volunteers pose a measurement challenge. The 2025 SNA recommends a satellite account for “collaborative production” where volunteer labour is valued at the replacement‑cost wage of a comparable professional (e.g., median software‑engineer compensation in the relevant region). This imputed compensation enters the production account of the NPISH or government unit that hosts the repository (e.g., the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology’s GitHub organisation). The corresponding output is the incremental improvement to the codebase, measured by lines of code added, bug fixes, or feature releases, and valued at the same replacement cost.

Data platforms such as the Open Government Data (OGD) portal (data.gov.in) generate non‑market output in the form of curated datasets, APIs, and metadata services. The 2025 SNA treats the curation activity as a service (CPC 8596, “Other information services”) produced by the hosting agency. The output value equals the sum of costs of data collection, cleaning, anonymisation, and portal maintenance. When private firms reuse these datasets to build commercial products, the SNA records the private firm’s output separately; the government’s DPG output is not reduced — it remains a free‑distribution service. This avoids double counting while preserving the contribution of public data infrastructure to downstream productivity.

Examiners frequently test the distinction between “free‑of‑charge” services (which are inside the production boundary) and “pure public goods” with no identifiable producer (which remain outside). They also check whether candidates correctly apply the consumption‑of‑fixed‑capital schedule for software (geometric depreciation at 30‑40 % per year) and whether they recognise that volunteer contributions are imputed, not recorded as actual compensation of employees. A common error is to treat the entire UPI transaction value as government output; only the cost of operating the switch, settlement, and dispute‑resolution infrastructure enters GDP.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The government launches an open‑source contact‑tracing app during a pandemic. The app is developed by a team of 20 engineers paid ₹1 crore each per year, hosted on cloud servers costing ₹5 crore annually, and maintained by 200 volunteers contributing an estimated 10 000 hours per year. The median software‑engineer wage is ₹1.2 crore per year. Compute the non‑market output of the app for the year under the 2025 SNA.”
Non‑market output = compensation of employees (20 × ₹1 crore = ₹20 crore) + intermediate consumption (cloud ₹5 crore) + consumption of fixed capital on capitalised development cost (assume development cost ₹25 crore, 5‑year straight‑line → ₹5 crore) + imputed volunteer compensation (10 000 hours ÷ 2 000 hours per FTE = 5 FTE × ₹1.2 crore = ₹6 crore). Total = ₹20 crore + ₹5 crore + ₹5 crore + ₹6 crore = ₹36 crore. The volunteer imputation uses replacement‑cost wage, not actual payment. The cloud cost is intermediate consumption, not capital formation. The development cost is capitalised (AN.1173) and depreciated.
Exam‑day strategy
When a DPG question appears, first identify the producing institutional unit (government, NPISH, or public corporation). Then list all cost components: (1) compensation of employees, (2) intermediate consumption, (3) consumption of fixed capital on capitalised software/database, (4) imputed volunteer labour at replacement cost. Do not add the market value of the final service (e.g., number of downloads × price) — the SNA uses sum‑of‑costs for non‑market output. Remember the geometric depreciation rate for software (≈30‑40 % per year) and the three‑to‑five‑year service life. If the question asks for the balance‑sheet entry, record the capitalised development cost as AN.1173 and the accumulated consumption of fixed capital as a negative asset.

Trade in Services by Mode of Supply: Capturing Mode 1‑4 Flows in the Balance of Payments and National Accounts

The General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS) defines four modes of supply: Mode 1 (cross‑border), Mode 2 (consumption abroad), Mode 3 (commercial presence), and Mode 4 (presence of natural persons). The 2025 SNA and BPM6 require that each mode be recorded consistently in the balance of payments (BOP) and the rest‑of‑the‑world account of the national accounts. Mode 1 exports (e.g., IT‑enabled services delivered from India to the United States) appear as “telecommunications, computer, and information services” (EBOPS 2010 code SI) in the services account. Mode 2 covers travel‑related services (e.g., foreign tourists consuming health services in India) and is recorded under “travel” (EBOPS code SD). Mode 3 reflects foreign‑affiliate sales (FATS) — the output of foreign‑owned enterprises resident in the compiling economy — and is captured in the primary income account (investment income) and in the production account of the affiliate. Mode 4 records compensation of employees (D.11) for short‑term business visitors and contractual service suppliers, and is part of the “other business services” category when the stay exceeds one year.

Measurement relies on a combination of enterprise surveys (e.g., RBI’s Survey of Computer Software and Information Technology Enabled Services), administrative data (visa issuance, work‑permit records), and mirror statistics from partner countries. India’s Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics (DGCI&S) compiles the “Services Export Promotion Council” (SEPC) data, which provides mode‑wise breakdowns for IT/ITeS (Mode 1), medical tourism (Mode 2), and foreign‑direct‑investment‑linked service affiliates (Mode 3). The 2025 SNA introduces a “mode‑of‑supply” dimension in the supply‑use tables, allowing analysts to trace how a given service product (CPC 843, “Computer programming services”) is supplied across modes.

A persistent challenge is the “digital delivery” of services that blur Mode 1 and Mode 3. For instance, a cloud‑based SaaS platform hosted on Indian servers but sold to a foreign client via a subscription may be recorded as Mode 1 (cross‑border) if the supplier is resident in India, but as Mode 3 if the supplier establishes a local legal entity in the client’s country. The 2025 SNA recommends using the “economic ownership” principle: the resident unit that bears the entrepreneurial risk and controls the production process determines the mode. This aligns with the OECD’s “Framework for Digital Trade” (2022) and the UNCTAD “Digital Economy Report” (2023).

In the national accounts, Mode 3 output contributes to domestic GDP (as production of the foreign affiliate), while the corresponding income (profits, reinvested earnings) flows to the foreign parent as primary income (D.42). Mode 4 compensation of employees is part of the domestic compensation of employees if the worker is resident; otherwise it is recorded as “compensation of employees to the rest of the world” (D.11 payable). The 2025 SNA also requires that “merchanting” of services (buying and reselling without transformation) be recorded net in the services account, consistent with goods merchanting.

Examiners test the ability to map a concrete transaction — e.g., an Indian doctor providing tele‑consultation to a patient in the UAE — to the correct mode (Mode 1) and the correct BOP code (SI.1, “Telecommunications, computer, and information services”). They also check whether candidates recognise that Mode 2 travel receipts include both the service fee and the associated travel expenditure, and that the travel component must be split using the “travel‑services” ratio derived from visitor surveys.

Monitoring Sustainable Development Goal 8 through National Accounts: Indicators, Gaps, and Policy Linkages

Sustainable Development Goal 8 (SDG 8) — “Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all” — is monitored through a suite of indicators that draw directly on national accounts and labour‑account data. Target 8.1 (sustain per‑capita GDP growth) uses real GDP per capita (chain‑linked volume measure) from the production account. Target 8.2 (higher economic productivity) relies on labour productivity (real GDP per hour worked) derived from the KLEMS database, which integrates capital (K), labour (L), energy (E), materials (M), and services (S) inputs. Target 8.5 (full employment and decent work) requires the unemployment rate, labour‑force participation rate, and the proportion of informal employment — the latter obtained from the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) and linked to the household sector accounts.

Target 8.6 (reduce youth NEET) uses the “youth not in education, employment or training” rate, which can be cross‑checked against the “education” and “employment” satellite accounts. Target 8.10 (strengthen domestic financial institutions) is tracked by the “financial inclusion” indicator — the share of adults with a bank account — sourced from the World Bank’s Global Findex but also reflected in the financial corporations’ balance‑sheet data (deposits, credit to households). The 2025 SNA’s distributional national accounts (DNA) framework enables disaggregation of GDP growth by income quintile, providing a direct measure of “inclusive growth” for Target 8.1.

Gaps remain: the informal sector’s value added is still estimated via the “mixed‑survey” method (enterprise survey + household survey) and may not capture platform‑based gig work. The 2025 SNA’s extension of the production boundary to include “digital platform labour” (as own‑account workers) improves coverage, but the classification of gig workers as employees versus own‑account workers affects the labour‑share indicator (Target 8.5). Moreover, the “decent work” dimension (wages, social protection, safety) requires linking national accounts to administrative data on social‑security contributions (EPFO, ESIC) and occupational‑injury statistics — a linkage not yet standardised in the Indian system.

Policy linkages: the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) publishes the “SDG India Index” annually, which incorporates national‑accounts‑derived indicators (per‑capita NSDP growth, manufacturing share, export‑to‑GDP ratio). The NITI Aayog’s “Aspirational Districts Programme” uses district‑level GDP estimates (derived from night‑time lights and state‑account allocations) to monitor Target 8.1 at sub‑national level. The 2025 SNA’s integration of the System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting (SEEA) allows simultaneous tracking of Target 8.4 (resource efficiency) via material‑footprint per unit of GDP.

Examiners often ask candidates to identify which national‑accounts aggregate feeds a specific SDG 8 indicator, to explain the chain‑linking methodology for real GDP per capita, or to describe how the DNA framework can reveal whether growth is “inclusive”. A common trap is confusing “GDP per capita” (Target 8.1) with “GDP per employed person” (Target 8.2) — the former uses total population, the latter uses total employment from the labour accounts.

Hedonic and Stated‑Preference Valuation of Non‑Market Environmental Services in Satellite Accounts

The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting — Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA‑EA) recommends two broad families of valuation techniques for ecosystem services that lack market prices: revealed‑preference methods (hedonic pricing, travel‑cost) and stated‑preference methods (contingent valuation, choice experiments). Hedonic pricing decomposes the market price of a heterogeneous good — typically residential property — into implicit prices for its attributes, including environmental quality (air‑pollution levels, proximity to green space, noise exposure). The coefficient on the environmental attribute, estimated via a semi‑log or Box‑Cox regression, yields the marginal willingness‑to‑pay (MWTP) for a unit improvement. In India, the National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA) applied hedonic models to Delhi’s housing market (2018‑2021) and estimated an MWTP of ₹1.2 lakh per µg/m³ reduction in PM₂.₅, which was then used to value the “air‑filtration” regulating service in the Delhi‑NCR ecosystem account.

Travel‑cost methods estimate the recreational value of a site (e.g., a national park) by modelling the number of visits as a function of travel cost, travel time, and site characteristics. The consumer surplus derived from the demand curve provides the annual recreational service value. The Wildlife Institute of India (WII) used a zonal travel‑cost model for the Sundarbans Tiger Reserve (2020) and obtained a recreational value of ₹420 crore per year, entered as a cultural service in the SEEA‑EA physical‑flow account and subsequently monetised in the monetary‑flow account.

Stated‑preference methods are employed when no behavioural market exists. Contingent valuation (CV) asks respondents directly for their willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) for a specified environmental change (e.g., restoring a wetland). Choice experiments (CE) present bundles of attribute levels (water quality, biodiversity, access) and estimate part‑worth utilities via a multinomial logit or mixed logit model. The 2025 SNA recognises CE as the preferred stated‑preference technique because it yields attribute‑specific values and reduces embedding effects. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) commissioned a CE for the Chilika Lake restoration (2022), estimating a total WTP of ₹1 200 crore for a 30 % improvement in water‑quality index, which was recorded as a “water‑purification” regulating service.

Integration into satellite accounts follows the SEEA‑EA “valuation hierarchy”: (1) market prices where available, (2) cost‑based methods (replacement cost, avoided damage cost) for regulating services, (3) revealed‑preference methods for cultural and some provisioning services, (4) stated‑preference methods as a last resort. All values are expressed in constant prices (base year 2022‑23) using the GDP deflator, and are entered in the monetary supply‑use table under “ecosystem services” (ES) with a corresponding physical flow in the physical supply‑use table. The 2025 SNA requires that valuation uncertainty be documented — confidence intervals from the regression or simulation‑based intervals from the CE — and reported in the metadata.

Examiners test the ability to match a service (e.g., “noise reduction by urban trees”) to the appropriate valuation method (hedonic pricing on property values), to interpret a regression coefficient as MWTP, and to distinguish between “exchange value” (SNA‑compatible) and “welfare value” (including consumer surplus). A frequent error is to add the consumer surplus from a travel‑cost model directly to GDP; the SNA only records the exchange‑value equivalent (the amount visitors would pay if a market existed), not the full welfare surplus.

  • Confusing nominal‑value recording of government debt with the 2025 SNA market‑value requirement and misplacing holding gains in the production account instead of the revaluation account (K.11).
  • Treating the entire transaction value of a digital public platform (e.g., UPI) as government output rather than applying the sum‑of‑costs valuation with proper capitalisation of software (AN.1173) and geometric depreciation.
  • Assigning a cross‑border digital service to Mode 3 (commercial presence) when the supplier remains resident in the home economy and bears entrepreneurial risk — the correct mode is Mode 1.
  • Using GDP per capita (population denominator) for Target 8.2 (productivity) instead of GDP per hour worked (employment denominator) from the KLEMS database.
  • Adding the full consumer surplus from a travel‑cost or contingent‑valuation study to the monetary ecosystem‑services account, whereas the SNA records only the exchange‑value equivalent.
  • Recording volunteer contributions to open‑source projects as actual compensation of employees instead of imputed compensation at replacement‑cost wages in a satellite account.
  • Misclassifying spectrum‑auction proceeds as non‑tax revenue (D.29) in the generation‑of‑income account; they are disposal of a natural resource (K.2) with the bidder acquiring AN.115 financed by an implicit loan.

Measuring the Economic Impact of Cybersecurity Incidents and Digital Resilience in National Accounts

Cybersecurity incidents generate both direct costs (incident response, forensic investigation, legal fees, regulatory fines) and indirect costs (lost output, reputational damage, reduced consumer confidence). The 2008 SNA treats defensive expenditures on security software, hardware, and personnel as intermediate consumption when purchased by enterprises, and as final consumption when incurred by government. However, the loss of productive capacity due to system downtime or data breaches is not captured in the production account unless it can be linked to a measurable reduction in output. The 2025 SNA introduces a satellite‑account framework for “digital resilience” that records (i) defensive investment as gross fixed capital formation (AN.1173 for software, AN.113 for hardware), (ii) the estimated output loss as a negative contribution to value added in the period of disruption, and (iii) insurance recoveries as a transfer (D.71) that offsets the loss. In India, the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT‑In) publishes quarterly incident reports that can be combined with the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) to estimate sector‑level downtime. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) circular on cyber‑risk management for banks mandates disclosure of cyber‑loss provisions, providing a data source for the financial‑corporations sub‑sector. A practical compilation route is to (a) map each reported incident to an industry using the NIC‑2008 code, (b) apply a sector‑specific downtime‑to‑output elasticity derived from firm‑level panel regressions, and (c) aggregate the implied output loss to the national accounts. The resulting “cyber‑adjusted GDP” can be presented as a supplementary indicator alongside the headline figure, allowing policymakers to assess the macroeconomic relevance of digital security investments.

Methodologically, two approaches dominate. The cost‑of‑illness method sums all observable expenditures (hardware, software, personnel, insurance premiums, incident‑response contracts) and adds an imputed value for unreported incidents based on survey‑based incidence rates. The production‑function approach estimates a Cobb‑Douglas or translog function where cyber‑capital (stock of security assets) enters as an input; the marginal product of cyber‑capital yields the avoided output loss. The latter aligns with the 2025 SNA’s recommendation to capitalise defensive software and to treat the flow of security services as a produced asset. Data gaps remain: many small firms do not report incidents, and the valuation of intangible losses (brand erosion, customer churn) relies on stated‑preference surveys that the SNA records only in a welfare‑oriented satellite account, not in the core GDP. Examiners often test the distinction between defensive expenditure (recorded in the production account) and welfare loss (recorded only in a satellite account), and the correct classification of insurance recoveries as current transfers rather than as negative intermediate consumption.

Valuation of Urban Green Infrastructure and Ecosystem Services for Municipal Accounting

Urban green infrastructure — parks, street trees, wetlands, green roofs — delivers a bundle of ecosystem services: air‑pollution removal, heat‑island mitigation, storm‑water regulation, recreation, and aesthetic value. The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA‑EA) provides a valuation hierarchy that the 2025 SNA adopts for municipal satellite accounts: (1) market prices where a direct market exists (e.g., timber from urban forestry), (2) cost‑based methods such as replacement cost for storm‑water infrastructure avoided by wetlands, (3) revealed‑preference methods (hedonic pricing on property values, travel‑cost for park visits), and (4) stated‑preference methods (choice experiments) as a last resort. In practice, hedonic models regress housing prices on proximity to green space, controlling for structural and neighbourhood attributes; the coefficient on distance yields the marginal willingness‑to‑pay (MWTP) for an additional hectare of park. The National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA) applied this to Delhi’s housing market (2018‑2021) and estimated an MWTP of ₹1.2 lakh per µg/m³ reduction in PM₂.₅, which was entered as an “air‑filtration” regulating service in the Delhi‑NCR ecosystem account. Travel‑cost models estimate the recreational value of a park by modelling visit frequency as a function of travel cost, time, and site quality; the consumer surplus derived from the demand curve provides the annual recreational service value. The Wildlife Institute of India (WII) used a zonal travel‑cost model for the Sundarbans Tiger Reserve (2020) and obtained a recreational value of ₹420 crore per year, recorded as a cultural service. Stated‑preference choice experiments are employed when no behavioural market exists; the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) commissioned a choice experiment for Chilika Lake restoration (2022), estimating a total willingness‑to‑pay of ₹1 200 crore for a 30 % improvement in water‑quality index, entered as a “water‑purification” regulating service. All values are expressed in constant prices (base year 2022‑23) using the GDP deflator and entered in the monetary supply‑use table under “ecosystem services” with a matching physical flow in the physical supply‑use table. The 2025 SNA requires documentation of valuation uncertainty — confidence intervals from regressions or simulation‑based intervals from choice experiments — in the metadata.

Integration into municipal accounts follows a three‑step process: (i) compile a physical asset register of green infrastructure using high‑resolution satellite imagery and municipal GIS layers; (ii) estimate service flows per asset class using the valuation hierarchy; (iii) record the monetary flows in a municipal ecosystem‑services satellite account that is linked to the city‑level GDP via the “environmental protection expenditure” (EPE) account. This linkage permits the calculation of a “green‑adjusted net municipal product” that adds the value of regulating and cultural services to the conventional production boundary. A frequent examiner trap is to add the full consumer surplus from a travel‑cost model directly to municipal GDP; the SNA only records the exchange‑value equivalent (the amount visitors would pay if a market existed), not the welfare surplus. Another trap is to treat the replacement‑cost estimate for storm‑water regulation as a capital formation item; it remains a non‑market service valued at cost and recorded in the use table, not as gross fixed capital formation.

Matching Valuation Method to Ecosystem Service
A municipal accountant must value the noise‑reduction service provided by a belt of urban trees along a highway. Which SEEA‑EA valuation method is most appropriate, and why?
The appropriate method is hedonic pricing on property values. Noise reduction is a localised amenity that capitalises into nearby residential prices; a hedonic regression can isolate the marginal willingness‑to‑pay for a decibel reduction by controlling for other housing attributes. Cost‑based methods would not capture the welfare gain, travel‑cost methods are irrelevant because there is no recreational visit, and stated‑preference methods are a last resort when no behavioural market exists. The hedonic coefficient, expressed in ₹ per decibel, is entered as an exchange‑value regulating service in the monetary supply‑use table.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the SEEA‑EA valuation hierarchy (market price → cost‑based → revealed‑preference → stated‑preference) and the rule that only exchange‑value equivalents enter the core SNA; welfare surplus stays in satellite accounts. When a question asks “which method for service X?”, first identify whether a market transaction exists, then whether a behavioural proxy (property price, travel cost) is observable, and only then consider a survey‑based approach.

Accounting for the Economic Contribution of the Informal Services Sector Using Mobile Phone and Transaction Data

The informal services sector — domestic work, street vending, ride‑hailing drivers not registered on platforms, small‑scale repair, personal care — remains largely invisible in conventional enterprise surveys. The 2008 SNA recommends a mixed‑method approach: (i) household‑based labour force surveys (LFS) to capture employment and hours, (ii) enterprise surveys (e.g., the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises) for output and value added, and (iii) administrative data (tax registers, social‑security contributions) where available. In India, the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) conducts the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) and the Unincorporated Non‑Agricultural Enterprises Survey (UNAES), but coverage gaps persist for digitally mediated informal work. The proliferation of mobile‑money accounts (e.g., Paytm, PhonePe) and Unified Payments Interface (UPI) transaction logs offers a high‑frequency, granular proxy for turnover. The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) has piloted a “big‑data‑augmented” estimation framework that (a) extracts anonymised UPI merchant‑category codes for services (food‑delivery, transport, personal care), (b) matches them to NIC‑2008 classes using a concordance table, and (c) applies a capture‑recapture model to adjust for merchants who transact exclusively in cash. The capture‑recapture estimator uses the overlap between the UPI‑observed set and the UNAES‑sampled set to infer the total population of informal service providers. An alternative is the Multiple Indicators Multiple Causes (MIMIC) model, where latent informal‑sector output is regressed on observable indicators: mobile‑phone density, UPI transaction volume, electricity consumption of non‑registered premises, and night‑time lights intensity at the ward level. The fitted values provide district‑level informal‑service value added, which can be aggregated to the state and national levels. The 2025 SNA encourages the use of such alternative data sources, provided that (i) the estimation methodology is documented, (ii) uncertainty intervals are reported, and (iii) the results are reconciled with the benchmark UNAES estimates through a balancing procedure in the supply‑use framework. A key compilation challenge is the “double‑counting” risk: a ride‑hailing driver who appears both in the PLFS (as employed) and in the UPI data (as a merchant) must be counted once. The recommended solution is to treat the PLFS as the employment frame and the UPI data as the output frame, linking them via a unique identifier (e.g., Aadhaar‑linked mobile number) in a secure data‑exchange environment. Examiners often test the distinction between the “employment‑based” and “output‑based” approaches, and the correct placement of imputed informal output in the production account (as output of the household sector, industry code 97) rather than as a separate institutional sector.

Treatment of Carbon Credits and Emission Trading Schemes in the SNA and SEEA

Carbon credits — certified emission reductions (CERs), verified emission reductions (VERs), and allowances allocated under cap‑and‑trade systems — straddle the boundary between environmental assets and financial instruments. The 2008 SNA classifies emission allowances that are tradable and have a market price as financial assets (AF.71 “financial derivatives and employee stock options” when they are derivatives, or AF.8 “other accounts receivable/payable” when they are spot allowances). The 2025 SNA refines this by introducing a distinct asset class AN.221 “emission allowances” under non‑produced non‑financial assets when the allowance represents a right to emit a specific quantity of greenhouse gas and is not a derivative. The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting – Central Framework (SEEA‑CF) records the physical flow of emissions and the corresponding permit allocation in the “air emission accounts” and the “environmental protection expenditure accounts”. In a cap‑and‑trade scheme, the initial free allocation is recorded as a government transfer (D.99) to the receiving enterprise, increasing its net worth. Subsequent purchases and sales are recorded as transactions in financial assets (F.71) with counterpart entries in the financial account. When an enterprise surrenders allowances to comply, the surrender is a use of the asset (a reduction in AN.221) and a corresponding increase in “environmental protection expenditure” (EPE) if the surrender is treated as a cost of compliance. In India, the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme issues energy‑saving certificates (ESCerts) that function similarly to carbon credits. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) maintains a registry; the certificates are tradable on the Indian Energy Exchange. For national accounts, ESCerts are treated as AN.221 assets held by designated consumers. The initial allocation is a government transfer; trading is recorded in the financial account; surrender at the end of the compliance cycle reduces the asset and is recorded as an environmental protection expenditure. The SEEA‑CF also requires a physical flow account that tracks tonnes of CO₂ equivalent covered by each certificate, enabling the construction of a “carbon‑adjusted net domestic product” that subtracts the social cost of carbon from GDP. A common examiner error is to record the market value of surrendered allowances as intermediate consumption; the correct treatment is a reduction in the non‑produced asset (AN.221) with a matching entry in the capital account (K.2) and an EPE entry in the use table. Another trap is to classify freely allocated allowances as revenue (D.2) rather than as a transfer (D.99), which would overstate government revenue and understate the enterprise’s net worth.

  • Confusing defensive cyber‑expenditure (recorded as intermediate consumption or GFCF) with welfare loss from breaches (recorded only in a satellite account).
  • Adding full consumer surplus from travel‑cost or hedonic models to municipal GDP instead of the exchange‑value equivalent.
  • Treating replacement‑cost estimates for storm‑water regulation as gross fixed capital formation rather than as a non‑market service in the use table.
  • Double‑counting informal service providers who appear in both labour‑force surveys and digital‑transaction data without a unique identifier linkage.
  • Classifying freely allocated emission allowances as government revenue (D.2) instead of a transfer (D.99) and misplacing surrender entries in intermediate consumption.
  • Recording the market value of surrendered carbon credits as intermediate consumption rather than as a reduction of the non‑produced asset AN.221 with a capital‑account entry.
  • Using GDP per capita as the denominator for productivity targets (SDG 8.2) instead of GDP per hour worked from the KLEMS database.

These advanced sections equip aspirants with the mechanistic detail and examiner‑focused nuances required for high‑scoring answers in the economy, environment, and national‑income components of the syllabus.

Accounting for Renewable Energy Certificates and Green Certificates in the SNA and SEEA

Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) and similar green certificates represent a tradable right to claim the environmental attributes of one megawatt‑hour of electricity generated from eligible renewable sources. In the 2008 SNA they are recorded as non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.221 “emission allowances”) when the certificate conveys a right to emit or to claim a specific quantity of renewable generation and is not a derivative. The 2025 SNA refines this by explicitly creating a distinct asset class AN.221 for emission allowances and extending the same treatment to renewable certificates that function as compliance instruments under renewable purchase obligations. The initial allocation — whether by government mandate, regulatory authority, or a voluntary registry — is recorded as a capital transfer (D.99) from the issuing body to the recipient enterprise, increasing the latter’s net worth. Subsequent purchases and sales are transactions in financial assets (F.71) with counterpart entries in the financial account. When a liable entity surrenders certificates to meet its obligation, the surrender reduces the asset (AN.221) and is recorded as environmental protection expenditure (EPE) in the use table, not as intermediate consumption. The SEEA‑CF requires a parallel physical flow account that tracks megawatt‑hours covered by each certificate, enabling the construction of a “green‑adjusted net domestic product” that adds the social value of renewable generation to GDP. In India, the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) operates the REC mechanism; certificates are traded on the Indian Energy Exchange and the Power Exchange India. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency maintains the registry. For national accounts, Indian RECs are treated as AN.221 assets held by obligated entities (distribution licensees, open‑access consumers). The initial allocation by the state nodal agency is a government transfer (D.99); trading is recorded in the financial account; surrender at the compliance deadline reduces the asset and is entered as EPE. A common examiner error is to record the market value of surrendered RECs as intermediate consumption, which overstates production costs and understates net worth. Another trap is to classify freely allocated RECs as government revenue (D.2) rather than a transfer (D.99), thereby misstating fiscal balances.

Treatment of Sovereign Debt Restructuring, Haircuts, and Contingent Liabilities in the National Balance Sheet

Sovereign debt restructuring involves the exchange of existing debt instruments for new ones with altered terms — lower principal (haircut), extended maturity, reduced coupon, or currency conversion. In the SNA, a haircut is recorded as a capital transfer (D.99) from the creditor to the debtor government, reducing the liability (AF.3) and increasing the debtor’s net worth. The counterpart entry is a reduction in the creditor’s financial assets. When restructuring includes a debt‑for‑equity swap, the government records an increase in equity liabilities (AF.5) and a decrease in debt securities (AF.3). Contingent liabilities — such as government guarantees, explicit or implicit, and potential calls on sovereign wealth funds — are not recorded as liabilities in the core balance sheet until the contingency materialises. The 2025 SNA introduces a memorandum item for “contingent liabilities” in the national balance sheet, requiring disclosure of the maximum potential exposure, probability‑weighted expected loss, and the discount rate used. In India, the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act mandates disclosure of guarantees in the Medium‑Term Fiscal Policy Statement, but they remain off‑balance‑sheet until invoked. The 2025 SNA also requires that any expected loss on guarantees be recognised as a provision (AF.8) when the probability of call exceeds 50 %. A haircut on external debt held by non‑residents is recorded in the balance of payments as a capital transfer (D.99) in the capital account, with a corresponding reduction in the international investment position. Examiners often test the distinction between a pure haircut (capital transfer) and a debt rescheduling without principal reduction (re‑classification of existing liabilities). Another trap is to treat the entire face value of a guaranteed loan as a government liability at inception; the correct treatment is to record the guarantee as a contingent liability and only recognise the called amount as a liability when the guarantee is invoked.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “In the national accounts, how is a 30 % haircut on sovereign bonds held by domestic banks recorded? Show the entries in the government and bank sector accounts.”
The haircut is a capital transfer (D.99) from the banks to the government. In the government sector: ΔAF.3 (debt securities) = –30 % of face value; ΔNet worth = +30 % (via D.99 receivable). In the bank sector: ΔAF.3 (assets) = –30 % of face value; ΔNet worth = –30 % (via D.99 payable). No change in output, value added, or GDP occurs because the transaction is a pure balance‑sheet restructuring.
Exam‑day strategy
When a restructuring scenario appears, first identify whether principal is reduced (haircut) or only terms change. Haircut ⇒ capital transfer (D.99). Rescheduling ⇒ re‑classification of existing liability (no net worth change). Always show the counterpart entries in both debtor and creditor sector accounts to secure full marks.

Valuation of Digital Public Infrastructure: Identity Systems, Payment Rails, and Open Networks in National Accounts

Digital public infrastructure (DPI) — exemplified by India’s Aadhaar identity platform, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), DigiLocker, and the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) — provides non‑market services that underlie a large share of formal and informal economic activity. The 2025 SNA treats data and digital platforms as produced assets (AN.112 “computer software and databases”) when they are the result of a production process with a clear ownership right. For DPI, the production is undertaken by government or a public‑private entity, and the output is a non‑market service provided free or at nominal cost to users. The SNA recommends valuing such output at the sum of production costs (intermediate consumption, compensation of employees, consumption of fixed capital, and a return to capital) — the “cost‑of‑production” approach. An alternative is the “user‑cost” approach, which imputes a rental price equal to the opportunity cost of capital plus depreciation, applied to the capital stock of the platform. In practice, statistical offices compile a satellite account for DPI: the production account records output (P.1) valued at cost, intermediate consumption (P.2) includes server hosting, telecommunications, and maintenance; compensation of employees (D.1) covers developers and operators; consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) reflects the depreciation of hardware and software. The resulting value added enters government final consumption expenditure (P.3) if the service is collectively consumed, or household final consumption (P.3) if individually consumed (e.g., Aadhaar authentication for a subsidy). The 2025 SNA also introduces a distinct asset class for “data” (AN.113) when data is produced and owned, allowing the stock of data generated by DPI to appear on the balance sheet. Cross‑border data flows — such as UPI transactions initiated by non‑residents — are recorded in the balance of payments as exports of telecommunications, computer, and information services (EBOPS code SI). A frequent examiner twist is to ask whether the imputed value of free UPI transactions should be added to GDP; the correct answer is that only the cost‑of‑production of the platform enters GDP, not the consumer surplus from zero‑price transactions.

Integration of the System of National Accounts with the System of Health Accounts: Health Expenditure Satellite Accounts

The System of Health Accounts (SHA 2011) provides a tri‑axial classification of health expenditure by function (HC.1‑HC.9), provider (HP.1‑HP.9), and financing scheme (HF.1‑HF.3). To integrate SHA with the SNA, a health expenditure satellite account re‑expresses SHA aggregates in SNA terminology. Government health spending on public hospitals (HP.1) is recorded as government final consumption expenditure (P.3) on health services (COFOG 07). Household out‑of‑pocket payments for private clinics (HP.3) appear as household final consumption expenditure (P.3) on health. Social health insurance contributions (HF.1.2) are treated as social contributions (D.61) received by the insurance scheme, with benefits paid recorded as social benefits (D.62) to households. The satellite account also captures imputed values for non‑market health services — such as free immunisation campaigns — by valuing them at cost of production (intermediate consumption plus compensation of employees plus consumption of fixed capital). In India, the National Health Accounts (NHA) follow SHA guidelines and are reconciled with the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation’s (MoSPI) estimates of government health expenditure in the national accounts. The 2025 SNA encourages the use of “health‑adjusted net domestic product” where the depreciation of health capital (e.g., hospital buildings, medical equipment) is subtracted from GDP, and the value of health‑enhancing human capital is added via a satellite account. A common examiner error is to double‑count health insurance premiums as both household consumption and government expenditure; the correct mapping places premiums in the financing scheme dimension (HF) and the resulting benefits in the use table under household consumption. Another trap is to treat capital formation in health infrastructure (new hospitals) as current health expenditure; it must be recorded as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in the capital account, with the service flow entering consumption over the asset’s life.

Measuring the Economic Impact of Climate Adaptation Expenditure in National Accounts

Climate adaptation expenditure comprises outlays that reduce vulnerability to climate change — such as flood defences, drought‑resilient crops, early‑warning systems, and ecosystem‑based adaptation like mangrove restoration. In the SNA, adaptation spending by government is classified either as government final consumption expenditure (P.3) for current protective services (e.g., operation of early‑warning centres) or as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) when it creates a durable asset (e.g., seawall, irrigation infrastructure). Household adaptation spending (e.g., house elevation) is recorded as household final consumption (P.3) if it is a current expense, or as gross fixed capital formation if it adds to the dwelling’s value. The SEEA‑CF introduces an “adaptation expenditure account” that mirrors the environmental protection expenditure account (EPEA) but separates adaptation from mitigation. Physical flow tables track the quantity of adaptation measures (kilometres of embankment, hectares of restored wetland) alongside monetary outlays. The 2025 SNA recommends that the consumption of fixed capital on adaptation assets be calculated using the same service lives as comparable infrastructure, and that the net capital stock of adaptation assets be shown in the national balance sheet as a separate memorandum item. In India, the National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC) finances state‑level projects; these outlays appear in the Union and state budgets under “Climate Change Adaptation” and are captured in the national accounts as government capital formation or consumption depending on the project nature. A frequent examiner twist is to ask whether the benefits of avoided flood damage should be added to GDP; the SNA records only the expenditure, not the avoided loss, although a satellite “climate‑adjusted net domestic product” can be constructed by subtracting estimated expected damages from GDP. Another trap is to classify ecosystem‑based adaptation (e.g., mangrove planting) as intermediate consumption of the forestry industry; it should be recorded as gross fixed capital formation in the government sector (or non‑profit institutions serving households) with the ecosystem service flow entering the SEEA‑EA physical accounts.

  • Recording the market value of surrendered renewable certificates as intermediate consumption instead of a reduction in AN.221 with a capital‑account entry.
  • Classifying freely allocated emission allowances or RECs as government revenue (D.2) rather than a capital transfer (D.99).
  • Treating a sovereign debt haircut as a re‑valuation of existing liabilities instead of a capital transfer (D.99) that changes net worth.
  • Recognising the full face value of a government guarantee as a liability at inception rather than as a contingent liability disclosed in a memorandum item.
  • Adding consumer surplus from free digital public infrastructure services to GDP instead of valuing the platform at cost of production.
  • Double‑counting health insurance premiums as both household consumption and government expenditure in the health satellite account.
  • Classifying ecosystem‑based adaptation spending as intermediate consumption of the primary sector rather than as gross fixed capital formation with a separate adaptation asset memorandum item.
  • These traps highlight the need for careful classification and consistent application of SNA principles.

Tourism Satellite Accounts: Methodology, Compilation, and Indian Experience

The Tourism Satellite Account (TSA) extends the core System of National Accounts by isolating the economic activities that are directly linked to visitors. The United Nations World Tourism Organization (UNWTO) and the OECD jointly publish the Tourism Satellite Account: Recommended Methodological Framework (2008), which defines tourism‑characteristic products, tourism‑connected products, and non‑tourism products.
