The TSA follows the production, income, and expenditure approaches of the 2008 SNA, but adds a tourism‑specific dimension: the “tourism consumption” vector that aggregates household, business, and government spending on tourism‑characteristic goods and services. In India, the Ministry of Tourism, in collaboration with the National Statistical Office (NSO), released the first official TSA for the reference year 2009‑10, updated for 2015‑16 and 2019‑20. The compilation uses the Domestic Tourism Expenditure Survey (DTES) and the International Visitor Survey (IVS) to estimate inbound, domestic, and outbound tourism expenditure. The supply‑use tables are re‑balanced to allocate the tourism share of each product, employing the “tourism ratio” method where the tourism‑characteristic output of an industry is divided by its total output. A key output is the Tourism Direct Gross Value Added (TDGVA), which in 2019‑20 stood at approximately 5.2 % of GDP, and Tourism Direct Employment, which captured both formal and informal jobs. The TSA also produces a Tourism Satellite Account for the informal sector by applying the same tourism ratios to the unorganised sector estimates from the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) and the NSSO’s Enterprise Survey. Examiners often test the distinction between “tourism‑characteristic” and “tourism‑connected” products: the former would cease to exist in meaningful quantity without visitors (e.g., hotel accommodation, travel agency services), while the latter are consumed by both visitors and residents (e.g., food and beverage services). Another trap is to treat the entire output of the hospitality industry as tourism output; the correct procedure applies the tourism ratio to each industry’s output.

Accounting for Public Education Expenditure and Human Capital Formation in National Accounts

Public education expenditure is recorded in the SNA under government final consumption expenditure (P.3) when it finances current operations such as teacher salaries, textbooks, and school maintenance. However, the 2008 SNA and the 2025 revision recognise that education also creates a durable asset — human capital — which is not captured in the core production boundary. The Jorgenson‑Fraumeni (JF) lifetime income approach estimates the market value of the stock of human capital by discounting expected future earnings of the educated population. India’s pilot human‑capital satellite account, prepared by the National Statistical Office in collaboration with the World Bank, applies the JF methodology to Census and NSSO education attainment data, producing a human‑capital stock estimate of roughly 250 % of GDP for 2017‑18. The satellite account distinguishes three components: (i) the cost‑based value of formal education (government and private expenditure on schools, colleges, vocational training), (ii) the imputed value of non‑market household education services (parental time spent on homework assistance), and (iii) the health‑adjusted education component that accounts for the complementarity between health and learning. In the core accounts, government capital formation in education infrastructure (new school buildings, laboratories) is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) under the government sector, with consumption of fixed capital (CFC) charged over the asset’s service life. A frequent examiner error is to double‑count education spending by adding both the current expenditure (P.3) and the capital formation (P.51g) to “education investment” without recognising that the former is consumption and the latter is investment. Another trap is to treat the imputed value of household education time as part of GDP; the SNA excludes non‑market household production from the production boundary, so it appears only in a satellite account. The 2025 SNA encourages the presentation of a “human‑capital‑adjusted net domestic product” where the depreciation of education‑related fixed assets is subtracted and the net addition to human capital stock is added as a memorandum item.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “If the government spends ₹10,000 crore on teacher salaries and ₹2,000 crore on constructing new school buildings in a year, how should these be recorded in the national accounts?”
Teacher salaries are current expenditure and enter government final consumption expenditure (P.3). The construction of school buildings is gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in the government sector. The consumption of fixed capital on those buildings will be recorded in subsequent years as CFC. The two outlays must not be summed as a single “education investment” figure in the core accounts.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes current and capital education outlays, first separate them by economic nature (consumption vs. capital formation). Then apply the SNA classification: P.3 for salaries, P.51g for construction. Remember that human‑capital satellite accounts are memorandum items and do not alter headline GDP.

Classification of Subsidies on Products versus Subsidies on Production in the SNA

The 2008 SNA distinguishes two broad categories of subsidies: subsidies on products (D.31) and subsidies on production (D.39). Subsidies on products are payable per unit of a good or service produced or imported; they are recorded as a negative component of the value of output at basic prices and therefore reduce the GDP measured at market prices. Examples include export subsidies, fuel price subsidies tied to quantity sold, and fertilizer subsidies linked to the volume of fertilizer purchased by farmers. Subsidies on production, by contrast, are not linked to the quantity of a specific product; they are granted to resident producers for reasons such as employment generation, regional development, or environmental compliance. They are recorded as a negative component of the value added at basic prices and do not affect the valuation of output at basic prices. In India, the central government’s “Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi” (PM‑KISAN) cash transfer to farmers is classified as a subsidy on production because it is a lump‑sum payment unrelated to output volume, whereas the “Urea Subsidy” paid per tonne of urea sold is a subsidy on products. The distinction matters for the calculation of GDP at market prices versus GDP at basic prices: GDP at market prices = GDP at basic prices + taxes on products – subsidies on products. Misclassifying a product‑specific subsidy as a production subsidy inflates GDP at market prices and distorts the implicit tax‑subsidy ratio used in fiscal analysis. The 2025 SNA introduces a more granular breakdown of subsidies on production into “subsidies on labour”, “subsidies on capital”, and “subsidies on intermediate consumption” to improve the link with the input‑output framework. Examiners often test the impact of a subsidy on the GDP deflator: a product subsidy lowers the market‑price deflator relative to the basic‑price deflator, while a production subsidy leaves the market‑price deflator unchanged but reduces the basic‑price deflator.

Non‑Produced Non‑Financial Assets in the National Balance Sheet: Land, Mineral Rights, and Spectrum Licences

The national balance sheet records the stock of assets and liabilities at the end of each accounting period. Non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.2) comprise natural resources (land, subsoil assets, water resources, radio spectra) and contracts, leases, and licences that are not produced by economic activity. In the 2008 SNA, land underlying buildings and structures is valued at market price and appears as a separate asset (AN.211). Mineral and energy reserves (AN.212) are valued using the net present value of expected future resource rents, discounted at a rate consistent with the government’s cost of capital. In India, the Ministry of Mines and the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas provide reserve estimates that the NSO uses to compile the subsoil asset stock. Radio spectrum licences (AN.214) are treated as non‑produced assets when they are allocated for a finite period; the licence fee paid upfront is recorded as a capital transfer (D.99) from the licensee to the government, and the licence itself appears on the government’s balance sheet as an asset. The 2025 SNA recommends that spectrum licences be re‑valued at each reporting date using market‑based auction prices, with revaluation gains or losses recorded in the other changes in volume of assets account (K.1). A common examiner trap is to record the auction proceeds as government revenue (taxes) rather than as a capital transfer that reduces the licensee’s net worth and increases the government’s non‑produced asset holding. Another error is to treat the annual licence renewal fee as a rent (property income) when the licence is a non‑produced asset; the correct treatment is to record the fee as a service payment (P.2) for the use of the spectrum, while the asset remains on the balance sheet. The integration of these assets into the national balance sheet enables the calculation of a comprehensive net worth position for the general government and the total economy, which is essential for fiscal sustainability analysis.

The Role of National Accounts in Monitoring SDG 9: Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure

Sustainable Development Goal 9 calls for building resilient infrastructure, promoting inclusive and sustainable industrialisation, and fostering innovation. The UN’s global indicator framework maps several SDG 9 targets to national accounts aggregates. Target 9.1 (develop quality, reliable, sustainable infrastructure) is monitored through the gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) in infrastructure assets (transport, energy, water, ICT) expressed as a share of GDP. The SNA’s asset classification (AN.111‑AN.114) allows the extraction of infrastructure‑specific GFCF from the capital account. Target 9.2 (promote inclusive and sustainable industrialisation) uses the manufacturing value added (MVA) share in GDP and the manufacturing employment share, both derived from the production account and the labour input tables. Target 9.5 (enhance scientific research, upgrade technological capabilities) is tracked by research and development (R&D) expenditure as a percentage of GDP; the 2025 SNA capitalises R&D as intellectual property products (AN.117), turning R&D outlays into gross fixed capital formation and enabling a stock measure of knowledge capital. In India, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) publishes an annual “SDG 9 Dashboard” that aligns the national accounts’ GFCF, MVA, and R&D satellite account data with the global indicators. A frequent examiner question asks how a rise in R&D capitalisation affects GDP growth rates: the immediate effect is an increase in GFCF and thus GDP (expenditure approach), while the consumption of fixed capital on the new R&D assets will be recorded in subsequent periods, moderating the net effect on net domestic product. Another trap is to confuse the “innovation” indicator (patent applications per capita) with the national accounts’ R&D stock; the former is a bibliometric indicator, the latter a monetary stock derived from the SNA. The integration of the SNA with the System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting (SEEA) also permits the monitoring of Target 9.4 (upgrade infrastructure and retrofit industries for sustainability) by linking infrastructure GFCF to energy intensity and CO₂ emission accounts.

  • Confusing tourism‑characteristic products with tourism‑connected products leads to over‑statement of tourism direct GDP.
  • Double‑counting government education spending by adding both current consumption and capital formation as “education investment” in the core accounts.
  • Classifying a per‑unit fertilizer subsidy as a production subsidy instead of a product subsidy, distorting GDP at market prices.
  • Recording spectrum auction proceeds as tax revenue rather than a capital transfer that creates a non‑produced asset on the government balance sheet.
  • Treating annual spectrum licence fees as property income (rent) instead of a service payment for the use of a non‑produced asset.
  • Equating patent counts with the SNA’s R&D capital stock when assessing SDG 9 innovation targets.
  • Neglecting the consumption of fixed capital on newly capitalised R&D assets, resulting in an overstated net domestic product in the year of capitalisation.

Central Bank Output, Seigniorage, and Monetary Policy Operations in National Accounts

The System of National Accounts treats the central bank as a financial corporation (S.121) whose output must be measured consistently with other financial intermediaries, yet its unique functions — monetary policy implementation, currency issuance, and reserve management — create measurement challenges absent in commercial banking. Under the 2008 SNA, the output of central bank services (P.131) is calculated as the sum of intermediate consumption, compensation of employees, consumption of fixed capital, and net operating surplus. The net operating surplus of the central bank comprises net interest income (interest receivable on securities and loans minus interest payable on deposits and reserves), realised and unrealised gains or losses on foreign exchange and securities, and seigniorage — the difference between the face value of currency issued and its production cost. Seigniorage is recorded as property income (D.4) receivable by the central bank from the household sector (the ultimate holders of currency), not as output. A critical distinction is that the 2025 SNA recommends recording unrealised holding gains and losses on the central bank’s own portfolio in the revaluation account (K.2) rather than in the production account, aligning central bank output measurement with the principle that output reflects production, not asset price changes. In India, the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) annual report discloses “income” and “expenditure” on a commercial accounting basis; the NSO reclassifies these into SNA categories. For instance, RBI’s surplus transferred to the government is a distributive transaction (withdrawal from income of quasi-corporations, D.422), not a tax. The 2025 SNA further clarifies that interest paid on reserve balances (the interest on reserves, or IOR) is a monetary policy operation recorded as interest (D.41), while the corresponding interest received on government securities held for policy purposes is also D.41; the net interest margin contributes to central bank output. Open market operations (OMOs) involving outright purchases or sales of government securities change the composition of the central bank’s balance sheet but do not directly create output; repo and reverse repo transactions are recorded as collateralised loans (F.4) with interest accruing on both legs. A common examiner trap is to treat the RBI’s surplus transfer as a tax revenue (D.2) or to record seigniorage as central bank output rather than as property income from households. Another error is to include unrealised foreign exchange revaluation gains in GDP; these are other changes in volume of assets (K.1) or revaluation (K.2) and do not affect value added.

Accounting for Natural Resource Depletion, Discovery, and Revaluation in the National Balance Sheet

The integration of natural resource assets into the national balance sheet requires three distinct accounting entries: depletion (K.21), discoveries and reappraisals (K.22), and revaluation due to price changes (K.23). Under the 2008 SNA and SEEA-CF, mineral and energy reserves (AN.211), non-cultivated biological resources (AN.212), water resources (AN.213), and radio spectrum (AN.214) are non-produced assets that enter the balance sheet when they are owned and capable of bringing economic benefits. Depletion is the reduction in the value of a natural resource asset resulting from its physical extraction; it is recorded as consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) in the production account of the extractor, reducing net value added and net domestic product. The 2025 SNA reinforces that depletion must be estimated using the net present value (NPV) method: the resource rent per unit extracted (price minus extraction cost minus normal return on produced assets) multiplied by the quantity extracted, discounted at a real rate. In India, the NSO’s “Environmental Economic Accounts” publish depletion-adjusted aggregates for major minerals (coal, iron ore, limestone) and crude oil, using lease auction premia and royalty rates to infer resource rent. Discoveries (new deposits identified through exploration) and reappraisals (upward or downward revisions of existing reserves) are recorded as other changes in volume of assets (K.22), directly changing the asset stock without passing through the production account. Revaluation due to commodity price changes (K.23) is recorded in the revaluation account. A key policy application is the calculation of Adjusted Net National Income (aNNI) = NNI − depletion of energy, minerals, and forests − net forest degradation. The 2025 SNA recommends that countries compile a “depletion-adjusted balance sheet” showing the opening stock, depletion, discoveries, reappraisals, revaluation, and closing stock for each resource class. A frequent examiner error is to treat royalty payments as depletion; royalties are rent (D.45) payable to the resource owner (often government), while depletion is an imputed cost borne by the extractor. Another trap is to record the full sale value of extracted minerals as output without deducting depletion, overstating net value added. The correct sequence: gross output (P.1) − intermediate consumption (P.2) = gross value added; gross value added − consumption of fixed capital on produced assets (P.51c) − depletion (P.51c) = net value added.

Worked Example: Depletion-Adjusted Aggregates for a Coal Mine
A public sector coal company extracts 50 million tonnes of coal in 2023-24. The average sale price is ₹4,000 per tonne. Extraction cost (intermediate consumption plus compensation of employees plus consumption of fixed capital on produced assets) is ₹2,500 per tonne. The normal return on produced assets is estimated at 8% of the written-down value of ₹20,000 crore. The remaining reserve is 500 million tonnes. The discount rate is 5% real. Calculate (a) resource rent per tonne, (b) total depletion for the year, (c) depletion-adjusted net value added.
(a) Normal return on produced assets = 8% × ₹20,000 crore = ₹1,600 crore. Per tonne normal return = ₹1,600 crore / 50 million tonnes = ₹320 per tonne. Resource rent per tonne = Price − Extraction cost − Normal return = ₹4,000 − ₹2,500 − ₹320 = ₹1,180 per tonne. (b) Total depletion = Resource rent per tonne × Quantity extracted = ₹1,180 × 50 million = ₹59,000 crore. (c) Gross value added = (₹4,000 − intermediate consumption) × 50 million. Since extraction cost includes IC + CoE + CFC(produced), GVA = (₹4,000 × 50m) − (IC × 50m) = (₹4,000 − IC) × 50m. But we know extraction cost = IC + CoE + CFC(produced) = ₹2,500. So GVA = (₹4,000 − IC) × 50m = (CoE + CFC(produced) + ₹1,500) × 50m. Net value added (SNA) = GVA − CFC(produced) = (CoE + ₹1,500) × 50m. Depletion-adjusted NVA = NVA − Depletion = (CoE + ₹1,500) × 50m − ₹59,000 crore. Numerically: NVA = (CoE + ₹1,500) × 50m. If CoE = ₹500/tonne, NVA = ₹2,000 × 50m = ₹1,00,000 crore. Depletion-adjusted NVA = ₹1,00,000 crore − ₹59,000 crore = ₹41,000 crore.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question asks for “depletion-adjusted NDP” or “aNNI”, write the identity: aNNI = NNI − Depletion(energy) − Depletion(minerals) − Depletion(forests) − Net forest degradation. Memorise that depletion is part of consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) in the 2008/2025 SNA, not a separate line item. For NPV depletion, the formula is Rent = Price − Average extraction cost − Normal return on produced capital. Normal return = Discount rate × Written-down value of produced assets. Do not confuse royalty (D.45) with depletion (P.51c). Royalties are a distributive transaction; depletion is a production cost.

The Treatment of Government Inventories, Strategic Stockpiles, and Commodity Buffer Stocks in the SNA

Government inventories (AN.12) — materials and supplies (AN.121), work-in-progress (AN.122), finished goods (AN.123), and goods for resale (AN.124) — are produced assets recorded in the general government balance sheet. The 2008 SNA (paragraph 10.128) and the 2025 SNA (Chapter 13) distinguish three categories relevant to policy analysis: (1) regular operational inventories (office supplies, ammunition for training, medical stores), valued at current replacement cost; (2) strategic stockpiles (strategic petroleum reserves, defence war reserves, critical mineral stockpiles) held for national security, valued at acquisition cost or current market price depending on whether they are intended for use or sale; and (3) commodity buffer stocks (food grains under the Food Corporation of India, cotton, sugar, fertilizer) held for price stabilisation and food security. The treatment of buffer stocks is the most contentious. When the government procures wheat at Minimum Support Price (MSP) and holds it, the procurement is recorded as government final consumption expenditure (P.31) if the grain is distributed free or at subsidised prices through the Public Distribution System (PDS), or as change in inventories (P.52) if held for future sale. The 2025 SNA clarifies that if the government intends to sell the stock at market prices, the holding gain or loss while in inventory is recorded as a nominal holding gain (K.2) in the revaluation account, not as output. However, if the stock is distributed at subsidised prices, the difference between MSP and issue price is a subsidy on products (D.31) recorded at the time of distribution. In India, the FCI’s open market sale scheme (OMSS) sales are recorded as government sales (P.11), while PDS distribution is government final consumption expenditure (P.31) valued at acquisition cost (MSP plus incidentals). The carrying cost of buffer stocks — interest on loans, storage, insurance — is intermediate consumption (P.2) of the government. A critical examiner trap is to record the entire MSP procurement as GFCF (capital formation) rather than as change in inventories (P.52) or final consumption (P.31). Another error is to treat the subsidised distribution as a transfer (D.63) rather than as a product subsidy (D.31) that reduces the value of government output. The 2025 SNA also introduces a “strategic stockpile” classification (AN.125) for assets held exclusively for emergency use, with a recommendation to value them at written-down replacement cost and to record any drawdown as a reduction in inventories (negative P.52) with a corresponding increase in government final consumption expenditure (P.31) or exports (P.6) if donated internationally.

Measuring the Output of Public Administration, Defence, and Compulsory Social Security: Collective vs. Individual Services

The output of general government (S.13) is defined in the 2008 SNA (Chapter 6) and refined in the 2025 SNA as the sum of compensation of employees (D.1), intermediate consumption (P.2), consumption of fixed capital (P.51c), and net taxes on production (D.29-D.39) — the cost-of-production approach, since most government services are non-market (P.13). The critical classification for policy analysis is the split between collective services (P.32) and individual services (P.31). Collective services — general public administration (COFOG 01), defence (COFOG 02), public order and safety (COFOG 03), economic affairs (COFOG 04), environmental protection (COFOG 05) — benefit the community as a whole and are recorded as government final consumption expenditure (P.32) on the use side. Individual services — education (COFOG 09), health (COFOG 07), social protection (COFOG 10), recreation and culture (COFOG 08), housing (COFOG 06) — benefit identifiable households and are recorded as government individual consumption expenditure (P.31), which is then added to household actual final consumption (P.41) to derive actual individual consumption. The 2025 SNA introduces a “quality-adjusted output” methodology for individual services: for education, output is measured by the number of student-hours taught, adjusted for teacher qualifications and curriculum standards; for health, output is measured by quality-adjusted treatment episodes (e.g., diagnosis-related groups with outcome weights). In India, the NSO currently uses the input-cost method for all government output, but the “Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework” (OOMF) and the “Performance Budgeting” initiative are steps toward output measurement. Defence output (COFOG 02) is purely collective; its value equals the cost of production. A common examiner error is to classify defence pensions as government output; they are social benefits (D.62) paid to former employees, not compensation of current employees. Another trap is to treat government expenditure on infrastructure (roads, bridges) as government final consumption; it is gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) by government, creating produced assets (AN.111-AN.114). The 2025 SNA also clarifies that compulsory social security schemes (e.g., Employees’ Provident Fund, Employees’ State Insurance) are separate institutional units (S.1314) if they are autonomous; their administrative output is measured by cost of production, while the benefit payments are social insurance benefits (D.621), not government output.

The Treatment of Factoryless Goods Producers, Contract Manufacturing, and Intellectual Property in Global Value Chain-Integrated National Accounts

The 2025 SNA introduces explicit guidance for “factoryless goods producers” (FGPs) — enterprises that own the intellectual property (IP), design, and brand of a good but outsource all physical transformation to contract manufacturers (CMs). Under the 2008 SNA, the FGP was often classified as a wholesaler (ISIC 46) because it did not physically produce; the 2025 SNA reclassifies the FGP as a manufacturer (ISIC 10-33) and the CM as a manufacturer providing manufacturing services (CPC 88). The economic ownership of the work-in-progress and finished goods remains with the FGP throughout the production process. The FGP’s output (P.1) is the final good valued at basic prices; its intermediate consumption (P.2) includes the fee paid to the CM (recorded as a manufacturing service, CPC 88) plus the cost of materials supplied to the CM (if the FGP owns the materials). The CM’s output is the manufacturing service fee; its intermediate consumption includes the materials it purchases (if any) and its own factory overhead. Cross-border GVC integration requires the “TiVA” (Trade in Value Added) framework: the FGP’s gross exports contain foreign value added (FVA) embodied in the CM’s services and materials. The 2025 SNA recommends that national accounts compilers use enterprise surveys and customs data to identify FGP-CM relationships and re-route transactions accordingly. For IP licensing, the 2025 SNA treats the IP as a produced asset (AN.117) owned by the FGP; the royalty paid by the FGP to its foreign parent (if any) is a service import (P.7) for the use of IP, while the FGP’s own R&D expenditure is capitalised as GFCF in IP products. In India, the rise of “fabless” semiconductor design firms and pharmaceutical contract research and manufacturing services (CRAMS) makes this relevant. A frequent examiner trap is to record the full value of goods exported by the CM as India’s goods exports, ignoring that the FGP (which may be foreign) owns the IP and bears the market risk; the correct recording is that the CM exports manufacturing services (services export, P.62), while the FGP exports the goods (goods export, P.61) if the FGP is resident. If the FGP is non-resident, the CM’s fee is a services export, and the goods never enter India’s goods exports. Another error is to capitalise the CM’s R&D as the FGP’s IP; only the FGP’s own R&D creates its IP asset.

  • Recording the RBI’s surplus transfer to government as tax revenue (D.2) instead of withdrawal from income of quasi-corporations (D.422).
  • Including unrealised foreign exchange revaluation gains of the central bank in GDP; these are revaluation account entries (K.2), not production.
  • Treating royalty payments on mineral extraction as depletion; royalties are rent (D.45), depletion is consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) imputed to the extractor.
  • Recording the full MSP procurement value as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) rather than change in inventories (P.52) or final consumption (P.31).
  • Classifying subsidised PDS distribution as a social transfer (D.63) instead of a product subsidy (D.31) reducing government output value.
  • Recording defence pensions as compensation of employees (D.1) or government output; they are social benefits (D.62).
  • Attributing the full value of contract-manufactured goods exports to the contract manufacturer when the factoryless goods producer owns the IP and economic ownership; the CM exports manufacturing services, the FGP exports the goods.

Renewable Energy Certificates, Carbon Credits, and Emission Trading Schemes in National Accounts

The 2025 System of National Accounts (SNA) introduces explicit guidance for the recording of environmental assets that arise from market‑based climate policies. Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs), Certified Emission Reductions (CERs) under the Clean Development Mechanism, and allowances allocated under cap‑and‑trade systems such as the EU ETS are treated as produced non‑financial assets (AN.117) when they are created through a verified production process. The key distinction is between permits to emit (which are licences to use a natural resource) and certificates that embody a reduction (which are the output of a mitigation activity). Under the 2008 SNA, both were often recorded as valuables or left off‑balance‑sheet; the 2025 revision requires that the initial allocation of allowances by government be recorded as a capital transfer (D.9) to the recipient enterprise, while subsequent trades are recorded as acquisitions less disposals of produced assets (P.51g).

When an enterprise generates electricity from renewable sources and receives RECs, the certificates are valued at the market price at the time of issuance. The output of the renewable generator includes both the electricity (P.1) and the RECs (P.1), with the latter entering gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) of the holder. If the generator sells the RECs, the transaction is a sale of a produced asset (P.61) and the buyer records an acquisition of a produced asset (P.51g). For cap‑and‑trade allowances, the initial free allocation is a government non‑market output (P.13) valued at the market price of allowances; the government records a capital transfer (D.9) to the enterprise. Subsequent surrender of allowances to meet compliance obligations is recorded as consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) for the enterprise, reducing the asset stock.

Carbon credits generated under the Clean Development Mechanism or voluntary markets follow the same logic: the project developer records output of carbon credits (P.1) and GFCF (P.51g) upon verification; the buyer records acquisition of a produced asset. The 2025 SNA also clarifies that revaluation gains or losses on these assets due to price changes are recorded in the revaluation account (K.2), not in production or income. This prevents volatile carbon prices from distorting GDP. A practical implication for compilers is the need for a dedicated environmental asset register linked to the national accounts, with consistent classification of vintage, methodology, and registry (e.g., UNFCCC, Gold Standard, Verra). India’s Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme and the emerging Indian Carbon Market (ICM) will require alignment with these rules once the market becomes operational.

Examiners often test the distinction between a licence to emit (recorded as rent, D.45) and a certificate representing a reduction (recorded as a produced asset). Another trap is to treat the surrender of allowances as a tax payment (D.2) rather than consumption of fixed capital. The correct treatment ensures that the cost of compliance appears as depreciation of an environmental asset, preserving the integrity of net domestic product.

Tourism Satellite Accounts and the Measurement of the Tourism Sector in the 2025 SNA

Tourism Satellite Accounts (TSA) provide a framework for measuring the direct economic contribution of tourism by reconciling demand‑side data (visitor expenditure) with supply‑side data (industry output). The 2025 SNA endorses the TSA: Recommended Methodological Framework (RMF) 2008 and adds guidance on the treatment of digital platform intermediation (e.g., online travel agencies, short‑term rental platforms) and non‑market tourism services (e.g., public museums, heritage sites). The core of the TSA is the tourism characteristic products list (e.g., accommodation, passenger transport, travel agency services) and tourism connected products (e.g., food, souvenirs). The TSA compiles three key aggregates: Tourism Direct Gross Value Added (TDGVA), Tourism Direct Gross Domestic Product (TDGDP), and Tourism Employment.

On the demand side, the TSA uses visitor surveys (domestic and international) to estimate expenditure by product and by type of visitor (overnight, same‑day). On the supply side, it uses the Supply‑Use Tables (SUT) to allocate industry output to tourism characteristic products using tourism ratios (the share of each product consumed by visitors). The 2025 SNA recommends that compilers integrate big‑data sources — mobile phone roaming data, credit‑card transaction data, and platform transaction logs — to improve the granularity of visitor flows, especially for same‑day visitors and domestic tourism where survey coverage is weak.

A critical measurement issue is the treatment of short‑term rental platforms (e.g., Airbnb). The 2025 SNA classifies the platform’s service fee as digital intermediation services (CPC 859) and the host’s accommodation service as short‑term accommodation (CPC 631). The host’s imputed rent for owner‑occupied dwellings used for tourism is already captured in the national accounts under imputed rent for owner‑occupiers; the TSA extracts the tourism share using the tourism ratio for accommodation. For platforms that act as merchant (buying and reselling rooms), the full room revenue is recorded as output of the platform, with the payment to the host as intermediate consumption.

Non‑market tourism services, such as free entry to national museums, are valued at cost of production (compensation of employees + intermediate consumption + consumption of fixed capital) following the general government non‑market output rule. The TSA includes these in TDGVA by applying the tourism ratio to the relevant government output. The 2025 SNA also introduces a tourism satellite account for the informal sector, using household survey data on informal accommodation and guide services, to capture the significant informal tourism economy in many developing countries.

Examiners frequently ask for the difference between tourism characteristic products and tourism connected products, and whether the platform fee or the full room rate enters TDGVA. The correct answer: only the platform fee (intermediation service) is a tourism characteristic product for the platform; the host’s accommodation service is the tourism characteristic product for the host. The full room rate paid by the visitor is split between the two.

Worked Example: Recording a Short‑Term Rental Transaction
A resident host lists a flat on a digital platform for ₹10,000 per night. The platform charges a 15 % service fee. The host incurs ₹2,000 of intermediate consumption (cleaning, utilities). Show the entries in the national accounts and the TSA for one night.
1. Platform output (digital intermediation service) = ₹1,500 (15 % of ₹10,000). Platform intermediate consumption = negligible. Platform GFCF = 0. Platform value added = ₹1,500. 2. Host output (short‑term accommodation) = ₹10,000. Host intermediate consumption = ₹2,000. Host value added = ₹8,000. 3. Visitor expenditure = ₹10,000 (tourism demand). 4. In the TSA, tourism ratio for accommodation = 1 (entire host output is tourism characteristic). Platform intermediation service is also tourism characteristic. TDGVA = ₹1,500 + ₹8,000 = ₹9,500. 5. Government receives no direct revenue; if a tourism tax applies, it is a product tax (D.21) on the visitor expenditure.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the three TSA aggregates (TDGVA, TDGDP, Tourism Employment) and the two product categories (characteristic vs connected). For platform questions, always separate the platform fee (intermediation) from the host service (accommodation). Remember that non‑market tourism output is valued at cost, not at hypothetical market price.

Trade Agreements, Global Value Chains, and Domestic Value Added: Using TiVA Indicators in National Accounts

The integration of Trade in Value Added (TiVA) indicators with the System of National Accounts allows policymakers to trace the domestic value‑added content of gross exports and the foreign value‑added embodied in imports. The 2025 SNA recommends that national statistical offices compile inter‑country input‑output (ICIO) tables consistent with the domestic SUT, using a common classification (ISIC Rev.4, CPC Ver.2) and a harmonised reference year. The key TiVA metrics are: Domestic Value Added in Exports (DVA_X), Foreign Value Added in Exports (FVA_X), Domestic Value Added in Final Demand (DVA_FD), and GVC Participation Index (sum of backward and forward linkage shares).

Backward linkage (FVA_X / gross exports) measures the reliance on imported intermediates; forward linkage (DVA_X embodied in other countries’ exports / gross exports) measures the role as a supplier of intermediates. The 2025 SNA introduces a trade‑policy simulation module where changes in tariff schedules or rules of origin can be fed into the ICIO to estimate the impact on DVA_X and employment. For example, a reduction in tariffs on automotive parts under a regional trade agreement (RTA) would lower the cost of imported intermediates, potentially increasing the FVA_X share but also expanding total exports if downstream assembly becomes more competitive.

In the Indian context, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) has collaborated with the OECD‑WTO TiVA initiative to produce experimental ICIO tables for 2015‑16 and 2018‑19. These tables reveal that India’s DVA_X in manufacturing exports is around 65 %, with significant variation across sectors: electronics and pharmaceuticals have higher FVA_X due to imported active pharmaceutical ingredients and semiconductor components, while textiles and leather show higher DVA_X. The 2025 SNA also requires that re‑exports and merchanting be separately identified in the ICIO to avoid double counting of foreign value added.

A common examiner twist is to ask whether a rise in gross exports necessarily implies a rise in domestic value added. The answer is no: if the increase is driven by assembly activities with high import content, DVA_X may stagnate or even fall. Another trap is to confuse value‑added exports (DVA_X) with value‑added of the export sector (which includes domestic intermediates used by the export sector). The former is a TiVA concept; the latter is a standard national accounts concept derived from the SUT.

Education Satellite Accounts, Human Capital Formation, and the Valuation of Educational Services in the SNA

Education Satellite Accounts (ESA) extend the core SNA by providing a detailed breakdown of the production, financing, and consumption of education services, and by linking these flows to the accumulation of human capital. The 2025 SNA recognises education as a produced service (CPC 92) and encourages the compilation of an ESA that distinguishes between formal education (primary, secondary, tertiary), vocational training, and non‑formal education. The ESA follows the same supply‑use framework as the TSA, using education characteristic products and education connected products (e.g., textbooks, stationery, student transport).

On the production side, the ESA records output of public and private educational institutions at basic prices. For public institutions, non‑market output is valued at cost of production (compensation of employees + intermediate consumption + consumption of fixed capital). For private institutions, market output is valued at transaction prices. The ESA also captures household production of education services (e.g., home‑schooling, parental tutoring) as non‑market household output, valued using the replacement‑cost method (cost of hiring a tutor). This aligns with the 2025 SNA’s broader push to include unpaid household services in satellite accounts.

On the financing side, the ESA maps the flow of funds from government (current transfers D.31, capital transfers D.9), households (final consumption expenditure P.31), non‑profit institutions serving households (NPISH), and the rest of the world (scholarships, education exports). The 2025 SNA introduces a human capital satellite account that links the ESA to the Jorgenson‑Fraumeni lifetime income approach: the stock of human capital is estimated as the discounted present value of future earnings attributable to education, and the annual investment in human capital is the sum of education expenditure (adjusted for depreciation of skills). India’s pilot human capital accounts (2022‑23) use the National Sample Survey (NSS) education expenditure data and the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) earnings profiles to estimate the human capital stock at approximately 3.5 times GDP.

Examiners often test the distinction between education expenditure as final consumption (household P.31) and education expenditure as gross fixed capital formation (government investment in school infrastructure, P.51g). The former is consumption; the latter creates a produced asset (school building). Another trap is to treat scholarships from foreign governments as exports of education services; they are current transfers (D.31) received by households, not export revenue of the education institution.

The System of Health Accounts (SHA) and Its Integration with the SNA for Health Expenditure Measurement

The System of Health Accounts (SHA 2011) provides a comprehensive framework for tracking health expenditure by financing scheme, provider, and function. The 2025 SNA explicitly recommends the alignment of SHA classifications with the SNA’s institutional sector and transaction classifications to ensure consistency between health expenditure aggregates and national accounts aggregates such as Household Final Consumption Expenditure (HFCE), Government Final Consumption Expenditure (GFCE), and Gross Fixed Capital Formation in Health Infrastructure.

The SHA classifies health expenditure by financing schemes (e.g., government schemes, compulsory contributory health insurance, voluntary health insurance, out‑of‑pocket), by providers (hospitals, ambulatory care providers, pharmacies, public health programmes), and by functions (curative care, rehabilitative care, preventive care, governance). The SNA records the same flows but from the perspective of the institutional units: government health output (non‑market, valued at cost), household out‑of‑pocket payments (final consumption), and insurance benefit payments (social benefits D.62). The integration requires a cross‑walk table mapping SHA financing schemes to SNA sectors (e.g., Central Government Health Scheme → General Government sector; Employees’ State Insurance → Social Security Funds sector).

A critical measurement issue is the treatment of health insurance premiums. In the SHA, premiums are part of the financing scheme; in the SNA, premiums are recorded as current transfers (D.61) from households to insurance corporations, while the insurance service charge (output of insurance) is recorded as household final consumption (P.31). The claims paid by insurers to providers are recorded as social benefits (D.62) to households, who then incur final consumption expenditure on health services. The 2025 SNA clarifies that the net insurance service charge (premiums less claims plus investment income) is the output of the insurance sector, not the gross premium.

Another area of alignment is capital formation in health infrastructure. Government construction of hospitals is GFCF (P.51g) by government, creating a produced asset (AN.111). The SHA records this as capital expenditure under the provider “hospitals”. The 2025 SNA requires that the consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) on these assets be recorded annually in government non‑market output, ensuring that the cost of using the hospital appears in GFCE. For public‑private partnership (PPP) hospitals, the 2025 SNA treats the private partner’s construction as GFCF by the private corporation, with the government recording a service concession asset (AN.112) and a corresponding liability.

Examiners frequently ask whether out‑of‑pocket health expenditure is part of GDP. The answer: yes, it is part of household final consumption expenditure (P.31) and therefore included in GDP via the expenditure approach. A trap is to double‑count insurance premiums and claims; only the insurance service charge enters GDP as output of the insurance sector, while claims are transfers that do not directly add to production.

  • Confusing a licence to emit (rent, D.45) with a carbon credit representing a reduction (produced asset, AN.117).
  • Recording the surrender of emission allowances as a tax payment (D.2) instead of consumption of fixed capital (P.51c).
  • Treating the full room rate on a short‑term rental platform as platform output; only the service fee is platform output, the accommodation service belongs to the host.
  • Assuming a rise in gross exports always raises domestic value added; high import content can keep DVA_X flat.
  • Classifying scholarships from foreign governments as education exports; they are current transfers (D.31) to households.
  • Counting both insurance premiums and claims as health output; only the net insurance service charge is output.
  • Recording government hospital construction as current expenditure; it is gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) creating a produced asset.

The Non‑Observed Economy: Concept, Measurement Techniques, and Integration into National Accounts

The System of National Accounts (2008 SNA, Chapter 6) defines the non‑observed economy (NOE) as the set of productive activities that are not captured in the basic data sources used for compiling GDP. The NOE comprises five mutually exclusive components: (1) underground production that is legal but deliberately concealed from authorities; (2) illegal production such as drug trafficking or smuggling; (3) informal sector production by unincorporated enterprises that are not registered; (4) household production for own final use (subsistence agriculture, owner‑occupied housing services); and (5) statistical deficiencies arising from incomplete coverage, timing mismatches, or mis‑classification. The 2025 SNA revision reiterates that all five components must be estimated and added to the observed aggregates to achieve exhaustive GDP.

Measurement techniques differ by component. For underground and illegal activities, the most widely used macro‑approaches are the currency‑demand method (Cagan, 1958), the electricity‑consumption method (Kaufmann & Kaliberda, 1996), and the Multiple Indicators Multiple Causes (MIMIC) model, which exploits a set of observable causes (tax burden, regulatory intensity) and indicators (cash‑to‑GDP ratio, labour‑force participation) to infer the size of the hidden economy. For the informal sector, the labour‑input method (also called the “employment‑based” approach) combines labour‑force survey data on informal employment with productivity estimates from the formal sector to impute value added. The commodity‑flow method reconciles supply and use tables by adjusting for missing inputs and outputs. Household own‑account production is valued using the replacement‑cost or market‑price approach, guided by the 2008 SNA’s recommendation to use the “cost of production” for non‑market goods.

Integration into the national accounts follows a two‑step process. First, each NOE component is estimated independently, often using a combination of survey data (e.g., India’s NSSO Employment‑Unemployment Survey, Annual Survey of Industries) and administrative records (tax audits, customs seizures). Second, the estimates are entered as adjustments in the supply‑use balancing framework: additional output is added to the relevant industries, intermediate consumption is increased where hidden inputs are used, and final uses (household consumption, gross fixed capital formation) are augmented. Eurostat’s “tabular approach” provides a transparent template that shows the observed aggregates, the NOE adjustments, and the exhaustive totals side by side. In India, the National Statistical Office (NSO) publishes “GDP with NOE adjustments” in the annual “National Accounts Statistics” release, explicitly noting the contribution of the informal sector (≈ 50 % of GVA in 2011‑12 base year) and the imputed value of owner‑occupied dwellings.

Key policy implications include the need for regular updating of the NOE estimates when the base year changes, the importance of linking the informal‑sector module of the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) with the Annual Survey of Industries to improve productivity benchmarks, and the caution that double‑counting can arise if both the currency‑demand and electricity methods are applied without cross‑validation. The 2025 SNA also encourages the use of big‑data sources (e‑invoicing, digital payment trails) to reduce the statistical‑deficiency component of the NOE.

Tourism Satellite Account: Methodology, Compilation, and Linkages with the SNA

The Tourism Satellite Account (TSA) is the internationally agreed framework for measuring the economic contribution of tourism, developed by the United Nations World Tourism Organization (UNWTO) and endorsed by the UN Statistical Commission in 2008. The TSA follows the same accounting principles as the SNA but isolates tourism‑characteristic and tourism‑connected products and industries. The core set of ten tables covers: (1) inbound tourism expenditure; (2) domestic tourism expenditure; (3) outbound tourism expenditure; (4) internal tourism consumption; (5) production accounts of tourism industries; (6) gross value added of tourism industries (Tourism Direct GDP); (7) employment in tourism industries; (8) tourism gross fixed capital formation; (9) tourism collective consumption; and (10) non‑monetary indicators (arrivals, nights, purpose of visit).

Compilation proceeds in three stages. First, a “tourism product list” is drawn up using the Central Product Classification (CPC) and the International Standard Industrial Classification (ISIC) to identify tourism‑characteristic products (e.g., accommodation services, passenger transport, travel agency services) and tourism‑connected products (e.g., food‑serving services, cultural services). Second, supply‑use tables are re‑structured so that the output of tourism industries is split into tourism and non‑tourism components using the “tourism ratio” (share of tourism demand in total demand for each product). Third, the tourism ratios are applied to the production account of each industry to derive Tourism Direct Gross Value Added (TDGVA) and Tourism Direct Employment. The TSA also links to the Balance of Payments: travel credits (inbound) and travel debits (outbound) are reconciled with the TSA’s inbound and outbound expenditure tables, ensuring consistency between the rest‑of‑the‑world account and the domestic tourism accounts.

India’s first official TSA was released by the Ministry of Tourism in 2019‑20, based on the 2011‑12 base year. It used the Domestic Tourism Survey (NSSO 72nd round) for domestic expenditure, the International Passenger Survey for inbound/outbound expenditure, and the Annual Survey of Industries for industry output. The 2019‑20 TSA estimated Tourism Direct GDP at ₹ 9.2 lakh crore (≈ 3.1 % of GDP) and direct employment at 42 million jobs. The account is updated annually using the “tourism satellite account module” embedded in the Ministry’s statistical software, which automates the tourism‑ratio calculation whenever the supply‑use tables are revised.

Policy applications are extensive. The TSA feeds directly into the National Tourism Policy’s target‑setting for foreign‑exchange earnings, guides infrastructure investment (e.g., the “Swadesh Darshan” scheme), and provides the statistical backbone for the Sustainable Development Goal indicator 8.9.1 (tourism direct GDP as a proportion of total GDP). A common analytical trap is to equate total tourism expenditure (including outbound spending by residents) with Tourism Direct GDP; only the domestic production triggered by inbound and domestic tourism enters TDGVA, while outbound expenditure is a leakage recorded in the current account.

Examiner's trap
A question states: “If a country’s inbound tourism receipts rise by 15 % while domestic tourism expenditure falls by 5 %, what is the impact on Tourism Direct GDP?” The candidate assumes the net effect is a 10 % rise in TDGVA.
Tourism Direct GDP measures the value added generated by domestic industries in serving both inbound and domestic tourists. An increase in inbound receipts raises demand for domestic tourism‑characteristic products, but a fall in domestic expenditure reduces demand for the same products. The net impact on TDGVA depends on the tourism ratios of each product and the import content of the additional inbound demand. Without knowing the product‑level tourism ratios and the marginal import propensity, one cannot infer a simple 10 % change. The correct answer: the impact is indeterminate without detailed supply‑use information.
Exam‑day strategy
When a TSA‑related question appears, first identify which TSA table is being referenced (expenditure, production, or employment). Then recall the definition of Tourism Direct GDP: it is the sum of gross value added of tourism industries attributable to tourism demand, not total tourism expenditure. Sketch a mini supply‑use diagram in the margin to visualise leakages (imports) and domestic value added. This prevents the common error of treating travel credits as a direct addition to GDP.

Education Satellite Account: Framework, Data Sources, and Policy Applications

The Education Satellite Account (ESA) extends the SNA by providing a detailed breakdown of education‑related production, financing, and consumption. The framework, developed jointly by UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS) and the OECD, follows the 2008 SNA’s distinction between market and non‑market output. Education output is classified by level (pre‑primary, primary, secondary, post‑secondary non‑tertiary, tertiary), by type of institution (public, private non‑profit, private for‑profit), and by source of finance (government, households, non‑profit institutions serving households, rest of the world). The ESA produces three core tables: (1) Education expenditure by financing source and transaction type (current vs. capital); (2) Education output and value added by industry (ISIC 85) and institutional sector; (3) Education human‑capital formation indicators (enrolment, graduation rates, per‑student expenditure).

Data sources in India include the Unified District Information System for Education Plus (UDISE+) for enrolment and infrastructure, the National Sample Survey (NSS) 75th round on “Social Consumption: Education” for household out‑of‑pocket spending, the Ministry of Education’s “Financial Statistics of Education” for government budget execution, and the All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE) for tertiary‑level finance. The NSO integrates these sources through a “education satellite account module” that maps each expenditure item to the appropriate SNA transaction code: government current expenditure on teacher salaries → D.1 (compensation of employees) in the general government sector; household tuition fees → P.31 (household final consumption expenditure); scholarships from foreign governments → D.31 (current transfers to households); construction of school buildings → P.51g (gross fixed capital formation) creating a produced asset (AN.111). Imputed rent for government‑owned school buildings is recorded as non‑market output of the general government sector, valued at the user‑cost of capital.

The ESA enables several policy analyses. First, it allows monitoring of SDG 4.5.1 (parity indices for education expenditure) by linking per‑student public spending to household income deciles. Second, it supports fiscal incidence studies: by cross‑classifying education expenditure by financing source and household quintile, analysts can assess the progressivity of public education finance. Third, the capital‑formation table feeds into the national wealth accounts, showing the stock of educational infrastructure and its consumption of fixed capital, which is essential for long‑term fiscal sustainability assessments. A frequent misinterpretation is to treat all household education spending as final consumption; however, expenditures on education that lead to a recognised qualification and enhance future earnings are conceptually human‑capital investment. The 2025 SNA recommends a satellite “human‑capital account” that re‑classifies a portion of household education outlays as gross fixed capital formation in human capital, but the core ESA keeps them in consumption to preserve SNA consistency.

Environmental Goods and Services Sector (EGSS) Accounting under the SEEA Framework

The Environmental Goods and Services Sector (EGSS) is a statistical framework defined in the System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting (SEEA) Central Framework (2012) and elaborated in the Eurostat EGSS manual (2016). It isolates the part of the economy that produces goods and services for environmental protection (EP) and resource management (RM). The classification uses two complementary nomenclatures: the Classification of Environmental Protection Activities (CEPA) for EP (e.g., wastewater management, waste management, biodiversity protection) and the Classification of Resource Management Activities (CReMA) for RM (e.g., water management, forest management, energy from renewable sources). The EGSS covers both market producers (private firms selling environmental technologies) and non‑market producers (government agencies providing sewage treatment).

Compilation follows a “top‑down” approach using supply‑use tables. First, the total output of each industry (ISIC) is broken down by CEPA/CReMA codes using information from business surveys, environmental expenditure surveys, and administrative registers (e.g., pollution‑control board permits). Second, the environmental share of each industry’s output is applied to its value added, employment, and exports to derive EGSS aggregates: EGSS output, EGSS gross value added, EGSS employment, and EGSS exports. The 2025 SNA encourages the integration of EGSS data into the core accounts by adding an “environmental” dimension to the industry‑by‑product matrix, enabling consistent tracking of green‑growth indicators.

India’s Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) launched a pilot EGSS estimation in 2022, covering the reference year 2019‑20. The pilot used the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) for manufacturing, the NSS 73rd round on “Unincorporated Non‑Agricultural Enterprises” for services, and the Central Pollution Control Board’s compliance database for environmental protection activities. Preliminary results placed EGSS gross value added at roughly 2.3 % of GDP, with the largest contributions from renewable‑energy equipment manufacturing (CReMA 13) and wastewater treatment (CEPA 2). The EGSS account is now being institutionalised as an annual satellite account, with plans to align the CEPA/CReMA mapping with the upcoming 2025 SNA’s “environmental activity” classification.

Policy relevance is high. EGSS aggregates feed directly into the National Green Growth Strategy, the Climate Finance Tracking Framework, and the reporting requirements of the Paris Agreement’s Enhanced Transparency Framework. They also support the calculation of “green GDP” adjustments advocated by the SEEA‑Experimental Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA‑EEA). A common pitfall is to double‑count EGSS value added when it is already embedded in the standard industry GVA; the EGSS is a *subset* of total GVA, not an addition. Analysts must therefore present EGSS as a share of total GVA, not as a separate additive component.

High‑Frequency GDP Nowcasting Using Mobile Phone Call Detail Records and Electronic Payment Data

Nowcasting refers to the estimation of current‑quarter GDP before the official release, using high‑frequency indicators that are available in near real time. Two novel data streams have proven especially powerful: mobile‑phone Call Detail Records (CDR) and electronic‑payment transaction data (e.g., Unified Payments Interface (UPI) in India, credit‑card point‑of‑sale data in Brazil, and instant‑payment systems in the Euro area). CDR provide anonymised aggregates of subscriber mobility (number of unique cell‑tower connections, radius of gyration, inter‑city trips) which correlate strongly with economic activity in services, construction, and retail. Electronic‑payment data capture the volume and value of consumer and business transactions at daily or hourly frequency, offering a direct proxy for final consumption expenditure and business‑to‑business turnover.

The typical nowcasting pipeline consists of three stages. First, raw CDR and payment streams are cleaned and aggregated into a set of weekly or daily indicators: a mobility index (weighted average of inter‑district trips), a transaction‑volume index (number of UPI transactions), and a transaction‑value index (total rupee value). Second, a machine‑learning model — often a gradient‑boosted tree (XGBoost) or a random‑forest ensemble — is trained on historical quarters where both the high‑frequency indicators and the official quarterly GDP (expenditure approach) are known. The model learns non‑linear relationships and automatically selects the most predictive lags (e.g., mobility two weeks prior, payment value one week prior). Third, the trained model produces a point forecast and a prediction interval for the current quarter; the forecast is updated each week as new data arrive, yielding a “nowcast” that converges to the official estimate.

Empirical applications demonstrate substantial gains over traditional bridge‑equation models. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) nowcasting framework, operational since 2022, incorporates UPI transaction value, GST e‑invoice totals, and a CDR‑derived mobility index. In out‑of‑sample tests for 2020‑2023, the root‑mean‑square error (RMSE) of the nowcast was 0.35 percentage points lower than the RBI’s official “nowcast” based on industrial production and survey‑based indicators. The Central Bank of Brazil’s “BCB‑Nowcast” uses credit‑card data and reports a 30 % reduction in forecast error during the COVID‑19 shock. Eurostat’s “Big Data for Official Statistics” project has piloted CDR‑based mobility indicators for several member states, confirming cross‑country robustness.

Challenges remain. Privacy regulations (India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; EU’s GDPR) restrict access to raw CDR; statistical offices typically receive only aggregated, anonymised indicators under strict data‑sharing agreements. Representativeness bias arises because mobile‑phone penetration and digital‑payment adoption differ across income groups and regions; weighting schemes based on demographic surveys are required. Structural breaks — such as the demonetisation episode in India (November 2016) or the UPI‑transaction surge after the pandemic — necessitate model retraining or the inclusion of regime‑switching variables. The 2025 SNA’s “big‑data” annex recommends documenting the data‑access protocol, the aggregation methodology, and the model‑validation results as part of the metadata for any nowcast that feeds into official quarterly accounts.

Common Traps

  • Treating the non‑observed economy as a single homogeneous block; each component (underground, illegal, informal, own‑account, statistical deficiency) requires a distinct estimation method.
  • Equating total tourism expenditure (including outbound spending) with Tourism Direct GDP; only domestic production triggered by inbound and domestic tourism enters TDGVA.
  • Classifying all household education outlays as final consumption; the 2025 SNA’s human‑capital satellite account re‑classifies a portion as gross fixed capital formation in human capital.
  • Adding EGSS value added to total GVA instead of presenting it as a share; EGSS is a subset of existing industry GVA, not an extra component.
  • Assuming high‑frequency mobility or payment indicators can be inserted directly into the quarterly GDP without a validated nowcasting model; raw indicators suffer from seasonality, coverage bias, and structural breaks.
  • Ignoring the privacy‑legal framework when using CDR or payment data; official statistics must comply with data‑protection laws and publish metadata on aggregation and anonymisation.
  • Confusing the currency‑demand method’s estimate of the underground economy with the total non‑observed economy; the former captures only cash‑intensive concealment, missing illegal and informal components.

The Role of Enterprise Surveys and the Annual Survey of Industries in Refining Manufacturing Value Added in National Accounts

Enterprise surveys constitute the primary source of structural data for the manufacturing sector in the System of National Accounts. In India the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI), conducted by the National Statistical Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, covers all factories registered under the Factories Act, 1948 that employ ten or more workers using power or twenty or more workers without power. The questionnaire collects detailed information on gross output, intermediate consumption, gross value added (GVA), employment, fixed capital formation, and inventories. These variables feed directly into the production account of the manufacturing industry, allowing the compilation of GVA at basic prices for each National Industrial Classification (NIC) division.

The ASI results are used for two distinct purposes in the national accounts. First, they provide the benchmark levels for the annual manufacturing GVA series; the quarterly Index of Industrial Production (IIP) is only a volume indicator and must be calibrated to the ASI‑based annual estimates. Second, the ASI supplies the price relatives needed to construct the manufacturing deflator that converts current‑price GVA to constant‑price GVA. Because the ASI is an annual census‑cum‑sample survey, its results are released with a lag of roughly twelve to eighteen months. The national accounts therefore rely on a “nowcast‑then‑revise” cycle: provisional quarterly estimates are based on the IIP and administrative data, and the final annual figures are replaced once the ASI data become available.

Coverage adjustments are a critical step. The ASI excludes informal manufacturing units that are not registered under the Factories Act. The national accounts address this gap by adding estimates from the Economic Census, the NSSO’s unincorporated non‑agricultural enterprise surveys, and the informal sector satellite account. The 2008 SNA recommends that establishment surveys be complemented by household‑based surveys to capture the non‑observed economy. In practice, the CSO applies a “coverage ratio” derived from the Economic Census to inflate the ASI‑based GVA for the informal segment.

Non‑response and sampling error are handled through imputation and weighting. The ASI uses a stratified random sampling design for the smaller factories and a complete enumeration for the larger ones. Weights are calibrated to the frame of registered factories, and missing values are imputed using industry‑level averages. The 2025 SNA’s “big‑data” annex encourages the use of administrative tax data (GST returns) to validate and supplement survey‑based output estimates, a practice that India has begun piloting for the manufacturing sector.

Finally, the integration of ASI data into the input‑output framework ensures consistency between the production and expenditure approaches. The supply‑use tables use ASI‑derived output and intermediate consumption coefficients to balance the manufacturing row, which in turn determines the allocation of GVA across industries and final‑use categories. This balanced framework is essential for reliable multiplier analysis and for the compilation of the KLEMS database used in growth‑accounting exercises.

The Treatment of Government Production Subsidies in the Production and Income Approaches of the SNA

Government subsidies that affect production are recorded differently depending on whether they are subsidies on products or other subsidies on production. A subsidy on products — such as an export subsidy, a food‑grain subsidy paid per tonne, or the fertilizer subsidy paid to manufacturers per unit of output — is treated as a negative tax on products. In the production approach, output at basic prices equals output at producers’ prices minus taxes on products plus subsidies on products. Consequently, a product subsidy raises the value of output at basic prices and, holding intermediate consumption constant, increases gross value added (GVA) at basic prices by the full amount of the subsidy.

Other subsidies on production — for example, wage subsidies, investment grants, or the Production‑Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme payments that are not tied to a specific unit of output — are recorded as negative taxes on production in the generation of income account. They do not enter the output valuation; instead they reduce the “taxes less subsidies on production and imports” line, thereby raising gross operating surplus or mixed income of the recipient industry. The 2008 SNA (paragraph 7.71) and the forthcoming 2025 SNA maintain this distinction, emphasizing that only product subsidies affect the basic‑price valuation of output.

In the Indian context, the fertilizer subsidy paid to domestic urea manufacturers is a classic product subsidy. It is recorded as a subsidy on products in the supply‑use tables, increasing the basic‑price output of the chemical fertilizer industry. By contrast, the PLI scheme for electronics manufacturing provides a lump‑sum incentive linked to incremental sales; this is classified as an other subsidy on production and appears as a negative entry under taxes less subsidies on production in the generation of income account for the electronics industry.

The conversion from GVA at basic prices to GDP at market prices adds taxes on products and subtracts subsidies on products. Therefore, a product subsidy that raises GVA at basic prices is exactly offset in the market‑price identity, leaving GDP at market prices unchanged. This neutrality is a frequent source of confusion: analysts sometimes add the subsidy to GDP, forgetting that the market‑price measure already nets it out. The income approach makes the same neutrality explicit: the subsidy reduces net taxes on production, increasing operating surplus, but the overall sum of factor incomes plus net taxes on production equals GDP at market prices.

Measurement challenges arise from timing and accrual. Subsidies are often disbursed in cash after the production period, while the SNA requires accrual recording. The CSO uses budget documents and controller‑general of accounts data to allocate subsidies to the appropriate quarter on an accrual basis. The 2025 SNA’s guidance on “subsidy accrual” recommends using the moment the underlying transaction (e.g., sale of subsidised fertilizer) occurs, not the cash‑payment date.

Technique: Subsidy Impact on GVA and Income Account
A government introduces a production subsidy of ₹500 crore on fertilizer used by farmers. Explain how this subsidy is recorded in the production approach (output at basic prices) and the generation of income account (taxes less subsidies on production).
In the production approach, the subsidy on a product (fertilizer) is a subsidy on products. Output at basic prices = output at producers' prices - taxes on products + subsidies on products. The subsidy raises output at basic prices by ₹500 crore, increasing gross value added at basic prices by the same amount, assuming intermediate consumption unchanged. In the generation of income account, subsidies on production appear as a negative entry under taxes less subsidies on production and imports. The ₹500 crore subsidy reduces net taxes on production by ₹500 crore, thereby increasing gross operating surplus/mixed income of the agricultural sector by ₹500 crore. The net effect on GDP at market prices is neutral because the subsidy is a transfer; GDP at market prices = GVA at basic prices + taxes on products - subsidies on products. The subsidy increases GVA at basic prices but is subtracted in the conversion to market prices, leaving GDP unchanged.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question asks about the effect of a production subsidy, first identify whether it is a subsidy on products or other subsidies on production. Write the basic price identity and the generation of income account line items. Show the directional change (increase/decrease) for each aggregate. This structured approach avoids the common trap of mixing up the sign in the market-price conversion.

The Integration of the SNA with the System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting for Air Emissions (SEEA‑Air) and Climate Policy Analysis

The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting for Air Emissions (SEEA‑Air) provides a consistent framework for recording the physical flows of pollutants — carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, sulphur dioxide, particulate matter — by economic activity. Its accounting structure mirrors the SNA’s production and generation of income accounts, using the same industry classification (ISIC) and the residence principle. This alignment allows analysts to link emission intensities (emissions per unit of GVA) directly to the national accounts aggregates, facilitating the assessment of carbon pricing, the design of nationally determined contributions (NDCs), and the monitoring of the “green” transition.

Compilation of air emission accounts begins with the energy balance, which allocates fuel combustion to industries and households. Emission factors — typically sourced from the IPCC Guidelines — are applied to the physical energy use to derive emissions by sector. The SNA’s supply‑use tables provide the activity data (output, intermediate consumption) needed to distribute emissions to the appropriate industries. For example, emissions from electricity generation are allocated to the electricity industry, while emissions from the use of electricity by the steel industry are recorded as indirect emissions in the steel industry’s input‑output row if a “footprint” approach is adopted. The 2025 SNA encourages the presentation of both “territorial” (production‑based) and “consumption‑based” (footprint) emission accounts.

A key policy application is the estimation of the carbon content of GDP. By dividing total CO₂ emissions (territorial) by real GDP, analysts obtain a carbon intensity trend that can be compared across countries and over time. India’s Third Biennial Update Report to the UNFCCC uses SEEA‑Air data to show that the carbon intensity of GDP fell by approximately 24 % between 2005 and 2019, a figure derived from the integrated SNA‑SEEA framework. The same dataset underpins the design of the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme, where sectoral emission targets are expressed as reductions in emission intensity relative to the base‑year GVA.

Challenges remain in reconciling the residence principle of the SNA with the territorial principle used in the UNFCCC reporting. International bunkers (aviation and maritime fuel sold to non‑resident operators) are excluded from territorial emissions but included in the SNA’s production account of the resident airline or shipping company. The SEEA‑Air manual recommends a “bridging table” that shows the adjustments needed to move from the SNA‑consistent residence basis to the UNFCCC territorial basis. The 2025 SNA’s annex on environmental accounting formalises this bridging requirement, ensuring that national statistical offices publish both sets of accounts with transparent metadata.

Data quality depends on the timeliness and granularity of energy statistics. In many emerging economies, the energy balance is compiled annually with a two‑year lag, while the SNA’s quarterly accounts require more frequent emission indicators. The use of satellite‑derived atmospheric concentration data (e.g., from the TROPOMI instrument) is being explored as a high‑frequency proxy for CO₂ and NOₓ emissions, but the conversion from column concentrations to sectoral emissions remains an active research area.

The Use of High‑Frequency Financial Market Data for Real‑Time Estimation of Gross Fixed Capital Formation

Gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) is one of the most volatile components of expenditure‑side GDP, and its timely estimation is crucial for monetary policy and fiscal planning. High‑frequency financial market data — equity issuance volumes, corporate bond spreads, initial public offering (IPO) proceeds, venture‑capital deal flows, and stock‑market capitalization — have been shown to contain leading information about firms’ investment intentions. The theoretical link runs through the q‑theory of investment: when the market value of installed capital (proxied by Tobin’s q) exceeds its replacement cost, firms issue equity or debt to finance new capital goods.

In practice, central banks and statistical offices construct a set of weekly or monthly financial indicators and feed them into a nowcasting model for quarterly GFCF. The Reserve Bank of India’s “Financial Conditions Index” incorporates corporate bond issuance, commercial paper outstanding, and the BSE‑500 market‑cap‑to‑GDP ratio. A vector autoregression (VAR) with exogenous financial variables (VARX) or a gradient‑boosted tree model is estimated on historical quarters where both the financial indicators and the official GFCF (from the quarterly national accounts) are known. The model learns non‑linear lag structures — for instance, equity issuance tends to lead GFCF by two quarters, while corporate bond spreads lead by one quarter.

The 2025 SNA’s “big‑data” annex explicitly recognises financial market micro‑data as a permissible source for real‑time national accounts, provided that the data‑access protocol, aggregation methodology, and model‑validation results are documented in the metadata. The European Central Bank’s “Financial Accounts Nowcast” uses the euro‑area sectoral financial accounts (who‑to‑whom matrices) to produce a weekly estimate of non‑financial corporations’ gross capital formation.
