In out‑of‑sample tests for 2015‑2023, the nowcast reduced the root‑mean‑square error by 22 % relative to a benchmark bridge equation based on industrial production and business‑survey data.

Limitations are significant. Financial market data reflect valuation changes as much as real investment; a stock‑market boom driven by sentiment can inflate the equity‑issuance indicator without a corresponding rise in capital expenditure. Moreover, a large share of GFCF in emerging economies is undertaken by the government and by unincorporated enterprises that do not access capital markets. The nowcasting model must therefore include fiscal‑expenditure indicators (capital outlay from the monthly treasury accounts) and construction‑permits data to capture the non‑corporate component. The Indian CSO’s experimental nowcast combines the RBI’s financial conditions index with the Ministry of Finance’s monthly capital‑expenditure releases and the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy’s project‑tracking database.

Finally, the integration of financial‑market‑based nowcasts into the official quarterly accounts requires a revision policy. The 2025 SNA recommends that nowcasts be published as “flash estimates” with a clear label, and that they be replaced by the survey‑based estimates once the latter become available. The revision cycle should be documented in the national accounts metadata, showing the size and direction of each revision, to maintain user confidence.

The Measurement of the Economic Contribution of the Non‑Profit Sector Beyond NPISH: Volunteer Labor and Social Enterprises

The System of National Accounts distinguishes non‑profit institutions serving households (NPISH) as a separate institutional sector. NPISH output is valued at the sum of compensation of employees, consumption of fixed capital, and intermediate consumption, because most NPISH services are provided free or at prices that are not economically significant. However, the non‑profit universe also includes social enterprises — organisations that generate a substantial share of revenue from market sales while pursuing a social mission — and a vast amount of volunteer labour that falls outside the core production boundary.

Volunteer labour is not recorded in the main sequence of accounts because it does not involve a monetary transaction. The 2008 SNA (Chapter 23) recommends a satellite account for household production that values volunteer time using the replacement‑cost method (the wage that would be paid to a hired worker performing the same task) or the opportunity‑cost method (the foregone earnings of the volunteer). India’s Time Use Survey (2019) provides the hours spent on unpaid volunteer work by activity and demographic group. Applying the replacement‑cost wage rate from the Periodic Labour Force Survey yields an estimate of volunteer output equivalent to roughly 0.8 % of GDP. This figure is published in the “Satellite Account for Unpaid Work” and is used in the Human Development Index adjustments.

Social enterprises pose a classification challenge. If more than 50 % of their revenue comes from market sales, the 2008 SNA classifies them as non‑financial corporations rather than NPISH. Their output is then valued at market prices, and their surplus is recorded as operating surplus. However, many social enterprises operate in a hybrid zone, receiving grants and donations alongside market revenue. The International Classification of Non‑Profit Organizations (ICNPO) and the “Social Enterprise” module in the 2025 SNA provide guidance: a “mixed‑income” approach splits the institution into a market‑producing unit (treated as a corporation) and a non‑market unit (treated as NPISH), each with its own production account. The UK Office for National Statistics has implemented this split for the “community interest companies” sector, producing a separate satellite account that shows the market and non‑market components side by side.

Data gaps remain acute. Most countries lack a comprehensive register of social enterprises, and volunteer hours are captured only in periodic time‑use surveys. The 2025 SNA encourages the use of administrative data — charity‑commission filings, tax‑exempt status registers, and crowdfunding platform records — to build a dynamic frame. In India, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs’ “Form MGT‑7” filings for Section 8 companies (non‑profit companies) and the NITI Aayog’s “Social Enterprise Registry” pilot are steps toward a statistical register that can feed into the national accounts.

From a policy perspective, the satellite accounts for volunteer work and social enterprises enable the measurement of the “care economy” and the “social economy” contributions to well‑being. They also inform the design of fiscal incentives: for example, the Indian government’s “Social Stock Exchange” framework requires quantified social impact metrics that can be linked to the satellite‑account estimates of volunteer‑equivalent output and social‑enterprise value added.

  • Confusing subsidies on products with other subsidies on production when tracing their effect through the generation of income account.
  • Assuming enterprise survey data are directly comparable across years without adjusting for coverage changes and frame updates.
  • Treating air emission accounts as a simple overlay on the SNA without reconciling residence versus territorial principles.
  • Overstating the predictive power of financial market indicators for real capital formation without accounting for valuation‑driven volatility.
  • Equating volunteer labour with market output in the core accounts rather than in the designated satellite account.
  • Ignoring the distinction between NPISH and social enterprises when compiling the non‑profit sector satellite account.
  • Using high‑frequency financial data without adjusting for mark‑to‑market changes that do not reflect real investment activity.

Valuation of Free Digital Services and the Production Boundary in the 2025 SNA

The 2025 revision of the System of National Accounts (SNA) explicitly recognises that a growing share of household consumption consists of digital services provided without a monetary price — search engines, social‑media platforms, mapping applications, and cloud‑based productivity tools. Under the 2008 SNA these services were largely excluded from the production boundary because no transaction occurs; the 2025 SNA, however, introduces a satellite‑account framework that values them as non‑market output produced by the platform enterprises on own account. The valuation follows the cost‑of‑production approach: the sum of compensation of employees, consumption of fixed capital, intermediate consumption (including server‑farm electricity, bandwidth, and data‑centre depreciation), and a return to capital estimated from the platform’s market‑based financing costs. This method mirrors the treatment of government non‑market output and ensures consistency with the general valuation principle for non‑market producers.

A key methodological choice concerns the allocation of joint costs between paid advertising services (which remain market output) and free user‑facing services. The 2025 SNA recommends a revenue‑proportional split based on the share of total platform revenue attributable to advertising versus other monetisation streams. Where reliable revenue breakdowns are unavailable, compilers may use a user‑time allocation derived from telemetry data (average session length, frequency of use) as a proxy. The Indian Central Statistics Office (CSO) has piloted this approach using anonymised aggregate data from major domestic platforms, reporting that the satellite account adds roughly 0.5‑1.0 % to gross value added (GVA) in the information‑communication sector. The satellite account is published separately from the core accounts, preserving the integrity of the headline GDP figure while providing policymakers with a measure of digital welfare gains.

Two practical challenges remain. First, the cross‑border nature of many platforms means that a portion of the cost base (e.g., global R&D, data‑centre infrastructure) is incurred outside the compiling economy. The 2025 SNA adopts the residence principle: only costs incurred by resident institutional units are recorded in the domestic satellite account; the remainder is captured in the rest‑of‑the‑world account and reflected in the balance of payments as imports of computer services. Second, the rapid obsolescence of digital capital requires chain‑linked volume measures with short asset‑life assumptions (typically 3‑5 years for software and server hardware). The CSO’s 2024 experimental estimates apply a geometric depreciation profile consistent with the KLEMS database, ensuring that volume growth of free digital services is not overstated by price‑index bias.

From an examination perspective, candidates should be able to distinguish three concepts: (i) the core production boundary (unchanged for market output), (ii) the satellite‑account boundary for free digital services (non‑market own‑account production), and (iii) the treatment of cross‑border cost allocation under the residence principle. A typical trap is to conflate the satellite‑account estimate with an upward revision of headline GDP; the 2025 SNA explicitly states that satellite accounts are supplementary and do not alter the main aggregates.

Accounting for Cybersecurity Expenditure and Digital Resilience in National Accounts

Cybersecurity spending — encompassing threat‑intelligence services, encryption hardware, security‑operations‑centre (SOC) personnel, and cyber‑insurance premiums — has risen sharply across both public and private sectors. The 2008 SNA classifies such outlays as intermediate consumption when purchased by enterprises for the protection of their own production processes, and as final consumption expenditure when incurred by government for the provision of collective security services. The 2025 SNA introduces a more granular breakdown: it recommends a distinct “digital resilience” product category within computer‑related services (CPC 843) to capture both market and non‑market cybersecurity output. This allows compilers to trace the flow of cybersecurity services from specialised providers (often classified in the information‑communication sector) to user industries, facilitating input‑output analysis of digital‑risk exposure.

A critical measurement issue is the capitalisation of internally developed security software. When an enterprise’s own IT staff write intrusion‑detection code, the 2025 SNA treats the resulting software as a produced fixed asset if it meets the criteria of control, economic benefit, and a service life exceeding one year. The asset is valued at the sum of direct labour costs, a share of overheads, and a mark‑up for the opportunity cost of the developers’ time. In India, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has issued guidance aligning the Government Accounting Standards Advisory Board (GASAB) capitalisation thresholds with the SNA recommendation, enabling the inclusion of home‑grown security platforms (e.g., the National Cyber Coordination Centre’s analytics suite) in the government’s capital stock.

Cyber‑insurance premiums pose a separate classification question. The 2025 SNA treats the net premium (premium minus expected claims) as a service charge — recorded as output of the insurance corporation and intermediate consumption of the policyholder. The claims paid are recorded as current transfers, not as production. This distinction matters for the measurement of the insurance sector’s value added and for the calculation of the non‑financial corporations’ operating surplus. Indian insurers reporting under the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (IRDAI) framework now provide the required split, allowing the CSO to implement the 2025 treatment from the 2025‑26 reference year.

Finally, the measurement of digital resilience as a stock is being explored through a satellite account that aggregates the capitalised value of security software, hardware (firewalls, hardware security modules), and the human capital embodied in certified security professionals. Pilot estimates for the Indian banking sector suggest that the stock of cybersecurity capital amounts to roughly 0.3 % of the sector’s total fixed capital, a figure that can be linked to the frequency of reported incidents to assess the marginal effectiveness of investment. Examiners often test the ability to differentiate between current expenditure (intermediate consumption) and capital formation (produced assets) in this context, and to apply the residence principle when a domestic firm purchases cloud‑based security services from a non‑resident provider.

Classification Exercise
A domestic e‑commerce company spends ₹120 crore in a year on the following: (i) ₹45 crore for a subscription to a foreign cloud‑based threat‑intelligence platform; (ii) ₹30 crore for salaries of its in‑house security analysts who develop proprietary detection algorithms; (iii) ₹25 crore for cyber‑insurance premiums (net of expected claims ₹5 crore); (iv) ₹20 crore for purchasing firewall appliances with a 5‑year life. Classify each item according to the 2025 SNA (output, intermediate consumption, gross fixed capital formation, import of services, etc.).
(i) Subscription to a non‑resident platform → import of computer services (BOP), intermediate consumption of the e‑commerce firm. (ii) In‑house development → own‑account gross fixed capital formation (produced software asset) valued at ₹30 crore plus overhead mark‑up; the corresponding labour cost is removed from compensation of employees and re‑routed to capital formation. (iii) Net premium (₹20 crore) → output of resident insurance corporation (if insurer resident) or import of insurance service (if non‑resident); intermediate consumption of the firm. The ₹5 crore expected claims are a current transfer, not production. (iv) Firewall appliances → gross fixed capital formation (acquired asset), recorded at purchaser’s price ₹20 crore; depreciation (consumption of fixed capital) begins in the same period under the 2025 SNA’s geometric profile.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question lists multiple cybersecurity outlays, first separate resident vs. non‑resident transactions (residence principle). Then apply the 2025 SNA hierarchy: own‑account software → GFCF; purchased security services → intermediate consumption (or import); insurance net premium → service output/import; hardware → GFCF. Remember that claims are transfers, not production. A quick mental checklist — “who produces? who uses? cross‑border?” — prevents the common error of lumping everything into intermediate consumption.

Measuring the Economic Value of Open Data and Public Sector Information

Open data — datasets published by government agencies under licences that permit free reuse — has become a recognised factor of production for downstream firms, researchers, and civic innovators. The 2025 SNA treats the creation and dissemination of open data as a non‑market service produced by general government. Its output is valued at the sum of costs: personnel engaged in data curation, metadata standardisation, portal maintenance, and the depreciation of the IT infrastructure hosting the repositories. Because the data are provided at zero price, the service is recorded as government final consumption expenditure (collective service) and simultaneously as intermediate consumption of the users who incorporate the data into their own production processes. This double entry ensures that the contribution of open data to downstream value added is captured without inflating government output.

A practical compilation challenge is the allocation of joint costs between open‑data portals and restricted‑access data services (e.g., statistical microdata released under licence). The 2025 SNA recommends a usage‑based split using portal analytics: the number of API calls, download volumes, and unique user sessions attributable to open versus restricted datasets. In India, the National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (NDSAP) portal provides such metrics, enabling the CSO to allocate roughly 65 % of the portal’s operating cost to open‑data production in the 2023‑24 accounts. The remaining 35 % is treated as a market service (sale of licensed microdata) and valued at the fees collected.

The valuation of the data asset itself — the stock of curated datasets — is addressed in a satellite account for knowledge capital. Following the 2025 SNA’s guidance on research‑and‑development (R&D) capitalisation, each dataset that meets the criteria of a produced asset (control, economic benefit, service life > 1 year) is capitalised at its production cost. The asset is then depreciated over an estimated useful life (typically 5‑10 years for statistical time series, longer for geospatial reference layers). This approach permits the construction of a public‑sector knowledge‑capital stock that can be linked to productivity analysis via the KLEMS framework. Pilot work by the Indian Statistical Institute (ISI) suggests that the capitalised value of core open datasets (census, agricultural surveys, health facility registers) amounts to about 0.2 % of GDP, a modest but policy‑relevant figure.

Examiners frequently test the distinction between open data as a non‑market service (government output) and open data as an intermediate input for private firms. A common mistake is to record the download of an open dataset as a market transaction, thereby creating a spurious export of services. The correct treatment recognises that the user’s benefit is captured through the intermediate consumption entry, while the provider’s cost remains in government consumption. Another trap is to capitalise the raw data (e.g., sensor readings) without the requisite curation; only the curated, documented, and maintained dataset qualifies as a produced asset under the SNA.

National Income Accounting for Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Adaptation Expenditure

Expenditure on disaster risk reduction (DRR) — such as early‑warning systems, flood‑defence infrastructure, building‑code enforcement, and community‑based preparedness programmes — and on climate adaptation (e.g., drought‑resilient crop varieties, coastal‑zone management, urban heat‑island mitigation) has grown in both public budgets and private investment. The 2008 SNA classifies these outlays according to their institutional sector and economic nature: government spending on DRR infrastructure is gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) when it creates a new asset or significantly extends the life of an existing one; recurrent spending on preparedness drills, insurance subsidies, and maintenance is intermediate consumption or final consumption expenditure depending on whether the service is used in production or consumed collectively. The 2025 SNA adds a “climate‑adaptation” product classification (CPC 949) to identify these flows explicitly in supply‑use tables.

A key accounting issue is the treatment of contingent liabilities arising from disaster‑risk insurance schemes (e.g., the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana). The 2025 SNA records the net premium as a service charge (output of the insurer, intermediate consumption of the farmer or government) and the claims paid as current transfers. However, the expected future claims embedded in the insurance contract are not recognised as liabilities in the core balance sheet; they appear only in the contingent‑liability memorandum of the government’s fiscal accounts. This distinction matters for debt‑sustainability analysis: the core national‑accounts debt stock excludes contingent claims, while the fiscal‑risk framework incorporates them.

For private firms, investment in adaptation measures (e.g., elevating machinery above flood levels, installing water‑recycling systems) is capitalised as GFCF if it meets the asset criteria. The 2025 SNA encourages the use of engineering‑based cost estimates to separate the adaptation component from routine replacement investment. In India, the Ministry of Finance’s “Climate‑Resilient Infrastructure” guidelines require project‑level tagging of adaptation costs, enabling the CSO to compile a satellite account of adaptation capital formation. Preliminary estimates for 2022‑23 indicate that tagged adaptation GFCF amounted to roughly 0.4 % of total GFCF, concentrated in the agriculture, water‑supply, and urban‑development sectors.

Another measurement frontier is the valuation of ecosystem‑based DRR — such as mangrove restoration for storm‑surge protection. The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting (SEEA‑EA) provides a framework to value the protective service as an ecosystem service flow (physical units: hectares of mangrove; monetary units: avoided damage). The 2025 SNA recommends recording the restoration expenditure as GFCF (produced asset: restored ecosystem) and the annual protective service as an intermediate consumption of the benefiting economic units (e.g., coastal property owners). This dual entry links the physical accounts of SEEA‑EA with the monetary accounts of the SNA, allowing a consistent assessment of cost‑effectiveness. Examiners often ask candidates to distinguish between (a) the capital expenditure that creates the protective asset, (b) the ongoing maintenance cost, and (c) the flow of ecosystem services — and to apply the correct SNA/SEEA codes to each.

The Treatment of Digital Public Infrastructure (e.g., Aadhaar, UPI) in the System of National Accounts

Digital public infrastructure (DPI) — population‑scale identity systems (Aadhaar), real‑time payment rails (Unified Payments Interface, UPI), and consent‑based data‑exchange layers (Account Aggregator framework) — represents a new class of government‑provided platform that is neither a traditional public good nor a conventional market service. The 2025 SNA treats the development and operation of DPI as non‑market output of general government (or of a public corporation if the platform is corporatised). Output is valued at cost: compensation of employees (including contracted developers), consumption of fixed capital on servers and network equipment, intermediate consumption (cloud hosting, telecommunications), and a return to capital for any equity invested by the state. Because the services are provided at zero or nominal price to end‑users, the output is recorded as government final consumption expenditure (collective) and simultaneously as intermediate consumption of the resident sectors that use the platform (banks, fintech firms, social‑protection programmes).

A critical classification decision concerns the ownership of the underlying intellectual property. In the Indian case, the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) holds the Aadhaar software as a government‑owned intangible asset; the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), a not‑for‑profit company owned by banks, operates UPI. The 2025 SNA recommends that when a public corporation provides a platform at non‑market prices, its output be valued at cost and the corporation be classified in the public non‑financial corporations sector. The resulting operating surplus (if any) is recorded as property income to the government. For UPI, NPCI’s surplus is minimal by design; its costs are covered by transaction‑fee revenue from banks, which the 2025 SNA treats as market output (payment‑processing services) rather than a transfer. This dual character — non‑market infrastructure layer plus market transaction layer — requires a split in the supply‑use table: the infrastructure layer (network, settlement engine) at cost, the transaction‑processing layer at market price.

The capitalisation of DPI assets follows the 2025 SNA’s rules for research‑and‑development and software. The initial build‑out (software architecture, biometric algorithms, encryption modules) is capitalised as a produced intangible asset with a service life of 7‑10 years, depreciated geometrically. Subsequent upgrades (e.g., addition of face‑authentication, offline KYC) are treated as major improvements and added to the asset’s value. The CSO’s 2024 experimental capital‑stock estimates place the net capital stock of Aadhaar‑related software and hardware at approximately ₹12,000 crore, representing about 0.05 % of the total produced fixed capital stock. This figure is used in the KLEMS growth‑accounting framework to assess the contribution of DPI to total factor productivity (TFP) in the financial‑services and public‑administration sectors.

From a fiscal‑transparency perspective, the 2025 SNA encourages the presentation of a DPI satellite account that shows (i) the cost‑based output, (ii) the user‑side intermediate consumption by sector, (iii) the capital stock and depreciation, and (iv) the estimated productivity spillovers (e.g., reduction in customer‑onboarding costs for banks). The Indian Ministry of Finance has adopted this template in the “Digital Economy” chapter of the Economic Survey, linking the satellite‑account aggregates to the government’s “Digital India” targets. Examiners may test the ability to differentiate between the non‑market infrastructure layer (cost valuation, government consumption) and the market transaction layer (fee‑based output, intermediate consumption of banks), and to apply the correct sector classification for the operating entity (UIDAI vs. NPCI). A frequent error is to record the entire UPI ecosystem as a single market service, thereby overstating NPCI’s output and missing the government’s non‑market contribution.

  • Confusing the satellite‑account valuation of free digital services with a revision of headline GDP.
  • Treating all cybersecurity outlays as intermediate consumption without separating own‑account software capital formation.
  • Recording open‑data downloads as market exports instead of intermediate consumption of a non‑market government service.
  • Capitalising raw sensor data as a produced asset without the required curation and documentation.
  • Mixing disaster‑risk insurance net premiums with claims in the production account; claims are current transfers.
  • Classifying the entire digital public infrastructure as a market service, ignoring the non‑market infrastructure layer valued at cost.
  • Overlooking the residence principle when a domestic firm purchases cloud‑based security or DPI services from a non‑resident provider.

Valuation of Publicly Funded Vocational Training and Skill Development Programs in National Accounts

The 2008 System of National Accounts (SNA) treats government‑provided education as non‑market output valued at cost, but the 2025 SNA revision introduces a more granular approach for vocational training that is explicitly linked to labour‑market outcomes. In India, the Skill India Mission (launched July 2015) and the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC) operate a network of over 12 000 training centres delivering courses aligned to the National Skills Qualification Framework (NSQF). The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) reports annual expenditure on these programmes; for FY 2023‑24 the budgeted outlay was ₹12 500 crore, of which ₹9 800 crore was disbursed as grants to training partners and ₹2 700 crore covered infrastructure and curriculum development.

Under the 2025 SNA, each training programme is recorded as a produced service (education) with output measured by the sum of compensation of trainers, consumption of fixed capital on training equipment, intermediate consumption (materials, utilities), and a return to capital for any public‑corporation‑run centres. Because trainees typically pay no fee, the output is entered as government final consumption expenditure (collective) and simultaneously as intermediate consumption of the household sector (human capital formation). The resulting increase in the household’s human‑capital stock is captured in the balance‑sheet account as a non‑produced asset, following the Jorgenson‑Fraumeni lifetime‑income approach piloted by the CSO in 2022.

A key measurement issue is the attribution of productivity gains. The 2025 SNA recommends a satellite account that links training output to subsequent wage‑premia observed in the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS). The 2023 PLFS shows that workers who completed NSQF‑level 4 or higher courses earned on average 18 % more than comparable untrained workers. This wage differential is used to estimate the rate of return on the training capital stock, which is then fed into the KLEMS growth‑accounting framework to assess the contribution of skill formation to total factor productivity (TFP) in manufacturing and services.

Another complication arises from the dual nature of many centres: some are run by private providers receiving outcome‑based grants. The 2025 SNA classifies such providers as market producers when they charge fees to trainees, but as non‑market when the bulk of revenue comes from government grants. The Indian implementation therefore splits the supply‑use table: the grant‑financed portion is valued at cost (government consumption), while any fee‑charging component is valued at market price. The CSO’s 2024 experimental satellite account for skill development shows a net capital stock of training infrastructure of ₹3 200 crore, representing 0.01 % of total produced fixed capital.

Examiners often test the distinction between the cost‑valuation of non‑market training output and the market valuation of fee‑based courses, and the correct sector classification of the training provider (general government vs. public corporation vs. private non‑profit). A frequent error is to record the entire Skill India outlay as a transfer, omitting the production account entry and thereby understating government consumption and human‑capital formation.

The Treatment of Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms and Their Recording in the SNA

The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), adopted in May 2023 and entering a transitional reporting phase from October 2023, imposes a carbon price on imports of cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen. From 2026 the mechanism will require importers to surrender CBAM certificates equivalent to the embedded emissions, effectively extending the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) to the border. The 2025 SNA provides guidance on recording such border carbon adjustments as a tax on products (D.21) when they are levied by the importing government, and as a subsidy on production (D.31) when the exporting country provides a rebate.

For the importing economy (the EU), the CBAM revenue is recorded as a tax on products in the generation of income account, increasing government revenue and reducing the net operating surplus of the importing firms. The corresponding carbon cost is reflected in the intermediate consumption of the importing industries, raising their production costs and, through the price deflator, the volume measure of output. In the balance‑sheet account, the CBAM certificates held by importers are treated as financial assets (AF.7) until surrendered, at which point they are extinguished and the tax liability is settled.

For the exporting economy (e.g., India), the embedded carbon cost borne by producers is recorded as a tax on production (D.29) if the domestic carbon price is lower than the CBAM rate, because the foreign tax effectively raises the cost of production for export‑oriented firms. If the exporting country has a domestic carbon tax that is creditable against CBAM, the net effect is a reduction in the tax on production. The 2025 SNA recommends a satellite account for carbon‑border flows that shows (i) the value of CBAM certificates purchased, (ii) the embedded emissions in physical units, and (iii) the resulting change in the terms of trade for carbon‑intensive sectors.

India’s Ministry of Finance, in its 2024 Economic Survey, estimated that CBAM could affect exports worth US$ 8 billion in the first year of full implementation, primarily in steel and aluminium. The CSO has begun a pilot to integrate CBAM‑related tax flows into the supply‑use tables for the metal‑products industry, using customs data on certificate purchases and the Ministry of Environment’s emissions‑intensity factors. The pilot shows an increase in the effective tax rate on steel exports from 0.3 % to 1.7 % of export value, which feeds into the sectoral deflator and reduces real export growth by an estimated 0.15 percentage points.

A common examination trap is to treat CBAM revenue as a current transfer rather than a tax on products, or to record the certificate purchase as a financial transaction without linking it to the production account. The correct treatment follows the 2025 SNA’s principle that any compulsory levy on goods crossing the border, irrespective of its environmental motive, is a tax on products and must appear in the generation of income account of the importing government.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "How should the revenue collected by the EU under the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism be recorded in the EU's national accounts?" The answer choices include (a) current transfer, (b) tax on products, (c) subsidy on production, (d) capital transfer.
The correct answer is (b) tax on products. Under the 2025 SNA, a compulsory levy on imported goods, such as CBAM certificates, is classified as a tax on products (D.21) in the generation of income account of the importing government. It is not a transfer because it is linked to the value of the imported product, nor a subsidy because it raises rather than lowers production cost. Recording it as a current transfer would misstate government revenue and the tax burden on importers.
Exam‑day strategy
When a new border carbon measure appears, first identify the imposing jurisdiction. If the levy is collected by the importing government on the value of the good, classify it as a tax on products (D.21). If the exporting government provides a rebate, treat it as a subsidy on production (D.31). Always check whether the SNA version referenced (2008 vs. 2025) changes the classification; the 2025 SNA explicitly addresses carbon‑border adjustments.

Accounting for the Economic Value of Urban Green Space Ecosystem Services under SEEA‑EEA

The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA‑EEA), adopted by the UN Statistical Commission in 2021, extends the production boundary to include ecosystem services that are not traded in markets. Urban green spaces — parks, street trees, wetlands, and peri‑urban forests — supply a bundle of regulating, provisioning and cultural services: air‑pollution removal, heat‑island mitigation, storm‑water regulation, recreation, and aesthetic value. The 2025 SNA recommends that these services be recorded in a satellite ecosystem account, with physical flows measured in biophysical units (e.g., tonnes of PM₂.₅ removed, cubic metres of runoff retained) and monetary values derived using replacement‑cost, avoided‑damage, or hedonic‑pricing methods.

In India, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) launched the Urban Ecosystem Accounts pilot in 2023 for five metropolitan areas (Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad). The pilot used high‑resolution satellite imagery (Sentinel‑2, 10 m) combined with the i‑Tree Eco model to estimate that urban trees in Delhi removed approximately 12 000 tonnes of PM₂.₅ annually, valued at ₹1 800 crore using the avoided‑health‑cost method (based on the Value of Statistical Life recommended by the WHO). Storm‑water retention by urban wetlands in Chennai was estimated at 45 million m³ per year, with a replacement‑cost valuation of ₹620 crore (cost of equivalent engineered drainage).

The ecosystem account records these services as intermediate consumption of the relevant economic sectors: air‑purification as intermediate consumption of the health sector, heat mitigation as intermediate consumption of the electricity sector (reduced cooling demand), and recreation as final consumption of households. The corresponding ecosystem assets (urban forest, wetland) appear on the balance sheet as non‑produced environmental assets, with a change in net worth reflecting degradation or enhancement. The 2025 SNA requires that the depletion of these assets be recorded as consumption of fixed capital (CFC) in the ecosystem account, ensuring that the net domestic product (NDP) reflects the loss of natural capital.

A measurement challenge is the avoidance of double counting with existing market services. For example, the cooling effect of street trees reduces household electricity consumption; the SNA already captures the reduced electricity use in the household final consumption expenditure. The SEEA‑EEA resolves this by recording the ecosystem service as a separate flow and adjusting the electricity sector’s intermediate consumption accordingly, leaving headline GDP unchanged but providing a richer analytical framework for policy.

Examiners may ask to distinguish between the physical flow account (biophysical units) and the monetary valuation account, and to identify the correct valuation method for each service type (replacement cost for storm‑water, avoided damage for air‑purification, hedonic pricing for recreation). A frequent mistake is to capitalise the entire urban park as a produced asset; under SEEA‑EEA it remains a non‑produced environmental asset unless the park infrastructure (paths, lighting) is separately identified as produced capital.

Measuring the Economic Impact of Digital Financial Inclusion Initiatives on Household Income Distribution

India’s Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY), launched in August 2014, had opened over 500 million basic savings accounts by March 2024, with a cumulative deposit balance exceeding ₹2 trillion. The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), operational since April 2016, processed 10.6 billion transactions in March 2024, representing a transaction value of ₹18.5 trillion. The 2025 SNA treats the provision of payment‑system infrastructure by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) as a mixed output: the core settlement network is a non‑market service valued at cost (government consumption), while the per‑transaction fee charged to banks is a market output (financial service).

To assess the distributional impact, the CSO has constructed a Distributional National Accounts (DNA) module linking household‑level survey data (Consumer Pyramids Household Survey, 2023) with national‑accounts aggregates. The DNA shows that households in the bottom income quintile increased their share of total financial‑service consumption from 3.2 % in 2015 to 5.8 % in 2023, driven largely by zero‑balance Jan Dhan accounts and UPI‑based direct‑benefit transfers (DBT). The DBT programme, which routed ₹3.5 trillion of subsidies through bank accounts in FY 2023‑24, reduced leakage estimated at 15 % under the previous cash‑based system, effectively raising the real income of beneficiary households by an average of ₹2 200 per annum.

The 2025 SNA recommends recording DBT flows as government social‑benefit transfers (D.62) to households, with the corresponding payment‑processing fees recorded as intermediate consumption of the government (financial services). The NPCI’s fee revenue (₹1 200 crore in FY 2023‑24) appears as output of the financial‑corporations sector and as intermediate consumption of the general government. This dual recording preserves the production boundary while allowing the DNA to trace the net transfer to each income group.

A further nuance is the treatment of interest earned on Jan Dhan balances. Since these accounts pay a nominal interest rate (4 % per annum), the interest income is recorded as property income (D.4) receivable by households and payable by the banking sector. The DNA uses this flow to adjust the primary‑income distribution, showing a modest but measurable reduction in the Gini coefficient of primary income from 0.48 to 0.46 between 2015 and 2023.

Common exam errors include treating the entire UPI ecosystem as a single market service, ignoring the non‑market infrastructure layer, or recording DBT amounts as government final consumption rather than as social‑benefit transfers. The correct approach follows the 2025 SNA’s split‑output treatment for NPCI and the DNA framework for distributional analysis.

The Role of National Accounts in Assessing the Fiscal Implications of Tax Expenditure Programs

Tax expenditures — revenue forgone due to exemptions, deductions, credits, and preferential rates — have been reported by the Government of India since the 2005‑06 Budget under the “Statement of Revenue Foregone”. The 2025 SNA treats tax expenditures as a component of government revenue (negative taxes on income, wealth, etc.) and recommends their explicit recording in the generation of income account to improve fiscal transparency. In the 2023‑24 Budget, the total revenue foregone was estimated at ₹7.2 trillion (approximately 2.8 % of GDP), with the largest items being the corporate‑tax holiday for new manufacturing units (₹1.1 trillion), the accelerated depreciation allowance (₹900 billion), and the exemption of long‑term capital gains on listed equity (₹850 billion).

To integrate tax expenditures into the national accounts, the CSO maps each provision to the relevant tax category (D.51 taxes on income, D.59 other current taxes) and records the foregone amount as a negative tax receipt. The corresponding benefit to taxpayers appears as a subsidy on production (D.31) for corporate provisions or as a social‑benefit transfer (D.62) for personal‑income provisions. This dual entry ensures that the net lending/borrowing of general government is unchanged, but the composition of revenue and expenditure is more informative for policy analysis.

The 2025 SNA also encourages a satellite account for tax expenditures that links each provision to its economic objective (e.g., investment promotion, export competitiveness, social equity) and to outcome indicators such as incremental capital formation, export growth, or poverty reduction. The Ministry of Finance’s 2024 Tax Expenditure Review used input‑output multipliers to estimate that the manufacturing‑sector tax holiday generated an additional ₹2.3 trillion of gross fixed capital formation over five years, yielding a fiscal multiplier of 2.1. Conversely, the long‑term capital‑gains exemption was found to have a negligible effect on household savings rates, suggesting a low efficiency.

A practical compilation issue is the timing of recognition. The SNA records tax expenditures on an accrual basis when the tax liability arises, whereas budget documents often present them on a cash‑foregone basis. The CSO reconciles these by adjusting for the lag between assessment and collection, using the Income Tax Department’s assessment‑year data. The 2023‑24 reconciliation showed a ₹150 billion difference between accrual and cash estimates, which is recorded as a timing adjustment in the financial account.

Examiners may test the classification of a specific tax expenditure (e.g., whether the Section 80C deduction is a negative tax on income or a subsidy on production) and the impact on the government’s net lending. The correct answer follows the 2025 SNA: personal‑income deductions are negative taxes on income (D.51) with a matching social‑benefit transfer to households; corporate‑investment incentives are negative taxes on corporate income with a matching subsidy on production.

  • Confusing the non‑market infrastructure layer of a digital payment system with its market transaction layer, leading to double counting of output.
  • Recording carbon‑border adjustment revenue as a current transfer instead of a tax on products.
  • Capitalising urban green‑space assets as produced capital rather than non‑produced environmental assets.
  • Treating direct‑benefit transfers as government final consumption rather than social‑benefit transfers.
  • Classifying personal‑income tax deductions as subsidies on production instead of negative taxes on income.
  • Omitting the timing adjustment between accrual and cash estimates of tax expenditures in the financial account.
  • Failing to split the output of a mixed public‑corporation platform into cost‑valued and market‑valued components.

Treatment of Carbon Credits and Emission Trading Schemes in National Accounts

Carbon credits and emission allowances have become significant financial instruments since the Kyoto Protocol introduced the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) in 1997 and the European Union launched its Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) in 2005. In the System of National Accounts (SNA) 2008, emission allowances are classified as produced non‑financial assets (AN.112) when they are created by a government or supranational body and allocated to enterprises. The initial allocation is recorded as a capital transfer (D.9) from government to the recipient, while subsequent purchases and sales are treated as transactions in existing assets (F.5). The 2025 SNA revision refines this by distinguishing between compliance allowances (used to meet regulatory caps) and voluntary credits (generated from offset projects). Compliance allowances remain produced assets; voluntary credits are recorded as financial assets (AF.7) because they represent a claim on future emission reductions rather than a physical permit.

India’s Perform Achieve Trade (PAT) scheme, notified under the Energy Conservation Act 2001, issues Energy Saving Certificates (ESCerts) that function similarly to emission allowances. The Central Electricity Authority allocates ESCerts to designated consumers; excess certificates can be traded on power exchanges. In the Indian national accounts, the initial allocation is a capital transfer from the Ministry of Power to the industrial sector, and the subsequent trading is recorded as a transaction in produced assets. The 2025 SNA recommends that the fair value of allowances at each reporting date be reflected in the balance sheet, with revaluation gains or losses recorded in the other changes in volume of assets account (K.11). This ensures that the national balance sheet captures the market risk associated with carbon pricing.

A practical compilation issue arises from the timing of surrender. Entities must surrender allowances equal to verified emissions by a compliance deadline (e.g., 30 April for EU ETS). The SNA records the surrender as a use of produced asset (P.51c) reducing the asset stock and increasing intermediate consumption (P.2) for the period in which emissions occur. If the surrender occurs after the reporting quarter, a timing adjustment is made in the financial account to align accrual‑based national accounts with cash‑based regulatory reporting. The 2023‑24 Indian National Accounts incorporated a ₹12 billion timing adjustment for PAT certificates surrendered in April 2024 but recorded in the March quarter.

Valuation of carbon credits follows the market price on the relevant exchange (e.g., EU ETS spot price, Indian Energy Exchange price for ESCerts). When no active market exists, the 2025 SNA permits the use of shadow prices derived from marginal abatement cost curves. The Indian Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) adopted a shadow price of ₹1,800 per tonne CO₂e for 2022‑23 based on the Integrated Energy Policy model. This valuation feeds into the adjusted net national income (ANNI) where the cost of environmental degradation is subtracted, linking carbon accounting to the SEEA‑EEA framework.

Examiners often test the distinction between a capital transfer at allocation and a subsidy on production when allowances are granted free of charge to support a nascent industry. The correct treatment under the 2025 SNA: free allocation to a new entrant is a capital transfer (D.9) because it increases the recipient’s net worth without a corresponding current‑period cost. Recording it as a subsidy (D.3) would overstate current‑period production subsidies and distort the generation of income account.

Accounting for the Economic Value of Data Localization Policies

Data localization mandates — requiring that certain categories of personal or strategic data be stored and processed within national borders — have proliferated since the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) 2018, China’s Cybersecurity Law 2017, and India’s draft Personal Data Protection Bill (PDPB) 2019 and subsequent Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023. These policies create a domestic data‑storage industry comprising data centres, cloud regions, and associated network infrastructure. In the SNA, the construction and operation of data centres are recorded as gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) in the information and communication technology (ICT) asset category (AN.1131). The 2025 SNA explicitly recognises data as a produced asset when it is the output of a data‑processing activity that meets the criteria of economic ownership, control, and ability to generate future benefits.

The economic value of localized data arises from two channels. First, the investment channel: firms incur capital expenditure to build or lease local server capacity. India’s data‑centre capacity grew from 350 MW in 2019 to 1,200 MW in 2023, attracting ₹45,000 crore of FDI. This investment is captured in the capital account and contributes to GDP through the production of construction and ICT services. Second, the productivity channel: localized data reduces latency for domestic digital services (e.g., UPI, Aadhaar authentication) and enables compliance‑driven innovation in fintech, health‑tech, and e‑governance. The 2025 SNA recommends a satellite account for data assets that links the stock of stored data (measured in petabytes) to a valuation based on the replacement cost of storage and the income approach using the marginal revenue product of data‑intensive services.

Valuation challenges include the non‑rival nature of data and the difficulty of observing market prices for proprietary datasets. The Indian pilot Data Satellite Account (2022‑23) used a cost‑based method for raw stored data (₹0.12 per GB per month) and a revenue‑share method for processed data services, allocating 15 % of the gross output of data‑driven platforms to the data asset. This yielded an estimated data‑asset stock of ₹3.2 trillion (≈1.2 % of GDP) for 2022‑23. The account also records cross‑border data flows as exports/imports of ICT services (BOP item S.1b) when data processing is performed by a non‑resident entity for a resident client, ensuring consistency with the Balance of Payments Manual (BPM6).

A common exam trap is to treat the regulatory cost of compliance (e.g., legal fees, audit expenses) as intermediate consumption of the data‑localization policy itself. The correct SNA treatment: compliance costs are intermediate consumption of the affected industry (e.g., banking, telecom) and do not create a separate policy asset. Only the resulting data‑centre investment and the data stock generated therefrom enter the national balance sheet as assets.

Classification of Data‑Localization Investment
A multinational cloud provider builds a new data‑centre region in India solely to comply with the 2023 Digital Personal Data Protection Act. The capital expenditure is ₹2,500 crore. How should this be recorded in the Indian national accounts for the year of completion?
The ₹2,500 crore is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) in the ICT asset category (AN.1131) of the non‑financial corporations sector. The output of the construction industry increases by the same amount (market‑price valuation). The data‑centre itself becomes a produced asset on the balance sheet of the cloud provider. No separate “policy asset” is created; the regulatory driver is noted in the satellite account for data assets but does not alter the core SNA entries. If the provider is non‑resident, the investment appears as a foreign direct investment (FDI) inflow in the financial account and as an import of construction services in the current account, with a matching GFCF entry in the domestic capital account under the “foreign‑controlled” sub‑sector.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question links a regulatory measure (data localisation, carbon pricing, PLI scheme) to national accounts, first identify the economic activity triggered (investment, production, transfer). Then map that activity to the appropriate SNA transaction code (P.51g for GFCF, D.9 for capital transfer, D.3 for subsidy). Remember that the regulation itself is not an asset; only the resulting tangible or intangible output enters the accounts.

Treatment of Virtual Assets and Metaverse Transactions in the System of National Accounts

The emergence of crypto‑assets, non‑fungible tokens (NFTs), and persistent virtual worlds (the “metaverse”) has prompted the 2025 SNA to issue explicit guidance on the classification of virtual assets. Crypto‑assets such as Bitcoin and Ether are treated as financial assets (AF.7) when they function primarily as a medium of exchange or store of value, and as produced non‑financial assets (AN.112) when they are created through a mining process that meets the production boundary (i.e., an activity under the control of an institutional unit that uses inputs of electricity, hardware, and labour to generate new tokens). The 2025 SNA distinguishes proof‑of‑work mining as production (output valued at the market price of newly minted coins) from proof‑of‑stake validation, which is recorded as a service (output of validation services) because no new tokens are created.

NFTs representing digital art, collectibles, or virtual land are classified as produced non‑financial assets (AN.112) when they are minted by a creator and sold on a marketplace. The initial minting is recorded as output of creative services (P.1) valued at the sale price; subsequent resales are treated as transactions in existing assets (F.5) with any price appreciation recorded as a holding gain in the revaluation account (K.11). Virtual land parcels in platforms such as Decentraland or The Sandbox are analogous to non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.211) when the platform operator retains ultimate control over the underlying server infrastructure, but they become produced assets when the user acquires a perpetual, transferable licence that confers economic ownership.

Metaverse platforms generate revenue through transaction fees, advertising, and subscription services. These are recorded as market output (P.11) of the platform operator. The 2025 SNA recommends a satellite account for virtual economies that tracks the stock of virtual assets, the flow of virtual‑currency transactions, and the conversion of virtual currency to fiat at market exchange rates. India’s pilot Virtual Economy Satellite Account (2023‑24) estimated the gross output of domestic metaverse platforms at ₹4,800 crore, with NFT minting contributing ₹1,200 crore and virtual‑land sales ₹600 crore. The account also captures cross‑border virtual‑currency flows as part of the financial account (F.7) when residents purchase foreign‑issued tokens.

Valuation of virtual assets follows the fair‑value hierarchy: Level 1 (quoted prices on active exchanges), Level 2 (observable inputs such as recent comparable sales), Level 3 (unobservable inputs, e.g., discounted cash‑flow models for income‑generating virtual property). The Indian Ministry of Finance’s 2024 guidance for tax purposes aligns with this hierarchy, requiring crypto‑asset holdings to be reported at fair value on the balance‑sheet date. A frequent exam error is to record the entire mining electricity cost as intermediate consumption of the mining industry without recognising the newly minted coins as output. The correct treatment: electricity and hardware depreciation are intermediate consumption; the market value of coins produced is output, yielding a gross value added for the mining activity.

Measuring the Economic Impact of Digital Infrastructure Investment on Regional Productivity

Large‑scale digital infrastructure programmes — notably India’s BharatNet (optical‑fibre backbone to gram panchayats), the 5G spectrum auctions of 2022‑23, and the Digital India stack (Aadhaar, UPI, DigiLocker) — have been analysed through the lens of national accounts using input‑output (I‑O) multipliers and regional KLEMS databases. The 2025 SNA encourages the compilation of regional supply‑use tables that break down GFCF in ICT assets (AN.1131) by state, enabling the estimation of capital deepening and total factor productivity (TFP) contributions at the sub‑national level.

The BharatNet programme, with cumulative capital expenditure of ₹1.3 trillion by March 2024, added an estimated 2.5 million km of fibre. Using the 2019‑20 I‑O table, the direct GFCF multiplier for construction of telecom infrastructure is 1.68, implying an induced output increase of ₹2.2 trillion. When the network becomes operational, the ICT services output multiplier (1.42) captures the productivity gains in sectors that intensively use broadband — education, health, finance, and e‑commerce. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) reported a 12 % rise in digital‑service transactions in connected gram panchayats between 2021 and 2023, which the regional accounts translate into a 0.35 % increase in state‑level GVA for the most connected states (Kerala, Punjab, Gujarat).

The 5G rollout, with spectrum proceeds of ₹1.5 trillion and projected capex of ₹3.5 trillion over five years, is modelled in a dynamic Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) framework linked to the national accounts. The CGE simulation (NITI Aayog, 2023) shows a cumulative GDP boost of 0.6 % by 2028‑29, driven by IoT‑enabled manufacturing (productivity elasticity 0.18) and remote‑health services (elasticity 0.12). The national accounts record the spectrum auction proceeds as a sale of a non‑produced asset (AN.211) — the electromagnetic spectrum — with a corresponding capital transfer to the government. The subsequent private‑sector capex appears as GFCF in telecommunications equipment (AN.1132).

Regional productivity analysis uses the KLEMS‑India database (capital K, labour L, energy E, materials M, services S) disaggregated to the state level. The 2022‑23 release shows that states with >80 % BharatNet coverage experienced an average annual TFP growth of 1.9 % versus 1.2 % for low‑coverage states. The difference is attributed to digital‑skill accumulation (quality‑adjusted labour input) and reallocation of labour from low‑productivity agriculture to higher‑productivity services. The SNA’s quality‑adjusted labour input (QALI) methodology captures this by weighting hours worked with skill premia derived from the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS).

A common pitfall is to attribute the entire GDP gain to the infrastructure investment alone, ignoring the complementary investments in human capital, firm‑level digital adoption, and regulatory reforms. The 2025 SNA’s growth accounting framework requires decomposing output growth into contributions from ICT capital deepening, non‑ICT capital, labour quality, and TFP. Only the ICT capital deepening component is directly attributable to the digital infrastructure programme; the residual TFP gain reflects the broader ecosystem effects.

The Role of National Accounts in Evaluating Production‑Linked Incentive Schemes

India’s Production‑Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, launched in 2020‑21 across 14 sectors (mobile manufacturing, pharmaceuticals, automobiles, telecom equipment, food processing, etc.), provide financial incentives linked to incremental sales and investment. The 2025 SNA treats PLI payments as subsidies on production (D.31) when they are contingent on output, and as capital transfers (D.9) when they are tied to qualifying capital expenditure. The Ministry of Finance’s 2023‑24 PLI dashboard reported cumulative disbursements of ₹1.1 trillion, with ₹620 billion classified as production subsidies and ₹480 billion as capital transfers.

In the national accounts, the production‑subsidy component reduces the net operating surplus of the recipient corporations in the generation of income account, while the capital‑transfer component increases their net worth in the capital account. The corresponding government expenditure appears as subsidies (D.3) and capital transfers payable (D.9) in the general government accounts, leaving net lending/borrowing unchanged but altering the composition of expenditure. The 2025 SNA recommends a PLI satellite account that links each scheme to outcome indicators: incremental GFCF, incremental output, employment generation, and export growth.

The mobile‑manufacturing PLI (scheme 1) illustrates the accounting flow. A qualifying firm invests ₹5,000 crore in a new assembly line (GFCF). The government disburses ₹800 crore as a capital transfer (D.9) upon verification of capex. In the same year, the firm achieves incremental sales of ₹12,000 crore, triggering a production subsidy of ₹1,200 crore (D.31). The firm’s output (P.1) rises by ₹12,000 crore; intermediate consumption (P.2) rises by ₹7,500 crore; gross value added (B.1g) increases by ₹4,500 crore. The subsidy reduces the firm’s net operating surplus by ₹1,200 crore, but the net effect on GDP is the full ₹4,500 crore GVA increase. The government’s net lending worsens by ₹2,000 crore (₹800 crore capital transfer + ₹1,200 crore subsidy) unless offset by higher tax revenues from the additional output.

Evaluation of PLI effectiveness uses input‑output multipliers derived from the 2019‑20 supply‑use tables. The mobile‑manufacturing multiplier for GFCF is 2.1, implying that the ₹5,000 crore investment generated ₹10,500 crore of economy‑wide output. The 2024 PLI Impact Report estimated a fiscal multiplier of 1.8 for the scheme, with an incremental tax‑revenue buoyancy of 0.9. The national accounts integrate these results by adjusting the government revenue projections in the medium‑term fiscal framework, linking the PLI satellite account to the debt‑sustainability analysis (DSA) through the intertemporal budget constraint.

Examiners may ask to classify a PLI payment that is conditional on both investment and export targets. The 2025 SNA rule: split the payment proportionally based on the verified shares of capex and incremental export sales. If the scheme design does not allow separation, the entire amount is treated as a subsidy on production because the export condition is an output‑linked criterion. Recording it wholly as a capital transfer would understate current‑period subsidies and overstate the government’s net lending.

  • Confusing the initial allocation of emission allowances (capital transfer) with a production subsidy.
  • Treating regulatory compliance costs of data localisation as a separate policy asset rather than intermediate consumption of the regulated industry.
  • Recording the full electricity cost of crypto mining as intermediate consumption without recognising the newly minted coins as output.
  • Attributing the entire regional GDP gain from digital infrastructure to the infrastructure investment alone, ignoring complementary human‑capital and firm‑level investments.
  • Classifying a PLI payment linked to both capex and export targets entirely as a capital transfer instead of splitting it between capital transfer and production subsidy.
  • Awareness of these pitfalls improves accuracy in national income analysis.

The Treatment of Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms in National Accounts and the Balance of Payments

The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), adopted in Regulation (EU) 2023/956 and entering its transitional phase on 1 October 2023 with full financial obligations from 1 January 2026, imposes a carbon price on imports of cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilizers, electricity and hydrogen. In the System of National Accounts (2008 SNA and the forthcoming 2025 SNA), the CBAM levy is recorded as a tax on production (D.2) payable by the importer, because it is levied on the value of the imported good at the border and is not a customs duty (which would be a tax on international trade, D.51). The importer’s payment increases the cost of intermediate consumption (P.2) for domestic producers using the imported inputs, thereby reducing their gross value added (B.1g). In the balance of payments, the CBAM payment appears as a current transfer (D.7) from the rest of the world to the EU budget, classified under “other current transfers” because it is not a tax on income or wealth. The corresponding credit entry is recorded in the EU’s general government revenue. For the exporting country, the CBAM does not generate a direct entry in its national accounts; however, the higher landed price may affect export volumes and thus the export of goods (P.6) and the associated trade balance. The 2025 SNA introduces a carbon‑border adjustment satellite account that links the CBAM revenue to the domestic carbon‑pricing framework (EU ETS) and tracks the allocation of revenues to climate‑finance programmes. Compilers must ensure that the CBAM levy is not double‑counted as both a production tax and a customs duty, and that the timing of recognition follows the accrual principle: the liability arises when the goods are released for free circulation, not when the payment is made.

Accounting for the Economic Value of Public Data Assets and Open Government Data

Governments increasingly treat data as a strategic asset. India’s Open Government Data (OGD) Platform, launched in 2012 under the National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (NDSAP), publishes over 300,000 datasets across sectors. The 2025 SNA recognises data as a produced non‑financial asset (AN.117) when it is created through a production process that incurs costs (collection, cleaning, storage) and yields future economic benefits. The valuation follows the cost‑of‑production approach for non‑market output: the sum of compensation of employees, intermediate consumption (including cloud‑storage fees), and consumption of fixed capital (depreciation of data‑center infrastructure). When the data are made freely available, the output is recorded as government non‑market output (P.13) valued at cost, and a corresponding transfer in kind (D.632) to households and enterprises is recorded in the redistribution of income account. If the government licences the data for a fee, the revenue is a sale of services (P.11) and the asset remains on the balance sheet. The 2025 SNA also introduces a data‑asset satellite account that tracks the stock of data assets, their depreciation (using a service‑life of 5‑10 years), and the flow of data‑related services. For international comparability, the UN‑ECE Guide on Measuring the Information Economy recommends reporting the value of open data as a separate line item in the government finance statistics (GFS) framework. In practice, statistical offices such as the UK ONS and Statistics Canada have piloted experimental estimates: the UK ONS 2022 pilot valued the UK’s open data stock at £12 billion, derived from the cost of data‑collection programmes (e.g., the Census, the Labour Force Survey) and the imputed user cost of the data‑infrastructure. Compilers must avoid double‑counting the same dataset when it is reused across multiple portals, and must distinguish between raw data (non‑produced asset) and processed data products (produced asset).

Classification of CBAM Revenue
A country imports steel worth €500 million from a non‑EU producer. The EU imposes a CBAM charge of €50 million on the importer. How should the €50 million be recorded in the importing country’s national accounts and in the balance of payments?
In the national accounts, the €50 million CBAM charge is a tax on production (D.2) payable by the importer. It raises the importer’s intermediate consumption (P.2) by €50 million, reducing the importer’s gross value added by the same amount. The government’s revenue increases by €50 million under taxes on production. In the balance of payments, the payment is a current transfer (D.7) from the rest of the world to the EU budget, recorded as a debit in the importing country’s current account under “other current transfers” and a credit in the EU’s general government revenue. It is not a customs duty (D.51) because it is based on carbon content, not on the value of the goods for tariff purposes.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the SNA classification of a new border carbon levy, first identify whether the levy is tied to the value of the good (customs duty) or to an environmental characteristic (tax on production). Remember the accrual timing: liability arises at customs clearance. In the BoP, any payment to a supranational budget is a current transfer, not a trade‑related flow. Practise with the CBAM example and the 2025 SNA satellite‑account terminology.

Measuring the Economic Contribution of the Platform Economy: Intermediation Services, Data Extraction, and Revenue Allocation

The platform economy — comprising digital marketplaces (e.g., Amazon, Flipkart), ride‑hailing apps (Uber, Ola), and gig‑work platforms (Upwork, Urban Company) — generates value through three distinct channels: intermediation services, data extraction and analytics, and revenue allocation via platform fees. The 2025 SNA treats the platform’s core activity as the production of intermediation services (CPC 859), valued at the total fees and commissions charged to third‑party sellers and service providers. This output is recorded in the platform’s production account (P.1) and the corresponding fees are recorded as intermediate consumption (P.2) by the sellers. The platform’s own consumption of cloud infrastructure, payment‑gateway services, and algorithm development is also intermediate consumption. Data extraction — the collection, processing, and monetisation of user‑behaviour data — is recognised as a produced asset (AN.117) when the platform invests in data‑science teams and storage. The 2025 SNA recommends capitalising the costs of data‑curation (labour, software licences) and amortising them over the expected useful life of the data asset (typically 3‑5 years). The resulting depreciation (consumption of fixed capital) enters the platform’s generation of income account. Revenue allocation — the split between platform fees, seller revenues, and any subsidies or incentives — must be consistent with the principal‑agent principle: the platform acts as an agent when it merely matches buyers and sellers, and the gross transaction value is not recorded as platform output. Only the net fee is output. When the platform holds inventory (e.g., Amazon’s first‑party sales), the full sales value is output and the cost of goods sold is intermediate consumption. India’s Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) 2023 pilot on “Digital Platform Services” used GST‑invoice data to separate marketplace fees from first‑party sales, estimating that platform intermediation contributed ₹1.8 trillion to GVA in 2022‑23, while data‑asset capital formation added ₹0.3 trillion. Compilers must avoid double‑counting the same transaction in both the platform’s output and the seller’s output, and must apply the residence principle for cross‑border platforms: a non‑resident platform providing services to resident sellers creates an export of services (P.6) for the platform’s home economy and an import of services (P.7) for the resident economy.

The Role of National Accounts in Assessing the Fiscal Implications of Universal Health Coverage

Universal Health Coverage (UHC) programmes such as India’s Ayushman Bharat‑Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (AB‑PMJAY), launched in September 2018, and Thailand’s Universal Coverage Scheme (2001) generate sizable fiscal flows that must be captured coherently in the national accounts. In the SNA, government health expenditure is recorded as final consumption expenditure (P.3) of general government when services are provided free at the point of use, valued at the cost of production (compensation of health workers, drugs, equipment depreciation). When the government purchases services from private hospitals under a reimbursement model, the payment is a social benefit in kind (D.632) to households, and the private hospital’s output is recorded as market output (P.11) valued at the reimbursed price. The 2025 SNA introduces a health‑satellite account that links the flow of health services to health‑outcome indicators (e.g., hospitalisation rates, out‑of‑pocket expenditure). For fiscal analysis, the national accounts provide the government net lending/borrowing (B.9) impact: the increase in health expenditure raises government final consumption, worsening net lending unless offset by higher tax revenues or reduced spending elsewhere. The IMF’s Fiscal Monitor (2023) used the SNA framework to estimate that India’s AB‑PMJAY added 0.15 percentage points of GDP to central government expenditure in 2022‑23, with a corresponding increase in the primary deficit. The accounts also enable distributional analysis through the Distributional National Accounts (DNA) framework: by linking household‑level health‑benefit receipts (from the scheme’s beneficiary database) to the household income distribution, analysts can assess progressivity. A key compilation challenge is the valuation of unpriced public health services (e.g., immunisation campaigns). The 2025 SNA recommends the cost‑of‑production method for non‑market output, supplemented by time‑use survey data for volunteer health‑worker time. Consistency with the Government Finance Statistics (GFS) 2014 framework requires that the same expenditure be classified as “health” (COFOG 07) in both SNA and GFS, ensuring that fiscal rules based on GFS aggregates (e.g., the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act targets) are aligned with the national accounts.

Integrating Satellite Remote Sensing Data with National Accounts for Real‑Time Agricultural Output Estimation

Timely estimation of agricultural gross value added (GVA) is critical for quarterly GDP compilation, especially in economies where agriculture contributes a large share of output. Since the 2010s, statistical offices have integrated satellite remote‑sensing indicators — primarily the Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) from NASA’s MODIS and the European Space Agency’s Sentinel‑2 — into the crop‑cutting experiment (CCE) framework. India’s Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, in collaboration with the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), launched the Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (MNCFC) in 2012, which produces fortnightly NDVI‑based crop‑condition maps for major cereals (rice, wheat, maize). The 2025 SNA encourages the use of big‑data sources as “auxiliary information” for the production account. The estimation procedure: (1) calibrate NDVI against historical CCE yields at the district level using a regression model; (2) apply the model to current‑season NDVI to generate a nowcast of district‑level yields; (3) aggregate to state and national levels using sown‑area estimates from the Digital Agriculture Mission (launched 2021). The resulting nowcast feeds the quarterly national accounts as a preliminary estimate of agricultural output (P.1), with a revision cycle aligned to the final CCE results released after harvest. The 2023‑24 Economic Survey reported that the NDVI‑based nowcast reduced the mean absolute percentage error of the first‑advance estimate of rice production from 6.2 % (traditional method) to 3.8 %. The SNA requires that the remote‑sensing input be documented in the metadata of the national accounts, specifying the sensor, spatial resolution (10 m for Sentinel‑2), temporal frequency (5‑day revisit), and the statistical model used. A key compilation issue is the treatment of crop‑failure insurance payouts: under the 2025 SNA, indemnity payments are recorded as non‑life insurance claims (D.72) receivable by farmers, increasing their disposable income, while the insurance corporation’s output is the insurance service charge (P.11). The satellite‑derived yield loss index can serve as the trigger for parametric insurance, linking the remote‑sensing data directly to the financial account. Compilers must ensure that the nowcast does not replace the final CCE‑based estimate but is clearly flagged as a preliminary, model‑based estimate subject to revision.

  • Confusing CBAM levies with customs duties and recording them as taxes on international trade (D.51) instead of taxes on production (D.2).
  • Valuing open government data at market price rather than cost of production, leading to overstatement of government non‑market output.
  • Recording the full transaction value of a platform marketplace as platform output instead of only the net fee, violating the principal‑agent principle.
  • Treating government health‑insurance reimbursements as subsidies on production rather than social benefits in kind (D.632).
  • Using satellite‑derived nowcasts as final agricultural GVA without flagging them as preliminary model‑based estimates.
  • These traps highlight the need for careful classification and transparent metadata in national income analysis.

Valuation of Public Infrastructure Maintenance Expenditure in National Accounts: Capital Consumption versus Current Expenditure

The System of National Accounts (2008 SNA) distinguishes between consumption of fixed capital (CFC) — the decline in the value of produced assets due to wear, obsolescence, and accidental damage — and current expenditure on maintenance that merely preserves the asset’s existing service potential. In practice, statistical offices must decide whether a given outlay on roads, bridges, water‑supply networks, or public buildings is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) or as intermediate consumption (P.2). The 2008 SNA (para. 10.71) states that “major improvements that extend the service life or increase the capacity of an asset are treated as capital formation”, whereas “routine maintenance and repairs that keep the asset in working order are treated as intermediate consumption”. India’s Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) follows this guidance in the Annual National Accounts, applying a threshold based on the proportion of the asset’s original cost: expenditures exceeding 10 % of the asset’s written‑down value in a given year are capitalised, while lower amounts are expensed.

The 2025 SNA revision refines the rule by introducing a “service‑life extension test”. If the maintenance activity adds at least five years to the expected remaining service life, the outlay is re‑classified as GFCF. This change aligns with the International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS) 17, which many state governments have adopted for their balance‑sheet reporting. A practical implication is the treatment of the National Highways Authority of India’s (NHAI) periodic resurfacing programmes. Prior to 2022, resurfacing costs were recorded as current expenditure, depressing the measured capital stock of the transport sector. After the 2025 SNA guidance, NHAI’s 2023‑24 resurfacing outlay of ₹12,400 crore was capitalised, raising the transport sector’s gross capital stock by roughly 1.8 % and increasing the sector’s CFC estimate in the subsequent year’s accounts.
