Compilers must also reconcile the SNA treatment with the Government Finance Statistics (GFS) 2014 framework, where the same outlay appears under “expense – maintenance” (GFS code 2111) if it is not capitalised. Consistency requires a mapping table that flags each line item in the Union Budget’s “Capital Outlay on Roads and Bridges” (Major Head 5054) as either GFCF or intermediate consumption based on the service‑life test. The 2023‑24 Economic Survey highlighted that mis‑classification of maintenance can bias the fiscal deficit by up to 0.15 % of GDP, because capitalised outlays are excluded from the revenue deficit calculation under the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act.

From an analytical perspective, the distinction matters for productivity measurement. Capitalising maintenance raises the measured capital input, which lowers the estimated total factor productivity (TFP) growth if output is unchanged. Researchers using the KLEMS database for India therefore adjust the capital stock series by adding back the capitalised maintenance component to isolate the “true” investment signal. The 2025 SNA also recommends that satellite accounts for infrastructure (e.g., the Infrastructure Satellite Account) present both the SNA‑consistent capital stock and a “maintenance‑adjusted” series to aid policy analysis.

Assessing the Fiscal Impact of Climate Adaptation Expenditure through National Accounts

Climate adaptation expenditure — spending on flood‑defence structures, drought‑resilient irrigation, heat‑resilient urban design, and early‑warning systems — has grown rapidly in India since the launch of the National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC) in 2015. The 2008 SNA treats such outlays as gross fixed capital formation when they create new produced assets (e.g., embankments, desalination plants) and as intermediate consumption when they fund recurring operations (e.g., maintenance of cyclone shelters). The 2025 SNA introduces a dedicated “climate adaptation” classification within the purpose classification (COFOG 05.3) and recommends that compilers tag each capital formation item with a climate‑adaptation flag, enabling the construction of a Climate Adaptation Satellite Account (CASA).

India’s 2022‑23 Union Budget allocated ₹4,800 crore to the NAFCC, of which ₹3,200 crore was earmarked for capital projects (construction of coastal protection walls in Odisha and Gujarat) and ₹1,600 crore for capacity‑building and community‑level resilience programmes. In the national accounts, the capital portion entered GFCF under “Other structures” (AN.112) and was simultaneously recorded in the CASA as “Coastal protection – capital”. The recurrent portion entered “Other services” (P.2) and appeared in the CASA as “Community resilience – current”. This dual recording permits analysts to track the share of adaptation spending that expands the produced asset base versus that which supports ongoing adaptive capacity.

The fiscal impact is assessed by linking the CASA to the government’s integrated financial management system (IFMS). The 2025 SNA recommends that the net lending/borrowing position (B.9) be decomposed into a “climate‑adjusted” component: B.9* = B.9 – (capital adaptation outlays financed by borrowing) + (returns from adaptation assets, e.g., reduced disaster relief outlays). A 2023 study by the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy (NIPFP) applied this decomposition to the central government’s accounts and found that climate‑adaptation capital formation reduced the primary deficit by 0.04 % of GDP in 2022‑23, because the assets generated future savings in disaster‑relief expenditure (recorded as social benefits D.62). However, the study cautioned that the valuation of avoided losses relies on counterfactual modelling and is not yet part of the standard SNA compilation.

Compilation challenges include the identification of adaptation‑relevant items in state‑level budgets, where coding follows the State Finance Accounts rather than COFOG. MoSPI’s 2024 pilot with the states of Kerala and Maharashtra used a keyword‑search algorithm on budget documents (terms such as “flood‑resilient”, “heat‑action plan”) to auto‑tag line items, achieving a 78 % match with manual classification. The 2025 SNA encourages the use of such machine‑learning aids, provided the tagging logic is documented in the metadata. A further issue is the treatment of international climate finance (e.g., Green Climate Fund grants). Under the 2008 SNA, grants are recorded as capital transfers (D.9) receivable by government, increasing net worth. The 2025 SNA adds a “climate‑finance” sub‑category to distinguish adaptation grants from mitigation grants, facilitating the monitoring of the $100 billion pledge under the UNFCCC.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “In the 2025 SNA, how is a government outlay on building a new cyclone shelter classified if the shelter also serves as a community centre during non‑emergency periods?”
The outlay creates a new produced asset (the shelter) and therefore is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) under “Other structures” (AN.112). The dual‑use nature does not change the capital formation classification; however, the 2025 SNA requires a climate‑adaptation flag on the asset and a COFOG 05.3 tag. The ongoing operating costs (staff, utilities) are recorded as intermediate consumption (P.2) and also carry the adaptation flag. Mis‑classifying the entire outlay as current expenditure would understate the capital stock and overstate the revenue deficit.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes asset creation with recurring services, first identify the asset boundary using the 2008/2025 SNA capital formation criteria (service‑life extension, capacity increase). Then apply the purpose classification (COFOG) and any satellite‑account flags. Remember that the same physical outlay can generate two entries: one in the production account (GFCF or P.2) and one in the relevant satellite account (CASA, Infrastructure SA).

Measuring the Economic Contribution of Renewable Energy Deployment to National Income and Employment

The rapid expansion of renewable energy capacity in India — solar photovoltaic (PV) installations rose from 2.6 GW in 2014 to over 70 GW by March 2024, while wind capacity crossed 44 GW — has direct implications for national income accounting. Under the 2008 SNA, the construction of solar farms and wind parks is recorded as gross fixed capital formation in “Other machinery and equipment” (AN.113) and “Other structures” (AN.112) respectively. The 2025 SNA adds a “renewable‑energy” sub‑category within the asset classification, enabling the compilation of a Renewable Energy Satellite Account (RESA) that tracks capacity additions, investment flows, and associated employment.

Investment data are sourced from the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) project‑level database, which records capital expenditure (CAPEX) for each commissioned project. For 2022‑23, total renewable‑energy CAPEX was ₹1.12 lakh crore, of which 62 % was solar, 28 % wind, and the remainder small hydro and bio‑energy. In the national accounts, this CAPEX appears as GFCF, raising the capital stock of the electricity sector. The corresponding consumption of fixed capital (CFC) is calculated using the perpetual inventory method (PIM) with service lives of 25 years for solar PV modules and 20 years for wind turbines, as recommended by the Central Electricity Authority (CEA). The resulting CFC for 2022‑23 was estimated at ₹9,800 crore, contributing to the sector’s gross value added (GVA) through the income approach (operating surplus plus CFC).

Employment measurement follows the International Labour Organization (ILO) guidelines for “green jobs”. The 2025 SNA encourages linking the RESA to the Labour Account, which integrates establishment‑survey data (Annual Survey of Industries) with the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS). For 2022‑23, the RESA‑Labour Account linkage estimated 1.35 million full‑time equivalent (FTE) jobs directly attributable to renewable‑energy construction, operation, and maintenance. Of these, 0.78 million were in construction (temporary) and 0.57 million in O&M (permanent). The indirect employment generated through supply‑chain linkages (e.g., glass, steel, inverter manufacturing) is captured via input‑output multipliers derived from the 2017‑18 Supply‑Use Tables, adding an estimated 0.9 million FTEs.

A key analytical use is the decomposition of electricity‑sector GVA growth into a “renewable‑capacity” effect and a “fuel‑cost” effect. The 2023‑24 Economic Survey reported that the renewable‑capacity effect contributed 0.12 percentage points to overall GDP growth in 2022‑23, while the reduction in coal‑import bills (recorded as a negative import of goods, P.7) contributed an additional 0.07 percentage points via the expenditure approach. The SNA framework also records the feed‑in tariff (FiT) payments as subsidies on production (D.31) when they are paid by the government to generators, and as current transfers (D.7) when paid by distribution utilities. The 2025 SNA clarifies that FiT payments that are guaranteed for the asset’s lifetime should be treated as a financial liability of the government (AF.8) and a financial asset of the generator, improving the consistency of the balance‑sheet presentation.

The Role of National Accounts in Evaluating Industrial Corridors and Special Economic Zones

India’s industrial corridor programme — notably the Delhi‑Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC), Chennai‑Bengaluru Industrial Corridor (CBIC), and the upcoming Amritsar‑Kolkata Industrial Corridor (AKIC) — involves large‑scale infrastructure investment, land acquisition, and policy incentives. The System of National Accounts provides the macro‑framework to assess the corridors’ contribution to output, capital formation, and regional income. The 2008 SNA treats corridor‑related infrastructure (roads, ports, power lines) as GFCF in “Other structures” (AN.112) and “Transport equipment” (AN.111). The 2025 SNA introduces a “spatial‑development” satellite account that tags each capital formation item with a geographic identifier (district or corridor code), enabling sub‑national aggregation consistent with the State Accounts.

Special Economic Zones (SEZs) receive fiscal concessions (tax holidays, duty‑free imports) that affect the distribution of national income. In the SNA, SEZ output is recorded in the production account of the resident institutional units (mostly private non‑financial corporations). The tax concessions appear as “other subsidies on production” (D.39) receivable by the SEZ units, reducing their net operating surplus and thereby lowering the sector’s contribution to GDP at factor cost. However, the 2025 SNA recommends that the revenue foregone be recorded as a “tax expenditure” in the Government Finance Statistics (GFS) and linked to the national accounts via the “tax‑expenditure satellite account”. This linkage permits a net‑benefit analysis: the increase in GVA from SEZ activity versus the fiscal cost of concessions.

Empirical work using the 2017‑18 Input‑Output Tables and the 2021‑22 Annual Survey of Industries shows that DMIC‑linked districts experienced a 3.4 % higher annual GVA growth rate than comparable non‑corridor districts between 2015‑16 and 2021‑22. The growth accounting decomposition attributes 1.1 % points to capital deepening (new infrastructure), 0.9 % points to total factor productivity gains (agglomeration effects), and the remainder to labour‑force expansion. The SNA’s regional accounts (State Domestic Product) capture the geographic distribution of this growth, while the Balance of Payments records the export orientation of SEZ units (over 60 % of SEZ output is exported, reflected in higher “exports of goods” P.6).

Compilation issues include the valuation of land transferred to corridor authorities. Under the 2008 SNA, land is a non‑produced asset (AN.211) and its transfer is recorded as a capital transfer (D.9) from government to the public corporation managing the corridor. The 2025 SNA adds a “land‑development” sub‑category to distinguish raw land acquisition from subsequent development expenditure (e.g., site levelling, utility provision). This distinction matters for the measurement of the corridor’s net capital formation: only development expenditure enters GFCF, while the land transfer affects net worth but not GDP. The 2023‑24 MoSPI pilot for the CBIC applied this rule, re‑classifying ₹4,200 crore of land acquisition as capital transfers and ₹1,800 crore of site development as GFCF, altering the corridor’s reported capital formation by 30 %.

Accounting for the Economic Value of Urban Ecosystem Services: Integrating SEEA‑EEA with Municipal Accounts

Urban ecosystems — parks, wetlands, street trees, peri‑urban forests — provide regulating services (air‑purification, heat‑island mitigation, flood regulation) and cultural services (recreation, aesthetic value). The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA‑EEA) provides a framework to measure these services in physical and monetary terms and to integrate them with the SNA. The 2025 SNA encourages the compilation of an Urban Ecosystem Satellite Account (UESA) that links ecosystem‑service flows to the production and asset accounts of municipal corporations.

In India, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) launched the “Urban Green Cover” survey in 2021, covering 4,500 urban local bodies (ULBs). The survey quantifies tree canopy cover, wetland area, and green‑space per capita. Physical flow accounts are built by applying biome‑specific service coefficients (e.g., 0.45 t CO₂ ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ for carbon sequestration by urban trees, 0.12 m³ ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ for storm‑water retention by wetlands) derived from the Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education (ICFRE) studies. For 2022‑23, the aggregate physical supply of air‑purification services by urban trees in the 50 largest cities was estimated at 1.8 million tonnes of PM₂.₅ removed.

Monetary valuation follows the “replacement cost” method recommended by SEEA‑EEA for regulating services: the cost of engineered alternatives (e.g., mechanical air‑filters, storm‑water drainage) that would deliver an equivalent service. The 2023‑24 Economic Survey applied this method and estimated the annual replacement cost of urban tree air‑purification at ₹22,500 crore and of wetland flood regulation at ₹9,800 crore. These values are recorded in the UESA as “ecosystem service use” (U.1) by the household sector (final consumption) and by the government sector (intermediate consumption for public health). The corresponding “ecosystem asset” values (the stock of urban green cover) enter the national balance sheet as “environmental assets” (AN.22) with a monetary valuation consistent with the 2025 SNA’s “environmental‑asset” classification.

Integration with municipal accounts requires mapping ULB budget lines (e.g., “Horticulture and Parks” under Major Head 2217) to the UESA. The 2025 SNA recommends a “budget‑to‑account” crosswalk that tags each expenditure line with an ecosystem‑service category. A 2024 pilot in Pune Municipal Corporation showed that 68 % of the horticulture budget (₹340 crore) could be linked to the maintenance of ecosystem assets, while the remainder funded recreational facilities (cultural services). This tagging enables the calculation of a “green‑expenditure multiplier” — the ratio of ecosystem‑service value generated per rupee of municipal green spending — which was estimated at 1.9 for Pune in 2022‑23.

Challenges remain in the valuation of cultural services (recreation, mental‑health benefits). The SEEA‑EEA suggests the “travel‑cost” or “hedonic‑pricing” methods, but data on urban residents’ willingness to pay are sparse. The 2025 SNA allows the use of “stated‑preference” survey results as supplementary information, provided the survey design is documented. The National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) conducted a 2023 pilot on urban recreation demand, yielding a marginal willingness‑to‑pay of ₹12 per visit to a neighbourhood park. Scaling this to the estimated 1.2 billion annual park visits in the top 100 cities gives a cultural‑service value of ₹14,400 crore, which can be added to the UESA as a “cultural‑service use” entry.

  • Confusing routine maintenance with capital‑forming improvements and mis‑classifying the outlay in GFCF versus intermediate consumption.
  • Omitting the climate‑adaptation flag on capital assets, preventing the construction of a Climate Adaptation Satellite Account.
  • Treating feed‑in tariff payments solely as subsidies on production without recognising the associated financial liability on the government balance sheet.
  • Recording land acquisition for industrial corridors as GFCF instead of a capital transfer, inflating measured capital formation.
  • Applying a single replacement‑cost coefficient to all urban tree species, ignoring biome‑specific sequestration rates.
  • Neglecting to link municipal horticulture budgets to ecosystem‑asset maintenance, breaking the budget‑to‑account crosswalk.
  • These traps illustrate the need for careful classification and transparent metadata in national income analysis.

Carbon Pricing, Emissions Trading, and Their Recording in the System of National Accounts

Carbon pricing mechanisms — carbon taxes, cap‑and‑trade systems, and credit‑based schemes — create explicit monetary flows that must be reflected in the production, income, and accumulation accounts of the SNA. The 2008 SNA treats a carbon tax as a tax on production (D.2) when levied on the emitter, and as a tax on products (D.21) when embedded in the price of fossil fuels. In a cap‑and‑trade system such as the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), the initial allocation of allowances is recorded as a government transfer (D.99) to the recipient enterprise; subsequent trading of allowances between enterprises is recorded as a financial transaction (F.5) with a corresponding change in the value of the allowance asset (AN.112). When an enterprise surrenders allowances to comply, the surrender is recorded as a use of the asset (P.51) and a reduction in the enterprise’s net worth. The 2025 SNA revision clarifies that allowances held for compliance are non‑produced, non‑financial assets (AN.112) and that the market price of the allowance at the reporting date determines their balance‑sheet value. In India, the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme operates a similar market for energy‑saving certificates (ESCerts). ESCerts are issued by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency and traded on the Indian Energy Exchange. The 2023‑24 Economic Survey notes that the aggregate value of ESCerts traded in 2022‑23 was approximately ₹1,200 crore, which should be entered as a financial asset (F.5) for the holder and a liability for the issuer. Carbon credits generated under the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) or voluntary markets are treated as produced intangible assets (AN.112) when they arise from a verified project; the sale of a credit is a disposal of an asset (P.51) and the revenue is recorded as output (P.1) of the project entity. A key compilation challenge is the timing of valuation: the SNA requires market‑price valuation at the end of each accounting period, yet many carbon markets exhibit thin trading and price volatility. The 2025 SNA recommends using the most recent observable transaction price, supplemented by a model‑based estimate when no trade occurs, and documenting the valuation method in the metadata. Failure to record the initial free allocation as a transfer, or to revalue allowances at period‑end, leads to an understatement of government net lending and an overstatement of corporate profits.

Valuing Public Data Infrastructure and Open Government Data in National Accounts

Governments increasingly invest in data platforms — open data portals, national statistical databases, geospatial infrastructures, and digital identity registries — that generate non‑market services used by households, firms, and researchers. The 2008 SNA classifies the production of such services as government non‑market output (P.13) valued at the sum of costs (intermediate consumption, compensation of employees, consumption of fixed capital, and other taxes on production). The 2025 SNA extends this by encouraging the creation of a “Data and Digital Infrastructure Satellite Account” that separates the asset value of the underlying data sets (AN.112) from the service flow. In India, the Open Government Data Platform (data.gov.in) launched under the National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (NDSAP) 2012 hosts more than 1.2 lakh datasets across ministries. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) estimates the annual operating cost of the platform at ₹150 crore, which is recorded as intermediate consumption (P.2) of the responsible ministry. The datasets themselves, once curated and documented, meet the SNA criteria for produced intangible assets: they are the result of a production process, have a identifiable owner (the government), and provide future economic benefits. The 2025 SNA recommends capitalising the development cost of high‑value datasets (e.g., the National Sample Survey micro‑data, the Agricultural Census database) as gross fixed capital formation (P.51) and amortising them over their useful life, typically 10‑15 years. A practical valuation approach uses the “replacement cost” method: the cost of recreating the dataset from primary sources, adjusted for quality and accessibility. For the 2022‑23 period, the replacement cost of the top 20 high‑impact datasets was estimated at ₹3,800 crore in a pilot study by the Indian Statistical Institute. This amount enters the national balance sheet as “data assets” (AN.112) and the annual amortisation appears as consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) in the government production account. The satellite account also records the “use” of data services by households (final consumption) and by firms (intermediate consumption) through a notional price derived from the marginal cost of access. A common compilation error is to treat the entire platform cost as current expenditure, thereby omitting the asset and understating government net worth.

Worked Example: Recording a Carbon Allowance Allocation
A government allocates 1 million free allowances to a steel plant under a cap‑and‑trade scheme. The market price of an allowance at the allocation date is ₹250. Show the SNA entries for the government and the plant at the moment of allocation and at the end of the reporting period when the plant surrenders 0.8 million allowances (market price ₹260).
At allocation: Government records a transfer payable (D.99) of ₹250 crore (1 m × ₹250) and a reduction in its net worth. The plant records a transfer receivable (D.99) of ₹250 crore and recognises an intangible non‑produced asset (AN.112) “Emission allowances” valued at ₹250 crore. At period‑end (surrender): The plant records a use of the asset (P.51) of 0.8 m × ₹260 = ₹208 crore, reducing the asset to ₹52 crore (0.2 m × ₹260). The government records a corresponding increase in its net worth of ₹208 crore as the allowances are extinguished. The plant’s profit and loss reflects the ₹208 crore cost of compliance; the government’s net lending improves by the same amount.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the SNA treatment of a carbon market instrument, first identify the instrument type (tax, free allowance, tradable credit). Then map each flow to the appropriate transaction code: D.2/D.21 for taxes, D.99 for free allocations, F.5 for secondary trades, P.51 for surrender or disposal. Remember the 2025 SNA re‑classification of allowances as AN.112 and the requirement to revalue at period‑end market price. A quick checklist — allocation, trade, surrender, valuation — prevents missing a leg of the entry.

Accounting for Fossil‑Fuel Subsidies and Energy Transition Expenditure in the SNA

Fossil‑fuel subsidies — price controls on petrol, diesel, LPG, kerosene, and electricity — are pervasive in many economies and have direct implications for the measurement of output, value added, and government net lending. The 2008 SNA records a subsidy on products (D.31) when the government pays a producer to keep the consumer price below the market‑determined level. The subsidy reduces the producer’s output value at basic prices (P.1) and appears as a negative component of taxes less subsidies on products in the generation of income account. In India, the central government’s petroleum subsidy bill (including the direct benefit transfer for LPG) exceeded ₹1 lakh crore in recent fiscal years. The 2025 SNA introduces a “subsidy‑by‑function” classification that separates subsidies supporting consumption (e.g., LPG for households) from those supporting production (e.g., diesel for agriculture). This distinction matters for the calculation of real GDP: consumption subsidies are treated as part of final consumption expenditure at purchasers’ prices, while production subsidies affect the volume measure of output through the input price deflator. Energy transition expenditure — capital outlays on renewable generation, grid modernisation, battery storage, and energy‑efficiency programmes — is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (P.51) when it creates a new asset, and as intermediate consumption (P.2) when it funds operational programmes such as demand‑side management. The 2025 SNA recommends tagging each energy‑transition outlay with a “climate‑mitigation” flag (consistent with the Climate Change Satellite Account) to enable the compilation of a “green‑capital formation” aggregate. A practical issue arises with the treatment of feed‑in tariff (FiT) payments to renewable generators. FiTs are a subsidy on production (D.31) but also create a contingent liability for the government if the tariff is guaranteed for a fixed period. The 2025 SNA advises recording the present value of the guaranteed stream as a government liability (F.8) at inception, with the annual FiT payment split between a subsidy component (D.31) and a reduction of the liability (F.8). Misclassifying the entire FiT as a current subsidy inflates the deficit and omits the future fiscal burden.

Measuring the Economic Contribution of Digital Identity Systems: The Aadhaar Case Study

Digital identity platforms generate economic value by reducing transaction costs, enabling targeted transfers, and fostering financial inclusion. The Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) launched Aadhaar in 2009; by 2023 over 1.35 billion residents were enrolled. The SNA treats the production of the Aadhaar infrastructure — enrolment centres, biometric hardware, central data‑centre, and authentication software — as government non‑market output (P.13) valued at cost. The capital expenditure on data‑centres and software development meets the criteria for produced intangible assets (AN.112) and should be capitalised as gross fixed capital formation (P.51) with a service life of 10‑12 years. The annual operating cost (staff, bandwidth, maintenance) is recorded as intermediate consumption (P.2). The authentication service provided to banks, telecom operators, and government schemes is a non‑market service used as intermediate consumption by those sectors; its value is imputed from the cost of the authentication platform (approximately ₹2,500 crore per annum in the 2022‑23 budget). A satellite account for “Digital Identity Services” can separate the asset (the Aadhaar database and authentication engine) from the service flow, allowing analysts to compute a “cost‑per‑authentication” metric and to assess the productivity impact on sectors such as banking (e‑KYC reduces onboarding cost by an estimated 70 %). The 2025 SNA encourages linking the digital identity asset to the “financial inclusion” indicator in the SDG monitoring framework. A common compilation trap is to expense the entire Aadhaar budget in a single year, thereby understating government net worth and overstating the current deficit. Another trap is to ignore the revenue from authentication fees charged to private entities (currently ₹0.50 per transaction), which should be recorded as sales of services (P.1) by the government and as intermediate consumption by the purchaser.

Integrating Disaster Risk Reduction Expenditure into National Accounts and the SEEA

Expenditure on disaster risk reduction (DRR) — early‑warning systems, resilient infrastructure, flood‑plain zoning, community‑based preparedness — is increasingly recognised as investment rather than consumption. The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015‑2030) calls for tracking DRR spending as a distinct category. The 2008 SNA records the construction of a cyclone shelter as gross fixed capital formation (P.51) under “Other structures” (AN.1122). The 2025 SNA adds a “disaster‑resilience” flag to the asset classification, enabling the compilation of a “Resilient Capital Stock” aggregate. Operational DRR outlays such as the maintenance of early‑warning radars, training of volunteers, and periodic mock drills are treated as intermediate consumption (P.2) of the relevant government agency. The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting (SEEA) provides a complementary physical flow account: the number of functional early‑warning stations, the length of embankments maintained, and the area of mangrove restored. These physical indicators can be linked to the monetary accounts through a “cost‑per‑unit‑of‑resilience” metric. In India, the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) reported DRR capital expenditure of ₹12,400 crore in 2022‑23, of which ₹8,200 crore was for resilient housing under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Gramin) and ₹4,200 crore for coastal protection works. The 2025 SNA recommends that the resilient housing component be recorded as a separate asset class (AN.11221) with a longer service life (50 years) and a higher depreciation rate reflecting climate‑stress testing. A frequent error is to lump all DRR spending under “General public services” (COFOG 01) without the resilience flag, which prevents the construction of the Resilient Capital Stock and hampers the assessment of fiscal sustainability under climate scenarios.

  • Treating free carbon allowances as a reduction in output rather than a government transfer (D.99) and an intangible asset (AN.112).
  • Expensing the full cost of open data platforms in the year incurred, omitting the capitalisation of high‑value datasets as produced intangible assets.
  • Recording feed‑in tariff payments solely as current subsidies (D.31) and ignoring the present‑value liability (F.8) created by long‑term guarantees.
  • Failing to capitalise Aadhaar enrolment and authentication infrastructure, thereby understating government net worth and overstating the fiscal deficit.
  • Classifying all disaster risk reduction spending under generic government consumption without applying the 2025 SNA resilience flag, which blocks the Resilient Capital Stock compilation.
  • Using a single market price for carbon allowances at allocation and ignoring period‑end revaluation, leading to inconsistent balance‑sheet values.
  • Omitting authentication fee revenue from the Aadhaar satellite account, which distorts both government output and private sector intermediate consumption.

The Treatment of Government Debt Securities and Interest Flows in the National Balance Sheet: Accrual Accounting, Discount Rates, and Fiscal Sustainability

Government debt securities are recorded in the System of National Accounts (SNA) as financial assets (AF.3) for the holder and as financial liabilities (FL.3) for the issuer. The 2008 SNA requires that interest on these instruments be accrued continuously (D.41) rather than recorded only when cash payments occur. The 2025 SNA revision extends this principle by mandating fair‑value measurement for marketable debt (AF.31) at each balance‑sheet date, with revaluation gains or losses recognised in the other changes in volume of assets account (K.1). For non‑marketable debt (AF.32) the nominal value remains the basis, but the accrual of interest must still follow the effective‑yield method.

In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) compiles the “Government Securities” (G‑Sec) portfolio for the central and state governments. The Quarterly Public Debt Management Report provides the market‑value series used for the national balance sheet. The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) adopts the RBI market‑value data for the “Financial Assets – Debt Securities” line in the Integrated Balance Sheet. A key compilation issue is the choice of discount rate for accruing interest on zero‑coupon bonds and on inflation‑indexed bonds. The 2025 SNA recommends using the market‑implied yield curve for each maturity bucket; MoSPI currently applies the RBI’s “Weighted Average Yield” for the 10‑year benchmark as a proxy, which can understate accrued interest when the yield curve is steep.

Fiscal sustainability analysis relies on the “net financial worth” of government, which equals financial assets minus financial liabilities. Because interest accrual raises liabilities continuously, the primary balance (revenue minus non‑interest expenditure) must be compared with the change in net financial worth to assess solvency. The 2025 SNA introduces a “debt‑service‑to‑revenue” ratio calculated on an accrual basis, which is now part of the IMF’s Government Finance Statistics (GFS) framework. Indian analysts should note that the “cash‑basis” fiscal deficit reported in the Union Budget excludes accrued interest on NSSF (National Small Savings Fund) securities, creating a systematic wedge between the budgetary deficit and the SNA‑based net borrowing requirement.

A common error is to treat the redemption of a bond at maturity as a reduction in liabilities without recognising the prior accrual of the discount. The correct entry is a simultaneous reduction in FL.3 (principal) and a reversal of the accumulated interest payable (D.41) that has been building up over the life of the instrument. Failure to reverse the accrued interest leads to double‑counting of interest expense in the non‑financial accounts.

The Role of National Accounts in Measuring the Impact of Trade Policy Changes: Tariff Revenue, Terms of Trade, and Real Gross Domestic Income

Changes in tariff rates affect three distinct national‑account aggregates: (1) taxes on products (D.21), which form part of GDP at market prices; (2) the terms‑of‑trade effect captured by the difference between real GDP (volume measure) and real gross domestic income (RGDI); and (3) the balance‑of‑payments current account through import values. Under the 2008 SNA, import duties are recorded as part of the value of imports at the border (CIF) and then added to GDP at market prices via the tax‑on‑products component. When a tariff is raised, the immediate effect is an increase in D.21, raising GDP at market prices even though the volume of domestic production may be unchanged.

The RGDI adjusts real GDP for the trading gain or loss arising from changes in the relative price of exports and imports. A rise in import tariffs that reduces import volumes but raises import prices can improve the terms of trade, increasing RGDI relative to real GDP. The 2025 SNA recommends chain‑linked volume measures with annually updated weights to capture this effect more accurately. In India, the Central Statistics Office (CSO) publishes both real GDP (base 2011‑12) and RGDI (derived from the implicit price deflators of exports and imports). The 2017 GST reform, which subsumed many central excise duties and state VATs, altered the composition of D.21 and shifted part of the tax burden from production to consumption, a shift visible in the divergence between GDP at factor cost and GDP at market prices after 2017‑18.

For balance‑of‑payments compilation, the IMF’s BPM6 treats import duties as part of the value of goods imported (goods debit) and does not record them separately in the services account. However, the “taxes on products” component in the SNA must be reconciled with the customs revenue reported by the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC). A practical compilation trap is to omit the “tariff revenue” from the government revenue account when the duty is collected at the border but not yet transferred to the treasury, leading to a timing mismatch between the SNA’s accrual basis and the cash‑based fiscal accounts.

Analysts evaluating trade‑policy shocks should therefore trace the full chain: tariff change → import price → import volume → customs revenue (D.21) → GDP at market prices → RGDI via terms‑of‑trade adjustment → current‑account balance. The 2025 SNA’s “trade‑policy satellite account” prototype, piloted by the OECD, provides a template for this integrated analysis.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "How is a 10 % import duty on electronic goods recorded in the national accounts and the balance of payments?"
In the SNA, the duty is part of the CIF value of imports; it raises the value of imports (P.7) and simultaneously increases taxes on products (D.21), which is added to GDP at market prices. In the BPM6 balance of payments, the full CIF value (including duty) appears as a goods debit; the duty is not shown separately in the services account. The government revenue account records the duty on an accrual basis when the customs liability arises, not when cash is received.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links trade policy to national‑income aggregates, first identify whether the aggregate is measured at factor cost, market prices, or real gross domestic income. Then map the tax instrument (tariff, GST, excise) to the correct SNA transaction code (D.21, D.29, D.51). Remember that the balance of payments records the duty inside the goods value, not as a separate service flow.

Accounting for the Economic Value of Public Education Expenditure: Human Capital Formation, Satellite Accounts, and Long‑Term Growth

Public education outlays are traditionally recorded as government final consumption expenditure (P.3) because the SNA treats education services as non‑market output valued at cost of production. The 2025 SNA, however, encourages the compilation of a “Human Capital Satellite Account” (HCSA) that re‑classifies a portion of education spending as gross fixed capital formation (P.51) in produced intangible assets (AN.112) when the expenditure creates durable skills embodied in the labour force. The Jorgenson‑Fraumeni lifetime‑income approach estimates the present value of future earnings increments attributable to schooling; this value can be used to impute the capital stock of human capital.

India’s Ministry of Education (MoE) and MoSPI launched a pilot HCSA in 2022 using the Unified District Information System for Education (UDISE+) enrolment data, the National Sample Survey (NSS) 75th round on education expenditure, and the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) for earnings by education level. The pilot applied a 5 % real discount rate and a 40‑year working‑life horizon, yielding a human‑capital stock estimate of ₹ 1,200 lakh crore for 2020‑21, equivalent to roughly 60 % of net national disposable income. The satellite account separates “formal schooling” (primary to tertiary) from “skill‑development programmes” (e.g., Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana), assigning different service lives (15 years for school, 10 years for vocational training) and depreciation rates.

A critical compilation issue is the treatment of teacher salaries. In the core accounts they are compensation of employees (D.1) within P.3. In the HCSA, the portion of teacher time devoted to curriculum development and pedagogical research can be capitalised as “educational research and development” (AN.1121) under the 2025 SNA’s expanded R&D asset boundary. The pilot used the “time‑use survey” of teachers (conducted by the National Council of Educational Research and Training in 2021) to allocate 12 % of teacher hours to R&D‑eligible activities, resulting in an additional ₹ 0.8 lakh crore of gross fixed capital formation.

Policy analysts should note that the HCSA does not alter the headline GDP figure; it provides a complementary balance‑sheet perspective. The 2025 SNA recommends linking the human‑capital stock to the “labour‑productivity” growth accounting framework (KLEMS) so that the contribution of education to total factor productivity (TFP) can be isolated. India’s KLEMS database (released 2023) now includes a “human‑capital deepening” term derived from the HCSA, enabling a more granular decomposition of growth into capital deepening, labour quality improvement, and TFP.

The Treatment of Cross‑Border E‑Commerce and Digital Services in the Balance of Payments and National Accounts

Cross‑border e‑commerce transactions involve a non‑resident digital platform (e.g., a foreign marketplace or streaming service) supplying goods or services to resident consumers. Under BPM6, the supply of digital services (streaming, software‑as‑a‑service, online advertising) is recorded as an import of “Telecommunications, computer, and information services” (EBOPS code SI) when the consumer is resident and the supplier non‑resident. The value of the service is the gross amount paid by the consumer, including any platform fees. For low‑value physical goods shipped directly to consumers (parcels below the customs de‑minimis threshold), customs data often miss the transaction; the 2025 SNA recommends using payment‑card and digital‑wallet data to estimate the import value of such goods.

In the SNA, the domestic household’s final consumption expenditure (P.31) includes the full price paid for the digital service. The non‑resident platform’s output is not part of domestic production; therefore, no domestic value added is generated. However, if the platform operates a local subsidiary that provides marketing, payment‑processing, or content‑moderation services, that subsidiary’s output is domestic and recorded under “Information and communication services” (J62‑J63). The 2025 SNA introduces a “digital‑platform intermediation” asset (AN.1123) for the platform’s algorithmic matching technology, which can be capitalised by the subsidiary if it meets the produced‑asset criteria.

India’s equalisation levy (introduced 2016, expanded 2020) taxes non‑resident digital advertising and e‑commerce operators at 2 % of gross consideration. In the government accounts, the levy is recorded as a tax on products (D.21) on an accrual basis when the liability arises. The RBI’s “International Trade in Services” survey captures the gross receipts of foreign platforms from Indian residents, but coverage gaps remain for peer‑to‑peer marketplaces. MoSPI’s 2023 “Digital Economy Satellite Account” pilot used anonymised UPI transaction data to estimate the value of cross‑border digital service imports at ₹ 1.4 lakh crore for 2022‑23, a figure not reflected in the standard BOP tables.

A frequent compilation error is to record the platform’s commission fee as a domestic service export when the platform is non‑resident. The correct treatment is to record the commission as part of the import of the digital service (the consumer pays the full price; the platform’s commission is an internal cost). Only when a resident platform intermediates a transaction between a non‑resident buyer and a resident seller does the commission appear as an export of “Other business services” (EBOPS code SJ).

  • Treating accrued interest on government securities as a cash‑flow item only, ignoring the 2025 SNA fair‑value revaluation requirement.
  • Confusing tariff revenue (D.21) with export subsidies (D.31) when analysing trade‑policy impacts on GDP at market prices.
  • Recording all public education spending as consumption (P.3) and omitting the human‑capital satellite account capitalisation of teacher R&D time.
  • Classifying cross‑border digital service imports as domestic output because a local payment gateway processes the transaction.
  • Using customs data alone to capture low‑value e‑commerce parcels, leading to systematic under‑estimation of goods imports.
  • Failing to reverse accumulated discount accruals on zero‑coupon bonds at redemption, causing double‑counted interest expense.

Valuation of Non‑Market Environmental Services in the SNA and SEEA: Methods and Policy Implications

The System of National Accounts (SNA) records only market transactions, while the System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting (SEEA) extends the production boundary to include ecosystem services that are not traded. The SEEA‑Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA‑EA) framework distinguishes three valuation approaches: (1) the resource rent method, which estimates the surplus earned by extracting a natural resource after deducting all production costs and a normal return to produced capital; (2) the replacement cost method, which values the cost of substituting the ecosystem service with a human‑made alternative (e.g., constructing a water‑treatment plant to replace wetland filtration); and (3) the damage cost avoided method, which measures the economic loss that would occur if the service were lost (e.g., flood damage avoided by mangrove buffers). The 2025 SNA revision recommends that countries compile a satellite account for ecosystem services using the SEEA‑EA physical flow tables (supply‑use of ecosystem services in physical units) and then apply one of the above monetary techniques to produce a monetary ecosystem asset account. India’s Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) launched a pilot in 2022 for the Western Ghats, using remote‑sensing derived forest‑cover change data combined with the InVEST model to estimate carbon sequestration, water regulation, and recreation values. The pilot reported a provisional annual flow of ecosystem services equivalent to 1.2 % of GDP, but the estimate is sensitive to the discount rate chosen for the asset valuation. Policy analysts should note that the SEEA‑EA does not alter headline GDP; it provides a complementary balance‑sheet perspective that can be used to adjust Adjusted Net National Income (ANNI) for natural capital depreciation, a metric increasingly referenced in the Union Budget’s “green accounting” annex.

Compilation challenges include the need for spatially explicit data, the treatment of joint production (e.g., a forest providing both timber and carbon storage), and the avoidance of double counting with existing SNA entries for timber harvest. The SEEA‑EA recommends a “ecosystem asset” classification (AN.211) separate from produced assets (AN.111) and non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.212). When the same physical asset yields both market and non‑market services, the SNA records only the market output, while the SEEA‑EA allocates the total ecosystem service flow across the relevant service categories. The 2025 SNA further introduces a “natural capital depletion adjustment” (D.99) that can be subtracted from net domestic product to derive a depletion‑adjusted measure, aligning with the “green GDP” concept advocated by the UN Statistical Commission. Indian state‑level accounts are beginning to incorporate these adjustments; for example, the Karnataka State Accounts 2023‑24 included a depletion adjustment for sand mining based on the resource‑rent method, reducing the state’s net domestic product by 0.4 %.

Measuring the Economic Impact of Digital Platform Monopolies on National Income Distribution

Digital platforms that operate as multi‑sided markets (e.g., e‑commerce marketplaces, ride‑hailing apps, food‑delivery aggregators) generate value through network effects, data aggregation, and algorithmic matching. The 2025 SNA treats the platform’s matching technology as a produced intangible asset (AN.1123) when the platform incurs development costs that satisfy the capitalisation criteria (controlled, identifiable, future economic benefits). However, the dominant platform often extracts a large share of the surplus via commission fees, which are recorded as intermediate consumption of the sellers (or as a reduction of sellers’ output) and as output of the platform under “Information and communication services” (J62‑J63). This accounting treatment can mask the distributional impact: the platform’s value added may appear modest relative to the total transaction volume, while the sellers’ value added is reduced. To capture the distributional consequences, the Distributional National Accounts (DNA) framework links macro aggregates to household‑level income by allocating platform commissions to the factor incomes of platform owners (capital income) and to the labour income of gig workers (who are classified as own‑account workers under the SNA). India’s Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) 2022‑23 introduced a module on platform work, enabling the estimation of gig‑worker earnings and the share of platform revenue accruing to labour versus capital. Preliminary DNA estimates suggest that in the ride‑hailing sector, roughly 65 % of platform revenue is retained as capital income (including returns to algorithmic asset), while 35 % flows to driver‑partners as mixed income. The 2025 SNA also recommends a “platform‑intermediation service” output measure that separates the pure matching service from ancillary services (payment processing, insurance, marketing), allowing a more granular decomposition of value added. Policy analysts should be aware that the equalisation levy (2 % on non‑resident digital advertising and e‑commerce) is recorded as a tax on products (D.21) and does not affect the platform’s value added; it merely shifts a portion of the surplus to government revenue. When assessing monopoly power, examiners often expect candidates to distinguish between market‑power rents (captured in operating surplus) and network‑effect externalities (which are not recorded in the SNA but can be approximated through the DNA’s capital‑income concentration indicators).

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "In the SNA 2025 framework, how should the commission fee charged by a non‑resident digital platform to resident sellers be recorded in the national accounts?"
The commission is part of the import of the digital intermediation service. The resident seller’s output is recorded net of the commission (i.e., the seller’s revenue minus the fee). The full fee is recorded as an import of “Information and communication services” (EBOPS SI) by the resident economy. The non‑resident platform’s output is not domestic production; therefore no domestic value added arises from the commission. If a resident subsidiary provides ancillary services (payment gateway, marketing), only that subsidiary’s output is recorded domestically. Recording the commission as a domestic service export is a common error.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes SNA recording rules with distributional analysis, first identify the institutional unit (resident vs non‑resident) and the transaction type (output, intermediate consumption, tax). Then apply the 2025 SNA asset boundary for digital platforms (AN.1123) and the DNA allocation rules. Sketch a quick T‑account for the platform, the seller, and the household sector to avoid double‑counting.

The Role of National Accounts in Assessing the Effectiveness of Monetary Policy Transmission under Inflation Targeting

Monetary policy transmission operates through several channels — interest‑rate, credit, exchange‑rate, and expectations — each of which leaves a trace in the national accounts. The interest‑rate channel is reflected in the property income account (D.4): a policy rate hike raises the interest payable on government securities and private debt, increasing the property income paid by the general government and non‑financial corporations to the financial sector. The credit channel appears in the financial account (F.3) as a slowdown in net lending/borrowing of households and firms, which can be tracked through the Flow of Funds matrix integrated with the SNA. The exchange‑rate channel influences the external account (B.11) via changes in export and import volumes and prices, captured in the goods and services account (P.6/P.7). The expectations channel is proxied by movements in gross fixed capital formation (P.51) and changes in inventories (P.52), as firms adjust investment plans in response to perceived future policy stance. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Monetary Policy Report routinely cites the output gap derived from the potential output estimate, which itself relies on a production‑function approach using capital stock (from the national balance sheet) and quality‑adjusted labour input (from the KLEMS database). The 2025 SNA’s recommendation to capitalise R&D and data assets improves the measurement of the capital stock, thereby refining potential output estimates. A practical illustration: during the 2022‑23 tightening cycle, the RBI raised the repo rate by 250 basis points. National accounts data showed a 0.6 % decline in real gross fixed capital formation in the subsequent two quarters, while household final consumption expenditure growth slowed from 7.2 % to 4.8 % year‑on‑year. Simultaneously, the financial account recorded a reduction in net borrowing by non‑financial corporations of ₹ 1.1 lakh crore, consistent with the credit channel. Analysts using the integrated SNA‑Flow of Funds framework can decompose the total effect on GDP into the sum of these channel‑specific contributions, providing a quantitative basis for evaluating whether the inflation‑targeting framework achieved its output‑stabilisation objective.

Key compilation points: (1) The property income series must be on an accrual basis, including accrued interest on zero‑coupon bonds, to avoid timing mismatches. (2) The financial derivatives positions (F.71) of banks affect the interest‑rate pass‑through and should be consolidated in the financial corporation sector. (3) The exchange‑rate valuation of external assets and liabilities (revaluation account) must be consistent with the BOP’s valuation principles (market prices). (4) The output gap estimation benefits from the chain‑linked volume measures introduced in the 2025 SNA, which reduce base‑year bias. Examiners often test the ability to link a policy rate change to specific national‑accounts aggregates; candidates should be ready to trace the transmission from the policy rate to property income, to sectoral saving‑investment balances, and finally to GDP components.

Accounting for the Economic Value of Public Infrastructure Maintenance and Deferred Maintenance in the National Balance Sheet

Public infrastructure — roads, bridges, water supply, power grids — constitutes a large share of the nation’s non‑financial produced assets (AN.111). The SNA records gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) when new assets are created, and consumption of fixed capital (CFC) as a cost of using up the asset over its service life. However, maintenance expenditure that merely preserves the existing service potential (e.g., routine resurfacing) is treated as intermediate consumption (P.2) and does not increase the asset stock. Major improvements that extend service life or enhance capacity are capitalised as GFCF. The distinction is critical for the national balance sheet: deferred maintenance leads to an understatement of CFC and an overstatement of the net capital stock, because the asset’s deterioration is not fully captured. The 2025 SNA introduces a “condition‑adjusted depreciation” approach, allowing compilers to adjust CFC upward when condition surveys indicate accelerated deterioration. India’s Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) conducts a biennial Pavement Condition Index (PCI) survey; the 2023 survey showed that 28 % of national highways were in “poor” condition, implying a higher effective depreciation rate than the standard 2.5 % per annum used in the perpetual inventory method (PIM). By applying a condition‑adjusted rate of 3.8 % for the poor‑condition segment, the revised CFC for the road network increases by approximately ₹ 0.3 lakh crore annually, reducing the net capital stock and the derived net national income accordingly. The same principle applies to water‑supply assets monitored by the Central Water Commission and to power‑transmission assets tracked by the Central Electricity Authority. A further nuance: public‑private partnership (PPP) assets under service‑concession arrangements are recorded on the government balance sheet only when the government controls the residual interest (IFRIC 12 / SNA 2025 guidance). Deferred maintenance on PPP assets is the responsibility of the private operator, but the government may bear contingent liability if the operator defaults; such contingent liabilities are recorded in the government guarantee memorandum items of the national balance sheet. For exam purposes, remember that (a) routine maintenance = intermediate consumption, (b) major renewal = GFCF, (c) condition‑adjusted CFC = higher depreciation when asset condition deteriorates, and (d) deferred maintenance creates an implicit liability that may be disclosed in the “other accounts payable” (F.8) of the government sector if a formal maintenance backlog is recognised.

  • Confusing routine maintenance (intermediate consumption) with capital‑forming renewal (GFCF) when classifying public works expenditure.
  • Applying a uniform depreciation rate to heterogeneous infrastructure assets without condition‑adjusted adjustments.
  • Omitting the revaluation of PPP concession assets when the government retains residual control, leading to an incomplete national balance sheet.
  • Treating deferred maintenance backlog as a mere footnote rather than a measurable liability in the government’s other accounts payable.
  • Neglecting the impact of accelerated CFC on net national income and the derived fiscal sustainability indicators.
  • Misclassifying the equalisation levy on digital platforms as a reduction of platform output instead of a tax on products (D.21).
  • Recording cross‑border digital service commissions as domestic exports when the platform is non‑resident, violating the 2025 SNA residency principle.

Accounting for the Economic Value of Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) in National Accounts

Digital public infrastructure — identity platforms, unified payment interfaces, consent‑based data exchange layers — has become a backbone of modern service delivery. The 2025 System of National Accounts (SNA) treats such infrastructure as a produced non‑financial asset (AN.111) when it satisfies the criteria of control, economic benefit, and a measurable service life. Compilers must therefore record the initial development outlay as gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) and subsequently charge consumption of fixed capital (CFC) over the asset’s expected operational period, which is typically aligned with the technology refresh cycle of five to seven years.

Because DPI services are often provided at zero or marginal price to users, the SNA requires an imputed output value based on the cost‑of‑production approach: the sum of intermediate consumption, compensation of employees, CFC, and a return to capital. This imputed output enters the production account of the general government sector (or the public corporation that operates the platform) and feeds into GDP through the output‑expenditure identity. The corresponding imputed final consumption expenditure of households is recorded under “social transfers in kind” (D.63), ensuring that the welfare contribution of free digital services is captured without inflating market‑price GDP.

A practical complication arises when the same infrastructure is used by both government and private agents. The 2025 SNA recommends a proportional allocation of CFC and return‑to‑capital based on observed usage metrics — transaction volumes, authentication requests, or data‑exchange calls — collected from system logs. In India, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) publishes quarterly usage dashboards for Aadhaar and UPI; these dashboards provide the empirical basis for the allocation. The resulting split ensures that the government’s production account reflects only the share of infrastructure serving public‑policy objectives, while the remainder is attributed to the market‑oriented output of payment‑service providers.

From a fiscal‑policy perspective, recognising DPI as an asset changes the government’s balance‑sheet position: the net capital stock rises, and the associated CFC reduces net operating surplus, which in turn lowers net lending/borrowing. Analysts evaluating fiscal sustainability must therefore adjust the primary deficit for the imputed depreciation of DPI, otherwise the fiscal stance appears more expansionary than it truly is. The 2025 SNA also introduces a “condition‑adjusted depreciation” option for digital assets, allowing compilers to accelerate CFC when cyber‑security incidents or technology obsolescence shorten the effective service life.

Examiners often test the ability to trace a policy decision — such as a mandate to expand UPI to feature‑phone users — through the national‑accounts chain: higher GFCF in the year of rollout, higher imputed output and CFC in subsequent years, a shift in household final consumption from market‑priced payment services to social transfers in kind, and a measurable impact on the government’s net worth. Candidates should be ready to illustrate each link with the relevant SNA transaction codes (P.51g, P.2, D.63, K.1).

Treatment of Green Hydrogen Production and Renewable Energy Certificates in the SNA

Green hydrogen — hydrogen produced by electrolysis powered exclusively by renewable electricity — has entered the energy‑transition agenda of many economies. The 2025 SNA classifies the electrolysis plant as a fixed asset (AN.111) and the hydrogen output as a product (CPC 1710) valued at basic prices. The renewable electricity consumed in the process is recorded as intermediate consumption (P.2) of the hydrogen‑producing establishment, while the associated renewable‑energy certificates (RECs) are treated as a separate intangible asset (AN.112) when they are tradable and confer a legal right to claim the environmental attribute.

When RECs are sold independently of the physical hydrogen, the transaction generates two distinct revenue streams: (i) the sale of hydrogen at market price, recorded as output (P.1) of the manufacturing sector; (ii) the sale of RECs, recorded as output of the “environmental‑services” industry (ISIC 3900) and as a transfer of the intangible asset from the producer to the buyer. The buyer — often a corporate seeking to meet a renewable‑energy mandate — records the REC purchase as gross fixed capital formation if the certificate is held for compliance over multiple periods, or as intermediate consumption if it is surrendered within the same accounting period.

The valuation of RECs follows the market‑price principle: the observable price on the certificate exchange (or the auction clearing price) is used. In the absence of an active market, the 2025 SNA permits a cost‑based estimate — the incremental cost of renewable generation over the fossil‑fuel benchmark — but this must be disclosed as a “non‑market valuation” in the metadata. India’s Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) operates a REC market; the quarterly clearing price provides a reliable market reference for national‑accounts compilers.

A further nuance concerns the treatment of the renewable electricity that powers the electrolyser. If the electricity is self‑generated by the hydrogen producer (e.g., a dedicated solar farm), the solar farm’s output is recorded as own‑account capital formation (P.51g) and the electricity used internally is imputed as intermediate consumption at the opportunity cost — the price the producer could have obtained by selling the electricity to the grid. This imputation prevents double counting of the renewable attribute between the electricity sector and the hydrogen sector.

For policy analysis, the SNA framework enables a clean decomposition of the green‑hydrogen value chain: (a) capital formation in electrolysis and renewable generation; (b) intermediate consumption of electricity; (c) output of hydrogen and RECs; (d) final use of hydrogen in industry, transport, or export; (e) final use of RECs for compliance or voluntary offsetting. This decomposition supports the measurement of “green‑value‑added” — the portion of GDP that can be attributed to low‑carbon production — and feeds directly into the SEEA‑Energy physical flow accounts.

Worked Illustration
A public‑sector electrolyser plant commissions a 100 MW solar farm (capital cost ₹ 500 crore) and an electrolysis unit (capital cost ₹ 300 crore). In year 1 the plant produces 10 000 tonnes of green hydrogen sold at ₹ 300 kg⁻¹ and generates 200 000 RECs sold at ₹ 1 500 each. Show the SNA entries for year 1.
  1. GFCF: Solar farm ₹ 500 crore (AN.111), Electrolyser ₹ 300 crore (AN.111).
  2. Output (P.1): Hydrogen 10 000 t × ₹ 300 kg⁻¹ = ₹ 3 000 crore (basic price). RECs 200 000 × ₹ 1 500 = ₹ 3 000 crore (environmental‑services output).
  3. Intermediate consumption (P.2): Electricity used = 100 MW × 8 760 h × capacity factor 0.25 = 219 GWh. Opportunity cost = 219 GWh × ₹ 3 kWh⁻¹ = ₹ 657 crore (imputed).
  4. Value added = Output (₹ 6 000 crore) – IC (₹ 657 crore) = ₹ 5 343 crore.
  5. Consumption of fixed capital (K.1): Straight‑line over 20 years for solar (₹ 25 crore/yr) and 15 years for electrolyser (₹ 20 crore/yr) = ₹ 45 crore.
  6. Net operating surplus = Value added – Compensation of employees – CFC – Other taxes on production.
  7. REC asset (AN.112) recognised at ₹ 3 000 crore; sale reduces asset, increases financial asset (F.2) of buyer.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the national‑accounts impact of a green‑hydrogen project, first list the two produced assets (generation and electrolysis), then write the output‑intermediate‑consumption‑value‑added chain for each product (hydrogen and REC). Remember that RECs are an intangible produced asset (AN.112) and their sale is a transfer of that asset, not a tax. Use the 2025 SNA transaction codes (P.51g, P.1, P.2, K.1, AN.112) to demonstrate precision.

Valuation of Publicly Funded Data Assets and Open Government Data in National Accounts

Governments increasingly invest in the creation, curation, and dissemination of large‑scale datasets — geospatial layers, administrative registers, sensor networks — that are released under open‑data licences. The 2025 SNA recognises such datasets as produced intangible assets (AN.112) when they are the result of a deliberate production process, are subject to control by the producing unit, and generate future economic benefits either directly (through licensing fees) or indirectly (by lowering transaction costs for private firms). The initial outlay — salaries of data scientists, cloud‑storage contracts, cleaning and annotation effort — is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in the general government sector.

Because open data are typically provided at zero price, the SNA requires an imputed output value using the cost‑of‑production method: the sum of intermediate consumption, compensation of employees, consumption of fixed capital, and a return to capital. This imputed output enters government production (P.1) and is matched by an imputed final consumption expenditure of the household sector under “social transfers in kind — non‑market services” (D.63). The approach mirrors the treatment of other non‑market government services such as public health or education.

A practical challenge is estimating the service life of a dataset. Unlike physical infrastructure, data can be updated continuously; the 2025 SNA allows a “rolling‑asset” approach where the asset is re‑valued each period to reflect the cumulative investment net of depreciation. Depreciation (CFC) can be modelled as a constant‑rate decline (e.g., 20 % per annum) reflecting obsolescence, or as a condition‑adjusted rate linked to usage analytics — download counts, API calls, citation indices — published by the data portal. India’s Open Government Data Platform (data.gov.in) provides monthly API‑usage statistics that can serve as the empirical basis for condition‑adjusted CFC.

When a private firm builds a commercial product on top of open government data, the firm’s own investment in value‑added services (algorithms, user interfaces) is recorded as its own GFCF. The open data itself remains on the government balance sheet; no transfer of ownership occurs. However, if the government enters into a data‑sharing agreement that grants exclusive commercial rights, the transaction is treated as a sale of an intangible asset (AN.112) and the government records a disposal (K.2) while the buyer records an acquisition (P.51g). The sale price becomes a market valuation for the dataset, replacing the cost‑based imputation for subsequent periods.

For fiscal analysis, recognising data assets improves the completeness of the government balance sheet and alters net worth. The imputed CFC reduces net operating surplus, which in turn lowers net lending/borrowing. Analysts assessing the fiscal impact of open‑data initiatives must therefore add back the imputed depreciation to the primary deficit to avoid overstating the fiscal stance. The 2025 SNA also encourages the compilation of a satellite account for “digital public assets” that links the national‑accounts entries to the SEEA‑Digital framework, enabling cross‑country comparability of data‑infrastructure investment.

Measuring the Economic Contribution of Urban Green Spaces and Ecosystem Services in National Accounts

Urban green spaces — parks, street trees, wetlands, green roofs — deliver a bundle of ecosystem services: air‑pollution removal, heat‑island mitigation, storm‑water regulation, recreation, and cultural‑heritage value. The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting — Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA‑EA) provides a physical‑flow framework that can be linked to the SNA through the “ecosystem‑asset” concept (AN.211). The 2025 SNA permits the capitalisation of ecosystem assets when they are subject to effective management and generate measurable economic benefits to institutional units.

Valuation follows a two‑step process. First, physical supply‑use tables quantify the flow of each service (e.g., tonnes of PM₂.₅ removed per hectare per year, cubic metres of runoff retained). Second, monetary valuation applies either (a) a replacement‑cost method — the cost of engineered infrastructure that would provide the same service (e.g., mechanical filtration plants for air purification) — or (b) a hedonic‑pricing method that isolates the marginal contribution of proximity to green space in residential property values. The 2025 SNA recommends the replacement‑cost approach for regulating services (air, water, climate) and the hedonic approach for cultural services (recreation, aesthetics).

In practice, municipal corporations compile a “green‑asset register” that records the extent, condition, and management regime of each green‑space parcel. Condition indicators — canopy cover, soil health, biodiversity indices — feed into a condition‑adjusted depreciation rate for the ecosystem asset, analogous to the condition‑adjusted CFC for built infrastructure. The resulting consumption of ecosystem capital (K.1) is recorded as a cost in the production account of the local‑government sector, reducing its net operating surplus and net worth.

The imputed output of ecosystem services is entered as non‑market output (P.13) of the general government sector, with a matching imputed final consumption of households (D.63). For services that are directly sold — e.g., entry fees to a botanical garden — the market revenue is recorded as market output (P.11) and the remainder of the service flow remains non‑market. This split ensures that the total economic contribution of urban green space is captured without double counting.

Policy analysts can use the integrated accounts to evaluate “green‑infrastructure investment” programmes: the GFCF for new park development, the annual CFC of existing green assets, the flow of regulating and cultural services, and the resultant change in household welfare (via imputed consumption). The framework also supports cost‑benefit analysis of alternative land‑use decisions — converting a vacant lot to a park versus a commercial building — by comparing the net present value of ecosystem‑service flows against the market rent foregone.

Accounting for the Economic Impact of Cybersecurity Investments in National Accounts

Cybersecurity expenditure — security‑operations centres, threat‑intelligence platforms, encryption hardware, incident‑response services — has risen sharply across public and private sectors. The 2025 SNA treats cybersecurity outlays as either intermediate consumption (P.2) or gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) depending on the nature and expected service life of the acquired item. Perpetual licences for security software, hardware appliances, and the build‑out of a dedicated security‑operations centre are capitalised as produced assets (AN.111 or AN.112) and depreciated over their useful lives (typically three to five years for software, seven to ten years for hardware). Recurring subscription fees, managed‑service contracts, and personnel costs for day‑to‑day monitoring are recorded as intermediate consumption in the period incurred.

When a government agency establishes a national Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT), the initial set‑up — facilities, network‑monitoring infrastructure, recruitment and training — constitutes GFCF. The ongoing operational budget — salaries of analysts, threat‑feed subscriptions, simulation exercises — is intermediate consumption. The output of the CERT is a non‑market service (P.13) valued at cost of production; the imputed output is matched by an imputed final consumption of the general government sector (D.63) and, where services are extended to private critical‑infrastructure operators, by an imputed social transfer in kind to the corporate sector.

A distinctive feature of cybersecurity is the “avoided‑loss” benefit: successful defence prevents production downtime, data‑breach fines, and reputational damage. The SNA does not record avoided losses as output; instead, the benefit appears indirectly through the preservation of the victim’s capital stock and output. However, the 2025 SNA encourages the compilation of a satellite account for “digital‑risk mitigation” that links cybersecurity investment (GFCF + IC) to a counterfactual estimate of lost output derived from incident‑reporting databases (e.g., the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team’s annual incident statistics). This satellite account informs cost‑effectiveness analysis without altering core GDP.

From a fiscal‑policy viewpoint, capitalising cybersecurity assets improves the government’s balance sheet: the net capital stock rises, and the associated CFC reduces net operating surplus. Analysts must adjust the primary deficit for the imputed depreciation to avoid overstating fiscal expansion. Moreover, the treatment of cyber‑insurance premiums — recorded as a service (output of the insurance sector) and as a current transfer (D.71) for the insured — interacts with the cybersecurity investment decision: higher capitalised security may lower insurance premiums, creating a feedback loop that can be modelled in a dynamic CGE framework.

Examiners may ask candidates to classify a mixed cybersecurity budget (e.g., ₹ 200 crore for a new SOC building, ₹ 50 crore for annual threat‑intelligence subscriptions, ₹ 30 crore for staff training) into GFCF and IC, compute the resulting CFC schedule, and trace the impact on government net lending/borrowing. Mastery of the distinction between produced assets (AN.111/AN.112) and current expenditures, and the ability to apply the cost‑of‑production valuation for non‑market output, are essential.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the imputed output of free digital public services with market output and therefore omitting the matching social transfer in kind.
  • Treating renewable‑energy certificates as a tax rather than an intangible produced asset, leading to mis‑classification of REC revenue.
  • Valuing open government data at market price when no market exists, instead of using the cost‑of‑production imputation required by the 2025 SNA.
  • Applying a single depreciation rate to heterogeneous urban green‑space assets without condition‑adjusted adjustments based on canopy cover or biodiversity indices.
  • Recording all cybersecurity spending as intermediate consumption, ignoring the capitalisation of software licences and hardware with multi‑year service lives.
  • Failing to adjust the primary fiscal deficit for the imputed consumption of fixed capital of newly recognised digital and ecosystem assets, which overstates the fiscal stance.

Accounting for Renewable Energy Certificates and Perform‑Achieve‑Trade Certificates in the SNA

Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) and Perform‑Achieve‑Trade (PAT) certificates are market‑based instruments that certify the generation of one megawatt‑hour of renewable electricity or the achievement of a verified energy‑efficiency improvement, respectively. Under the 2008 SNA, such certificates were often recorded as financial assets (F.5) because they are tradable, but the 2025 SNA introduces a clearer distinction based on their origin. Since both RECs and PAT certificates are created through a verifiable production process — renewable generation for RECs and measured energy‑saving investments for PAT — they satisfy the definition of a produced asset. Consequently, the 2025 SNA classifies them as intangible produced assets (AN.112) rather than non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.211) such as emission permits.

Valuation follows the hierarchy in the 2025 SNA. When an active secondary market exists, the certificates are valued at the prevailing market price, which reflects the marginal value of the underlying environmental service. In the Indian context, the REC market on the power exchanges provides observable prices for solar and non‑solar RECs, and the PAT trading platform yields prices for energy‑saving certificates. Where trading is thin or absent — for example, in the early years of a state‑level REC scheme — the SNA requires valuation at the cost of production. For RECs this is the incremental levelised cost of renewable generation that generated the certificate; for PAT certificates it is the verified incremental investment cost of the energy‑efficiency measure. The cost‑of‑production approach ensures that the asset value enters the balance sheet of the generating unit (or the designated obligated entity) and that the corresponding consumption of fixed capital (CFC) is recorded over the certificate’s useful life, typically the compliance period of the relevant regulation.

The recording of transactions involving these certificates affects several accounts. The initial issuance is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) by the producer, increasing the stock of AN.112. Subsequent sales are treated as disposals of a produced asset (negative P.51g for the seller, positive for the buyer) and are accompanied by a financial transaction (F.5) for the cash settlement.
