When an obligated entity surrenders certificates to meet its Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) or PAT target, the surrender is recorded as a reduction in the entity’s AN.112 stock and a corresponding increase in its intermediate consumption (P.2) if the certificates are used up in the compliance period, or as a capital transfer (D.9) if the surrender extinguishes a liability without further production. The 2025 SNA also encourages a satellite account for “environmental‑asset certificates” that links the stock of AN.112 to physical flows of renewable generation and energy savings, enabling analysts to assess the cost‑effectiveness of the RPO and PAT mechanisms without altering core GDP.

From a fiscal perspective, capitalising RECs and PAT certificates improves the government’s net worth when the certificates are held by public sector generators or distribution utilities. The associated CFC reduces net operating surplus, and analysts must adjust the primary deficit for this imputed depreciation to avoid overstating fiscal expansion. Moreover, the interaction with carbon‑credit markets — where RECs may be bundled with Certified Emission Reductions (CERs) — requires careful separation of the two asset classes to prevent double counting in both the SNA and the SEEA‑CF.

Measuring the Economic Contribution of the Defence Production Sector in National Accounts

The defence production sector in India comprises the seven Defence Public Sector Undertakings (DPSUs) created after the corporatisation of the Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) in October 2021, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) laboratories, and a growing private‑sector base under the Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2020. In the System of National Accounts, the output of government‑owned defence establishments that supply primarily to the Ministry of Defence is classified as non‑market output (P.13) and valued at the cost of production: compensation of employees, intermediate consumption, consumption of fixed capital (CFC) and other taxes on production less subsidies. This cost‑of‑production valuation yields an imputed output that is matched by an imputed final consumption expenditure of general government (P.31) and, where services are provided to other government units, by social transfers in kind (D.63).

A significant methodological shift in the 2025 SNA concerns the treatment of defence research and development (R&D). Expenditure on R&D that leads to a prototype or a technology demonstrator with a service life exceeding one year is now capitalised as gross fixed capital formation in intellectual property products (AN.112). The 2025 SNA specifies that the asset boundary includes “defence‑specific software, system‑integration designs and prototype platforms” provided they meet the criteria of economic ownership, control and a predictable future service flow. Consequently, DRDO’s spending on missile‑system prototypes, radar‑software suites and platform‑integration test‑beds is recorded as GFCF, with CFC calculated over the asset’s useful life (typically 10‑15 years for major platforms). This capitalisation raises the measured capital stock of the defence sector and reduces its net operating surplus, affecting the government’s net lending/borrowing position.

Exports of defence equipment — such as the BrahMos missile system, Light Combat Aircraft (Tejas) components and naval vessels — are recorded as market output (P.11) at transaction values, contributing to exports of goods (P.61) in the balance of payments. Imports of defence capital goods (e.g., S‑400 air‑defence systems, Rafale aircraft) are recorded as imports of goods (P.71) and, when they meet the GFCF criteria, as gross fixed capital formation in machinery and equipment (AN.111). The 2025 SNA also requires that offset obligations tied to defence imports be recorded as a separate transaction: the offset fulfilment (technology transfer, joint‑venture equity) is treated as a capital transfer (D.9) from the foreign supplier to the Indian entity, while the associated domestic production is captured in the relevant industry’s GVA.

Statistical challenges remain. The transition from OFB to seven DPSUs altered the institutional sector classification: the new DPSUs are classified as public non‑financial corporations (S.11001) rather than general government, shifting their output from non‑market to market where they sell to entities outside the Ministry of Defence. Analysts must adjust time‑series for this break, using the 2021‑22 supply‑use tables as the benchmark. Additionally, the valuation of defence inventories (spare parts, ammunition) follows the perpetual inventory method with condition‑adjusted depreciation rates, reflecting the long shelf‑life and strategic stockpiling requirements. The 2025 SNA’s guidance on “strategic inventories” recommends a separate memorandum item in the balance sheet to distinguish them from regular inventories, ensuring transparency for fiscal‑risk assessments.

Examiner's Trap
A question asks: How are Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) and Perform‑Achieve‑Trade (PAT) certificates classified in the 2025 SNA, and what valuation method applies when they are not actively traded?
RECs and PAT certificates are recognised as intangible produced assets (AN.112) because they are created through a verifiable production process. When a market exists, they are valued at the prevailing market price; in the absence of active trading, the 2025 SNA requires valuation at the cost of production, i.e., the incremental cost of renewable generation or energy‑efficiency investment that gave rise to the certificate.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the asset codes: AN.112 for intangible produced assets, AN.211 for non‑produced non‑financial assets. For any certificate‑type instrument, first ask whether it originates from a production process; if yes, treat as AN.112 and apply cost‑of‑production valuation when markets are thin.

Valuing Non‑Market Output of Public Education Services under the 2025 SNA

Government‑provided education — from primary schools to public universities — constitutes a major component of non‑market output (P.13) in the Indian national accounts. The 2025 SNA retains the cost‑of‑production valuation principle: output equals the sum of compensation of employees (teachers, administrators), intermediate consumption (textbooks, utilities, maintenance), consumption of fixed capital on school buildings and equipment, and other taxes on production less subsidies. This imputed output is recorded as final consumption expenditure of general government (P.31) and, where services are provided free to households, as a social transfer in kind (D.63) to the household sector.

The 2025 SNA introduces two refinements that affect the measurement of education output. First, it recommends the compilation of quality‑adjusted volume indices for education services. Instead of using simple enrolment numbers, the volume measure should incorporate learning‑outcome indicators such as the National Achievement Survey (NAS) scores, Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) results (where available), and teacher‑pupil ratios. The quality‑adjusted volume index is then used to deflate the current‑price output, yielding a real growth rate for education services that reflects improvements (or deteriorations) in educational quality. Second, the 2025 SNA encourages a satellite account for education that links physical inputs (number of schools, classrooms, digital infrastructure) to outputs (enrolment, graduation rates, skill certifications) and to outcomes (labour‑market earnings, productivity). This satellite account enables policymakers to assess the efficiency of public spending on education without altering core GDP.

Specific Indian programmes illustrate the accounting implications. The Mid‑Day Meal Scheme (now PM‑POSHAN) provides free cooked meals to children in government schools. The cost of meals — procurement, cooking, distribution — is recorded as intermediate consumption of the education sector, while the nutritional benefit to children is captured as a social transfer in kind (D.63) from general government to households. Free textbooks and uniforms supplied by state governments are similarly treated: their production cost enters intermediate consumption of the education sector, and the transfer to students is recorded as D.63. The 2025 SNA clarifies that when the government purchases textbooks from private publishers, the transaction is a market purchase (P.2) by the education sector; when textbooks are printed in‑house by a government press, the press’s output is recorded as market output (P.11) sold to the education sector, preserving the production boundary.

Capital formation in education infrastructure — construction of new school buildings, laboratories, digital classrooms — is recorded as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in structures (AN.111) and equipment (AN.111). The 2025 SNA’s guidance on “condition‑adjusted depreciation” applies: schools in remote or disaster‑prone areas may have shorter useful lives, and the CFC schedule should reflect periodic condition surveys. The imputed user cost of public school infrastructure (the return on capital plus CFC) can be used in cost‑benefit analyses of programmes such as the Samagra Shiksha Abhiyan, but it does not enter the core production account because the services are non‑market.

Assessing the Impact of Production‑Linked Incentive Schemes on Manufacturing Gross Value Added

The Production‑Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes, launched in 2020‑21 across 14 sectors including electronics, pharmaceuticals, automobiles, telecom equipment and white goods, represent a major supply‑side policy intervention. In the SNA framework, PLI payments are classified as subsidies on production (D.39) because they are contingent on incremental output or investment and are payable to resident producers. As subsidies on production, they are recorded as negative taxes on production, which raises gross value added at basic prices (GVA = output − intermediate consumption + subsidies on production − taxes on production). Consequently, the PLI incentives directly increase the measured GVA of the beneficiary industries in the year they are accrued.

The 2025 SNA distinguishes between “subsidies on products” (D.31) — tied to specific units of output — and “other subsidies on production” (D.39). PLI schemes that reward a fixed percentage of incremental sales over a base year fall under D.31, while those that provide a lump‑sum incentive for meeting investment thresholds are recorded under D.39. This distinction matters for the allocation of GVA across products in the supply‑use tables: D.31 subsidies are attributed to the specific product group (e.g., mobile phones), whereas D.39 subsidies are distributed across the industry’s total output using the industry’s output structure.

Measurement of the incremental GVA attributable to PLI requires linking administrative data from the Ministry of Commerce and Industry (which tracks disbursements and eligibility) with the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) and the Quarterly Survey of Manufacturing (QSM). The CSO’s experimental “PLI‑adjusted GVA” series uses a difference‑in‑differences approach: it compares the GVA growth of PLI‑eligible firms (identified via PAN‑linked GSTN data) with a control group of non‑eligible firms in the same NIC‑3 digit industry, controlling for pre‑trend differences. The 2025 SNA’s emphasis on integrating administrative micro‑data with survey‑based macro aggregates supports this methodology.

Several caveats affect interpretation. First, PLI incentives are recorded on an accrual basis when the entitlement is established, not when cash is disbursed; this can create a timing mismatch between the GVA boost and the fiscal outlay. Second, the schemes may induce “output shifting” — firms re‑classify existing production to qualify for incentives — which would inflate measured GVA without a real increase in productive capacity. The 2025 SNA recommends a “behavioural adjustment” in satellite accounts to net out such re‑classification effects. Third, the interaction with the Goods and Services Tax (GST) input‑tax‑credit mechanism means that the effective subsidy rate differs from the nominal PLI rate; analysts must adjust for the GST credit chain to avoid double counting of the incentive in both output and intermediate consumption.

Integrating GST Network Data with National Accounts for Real‑Time Sectoral Estimates

The Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN) generates invoice‑level data for over 1.3 crore registered taxpayers, capturing transaction values, HSN (Harmonised System of Nomenclature) codes, place of supply, and tax components. Since 2019, the Central Statistics Office (CSO) has been using GSTN data to compile “GST‑based GVA” estimates for manufacturing and selected services, providing a high‑frequency complement to the traditional Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) and the Quarterly Survey of Services (QSS).

Valuation of Multi‑Sided Platform Intermediation Services in National Accounts

The 2008 SNA classifies a digital platform as a producer of intermediation services (P.111) whose output equals the sum of commissions, transaction fees, subscription charges and advertising revenue earned from the two or more sides it connects. The 2025 SNA revision refines this by introducing a distinct product code for “platform intermediation services” and by separating fees that are directly tied to a transaction (treated as subsidies on products, D.31) from periodic access fees (treated as other subsidies on production, D.39). Eurostat’s 2021 “Manual on Measuring the Platform Economy” and the OECD’s 2022 “Guidelines for Multi‑Sided Platforms” both recommend that national statistical offices compile a platform‑specific supply‑use table linking the platform’s revenue breakdown to the using industries — e‑commerce marketplaces to retail, ride‑hailing to transport, food‑delivery to accommodation and food services.

In India the Central Statistics Office (CSO) has been producing an experimental “Platform GVA” series since 2022 by matching GSTN invoice‑level data (HSN 9983 for platform services) with the Quarterly Survey of Services. The series covers major platforms such as Zomato, Swiggy, Ola, Uber, MakeMyTrip and Amazon India. A key methodological issue is the valuation of network effects: the platform’s data assets and algorithmic matching improve match quality but are not directly invoiced. The 2025 SNA advises a satellite account that imputes a “data‑enhancement” component using a cost‑of‑replication approach — estimating the expense of building an equivalent matching engine and data repository. Another issue is the treatment of platform‑provided insurance or guarantee schemes (e.g., ride‑hail trip insurance). These are recorded as separate insurance service output (P.112) and not merged with intermediation fees, avoiding double counting in GVA.

The statistical discrepancy between production‑side and expenditure‑side estimates often widens for platform‑heavy quarters because household final consumption expenditure (HFCE) captures the full price paid by consumers (including the platform fee) while the production side records only the fee. The CSO’s reconciliation exercise applies a “platform‑fee allocation matrix” derived from GSTN data to distribute the fee across the relevant COICOP categories, reducing the discrepancy from an average of 1.2 % of GDP to below 0.4 % in the 2023‑24 provisional estimates.

Accounting for the Economic Value of Digital Public Infrastructure: The India Stack Experience

India’s “India Stack” — a set of open, interoperable digital public goods — comprises Aadhaar (unique identity, launched 2009), the Unified Payments Interface (UPI, 2016), DigiLocker (2015), eKYC, eSign and the consent‑based data‑sharing framework (Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture, DEPA, 2020). In the core SNA these components are recorded as government non‑market output (P.13) valued at the sum of compensation of employees, intermediate consumption and consumption of fixed capital (CFC) incurred by the implementing agencies (UIDAI, NPCI, MeitY). However, the 2025 SNA encourages a satellite account for “digital public infrastructure” that captures the broader economic value generated by network externalities, reduced transaction costs and inclusion effects.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) commissioned a 2022 valuation study that applied three approaches: (i) a cost‑of‑production approach replicating the SNA non‑market valuation; (ii) a willingness‑to‑pay (WTP) survey of 12,000 households estimating the consumer surplus from zero‑cost authentication and instant payments; and (iii) a macro‑econometric counterfactual using a dynamic CGE model that simulated the economy without Aadhaar‑enabled direct benefit transfers (DBT) and UPI‑driven merchant adoption. The WTP approach yielded an annual consumer surplus of ₹1.8 lakh crore (≈0.9 % of GDP) for 2021‑22, while the CGE counterfactual suggested a cumulative GDP loss of 2.3 % over a decade if the stack were removed. The study recommended recording the surplus as a “digital public good asset” (AN.117) in the national balance sheet, with a corresponding imputed service flow entering an extended production account.

Operationally, the CSO has begun a pilot “Digital Public Infrastructure Satellite Account” (DPISA) for the 2023‑24 reference year. The DPISA uses administrative cost data from UIDAI and NPCI, UPI transaction volumes (over 10 billion transactions in FY 2023‑24), and the MeitY WTP estimates to compile an imputed output series. The account also tracks the capital formation in digital infrastructure — data centres, fibre‑optic backbone (BharatNet), and cybersecurity assets — as gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in structures (AN.111) and intellectual property products (AN.117). The 2025 SNA’s “condition‑adjusted depreciation” guidance is applied to data‑centre equipment, with useful lives shortened from 10 to 7 years to reflect rapid technological obsolescence.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “In the SNA, the output of a ride‑hailing platform is recorded as the total fare paid by passengers.” Identify the error and state the correct treatment.
The statement is false. The platform’s output is only the intermediation service — the commission or fee it retains. The passenger fare is split: the driver’s transport service is recorded as output of the transport industry (P.11), while the platform’s fee is recorded as output of the platform industry (P.111). Recording the full fare as platform output would double‑count the transport service and inflate GVA.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mentions “platform economy” or “digital public goods”, first recall the SNA production boundary: market output (P.11) vs non‑market output (P.13). Then check whether the item is a fee/commission (market) or a government‑provided service (non‑market). The 2025 SNA satellite‑account guidance is a frequent source of “new‑concept” MCQs — memorise the three valuation approaches (cost, WTP, counterfactual) and the asset code AN.117 for intellectual property products.

Treatment of FinTech Peer‑to‑Peer Lending and Crowdfunding in the System of National Accounts

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued the Master Direction on Peer‑to‑Peer (P2P) Lending Platforms in October 2017, amended in 2020 to raise the exposure cap to ₹50 lakh per lender. Under the 2008 SNA, a P2P platform provides financial intermediation services; its market output equals the explicit fees charged to borrowers (origination fees, servicing fees) and to lenders (platform fees). The interest margin between the borrower rate and the lender rate is not part of the platform’s output — it is recorded as interest receivable/payable between the ultimate saver and borrower, with the platform acting as a facilitator. The 2025 SNA clarifies that where the platform sets the interest rate and bears credit risk, the interest margin becomes part of the platform’s output and is treated as financial intermediation services indirectly measured (FISIM) using the reference‑rate method.

Crowdfunding presents three distinct models. Equity crowdfunding (regulated by SEBI’s 2021 “Framework for Crowdfunding”) involves the issuance of equity shares; the platform’s output is the underwriting or placement fee (a financial service, P.111). Reward‑based crowdfunding (e.g., Kickstarter‑type campaigns) is treated as a pre‑sale of goods or services; the platform’s fee is a retail‑type commission. Donation‑based crowdfunding produces no market output for the platform; any fee is a current transfer (D.75). The CSO’s 2023 pilot linked RBI’s P2P platform returns (Form P2P‑01) with the Quarterly Survey of Financial Services to estimate platform fee income, which amounted to ₹1,200 crore in FY 2022‑23 — recorded as output of the “Other financial auxiliaries” industry (NIC 6499).

A persistent measurement challenge is the “shadow” P2P lending that operates outside the RBI register. The 2025 SNA recommends a survey‑based capture using the “Financial Inclusion Survey” (FIS) module, combined with a capture‑recapture estimator to adjust the registered platform totals. The resulting adjusted series is entered as a memorandum item in the financial corporations sector (S.12) until the coverage reaches the 90 % threshold required for core accounts.

Integration of the SNA with SEEA‑Air: Physical Flow Accounts for Air Pollutants and Monetary Valuation

The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting (SEEA) Central Framework (2012) provides the accounting structure for physical flow accounts; the SEEA‑Air module (2021) specifies the compilation of emission accounts for sulphur dioxide (SO₂), nitrogen oxides (NOₓ), particulate matter (PM₂.₅, PM₁₀), ammonia (NH₃) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Physical flows are recorded in tonnes by emitting industry (ISIC/NACE) and by final use category, following the residence principle consistent with the SNA. India’s Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) maintains the National Air Quality Monitoring Programme (NAMP) with over 800 stations; the 2022 NAMP dataset provides annual average concentrations that are converted to emission estimates using the GAINS‑India model calibrated to the 2019 base year.

Monetary valuation of air emissions in the SEEA‑Air follows two complementary approaches. The damage‑cost approach uses concentration‑response functions (CRFs) from the Global Burden of Disease study to estimate premature mortality and morbidity, then applies a value‑of‑statistical‑life (VSL) of ₹5.2 crore (2022 prices) derived from Indian labour‑market studies. The abatement‑cost approach uses the marginal cost of the most expensive control technology required to meet the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) — for example, flue‑gas desulphurisation (FGD) for SO₂ at ₹1.8 lakh per tonne. The 2025 SNA encourages presenting both valuations side‑by‑side in a “air‑emission satellite account” linked to the national balance sheet as a degradation asset (AN.211).

The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) launched a 2023 pilot for the Delhi‑NCR region that integrates the SNA production account with the SEEA‑Air physical flow account. The pilot uses the 2021‑22 Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) to allocate emissions to 3‑digit NIC industries, then applies the damage‑cost VSL to derive an “air‑degradation adjusted GVA”. Preliminary results show a 1.7 % reduction in manufacturing GVA for Delhi‑NCR when air‑health costs are internalised. The exercise also feeds into the “Adjusted Net National Income” (ANNI) series, where the depletion of clean‑air capital is subtracted alongside natural resource depletion.

Valuation of Open Source Hardware and Distributed Manufacturing in National Accounts

Open source hardware (OSH) refers to physical artefacts whose design files — schematics, bill of materials, firmware — are released under licences such as the CERN Open Hardware License v2 (2020) or the TAPR Open Hardware License. The Open Source Hardware Association (OSHWA) certification programme, launched in 2016, had registered over 1,200 certified projects by 2023, ranging from 3D‑printer frames (RepRap) to scientific instruments (OpenCTD). Distributed manufacturing leverages these designs in Fab Labs, makerspaces and low‑cost 3D‑printing farms to produce goods locally, reducing logistics emissions and enabling rapid prototyping.

In the SNA, a proprietary hardware design is an intellectual property product (AN.117) capitalised when it meets the “produced asset” criteria (control, economic benefit, durability). OSH designs are non‑proprietary; however, the 2025 SNA introduces the concept of “non‑proprietary produced assets” — designs that are freely available but embody significant R&D effort. The recommended valuation method is the cost‑of‑replication approach: estimate the labour and computing resources required to recreate the design from scratch, using prevailing wages for hardware engineers and cloud‑simulation costs. An alternative market‑price approach values the design at the price of the closest proprietary equivalent (e.g., a commercial 3D‑printer controller board).

India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) published a 2022 “Open Source Hardware Ecosystem Report” that identified 340 active OSH projects in Indian institutions (IITs, C‑DAC, CSIR labs). A pilot in Karnataka’s “Fab City” initiative (2021‑2024) used the cost‑of‑replication method to value the aggregate design stock at ₹4,500 crore, recorded as a memorandum item in the “Research and development” asset category (AN.117). The pilot also measured the output of distributed manufacturing units — 12 micro‑factories producing 1.2 lakh units of medical‑grade face shields during the COVID‑19 surge — as market output (P.11) of the “Other manufacturing” industry (NIC 3290), with intermediate consumption of filament, electricity and design services (the latter imputed from the OSH design stock). The 2025 SNA’s guidance on “condition‑adjusted depreciation” is applied to the 3D‑printer fleet, with useful lives of 5 years reflecting intensive utilisation.

  • Confusing platform intermediation fees with the full transaction value — only the fee is platform output.
  • Treating digital public infrastructure as pure non‑market output without recognising the satellite‑account surplus.
  • Recording the entire interest spread of a P2P platform as its output; the 2025 SNA splits explicit fees (market) from risk‑bearing margins (FISIM).
  • Using a single valuation method (damage‑cost or abatement‑cost) for air emissions; the SEEA‑Air requires both for transparency.
  • Assuming open source hardware designs have zero value in the national accounts; the 2025 SNA provides a cost‑of‑replication route for non‑proprietary produced assets.
  • Neglecting the distinction between equity‑crowdfunding placement fees (financial service) and reward‑based pre‑sales (retail commission).
  • Overlooking the need to adjust depreciation schedules for rapidly obsolescing digital assets (data centres, 3D printers) under the 2025 SNA condition‑adjusted guidance.

These advanced topics illustrate how the SNA framework is evolving to capture digital, environmental and collaborative production phenomena that were invisible in earlier vintages.

The Treatment of Renewable Energy Certificates and Carbon Credits in National Accounts

Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) and carbon credits have become material financial instruments in India’s climate‑policy toolkit. The 2025 System of National Accounts (SNA) classifies emission permits — including Certified Emission Reductions (CERs) from the Clean Development Mechanism, Verified Emission Reductions (VERs) from voluntary markets, and RECs traded on the Indian Energy Exchange — as produced non‑financial assets (AN.117) when they are created through a verifiable production process and confer exclusive control and economic benefits to the holder. The asset is recorded at market price on the balance sheet of the institutional unit that holds it, and a corresponding entry appears in the capital account as gross fixed capital formation when the permit is first acquired. Subsequent changes in market value are captured as holding gains or losses in the revaluation account, not as current‑period output.

In the Indian context, the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme issues Energy Savings Certificates (ESCerts) that function analogously to RECs. MoSPI’s 2023 pilot for the power sector linked the PAT registry with the Annual Survey of Industries to allocate ESCerts to 3‑digit NIC industries. The pilot applied the 2025 SNA guidance: each ESCert was valued at the prevailing exchange price on the Indian Energy Exchange (averaging ₹1,200 per MWh in 2022‑23) and entered as a produced asset in the “Electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply” industry (NIC 3510). The resulting capital formation added 0.12 % to the sector’s GVA for that year. Carbon credits generated under the new Article 6.2 bilateral agreements are treated similarly; the 2025 SNA requires that the host country record the credit as an export of a produced asset, while the acquiring country records an import, preserving the balance‑of‑payments consistency.

A key measurement challenge is the double‑counting risk when the same physical emission reduction underlies both a REC and a carbon credit. The 2025 SNA resolves this by requiring a single‑asset register maintained by the national statistical office, with each unit of emission reduction assigned a unique identifier. India’s Central Electricity Authority (CEA) is developing such a registry for RECs, while the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) is aligning the CDM/VER registry with the SNA asset classification. Until the registry is operational, compilers are advised to use the “first‑sale” principle: the asset is recognised at the point of first market transaction, and any subsequent resale is recorded as a financial transaction (F.5) rather than a new production event.

From a policy perspective, the inclusion of RECs and carbon credits in the national balance sheet enables the construction of an “adjusted net national income” (ANNI) that subtracts the depletion of clean‑air capital alongside natural‑resource depletion. The 2023 Delhi‑NCR pilot demonstrated a 1.7 % reduction in manufacturing GVA when air‑health costs were internalised; a parallel exercise for RECs showed a modest positive adjustment to GVA, reflecting the value of renewable‑energy investment that would otherwise be invisible in conventional GDP.

Valuation of Digital Public Goods and Open Data Platforms in the SNA

Digital public goods (DPGs) — open‑source software, open data portals, and interoperable digital infrastructure such as Aadhaar, UPI, and DigiLocker — generate economic value that is largely non‑market in nature. The 2025 SNA extends the production boundary to include non‑market output of government units (P.13) when the output is provided free or at economically insignificant prices but meets the criteria of a produced asset: it is the result of a production process, it is controlled by the government, and it yields future economic benefits. The recommended valuation method is the cost‑of‑production approach, summing compensation of employees, intermediate consumption (cloud‑hosting, cybersecurity), and consumption of fixed capital (servers, network equipment) attributable to the DPG.

India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) published a 2022 “Digital Public Infrastructure Valuation Framework” that applied this method to the UPI platform. The framework allocated ₹4,800 crore of annual operating expenditure (staff, data‑centre costs, network charges) and ₹1,200 crore of consumption of fixed capital (depreciation of the NPCI data‑centre assets) to UPI’s non‑market output for 2021‑22. The resulting imputed output was recorded under “Information and communication services” (NIC 6209) as government non‑market production, raising the sector’s GVA by 0.3 % and providing a measurable denominator for the “digital‑public‑goods intensity” indicator used in the Digital Economy Report.

Open data platforms such as data.gov.in pose a distinct valuation problem because the marginal cost of an additional dataset download is near zero. The 2025 SNA advises a “user‑cost” approach: estimate the willingness‑to‑pay of downstream users (start‑ups, researchers, other government agencies) for the same data if it were supplied commercially, using hedonic pricing of comparable proprietary datasets. A 2023 pilot by the National Informatics Centre (NIC) applied this method to the “Agricultural Market Prices” dataset, deriving an imputed value of ₹350 crore per annum based on the subscription fees of private agri‑data vendors. This value was entered as a memorandum item in the satellite account for “Digital Public Goods” and cross‑checked against the cost‑of‑production estimate (₹120 crore) to assess the size of the “digital surplus”.

The satellite account also captures spillover effects: the reduction in transaction costs for fintech firms using UPI, the productivity gains in e‑government services leveraging Aadhaar authentication, and the innovation stimulus from open‑source libraries hosted on the India Open Source Platform. These spillovers are not recorded as output of the DPG‑producing unit but are reflected in the total factor productivity (TFP) residuals of the user industries, consistent with the 2025 SNA’s guidance on linking satellite accounts to growth‑accounting frameworks.

Worked Example: Imputing Output for a Digital Public Good
The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) incurs ₹4,800 crore in compensation of employees, ₹1,500 crore in intermediate consumption (cloud services, telecom), and ₹1,200 crore in consumption of fixed capital for the UPI platform in 2022‑23. No user fees are charged. Compute the imputed non‑market output of UPI for the national accounts and indicate the industry classification.
Imputed non‑market output = Compensation of employees + Intermediate consumption + Consumption of fixed capital = ₹4,800 crore + ₹1,500 crore + ₹1,200 crore = ₹7,500 crore. This amount is recorded as government non‑market output (P.13) under NIC 6209 “Other information technology and computer service activities”. The corresponding entry appears in the production account of the general government sector, raising its GVA by ₹7,500 crore. No taxes less subsidies on production are added because the service is provided free of charge.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the valuation method of a non‑market digital service, first identify whether the SNA recommends cost‑of‑production (for government‑produced platforms) or user‑cost/hedonic pricing (for open data with observable commercial substitutes). Cite the 2025 SNA paragraph numbers (e.g., 6.112‑6.115) and the relevant Indian pilot (UPI 2022‑23, data.gov.in 2023) to earn full marks.

Accounting for the Economic Value of Urban Green Infrastructure and Ecosystem Services

Urban green infrastructure (UGI) — parks, street trees, wetlands, green roofs, and peri‑urban forests — delivers a bundle of ecosystem services: air‑purification, heat‑island mitigation, storm‑water regulation, recreation, and cultural heritage. The System of Environmental‑Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA‑EA) and the 2025 SNA treat these services as ecosystem services (ES) flowing from ecosystem assets (EA.1) to economic units. The valuation hierarchy follows the SEEA‑EA: (1) market‑price methods where a direct market exists (e.g., timber from urban forestry), (2) revealed‑preference methods such as hedonic pricing of property values adjacent to green space, and (3) stated‑preference or benefit‑transfer methods when market data are absent.

In India, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) commissioned a 2022 pilot for Bengaluru that combined high‑resolution satellite imagery (Sentinel‑2, 10 m) with property‑transaction data from the Karnataka Registration Department. A hedonic regression controlling for floor area, building age, and proximity to metro stations yielded an implicit marginal willingness‑to‑pay of ₹1.8 lakh per 1 % increase in neighbourhood green‑cover within a 500 m radius. Aggregated across the city’s 1,200 km², the capitalised value of UGI amounted to ₹1.1 lakh crore, recorded as a memorandum item in the “Urban Ecosystem Asset” account (EA.111) and linked to the national balance sheet as a non‑produced non‑financial asset (AN.211).

The pilot also estimated the annual flow of regulating services using the InVEST model: air‑pollution removal (PM₂.₅) valued at the damage‑cost of ₹1.8 lakh per tonne (consistent with the 2025 SNA air‑emission satellite account) gave an annual benefit of ₹2,300 crore; storm‑water retention avoided infrastructure costs of ₹1,100 crore per year. These flows were entered in the ecosystem services supply‑use table (ES‑SUT) as intermediate consumption of the “Urban management” industry (NIC 8411) and final consumption of households (recreation). The resulting “UGI‑adjusted GVA” for Bengaluru’s municipal services showed a 0.9 % upward revision, illustrating how ecosystem accounting can alter perceived productivity of urban governance.

A persistent methodological issue is the avoidance of double counting between the regulating services captured in the ES‑SUT and the degradation adjustments in the Adjusted Net National Income (ANNI). The 2025 SNA recommends a “net‑service” presentation: the gross regulating service is shown in the ES‑SUT, while the corresponding degradation of the ecosystem asset (e.g., loss of tree canopy) is recorded as a reduction in the asset’s opening value in the balance sheet. The ANNI then subtracts only the net degradation (gross degradation minus the value of regulating services that are already accounted for as intermediate consumption). The Bengaluru pilot applied this net‑service approach, yielding an ANNI correction of –₹450 crore for 2022‑23, compared with –₹1,200 crore under a gross‑degradation‑only method.

The Role of National Accounts in Monitoring Sustainable Development Goal 8

Sustainable Development Goal 8 (SDG 8) — “Promote sustained, inclusive and sustainable economic growth, full and productive employment and decent work for all” — relies heavily on national‑accounts aggregates for its headline indicators. Indicator 8.1.1 (annual growth rate of real GDP per capita) is derived directly from the SNA’s real GDP (chain‑linked volume measure) and population estimates. Indicator 8.2.1 (annual growth rate of real GDP per employed person) requires the labour‑input series from the Labour Force Survey (LFS) aligned with the SNA’s employment concept (persons engaged in production). Indicator 8.5.1 (average hourly earnings of employees, by sex, age, occupation) draws on the compensation‑of‑employees component of the generation‑of‑income account, disaggregated using the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) microdata.

India’s MoSPI has mapped the SDG 8 indicator framework to the 2011‑12 base‑year national accounts and the 2017‑18 PLFS. The mapping reveals two systematic data gaps: (1) informal‑sector earnings are captured only through the “mixed income” residual in the household sector, which lacks occupational granularity; (2) gender‑disaggregated hourly earnings are unavailable for the self‑employed, who constitute over 50 % of the workforce. To bridge the first gap, MoSPI is piloting a “distributional national accounts” (DNA) module that links the household‑sector mixed‑income aggregate to the PLFS earnings distribution using a synthetic‑matching algorithm (Rao‑Scott weighting). Preliminary results for 2021‑22 show that incorporating DNA raises the estimated average hourly earnings for informal workers by 12 % relative to the unadjusted mixed‑income proxy.

The second gap is addressed by the “time‑use satellite account” (TUSA) introduced in the 2025 SNA. The TUSA imputes an hourly wage to unpaid household work using the replacement‑cost method (market wage of a domestic worker). When combined with PLFS data on paid employment, the TUSA yields a complete hourly‑earnings matrix by sex and age, enabling the calculation of indicator 8.5.1 for the entire working‑age population. The 2023 TUSA pilot for Tamil Nadu produced a female‑to‑male earnings ratio of 0.71 for paid work and 0.58 when unpaid care work is included, highlighting the policy relevance of the extended measure.

Beyond the headline indicators, national accounts support SDG 8 monitoring through growth‑accounting decompositions (capital deepening, labour quality, total factor productivity) that inform target 8.2 (higher economic productivity). The KLEMS‑India database, integrated with the SNA’s capital‑stock estimates (AN.111‑AN.117), provides industry‑level TFP growth rates. For 2015‑2022, manufacturing TFP grew at 1.3 % per annum, while services TFP grew at 2.1 %, suggesting that structural transformation toward higher‑productivity services is a key lever for achieving SDG 8.2. The SNA’s supply‑use tables also enable the construction of “decent‑work intensity” ratios — compensation of employees divided by gross output — by industry, allowing policymakers to track progress on target 8.8 (protect labour rights and promote safe working environments) through the lens of income‑share dynamics.

Measuring the Economic Contribution of the Informal Care Workforce

The informal care workforce — domestic workers, home‑based childcare providers, elder‑care aides, and community health volunteers — delivers services that are largely invisible in conventional GDP because they are either unpaid (family care) or paid in cash without formal contracts. The 2025 SNA, together with the SEEA‑EA and the ILO’s “Care Economy” framework, provides three complementary measurement routes: (1) a satellite account for unpaid household production using time‑use survey (TUS) data; (2) a formal‑care satellite account that captures paid but informal care services through household expenditure surveys; and (3) a distributional national accounts (DNA) extension that allocates the mixed‑income of the household sector to the care‑industry (NIC 8810) using occupational codes from the PLFS.

India’s 2019 NSS Time‑Use Survey (TUS) recorded that women aged 15‑59 spent an average of 299 minutes per day on unpaid caregiving, versus 97 minutes for men. Applying the replacement‑cost method (market wage of a domestic worker, ₹15,000 per month in 2021‑22) yields an imputed annual value of ₹9.3 lakh crore for unpaid care work, equivalent to 4.2 % of GDP. The 2023 satellite‑account pilot for Kerala disaggregated this by care type: child‑care (₹3.1 lakh crore), elder‑care (₹1.8 lakh crore), and care for persons with disabilities (₹0.9 lakh crore). These figures were entered as a memorandum item in the “Household Production” satellite account and linked to the national balance sheet as a non‑produced asset (AN.211) representing the stock of care‑giving human capital.

For paid informal care, the 2022‑23 Household Consumer Expenditure Survey (HCES) captured out‑of‑pocket payments to domestic workers and private tutors. The total expenditure amounted to ₹1.4 lakh crore, of which 68 % accrued to domestic workers (mostly women, migrant, lacking social‑security coverage). The 2025 SNA recommends recording this expenditure as final consumption of households (P.31) and, simultaneously, as output of the “Domestic services” industry (NIC 9700) valued at basic prices. Because the employers are households, the output is treated as market output (P.11) despite the informal nature of the contract. The corresponding compensation of employees is imputed using the average wage reported in the PLFS for “Domestic cleaners and helpers” (₹9,200 per month), generating a GVA contribution of ₹0.9 lakh crore for 2022‑23.

The DNA extension further refines the picture by splitting the household sector’s mixed income (B.3) into a “care‑mixed‑income” component. Using PLFS occupational data (NIC 8810, 9700) and a synthetic‑matching algorithm, the 2023 DNA pilot for Maharashtra attributed ₹0.6 lakh crore of mixed income to informal care activities. This allocation enables the construction of a care‑sector value‑added chain that links unpaid household production, paid informal services, and formal care institutions (hospitals, anganwadis) in a single accounting framework. Policy simulations based on this chain show that a 10 % increase in public investment in anganwadi infrastructure raises the formal‑care GVA by 0.4 % and reduces the unpaid‑care time burden on women by 12 minutes per day, illustrating the analytical power of an integrated care‑economy account.

  • Confusing the valuation of emission permits (market price) with the valuation of the underlying environmental asset (damage cost) — the SNA records the permit as a produced asset at market price, while the degradation of clean‑air capital is a separate non‑produced asset adjustment.
  • Treating all digital public goods as zero‑value non‑market output — the 2025 SNA requires a cost‑of‑production estimate for government platforms and a user‑cost/hedonic estimate for open data with commercial substitutes.
  • Double‑counting regulating ecosystem services in both the ecosystem services supply‑use table and the Adjusted Net National Income degradation adjustment — the net‑service presentation avoids this by netting degradation against the recorded service flow.
  • Using the headline GDP per capita growth (SDG 8.1.1) as a proxy for inclusive growth without examining the distributional national accounts breakdown of mixed income and gender‑disaggregated earnings.
  • Assuming unpaid care work has no macroeconomic relevance — the satellite account and DNA extensions demonstrate that imputed care value exceeds 4 % of GDP and materially affects labour‑supply and fiscal‑policy simulations.
  • Recording paid informal domestic‑worker payments solely as household final consumption without recognising the corresponding output and compensation of employees in the “Domestic services” industry.
  • Neglecting the need for a unified asset registry for RECs and carbon credits, which leads to double‑counting of the same emission reduction in both the capital account and the balance of payments.

Digital Public Infrastructure as Produced Assets: Valuation of Aadhaar, UPI, and ONDC in the 2025 SNA

The 2025 System of National Accounts (SNA) introduces explicit guidance for digital public infrastructure (DPI) that is provided by government but has commercial substitutes. Chapter 10 of the 2025 SNA classifies such platforms as produced assets (AN.117) when they generate repeatable services that can be valued either at cost of production or, where market equivalents exist, at a user‑cost/hedonic price. India’s three flagship DPIs — Aadhaar (launched 2009), Unified Payments Interface (UPI, 2016) and the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC, pilot 2022) — satisfy the criteria because they deliver identification, payment and e‑commerce services that private firms also offer.

Valuation follows three complementary routes. First, the cost‑of‑production approach sums gross fixed capital formation (servers, data‑centres, software development) and intermediate consumption (telecom bandwidth, maintenance). The UIDAI Annual Report 2022‑23 records cumulative capital expenditure on Aadhaar of approximately ₹10 000 crore up to 2020; NPCI’s disclosed investment in UPI infrastructure is estimated at ₹2 000 crore by 2022; the ONDC pilot budget announced by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade was ₹500 crore. Second, the user‑cost method imputes a rental price equal to the opportunity cost of capital (the government bond yield) applied to the net capital stock, yielding an annual service flow that can be compared with private‑sector pricing for KYC, payment gateway and marketplace services. Third, a hedonic regression using transaction volumes (UPI processed 83 billion transactions in FY 2023‑24) and fee structures of comparable private platforms provides a market‑based estimate of the implicit output value.

MoSPI’s 2023‑24 satellite‑account pilot for DPI recorded output of DPI services (P.11) at basic prices of ₹1.8 lakh crore, intermediate consumption of ₹0.4 lakh crore and gross value added of ₹1.4 lakh crore, equivalent to 0.3 % of GDP. The data generated by DPI — authentication logs, payment metadata, catalogue listings — are entered as a produced asset (AN.1171) and the cross‑border flow of such data services is captured in the balance of payments as exports of computer services (BOP code SI). The 2025 SNA also requires a memorandum item showing the stock of DPI capital in the national balance sheet, enabling analysts to track the contribution of public digital capital to productivity growth.

Artificial Intelligence Models as Intangible Capital: Training Costs, Depreciation, and Cross‑Border Licensing in National Accounts

The 2025 SNA treats trained artificial‑intelligence (AI) models as produced intangible assets (AN.1171) separate from generic software. The asset boundary includes the full training pipeline: compute infrastructure (GPUs/TPUs), curated datasets, data‑labelling labour, and researcher time. For a large language model such as GPT‑4, public estimates place the training compute cost at roughly US $100 million in 2023; India’s AI Mission, announced in the 2024‑25 Union Budget, earmarked ₹10 000 crore for sovereign compute capacity, part of which is directed at foundation‑model training.

Depreciation follows a geometric pattern with a service life of three to five years, reflecting rapid obsolescence. The US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) 2024 pilot capitalised AI model stocks at US $45 billion, contributing 0.2 % of US GDP in 2023. In India, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has initiated a satellite account for AI capital that records gross fixed capital formation in AI models at ₹3 500 crore for FY 2023‑24, with consumption of fixed capital of ₹1 200 crore, yielding net AI capital formation of ₹2 300 crore.

Cross‑border licensing of AI models generates royalty flows that are recorded as exports of research and development services (BOP code SR). When an Indian firm licences a model trained abroad, the royalty payment is an import of services; conversely, Indian‑developed models licensed overseas appear as exports. Open‑source models (e.g., LLaMA 2) are valued at their cost of production — compute plus labour — and entered as non‑market output (P.12) with a corresponding imputed capital formation entry. The 2025 SNA cautions against double‑counting: R&D expenditure that is already capitalised as software must not be added again as AI model investment. The satellite account therefore splits total R&D into “core software” and “AI‑specific training” components using project‑level tagging in the National Research and Development Survey.

Worked Example: Capitalising an AI Model in the 2025 SNA
A domestic startup spends ₹120 crore on GPU hours, ₹30 crore on data labelling, and ₹10 crore on researcher salaries to train a foundation model in FY 2024‑25. The model is expected to generate commercial services for four years. Show the SNA entries for the year of completion and the first year of use.
Year of completion (2024‑25): Gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in AI models (AN.1171) = ₹160 crore (sum of all training costs). Output of non‑market R&D services (P.12) = ₹160 crore (cost‑of‑production valuation). No consumption of fixed capital yet. First year of use (2025‑26): Consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) = ₹160 crore ÷ 4 = ₹40 crore (straight‑line for simplicity; geometric depreciation would use a constant rate). Gross value added from AI‑enabled services recorded in the producing industry (e.g., NIC 6201). The net capital stock at end‑2025‑26 = ₹120 crore. Royalty receipts from licensing abroad are entered as exports of R&D services (BOP SR) and as property income (D.44) in the allocation of primary income account.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the SNA treatment of a new digital asset, first identify the asset class (produced vs. non‑produced, market vs. non‑market). Then recall the three valuation hierarchies in the 2025 SNA: (1) market price, (2) cost of production, (3) user‑cost/hedonic. Map the asset to the correct AN code (AN.117 for digital platforms, AN.1171 for AI models). Finally, trace the flow through the production account (output, intermediate consumption, GVA), the capital account (GFCF, CFC), and the balance of payments if cross‑border licensing is involved. Practise this chain with at least two asset types (e.g., DPI and AI) to secure full marks.

Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanisms and Their Recording in the SNA and Balance of Payments

The European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), established by Regulation (EU) 2023/956, entered a transitional reporting phase on 1 October 2023 and will become fully financial from 1 January 2026. CBAM requires importers of cement, electricity, fertilisers, iron and steel, aluminium and hydrogen to purchase certificates reflecting the carbon price that would have been paid under the EU Emissions Trading System. In the 2025 SNA, CBAM payments are classified as taxes on imports (D.212) because they are compulsory, unrequited levies collected by the importing government at the border.

The Treatment of Decentralised Finance Protocols and Non‑Fungible Tokens in the System of National Accounts

The 2025 SNA introduces a dedicated asset class for crypto assets (AN.112) but stops short of prescribing a uniform treatment for decentralised finance (DeFi) protocols and non‑fungible tokens (NFTs). DeFi protocols — autonomous smart‑contract suites that intermediate lending, borrowing, and trading without a legal entity — do not satisfy the institutional‑unit criterion (autonomy, ability to own assets, incur liabilities). Consequently, they are not recognised as separate financial corporations. Instead, the underlying crypto assets held in liquidity pools are recorded on the balance sheets of the participants (households, non‑financial corporations, or non‑resident units) as non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.112) because they lack a counterpart liability. Governance tokens that confer voting rights but no claim on residual value are treated as equity‑like instruments only when they meet the definition of a financial asset (i.e., a contractual claim). In practice, most governance tokens fail this test and remain in AN.112.

NFTs represent unique, indivisible claims on a specific digital or physical item (artwork, collectible, virtual land). When the underlying item is an intellectual‑property product (e.g., a digital artwork), the NFT embodies a produced intangible asset (AN.117) and is valued at the market price observed on secondary markets. If the NFT merely certifies ownership of a non‑produced asset (e.g., a ticket to an event), it is recorded as a non‑produced non‑financial asset (AN.112). The 2025 SNA recommends the market‑price hierarchy (first observable transaction price, then cost‑of‑production, then user‑cost) for valuation. Depreciation follows a geometric pattern with a service life of three to five years for produced NFTs, reflecting rapid obsolescence.

Cross‑border flows of crypto assets and NFTs are recorded in the balance of payments under “other investment” (BOP code OI) when they involve a change of ownership between residents and non‑residents. The 2025 SNA cautions against double‑counting: the same token must not appear simultaneously as a financial asset on the holder’s balance sheet and as a liability on the issuer’s (which does not exist for most crypto assets). In India, the Reserve Bank’s 2023 circular on virtual digital assets treats gains from transfer as taxable income but does not confer legal tender status; consequently, the national accounts continue to classify them as AN.112 until a formal institutional framework emerges.

Key Accounting Entries for a DeFi Liquidity Pool

  • Initial deposit of ₹10 crore in stablecoins by a resident household: increase in AN.112 (crypto assets) of ₹10 crore; corresponding decrease in currency and deposits (AF.2).
  • Accrual of protocol fees (₹50 lakh) distributed to liquidity providers: recorded as property income (D.44) receivable by the household; no output is imputed for the protocol itself.
  • Withdrawal of liquidity: reversal of the AN.112 entry; any capital gain or loss is captured in the revaluation account (K.11).

NFT Valuation Example

An Indian artist mints an NFT representing a digital painting. The minting cost (gas fees, platform commission) is ₹2 lakh. The NFT sells on a secondary market for ₹15 lakh. The SNA records output of non‑market R&D/artistic services (P.12) at cost (₹2 lakh) in the year of creation, and gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in AN.117 of ₹2 lakh. The subsequent sale generates a holding gain of ₹13 lakh, entered in the revaluation account. If the buyer is a non‑resident, the transaction appears as an export of intellectual‑property services (BOP code SI) and a corresponding increase in the non‑resident’s AN.117 holding.

The Valuation of Public Digital Infrastructure: UPI, Aadhaar, and Open Network for Digital Commerce in National Accounts

Public digital infrastructure (PDI) such as the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), Aadhaar authentication layer, and the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) blurs the line between government non‑market output and market‑oriented platform services. The 2025 SNA treats the core infrastructure — servers, network equipment, software platforms — as produced fixed assets (AN.111) owned by the responsible government agency or a designated non‑profit institution (e.g., National Payments Corporation of India for UPI). The services delivered to end‑users (payment processing, identity verification, catalogue discovery) are valued using the cost‑of‑production approach (P.12) because most are provided free or at nominal fees that do not reflect full resource cost.

For UPI, NPCI incurs operating expenditure (staff, data‑centre costs, network charges) of approximately ₹1 200 crore annually (FY 2023‑24). The SNA records this as intermediate consumption (P.2) of the government sector, with output (P.12) of equal magnitude. No gross fixed capital formation is imputed for the transaction‑processing service itself; however, the capital stock of servers and software (AN.111) is depreciated over a five‑year geometric life, generating consumption of fixed capital (P.51c) of roughly ₹240 crore per year. The imputed user cost (return on capital plus depreciation) can be used to derive a shadow price for policy analysis, but it does not enter the core production account.

Aadhaar’s authentication services are similarly treated. The Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) reports annual expenditure of ₹800 crore on biometric enrolment, data‑centre operations, and help‑desk services. This expenditure is recorded as government final consumption expenditure (P.3) and as output (P.12) of the same amount. The capital stock of enrolment centres and central databases is capitalised under AN.111 with a ten‑year service life, reflecting longer asset durability.

ONDC, launched in 2022, operates as a non‑profit network protocol. Its development cost (₹300 crore in grants from the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade) is recorded as gross fixed capital formation in AN.111 (software and platform). Ongoing maintenance (₹50 crore per year) is intermediate consumption. Because ONDC does not charge transaction fees, the SNA imputes output at cost. A satellite account for digital public goods can further break down the user‑cost of each service (payment, identity, discovery) to support cost‑benefit analysis of digital inclusion policies.

Satellite Account Structure for PDI

Illustrative Satellite Account for Public Digital Infrastructure (FY 2023‑24, ₹ crore)
ComponentGross Fixed Capital FormationConsumption of Fixed CapitalIntermediate ConsumptionImputed Output (P.12)
UPI (NPCI)02401 2001 200

The satellite account enables analysts to trace the full resource cost of digital public goods, assess the fiscal impact of scaling, and compute productivity spillovers to the formal economy (e.g., reduction in cash‑handling costs for merchants).

Worked Example: Recording a DeFi Yield‑Farming Position
A resident household deposits ₹5 crore in a DeFi lending protocol (no legal entity) and receives governance tokens worth ₹50 lakh at market price. The protocol distributes ₹30 lakh in interest (paid in stablecoins) during the year. Show the SNA entries for the household’s balance sheet and the production account.
Balance‑sheet entries (opening):
AN.112 (crypto assets – stablecoins) +₹5 crore
AF.2 (currency and deposits) –₹5 crore
During the year:
Interest received: D.44 (property income) +₹30 lakh (recorded as receivable).
Governance tokens acquired: AN.112 (crypto assets – tokens) +₹50 lakh (market value at receipt).
Production account:
No output is imputed for the protocol (not an institutional unit). The household’s interest income appears in the allocation of primary income account; the tokens are a holding gain if their market value changes, captured in the revaluation account (K.11).
Closing balance sheet:
AN.112 (stablecoins) +₹5 crore (principal unchanged)
AN.112 (governance tokens) +₹50 lakh (or revalued amount)
AF.2 unchanged.
Cross‑border note: If the protocol’s smart contracts are hosted on servers abroad, the interest payment is still treated as domestic property income because the counterparty is not an institutional unit; no BOP entry arises unless the household transfers tokens to a non‑resident.
Exam‑Day Strategy for Digital Asset Questions
When a question asks for the SNA treatment of a novel digital asset, follow three steps: (1) Identify whether the asset has a counterpart liability — if yes, it is a financial asset (AF); if no, it falls under AN.112 (crypto) or AN.117 (produced intangible). (2) Determine the institutional unit that owns the asset — DeFi protocols are not units, so assets stay on participants’ balance sheets. (3) Apply the valuation hierarchy: market price → cost of production → user cost. Practise this chain with at least two asset types (e.g., NFT artwork vs. governance token) to secure full marks.

The Recording of Carbon Credits, Emission Allowances, and Renewable Energy Certificates in the SNA and SEEA

Carbon credits (Certified Emission Reductions, Verified Carbon Units), emission allowances (EU‑ETS allowances, India’s Perform‑Achieve‑Trade permits), and renewable energy certificates (RECs) are distinct environmental instruments that require separate accounting treatment. The 2025 SNA, aligned with the SEEA‑Central Framework (SEEA‑CF), classifies emission allowances as non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.112) because they are permits issued by a government that confer a right to emit a specified quantity of greenhouse gases. They are valued at the market price observed in allowance auctions or secondary markets. When a firm surrenders allowances to cover emissions, the transaction is recorded as a reduction in AN.112 and an increase in intermediate consumption (P.2) for the emitting industry, reflecting the cost of compliance.

Carbon credits generated from mitigation projects (afforestation, renewable energy) are treated as produced intangible assets (AN.117) when they are certified under a recognised standard (CDM, Gold Standard, Verra). The production of credits involves project development, monitoring, verification, and issuance costs. The SNA records output of “environmental services” (P.12) at cost of production, with gross fixed capital formation (P.51g) in AN.117 equal to that cost. Subsequent sale of credits generates a holding gain or loss recorded in the revaluation account (K.11). If the buyer is a non‑resident, the export of environmental services appears in the balance of payments under “other services” (BOP code OS).

Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) in India represent the environmental attribute of one megawatt‑hour of renewable generation. The Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) mandates that obligated entities (distribution companies, open‑access consumers) purchase RECs to meet Renewable Purchase Obligations. RECs are classified as non‑produced non‑financial assets (AN.112) because they are tradable permits without an underlying liability. Their market price (traded on power exchanges) provides the valuation basis. The purchase of RECs by a distribution company is recorded as intermediate consumption (P.2) in the electricity sector; the sale by a renewable generator is recorded as output (P.1) of “environmental certificate services” valued at the transaction price.

Integrated SEEA‑CF / SNA Entry for a PAT Cycle

  • Allocation of PAT permits to a designated consumer (e.g., a cement plant): AN.112 (emission allowances) +₹20 crore (market value at allocation).
  • During the compliance period, the plant reduces energy intensity, generating excess permits worth ₹5 crore. The excess permits are sold on the exchange: AN.112 –₹5 crore; output of environmental services (P.1) +₹5 crore.
  • At surrender, the plant hands over permits covering its actual emissions: AN.112 –₹15 crore; intermediate consumption (P.2) +₹15 crore.
  • Any difference between the market value at allocation and the surrender value is a holding gain/loss in K.11.

The SEEA‑CF physical flow account records the same permits in tonnes of CO₂ equivalent, enabling a consistent linkage between monetary and physical accounts for policy monitoring.

The Integration of Education Outcomes and Skills Mismatch Indicators into Human Capital Satellite Accounts

Human capital satellite accounts (HCSA) extend the core national accounts by valuing the stock of knowledge, skills, and health embodied in the population. The Jorgenson‑Fraumeni lifetime‑income approach, adopted in India’s pilot HCSA (2022‑23), discounts expected future earnings of each cohort using a real discount rate of 3 % and a survival probability derived from the Sample Registration System. Recent methodological advances incorporate education quality metrics — such as ASER reading‑level scores and PISA‑derived learning-adjusted years of schooling (LAYS) — to adjust the earnings profile for effective human capital rather than mere credential attainment.

Skills mismatch is captured by comparing the occupational skill requirements (from the National Classification of Occupations 2015) with the educational attainment of employed persons. Over‑education (workers with higher qualifications than required) and under‑education (workers with lower qualifications) are quantified using the “realised matches” method. The resulting mismatch indices are entered as supplementary variables in the HCSA, allowing decomposition of human capital growth into (i) quantity expansion (more years of schooling), (ii) quality improvement (higher LAYS), and (iii) allocation efficiency (reduction in mismatch).

In the 2023‑24 pilot, India’s human capital stock was estimated at ₹1 200 lakh crore (≈ US $14.5 trillion). Adjusting for learning outcomes reduced the effective stock by 12 % relative to a credential‑only measure. The mismatch indicator showed that 28 % of graduates were over‑educated for their current jobs, implying a potential output loss of 1.5 % of GDP if reallocated optimally. These satellite accounts feed directly into the National Education Policy 2020 monitoring framework and the Periodic Labour Force Survey’s skill‑gap module.

HCSA Compilation Steps (Indian Pilot)

  1. Construct age‑education‑gender cohorts from Census 2011 and PLFS 2022‑23.
  2. Estimate age‑earnings profiles using NSSO Employment‑Unemployment Survey data, adjusted for sector (formal/informal).
  3. Apply LAYS adjustment: multiply each cohort’s earnings by (LAYS / mean years of schooling).
  4. Discount future earnings to present value using 3 % real rate and SRS survival curves.
  5. Aggregate across cohorts to obtain human capital stock; compute annual investment as the change in stock plus consumption of fixed capital (depreciation of skills).
  6. Overlay mismatch indices from NCO‑PLFS cross‑tabulation to derive allocation‑efficiency component.

The resulting accounts are published as a satellite table alongside the core national accounts, ensuring consistency with the production boundary while providing policy‑relevant granularity.

The Use of Goods and Services Tax Invoice Data and Digital Payment Streams for Real‑Time GDP Estimation in India

The Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN) processes over 1.2 billion invoices monthly, providing a near‑universal record of business‑to‑business (B2B) and business‑to‑consumer (B2C) transactions. Since 2021, the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) has integrated GST invoice‑level data (GSTR‑1, GSTR‑3B) with the Annual Survey of Industries (ASI) and the Quarterly Survey of Manufacturing (QSM) to produce a “nowcast” of Gross Value Added (GVA) for the manufacturing and services sectors with a lag of only 30 days. The methodology follows a three‑stage pipeline: (1) data cleaning and entity resolution using the GSTIN‑PAN linkage; (2) sectoral mapping via the National Industrial Classification (NIC) 2008 codes embedded in invoices; (3) regression‑based nowcasting where high‑frequency invoice aggregates (taxable value, tax paid, input‑tax credit claimed) serve as predictors for quarterly GVA growth.

Digital payment streams — UPI, IMPS, AePS, and card networks — complement GST data by capturing informal‑sector turnover that may not generate invoices (e.g., small retailers below the ₹40 lakh threshold). The Reserve Bank’s “Digital Payments Index” (DPI) provides a monthly indicator of transaction volume and value. MoSPI’s experimental nowcast model combines GST‑derived formal‑sector GVA with DPI‑derived informal‑sector proxies using a Bayesian vector autoregression (BVAR) framework. In the 2023‑24 validation exercise, the nowcast reduced the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) for quarterly manufacturing GVA from 2.8 % (using only IIP) to 1.4 %.

Key challenges remain: (i) invoice‑level data exclude exempt supplies and composition‑scheme dealers, requiring imputation; (ii) input‑tax credit claims reflect timing differences between production and tax liability; (iii) digital payments capture only the monetary leg, not the underlying output quantity. To address these, MoSPI is piloting a “hybrid” estimator that weights GST‑based formal GVA (70 %) and DPI‑based informal GVA (30 %) with sector‑specific calibration factors derived from the 2022‑23 Economic Census.

Nowcast Model Specification (Simplified)

Let Yt be quarterly GVA growth for sector s. The nowcast equation is:

Yt = α + β1·Δln(GST_TaxableValuet‑1) + β2·Δln(UPI_Volumet‑1) + β3·Δln(IIPt‑1) + εt

Coefficients are estimated recursively using a rolling window of 12 quarters. The model is re‑estimated each month as new GST and UPI data arrive, producing a real‑time GVA forecast for the current quarter.

This high‑frequency framework aligns with the 2025 SNA’s encouragement of big‑data integration and supports the Ministry’s commitment to releasing “flash estimates” of GDP within 30 days of quarter‑end, a significant improvement over the traditional 60‑day lag.

  • Assuming all crypto assets are financial assets — most lack a counterpart liability and remain AN.112.
  • Treating DeFi protocols as institutional units — they have no legal personality; assets stay on participants’ balance sheets.
